Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:55:53 GMT

The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.

Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.

They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.

Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.

Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.

Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.

In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.

Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.

"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.

"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."

During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.

They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.

The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.

Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.

"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.

"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."

One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.

The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.

But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests.

"The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.

He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."

Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'".

"Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.

The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.

Passengers thought mass train attack 'was a joke'

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:20:59 GMT

Some train passengers initially remained sitting down and thought a man was joking after he told people "I've been stabbed, run", a court has heard.

Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people on the train which made an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard the first person who was stabbed, Jonathan Gjoshe, later asked hospital staff "am I going to die today?".

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder, and four other alleged attempted murders in earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

A second stabbing victim said Williams ran away when his pet cockapoo fought back, and another said he threw luggage at the attacker to fend him off.

Jurors have seen CCTV footage of Williams' attack, which took place on the York to London King's Cross LNER service, after it had left Peterborough.

The court was played a video interview with Gjoshe, who said he was on his phone in carriage J at the time and initially thought Williams was someone he knew.

"I've made eye contact with him… he's pulled a knife, but I just think it was the way he's poked me, the way he's stabbed me, it was a bit weird because it was slow."

Gjoshe said that once he felt a shock "that's when the adrenalin kicked in" and he jumped over the train table.

He said his whole arm was "drenched with blood" and went through the carriage telling people "I've been stabbed, run", but said some other people on the train remained "sitting down, thinking it was a joke".

"It was like a movie, it was quite horrific."

He spent four days in hospital and asked staff "am I going to die today or not? please tell me this".

Jurors then watched a video interview with another stabbing victim, Sachin Balakrishnan, who was a passenger in the same carriage.

He said he heard "screaming", then saw "people trying to jump over the seats" and running, then a man with a "big knife" who "was saying something but nothing meaningful".

Balakrishnan said he "ran and ran and ran", adding: "This guy was running behind me, there was nowhere to go. Nowhere was safe."

He said "everyone was running for their lives" and then he felt pain in his right arm.

The court also heard from David Presland, who said he was on his hands and knees on the floor when he was stabbed by Williams.

The 73-year-old said "I thought I was going to die" and "I'm lucky I survived."

Presland said another passenger called Kevin came to his aid.

Scott Green, who was travelling with his cockapoo Poppy in the next carriage along, said he initially thought there was a fight happening, before he "felt a jab" into his side.

In a recording of his interview, he said he fought back and told himself, "If I don't get this knife now I think he's going to kill me".

"I've tried to yank it... but I couldn't remove it," said Green.

He said his dog "went into attack mode" and startled the attacker, before Williams "done a runner".

Green described how a woman had "thrown him" to safety into a toilet, who subsequently joked: "I don't usually get in with men who I just met in the toilet".

He said the attacker was "just dead in the eyes, real dead... like he weren't there".

A fifth passenger, Kevin Deely, remembered shouting to Williams: "You don't have to do this, you don't have to do this."

In his recorded account, he described trying to shield a woman and throwing a piece of luggage at the assailant.

"It started to dawn on me I've been stabbed but I've no recollection of the event itself," Deely recalled.

He said his head was bleeding and others "started passing clothing back to us" to stem the bleeding.

"I remember feeling I was going to die there," he remembered.

Williams is also accused of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Scott Bletcher, Stephen Crean, Kevin Deely, Michael Paffett, and Samir Zitouni on the London-bound train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on 1 November.

Prosecutors further allege that on 31 October, Williams tried to kill three people in Peterborough, before attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.

Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question - the court has been told - but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.

The trial continues.

Zverev lost to Italy's Lorenzo Musetti at the Paris Masters on Wednesday - his first match since becoming the ATP Tour's number one for the first time.

Before this year's French Open, Sinner and Alcaraz had shared the past nine Grand Slam titles, with Sinner beating Zverev in last year's Australian Open final.

Zverev has lost in each of his 10 most recent meetings with Sinner, who has not played since Wimbledon after injuring his knee and has subsequently dropped to number two in the rankings.

He has also lost four of his past five matches against Alcaraz, who missed large parts of the season with a wrist injury.

"I was a bit annoyed, to be honest, because achieving the world number one status is something that every player dreams of," said Zverev, who won this year's French Open and US Open titles and lost to Sinner in the final of Wimbledon.

"But then I feel like I'm the only world number in tennis history that has to explain why it's OK for me to be world number one, which I find quite difficult, because I think I deserve to be where I am, even though I lost today."

Zverev did not specify which issues had been annoying him after going to the top of the rankings.

His ascent has led to previous accusations of physical abuse by two of his former partners being highlighted again.

Zverev has always firmly maintained his innocence and has insisted the allegations are baseless.

He was presented with the world number one trophy in Paris on Monday but, after receiving a bye through the first round, was beaten 7-6 (7-5) 6-2 by Musetti.

Looking at his performance on Wednesday, Zverev said: "To simplify it, he played really good and I played really bad.

"I think this was not a very good match from me, I think it might be one of the worst in the last couple of months."

'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:40:38 GMT

This video can not be played

Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De Miguel

FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.

The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.

Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally".

"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement.

"I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened.

"I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him.

"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing.

"Rest in peace, Jesus."

Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.

Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.

Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.

"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."

Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.

Football world mourns Tenerife striker De Miguel

Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.

Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.

The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.

Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.

The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.

Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.

Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.

Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.

The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player.

"As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.

Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year deal

On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.

Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.

The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.

Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".

"Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.

Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

Brigitte Bardot inheritance row deepens after private letter to partner leaked

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:31:14 GMT

A row over the inheritance of late screen legend Brigitte Bardot has intensified after a private letter was made public which appears to show her cutting off relations with her last partner.

Dated November 2022 – three years before she died at her home in Saint Tropez – the hand-written note accuses Bernard de Chiara, her companion of more than 30 years, of "patiently destroying me day after day".

The leaked letter is a useful weapon for the other side in the Bardot legacy battle - the animal rights foundation that bears her name - which is accused by de Chiara of rushing to dispose of her estate without regard for friends and intimates.

A week ago de Chiara, who is 85, was forced to leave the seaside house known as La Madrague which he shared with Bardot from the early 1990s.

After being looked after financially by her for so many years, he is reported to possess neither a bank account nor a social security card.

He was also furious after the Brigitte Bardot Foundation organised a sale in September of household objects mainly taken from the late actress's Paris flat. The sale raised nearly €1m (£835,000), shared between the Foundation and Bardot's only son Nicolas Charrier.

"I found it extraordinary that just a few months after Brigitte's death, they already wanted to make a souvenir out of her. I did not appreciate that one bit," de Chiara said.

In the letter, which begins "Bernard, it's a failure!", Bardot said she had given "everything" in the hope of finding a "companion would could offer back my love, share my joys and immense sorrows... who is happy at the life I am giving him."

But she concluded: "Today I have reached the end-point of my distress... I am so in need of a shoulder, a support, a tenderness, a presence – which you are incapable of giving."

Widely known under the adopted name d'Ormale (a pun on the French dort mal – sleeps badly), de Chiara was a businessman and one-time associate of far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.

Friends say that he and Bardot had an up-and-down relationship. They were never married under French law, but he was living with her to the end and cared for her as she was dying.

When her will was read after her death last December, it divided the estate between the Foundation and her son, who lives discreetly in Oslo. There was no mention of de Chiara, and Bardot also stipulated that La Madrague should be unoccupied within six months of her death.

As lawyers now draw up a definitive list of the late actresses' assets, the Foundation accused de Chiara of removing items from La Madrague, including her Mini Moke jeep. "I am not accusing him of theft, but it's gone and that's a problem," said Foundation President Max Guazzani on Tuesday.

According to the Foundation, de Chiara has no legal claim except for a share of the Paris flat, which is now up for sale. In the meantime he is living in an apartment rented from the town hall of Saint Tropez.

Guazzini said that "on a human level one can understand [de Chiara's reluctance to leave La Madrague]. But it's the law and it's also what Brigitte Bardot wanted.

"It's not our fault that she did not leave him the right to live there. What else are we supposed to do?"

The high cost of maintaining La Madrague – and Bardot's second home La Garrigue in the hills behind the Mediterranean coast – means the Foundation needs to find ways to make the properties pay. Both houses were in a poor state when she died, and now need round-the-clock security.

An idea for a museum has been abandoned because La Madrague is inaccessible by car. Instead the house could be opened up for guided tours, as well as for fashion displays and film shoots.

After Bardot left the world of cinema in 1973 she devoted her life to animal welfare and her foundation says it now cares for 13,000 animals.

Bardot was married three times before she met de Chiara: to filmmaker Roger Vadim, actor Jacques Charrier and industrial heir Gunter Sachs.

French media say she married de Chiara at a ceremony in Norway but this was never registered in French law.

UK government to outlaw new North Sea drilling

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:28:03 GMT

The UK government has moved to ban any new exploration for oil and gas in the North Sea.

The Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority's ability to grant new oil and gas licences.

The legislation will not affect the decision on whether to allow drilling at Rosebank off Shetland - the UK's largest known untapped field - which was approved in 2022 before being subject to legal challenges.

The UK government said it was upholding Labour's 2024 manifesto vow not to issue licences for new oil and gas fields, as well as underpinning its commitment to reducing global warming.

The Conservatives described the bills as "dangerous", accusing Labour ministers of being "totally oblivious the economic and energy threats this country faces".

The Energy Independence Bill, if passed at Westminster, would introduce Transitional Energy Certificates, which would allow existing oil and gas fields to provide additional production from "areas bordering or in close proximity to already licensed fields" or in areas that are already part of an existing field.

The government said the move could produce about 60 million barrels of oil and support hundreds of jobs.

It vowed to sustain "growth and investment across North Sea communities as the energy sector transitions".

The wide-ranging bill would also formally scrap gas standing charges and introduce reforms designed to speed up grid connections.

The UK government has also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Together, these changes will bring bills down for good, give families greater security and put Britain back in control of its energy future."

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the bill would help to "build a clean energy future which people feel in their pockets, households and communities, ensuring support reaches those who need it most".

It comes two weeks after the UK government approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

Ministers said the site, off the coast of Aberdeen, would help heat millions of homes.

Environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank were approved by the previous Conservative government.

However, after being subject to legal challenges from environmental groups, Labour ministers have had to decide whether to continue with the projects.

Situated 80 miles north-west of Shetland, Rosebank is thought to contain between 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

Backers say it would be a vital lifeline to the energy industry in the north east of Scotland, and improve energy security at a time when global supply chains are disrupted by conflict.

Opponents say it would accelerate the climate crisis, slow down the transition to greener energy sources and do little to improve energy security since its produce would largely be exported overseas to be refined.

Greenpeace UK called the bill a "positive step forward for the clean energy transition".

However, it called on the UK government to reject Rosebank.

Amy McCarthy, the campaign group's head of politics, said: "Saying a resounding no to this oil field - a project that would annihilate every single climate or cost-of-living benefit achieved through this bill - must be step one to securing our power and protecting lives."

Aberdeen and Grampian Chamber of Commerce chief executive Russell Borthwick argued that it made "no sense" to wind down North Sea oil and gas production.

"Britain will continue to need oil and gas for decades to come," he added.

"The question is whether we produce more of it here, supporting British jobs, investment and energy security, or pay other countries to produce it for us."

David Whitehouse, chief executive of industry body Offshore Energies UK, said the government was right to target energy affordability, but said it should also prioritise energy security.

"Today, Britain imports more than 40% of the energy it needs, leaving households and businesses exposed in an increasingly volatile world," he said.

"We should be making the most of the energy we produce here at home rather than relying on imports."

Shadow Energy Secretary Andrew Bowie, Tory MP for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine, called Labour ministers "utterly delusional".

He accused them of being "totally oblivious" to the "economic and energy threats this country faces".

Bowie added: "Might as well hang a closed for business sign over Aberdeen and the North Sea."

Scotland's First Minister has declined to give a definitive position on whether the UK government should grant the go-ahead for Rosebank.

Pressed repeatedly on his position at Holyrood last month, John Swinney told MSPs: "The carbon emissions that come out of the development of an individual site have to be assessed ... as to whether it is compatible with our journey to net zero.

"That is the legal obligation and that is the test and the assessment the United Kingdom government has got to go through."

Why Man Utd's Roma comeback has echoes of Mourinho and Solskjaer

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:12:46 GMT

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick (second left) hugs Shea Lacey after the 3-2 Champions League victory against Roma

It was impossible not to get swept up in the emotion and delirium of Manchester United's late 3-2 Champions League comeback win against Roma.

Old Trafford was transformed from a mutinous, baying cathedral of distrust and fury to one of joy and celebration.

Nine games and almost eight weeks is an eternity to wait for a victory at a club of Manchester United's size.

It didn't take Michael Carrick long to calm the mood.

"It's one win, so we're not getting too carried away with things, but it was an important win."

It was a huge result in the sense it bought Carrick some time. But given United's general state, no-one can be sure how much.

And, as was quickly pointed out in the aftermath of the victory, Manchester United have been here before.

Man Utd produce incredible second-half comeback to beat Roma

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

Jose Mourinho (centre) was sacked after a 3-1 defeat at Liverpool in December 2018

'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'

As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.

Saturday, 6 October 2018.

As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable.

Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.

Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.

After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.

While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".

Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.

As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.

Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.

Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.

Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.

Man Utd beat Roma - the other great Champions League comebacks

Fernandes critical of media 'lies' about Carrick relationship

Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes celebrates Matheus Cunha's winner against Roma

One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

That is Carrick's challenge.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with £70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:35:09 GMT

Andy Burnham has said the results of the US midterm elections meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".

Speaking to broadcasters from the Commonwealth leaders summit, the prime minister promised to push for a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine in the wake of the US elections that saw Donald Trump's Republicans suffer heavy losses.

He said he couldn't ease cost of living pressures until the US's conflict in Iran had been resolved.

Responding to the midterm results, the US president acknowledged that rising fuel prices - caused by the Iran war - had played a part in his party's defeats.

Speaking to Fox News, President Trump said: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."

Giving his reaction to the results, Burnham said the voters in the US have said they want to "see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people".

Asked whether he thought the results might make the US president more unpredictable, Burnham said: "President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living.

"That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves.

"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.

"These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that.

"And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do."

The subject of the US midterm elections was raised at Prime Minister's Questions, which, in Burnham's absence, was taken by Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh.

The Liberal Democrat's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said American voters had rejected Trump's "warmongering and the economic chaos that it has caused".

She expressed concern that the US president was planning further strikes on Iran and urged the government to "stand together with our reliable allies and send a clear message to Trump and Netanyahu: there must be no more strikes."

Haigh replied: "The US are one of our most important allies and our priority absolutely is de-escalation."

She said the Iran war had been "catastrophic for the cost of living crisis" and said the Conservatives and Reform should "consider very carefully their judgment in calling for us to jump so readily into it".

Asked about suggestions there could be an attack on Iran in the coming week, Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday: "The US was "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".

Indirect talks between the two sides have been stalled for months and some analysts close to the Iran regime have suggested prolonging the negotiations, in the hope that the rising cost of fuel would damage Trump electorally.

Although the US Congress, now controlled by the Democrats, can restrict funding, Trump will still have significant authority over foreign policy.

Burnham is preparing a 10-year plan for government, and will be hoping that his strategy isn't blown off course by the actions of an unpredictable US president in his last two years in the White House.

Zelensky gives Melania Trump Ukraine's highest award after Oleshky ceasefire

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:01:10 GMT

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump.

The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, was awarded to Melania Trump for her "significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine", according to the presidential decree.

It comes after the end of ceasefire in Ukraine's southern region of Kherson, which allowed for the evacuation of several hundred people from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

Russian and Ukrainian delegations - made up of ombudsmen who were involved in the evacuation mission as well as senior officials - are due to meet at the White House on Thursday on Melania Trump's invitation.

The White House said that Melania Trump had "independently initiated engagement between the two warring nations and successfully secured a ceasefire".

"This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady", it added.

Both the Russian and Ukrainian sides repeatedly thanked Melania Trump for brokering the ceasefire, though neither elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement.

The delegations travelling to the White House on Thursday will include Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Russian senior official Kirill Dmitriev.

Lubinets and Lantratova travelled together into Oleshky last week, in an unusual show of cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials.

Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament, has previously been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team during peace talks with Russia.

He was responsible for informal contact between the White House and Moscow during the ceasefire, according to diplomatic sources quoted by Ukrainian media, and has confirmed he will take part in Thursday's talks.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian delegation will be made up of Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian businessman close to the Kremlin who has frequently taken part in US-brokered ceasefire talks.

Dmitriev and Arakhamia are veteran participants in high-level peace negotiations, and it is unusual for meetings involving such senior representatives to be convened through an initiative led by a US First Lady.

No details of what the White House event will entail have been shared. "There are important meetings ahead," said Lubinets in a social media post while announcing he was on his way to the US.

On Thursday Melania Trump will also deliver remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at 11:00 (16:00 GMT), the White House website said.

Zelensky's decree also cited Melania Trump's wider humanitarian work, including her efforts concerning Ukrainian children affected by the war, as reasons for giving her the Princess Olga award.

Melania Trump has largely remained discreet on foreign policy matters, but in 2025 she said an "open channel of communication" had been established with Russian President Vladimir Putin, allowing for Ukrainian children displaced in the war to be reunited with families.

Earlier this year the UN said the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime.

According to Ukraine, almost 20,000 children have been illegally sent to Russia and Belarus since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russian, Ukrainian and American representatives are also going to meet in Abu Dhabi next week in the first trilateral meeting since February. The talks will be focused on postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:05:42 GMT

Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate.

Here is everything you need to know about some of the big Democratic wins and some historic firsts.

Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Trump two years ago in the presidential election.

With James Talarico winning a seat in the US Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa being elected state governor, Democrats scored two statewide victories in Texas - ending a string of defeats they have endured for almost two generations.

Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.

Hinojosa became the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.

Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.

Senior party figures who cheered the results included Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.

"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.

If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.

Trump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".

He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Congress.

Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."

He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote. Trump argued that high fuel prices meant voters could not see how well his economy was doing "as much as they should have", adding: "The gasoline was caused by Iran."

Abdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate - after claiming victory in Michigan in what was one of a handful of closely fought contests. His win means the seat stays in Democratic hands.

He defeated Republican opponent Mike Rogers, who received the surprise backing of El-Sayed's Democratic rival in the primary contest, Haley Stevens, who changed her endorsement at the eleventh hour.

The race was one of the bitterest of the midterms. Trump invoked 9/11 and even called El-Sayed a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

El-Sayed's supporters went wild when he took the stage to celebrate his claimed victory, wrote the BBC's Nada Tawfik. He said: "Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say 'inshallah,' or 'God willing,' whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned."

He went on to say: "But today, tonight, we can turn that 'inshallah' into 'alhamdulillah'. For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'"

The defeat of Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, was one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses.

She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.

In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years.

The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.

Collins entered the race as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.

Ashley Hinson suffered the same fate in Iowa, losing that closely-fought Senate seat to Josh Turek. Hinson had slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.

Among the other firsts of the night were in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor, following a hearty endorsement from Trump.

Donalds, who will take over the job from Ron DeSantis, said his state was the "envy of the nation", and that he would work to make the state more affordable.

The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans.

In the neighbouring state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, won the governor's race, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.

The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue. Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive. The state has also not had a Democratic governor for more than 20 years.

Elsewhere, Democrat Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.

Pappas defeated former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race, whom he thanked on Tuesday, saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."

In Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first woman elected to Congress from Gen Z - meaning those who were born between 1997 and 2012.

Could Hyrox's Olympic ambition spell the end for triathlon?

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:52:19 GMT

This video can not be played

Could Hyrox spell the end for triathlon?

"Our biggest concern is that they're not just here to take part, they're here to take over."

British triathlete Max Stapley first saw the news on Instagram. Last week, World Triathlon announced it was partnering with Hyrox - the fitness craze which combines running with exercise stations.

The agreement means Hyrox becomes a recognised discipline within World Triathlon. And now it sits under a recognised international federation, it could be eligible for inclusion at the Olympics and Paralympics.

It is too late for the Los Angeles 2028 Games but is there room for both hybrid racing and triathlon to feature at a future Olympics? Or could one replace the other?

For triathlon, a sport which has been in the Olympics since 2000, and has long-established professional circuits, its athletes are questioning whether they'll reap any rewards from this partnership - or even, whether it could "kill" the sport altogether.

Hyrox, launched in 2017, has entered into a partnership with World Triathlon

Stapley, who spoke to BBC Sport from a training camp in Thailand, was having dinner with friends when his phone started pinging with news of the proposals and reaction to them.

"I was like, hold on a minute, what's this?", said Stapley.

"We don't even get an early notification, we found out on Instagram".

The post read, external: 'Hyrox x World Triathlon are officially introducing 'Hybrid Racing' as a new discipline within the World Triathlon family.'

Sophie Evans - who won gold as part of England's Commonwealth Games mixed relay team in Birmingham in 2022 - said she was "surprised" to receive the news like that.

"I'm not actually against it being part of World Triathlon. It's more the fact we were blindsided, it's just like it's here," she added.

Stapley accused World Triathlon of not caring about its athletes because he did not receive any communication from his sport's governing body prior to and after the announcement was made.

"They have no respect for us," he said. "They don't even contact us like 'hey, do you guys actually care about this, or what do you think?'"

In response, a World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport: "The World Triathlon Executive Board approved the partnership. The board includes representatives of the World Triathlon Athletes' Committee elected by their peers.

"Athlete representatives are involved in every executive board discussion, and their voice is always heard.

"The announcement was communicated through the same procedures followed for all World Triathlon releases."

Stapley questioned whether the partnership brought 'any positive outcome' for triathlon

World Triathlon says the partnership is designed to "benefit the entire World Triathlon movement",, external with new opportunities to engage athletes and audiences, and a stronger platform to grow triathlon and multisport from grassroots to elite level.

The question for athletes is, how?

European champion Roksana Slupek, of Poland, said she was "not against the idea", but wanted more information.

"What's the benefit for us, for triathlon? It's nothing against Hyrox," said Slupek.

However, Stapley called the move an "attack on our whole existence" and is concerned that World Triathlon could direct attention and resources towards Hyrox's Olympic ambition - at the expense of his own sport.

"How does Hyrox grow triathlon? If anything they've killed triathlon," he said, while also suggesting brands would rather get in early with Hyrox athletes before they potentially appear at an Olympics.

"Sponsorships have reduced because there's no visibility on TV, you have to pay to watch us.

"We are triathletes that do the short distance, which is the Olympic distance, and we've trained all our lives for it.

"There's no swimming, there's no biking, it's indoors. [Hyrox] has got nothing to do [with triathlon]".

"It seems like our sport's gone, 'no worries, come along, use our structure, use our access to the International Olympic Committee, and perhaps take our space'.

"We've got an opportunity to win medals in Los Angeles [at the 2028 Olympics], but will we have it further down the track?"

Evans said that while triathlon was an "established" Olympic sport, that has provided high quality racing since its introduction to the Games 26 years ago, this new partnership has introduced a "level of uncertainty".

"A lot of the resistance has come from athletes, because you don't know," she added.

A World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport, it is continuing to "increase its focus and involvement in the Olympic and Paralympic families" and that it is in the "planning phase" for Brisbane 2032, adding that "triathlon is, and will remain, at the heart of everything we do".

BBC Sport approached Hyrox for comment, but they referred us to the statements made by World Triathlon.

Sam Dickinson - who won an Olympic triathlon bronze in Paris as part Team GB's relay quartet - can see why the move makes sense but wants more clarity.

"It's trying to get people active not from an elite side but from a participation side," Dickinson told BBC Sport.

"So in that sense it does make sense that as a multi-sport it comes under the World Triathlon umbrella.

"But it's early days, we don't have any of the bread and butter of exactly what's going on."

And there lies the crux of the problem - the lack of clarity has fuelled speculation about what the future holds.

World Triathlon does have other disciplines in its remit, such as Aquathlon and duathlon.

BBC Sport has been told that 'Fitness Racing' was first included as a discipline in the World Triathlon Constitution in October 2025, a move supported by the majority of the governing body's National Federations.

A World Triathlon spokesperson added that the partnership provides opportunities to 'reach new audiences' through collaborating with global partners.

Founded in 2017, Hyrox's popularity has continued to grow rapidly. A total of 1.5m athletes took part during the 2025/26 season - up from 650,000 the year before - with participation projected to surpass 2m in the current season.

British Triathlon, one of World Triathlon's national federations, told BBC Sport it recognises "World Triathlon's work to grow, develop and strengthen the sport of triathlon, multi-sport and its community", but is waiting to hear the "full operational, governance and commercial framework" for the partnership.

Government needs to act faster on grooming gang inquiry, says survivor

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:31:57 GMT

A survivor of grooming gang abuse has accused the Scottish government of taking too long to deliver the public inquiry it promised "at pace" almost nine months ago.

Holly Alex, 36, went into care at the age of 14 after her stepfather went to prison and her relationship with her mother broke down.

Holly's social care records, seen by BBC Scotland News, show that staff recorded concerns that she was being "groomed" for sex by "adult Asian men" as a teenager. They also indicate social workers and police knew of the risks she faced.

Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said safeguarding children was the government's priority, and the planned statutory inquiry was a core part of this work.

Contains some upsetting scenes.

The Scottish government ordered a public inquiry into grooming gangs in February following mounting political pressure.

Between the ages of 14 and 17, Holly lived in five different children's homes across Edinburgh.

Police Scotland has confirmed it was made aware of some reports made by Holly during this time period and an investigation is ongoing.

Holly's care records contain repeated references to her going missing from her accommodation before returning intoxicated, with unexplained sums of money.

At the same time, professionals described her as "sexually promiscuous" and "flirtatious".

Holly said roughly 25 to 50 men were involved in her abuse in a series of flats in Edinburgh and Livingston during her time in care.

What initially appeared to be friendship and generosity, soon became exploitation and abuse.

"At the start, 14-year-old Holly felt this was great," she said. "But then slowly realised these men expected something from you.

"It was explicitly told to me: 'You basically need to give us something back, because we gave you all this money, drink, cigarettes, food. We need something back.'

"For a while, I thought I was clever because I used to manage to escape before anything happened.

"But they caught on to that very quickly and my opportunities to leave became far and few between.

"And if I tried to leave, I was met with physical violence."

She added: "Sometimes you'd go to a property and there was maybe two people there, sometimes… seven men there.

"I was taken to a specific house and when I arrived there were several men and several young girls.

"You never knew what you were walking in to."

When asked how she feels about her experience now, Holly said: "Younger me would have said 'disgusting', but it's not my fault."

The Scottish government announced plans for a public inquiry into group-based child sexual abuse and exploitation in February, with the then Education Secretary Jenny Gilruth pledging to "leave no stone unturned".

Almost nine months on, Holly said survivors were still waiting for meaningful progress.

"I want them to know that survivors have been waiting, some of us for absolute decades," she said.

"If you say you'll do something at pace, do it at pace.

"Don't just pay lip service to it. Some people's lives depend on the truth coming out."

Holly also argued that the term "grooming gang" had become weaponised, creating misconceptions about the nature of the abuse and sometimes "twisted to suit certain narratives".

"I am in contact with a lot of survivors who are victims of child sexual exploitation, not by Asian perpetrators, by other perpetrators," she said.

She said some survivors had told her they feared being excluded from the inquiry because their abusers did not fit a particular ethnic profile.

"A grooming gang is a group of two or more perpetrators, regardless of ethnicity or race," she said.

"I don't tie grooming gangs specifically to an ethnicity."

Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said sexual abuse and exploitation were "abhorrent crimes" that left a devastating effect on victims and their families.

She said: "Safeguarding children is our utmost priority, and we are taking determined action to establish the extent and scale of this abuse so we can prevent it.

"The statutory inquiry is a core part of this work, to be chaired by Prof Alexis Jay with the fullest investigatory powers."

A national review of group-based child sexual abuse in Scotland, published in September, found there is no reliable national picture of the scale of grooming gang offending because of inconsistent data collection and the absence of an agreed definition.

The review was also overseen by Prof Jay, who is a child sexual abuse expert.

Before evidence can be heard at the inquiry, its terms of reference must be formally agreed.

Ministers are expected to provide an update on the inquiry at Holyrood on Thursday.

Holly has been invited to take part in the Scottish government's Truth Project pilot, an exercise to listen to survivors, which is running alongside the public inquiry.

Then Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced a statutory independent investigation into grooming gangs in England and Wales in June 2025, with its terms of reference published earlier this year.

Police Scotland said it was committed to tackling all forms of child sexual exploitation, regardless of the passage of time.

A spokesperson added: "We know how difficult it can be to come forward and the needs of survivors are always at the heart of our victim-centred approach.

"We will continue to work with partners to identify and to protect potential victims, and to tackle child sexual exploitation and grooming."

Holly also experienced sexual abuse at a secure unit in Edinburgh.

Her evidence played a crucial role in convicting her abuser, carer Gordon Collins.

He was sentenced to 10 years in 2016 for indecent behaviour towards Holly and three other young people in his care.

The court heard he raped one girl over the course of a year.

Amanda Hatton, from City of Edinburgh Council, said: "We want to repeat our apology to Holly - and praise her and others who have bravely come forward to tell their stories.

"Testimonies like Holly's have already helped us to make significant changes to the service, including the closure of all secure residential accommodation across the city, and we're confident that children and young people in our care are now safer and better supported."

Hatton said the council was listening to young people but acknowledged there was more work to be done to "learn lessons from the past".

"If and where any criminality is suspected, we will always report this to Police Scotland urgently," she added.

How America voted in maps and charts

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 09:53:18 GMT

It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats in the US midterms.

They have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives too.

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but the previously deep red state of South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.

Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine also turned blue and the Democrats held Michigan. There are two seats remaining, Alaska and Mississippi, both are on a knife edge.

The shift from Republican to Democrat happened across the country. Some of the biggest swings were in Texas where the Democrats took the Senate seat and the governor.

The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday).

Now it's a question of how big that win will be as counting continues.

Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.

The redistricting saw both districts move from having a majority of 2024 Kamala Harris voters to having a majority of people who voted for Donald Trump.

Florida 22, which was also redrawn to favour the Republicans, saw a victory for the Democrats too.

A huge poll of voters suggests women turned out in numbers and most voted Democrat. Men on the other hand were evenly split between the two main parties.

Hispanic voters look to be one of the key groups in the elections in Florida. The poll suggests this group backed the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon by 55% to 44% for the Republican Ashley Moody.

This is a turnaround from the estimated 55% of Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024.

The poll also asked what issues voters were most concerned about. It suggests that across the country the economy was the biggest issue, followed by the state of democracy.

When voters were asked if Donald Trump's policies impacted economic conditions, the poll suggests that two-thirds believe they had made things worse.

Code cracked for shipwreck padlock solving 400-year-old mystery

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:12:52 GMT

Experts have cracked a four-letter code to open an ancient padlock from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast using modern scanning technology.

The 400-year-old brass lock was discovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes in the sand near Margam in Port Talbot, in 1999.

It forms part of a wider treasure hoard from the Ann Francis ship that was caught in a storm on 28 December 1583 on the way back from Spain. Its cargo was hidden beneath the sand for centuries.

Museum experts have used CT scanning to examine the lock's internal mechanism, identify the correct letter combination and solve the mystery.

Peter Hughes, from Maesteg, said the padlock was one of hundreds of artefacts he found after decades of searching on Morfa beach.

Found near a collection of Spanish silver coins and close to two coin weights, it is thought the lock may have protected these objects or secured a chest containing valuable items that did not survive, like documents or textiles.

"It was by chance - a day off. I was walking along the beach with my metal detector on a day off, and I came across a coin," the 69-year-old said.

"That was the start of a journey that lasted 21 years."

He said he was "delighted" that the expert team at Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University cracked the padlock code after he spent years trying to solve the mystery himself.

"I tried to unlock it for about 20 years, I tried moving the dials, finding the right combinations, and I failed," he said.

"But with the aid of modern technology we've been able to crack what's like the Da Vinci code, really.

"For me, it's like opening the Ark of the Covenant, and I'm delighted, truly thrilled."

Dr David Williams, a research associate based at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said he was "sceptical" when he was asked to use a scanning device to try and solve the mystery.

"It's challenging, the device we have is not designed to this particular purpose," he said.

"This is micro CT scanning, something you'd get at the hospital, but for smaller items."

Williams said he was "always open to a challenge" and trying to "figure out a puzzle".

"We did a first scan to see if we could see anything and we were quite surprised that we could see letters," he said.

"The second scan went terribly, but with the third scan, we tried a different approach, and figured out the code.

"I was blown away that we actually cracked it."

Hughes passed on the hoard of artefacts to Amgueddfa Cymru in 2017, and the collection, with the lock in the centre, was put on display at Swansea Waterfront Museum in July 2026.

Senior curator Alastair Willis said the discovery of the code, which spells out ANCE, was "incredible".

"It's really complex because there are so many combinations," he said.

"There are four different rings, and because there are six different letters on each of the rings, there are 1,296 different combinations, and you have to make sure they're aligned with the loop at the top."

"Also, confusingly, there are other letters on the ends which don't move, which are unrelated, and it's like they were to mislead any potential burglar," he added.

His colleague at Amgueddfa Cymru, senior curator Siân Iles, said the lock was in "excellent condition" and paints a picture of the period.

"This is a wonderful example of one that still functions as it would have done hundreds of years ago," she said.

"Because it was found so close to the wreck of the Ann Francis and with all the material that's part of that collection, it provides a really good context, it allows us to really tightly date it.

"I've seen others, and they're usually corroded and in different parts, but it was in wonderful condition.

"It's a small object so it probably would have been a lock for a chest or a small box, we don't know the content, and that's part of the story, there are some things we'll never know, but it's something that would have meant something to the person who knew that code."

Treasure has a variety of definitions, as per the Treasure Act of 1996.

In Wales, if you find treasure it must be reported to a Finds Liaison Officer within 14 days of first finding it or within 14 days of realising an item might be treasure, even if you have had it for longer.

Only items officially defined as treasure need to be reported and there is a fine or up to three months in prison for not reporting.

There are different rules for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

After a find is reported, you will be contacted by either a Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator to talk about how and where you made the find.

The Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator will then write a report on the find and the coroner will hold an inquest.

The Finds Liaison Officer will help you get the coins assessed by experts to determine if they meet the legal definition of "treasure" under the Treasure Act 1996.

If a museum wants the treasure, the Treasure Valuation Committee will ask an expert to value the find.

They will recommend to the Secretary of State for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport how much the treasure is worth and how much should go to anyone eligible for a share of a reward.

Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'

BBC News Wed, 04 Nov 2026 00:52:19 GMT

It was meant to be Kim Kardashian's triumphant debut as a leading actor - but last year's legal drama All's Fair was so universally panned by critics that it actually broke streaming records as audiences clambered to see what all the fuss was about.

Kardashian, who is best known as a media personality and businesswoman, tells the BBC she had no choice but to "lean into" the discourse and come back for a second series.

"We thought we were this law show, dealing with some really serious issues," she jokes.

But viewers mostly enjoyed its comedy value - with outlandish outfits and zingy one-liners from co-stars Sarah Paulson and Glenn Close sending the show straight into the pantheon of 'camp classics'.

"We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."

All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.

Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.

The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".

But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.

Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?

"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"

Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.

"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.

While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.

Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.

"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."

But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.

"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.

"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.

"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.

Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.

Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.

As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season".

"She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."

One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know".

"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease

New Scientist November 04, 2026

A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes.

“The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.”

How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants

Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population. Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss.

Advertisement

But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles, although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque, but they are dependent on batteries.

Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure, prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic.

Free newsletter

The idea was that, as the bristles bend during brushing, they would generate electricity, triggering chemical reactions that produce molecules called reactive-oxygen species that damage bacteria, while the bristles physically remove plaque.

The researchers made two sets of bristles of different thicknesses, both of which met Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. The team also detected reactive-oxygen species on the brushes, which remained soft and retained their electrical properties after three months of use.

Next, the researchers exposed two common oral bacteria to their bristles and nylon ones, which are used in standard toothbrushes, in laboratory experiments, including simulated brushing movements. The thicker piezoelectric bristles were particularly effective, killing about 53 per cent of Streptococcus mutans, which causes cavities, and 78 per cent of Porphyromonas gingivalis, which contributes to gum disease, compared with just 9 and 8 per cent, respectively, for nylon bristles.

The team also grew plaque from human mouths on pieces of cow enamel and brushed them for 3 minutes. The new toothbrushes removed more than 99 per cent of the plaque, compared with about 80 per cent for conventional nylon brushes.

Finally, the team tested the toothbrushes in 109 adults with dental plaque and gum inflammation, who were randomly assigned to use either a piezoelectric or nylon toothbrush twice daily for three months. Dental examinations revealed reductions of roughly 40 per cent in plaque build-up, gum inflammation and bleeding among those using the piezoelectric brushes, compared with around 15 per cent for those using conventional brushes.

Genetic sequencing of the dental plaque from the piezoelectric group also revealed a decline in the relative abundance of harmful bacteria and an increase in some potentially beneficial bacteria.

Larger studies now need to establish whether the toothbrush actually prevents issues like cavities and tooth loss, says Jakubovics.

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeg5744

A dyslexia diagnosis can help struggling children, but what about the rest?

New Scientist November 04, 2026

In years gone by, children who struggled to learn to read and spell were labelled “stupid”, “lazy” or “dim”. Today, of course, we are much more enlightened – now we label many of these children as “dyslexic”. But perhaps this label is still a bad idea.

Picture two 9-year-olds reading at the level of an average 6-year-old. One gets a diagnosis of dyslexia. This positively affects her wellbeing. Her teachers now understand she has dyslexia and that she can get tailored help.

The other child isn’t so lucky. Maybe his parents can’t afford a dyslexia test – in the UK, assessment isn’t available on the NHS and can cost several hundred pounds. In the US it could set parents back thousands of dollars. Or perhaps he was tested but the result was negative. Until very recently, this outcome was common for already disadvantaged children, because the official definition of dyslexia included the idea of “discrepancy” – that reading problems should be unexpected given a child’s other cognitive abilities. Assessing ability using IQ tests can also be biased against those from lower socioeconomic groups or learning to read in a second language. By extension, this second child is just bad at reading or lazy, or both, and not eligible to receive extra help with reading.

Advertisement

Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help, the other does not

Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help and understanding and the other doesn’t, all because of a label. Yet this label is based on a questionable assessment. Despite trials using a wide range of cognitive processes, researchers have been unable to find meaningful ways to identify dyslexia.

So, why not just help all children who struggle to read? Each has a unique combination of risk and remediation factors, but all will benefit most if we intervene when the problem first shows up, instead of waiting years for them to fail and then receive a diagnosis. Our newfound understanding of what is happening in their brains even suggests some surprisingly simple ways to help. Giving every child the best possible chance to overcome their challenge is what matters, not the label we attach to them.
