Arrival is 10 years old. This first-contact film is as brilliant as ever

New Scientist November 04, 2026

ArrivalDenis Villeneuve

Here’s something remarkable: for a decade now, one of the finest directors working anywhere in the world has been exclusively focused on science fiction. That isn’t a blessing we’re often afforded. More remarkable still is that each of the four films he has released in this period has been a success – and his fifth, the final part of the Dune trilogy, out this December, looks likely to be one, too.

Yes, I’m talking about Denis Villeneuve. But instead of looking ahead at Dune: Part Three, I want to look back at his first (and probably best) foray into sci-fi, released in the UK 10 years ago this month. The best word I can think of to describe it is “staggering”.

Advertisement

With a new 28 Days Later movie and a new Dune, not to mention films from Stephen Spielberg and Ridley Scott, this is shaping up to be a vintage year for sci-fi, says Simon Ings

Arrival starts with a world-ending event: the death of a child. In a 2-minute opening montage, the brief life of 12-year-old Hannah elapses with cruel linearity. What little we see of her in the film we mostly sense through her mother, Louise (Amy Adams), and the way that Hannah’s presence and absence come to shape a defining moment of human history.

Louise is a linguist who is called upon in unlikely circumstances: a mysterious craft, hundreds of metres tall, has landed in Montana – one of 12 such “shells” around the world. The US Army is trying desperately to assess what the life forms inside it want and whether they pose a threat. Partnered with physicist Ian (Jeremy Renner), who would rather approach the aliens through the purity of maths, Louise is given the near-impossible task of translating for these strange, striking, seven-limbed “heptapods”.

It is fascinating to watch Louise slowly work out the heptapods’ means of communication

Arrival‘s script is beautifully spare. Appropriately enough for a film about language, it conveys a great deal with every exchange between the people who have converged on Montana. When Louise and Ian arrive at the military camp, a scientist reveals that the heptapods usher the humans out of their craft after around 2 hours, apparently to prevent them suffocating. CIA agent David Halpern (Michael Stuhlbarg) questions why it takes 18 hours to establish contact again.

In a lesser film, this would be a load-bearing piece of plot, explicated simply to justify a later happenstance. Here, it is rich with theme. When Ian explains that differences between the heptapods’ atmosphere and our own could affect how long it takes to pump in fresh air, agent Halpern’s response is: “So you’re saying they could suffocate us if they wanted?”

The aliens’ intent, it seems, is in the eye of the beholder, and Louise is one of vanishingly few people with the skills to unravel what is actually going on. To do so, she has to talk relativity – linguistic relativity, that is, the idea that the structure and style of the language we use influences our perception. It is fascinating to watch her slowly work out the heptapods’ means of communication, and how, in turn, to present this knowledge to her human compatriots without triggering all-out war.

On top of all this delicious intellectualism, Arrival is a stunningly shot film. Villeneuve and cinematographer Bradford Young work wonders with the hermetic interior of the heptapods’ inky black shell.

Aside from a few bits of dodgy CGI, nothing about Arrival has aged. It is as heartbreaking and life-affirming as ever. And if reports that Villeneuve is set to direct an adaptation of Arthur C. Clarke’s Rendezvous with Rama are correct, then we can be grateful he hasn’t yet left the realm of sci-fi behind.

BookExtraterrestrial LanguagesDaniel OberhausHow should we talk to aliens? If the questions posed in Arrival make you want to find out more, try this primer, which draws on ideas from maths, linguistics and philosophy

FilmDune; Dune: Part TwoDenis VilleneuveGetting it right once takes talent. Getting it right twice takes brilliance. While we wait to see if Villeneuve will pull off a hat trick with Dune: Part Three, why not revisit the previous films?

Bethan Ackerley is a subeditor at New Scientist. She loves sci-fi, sitcoms and anything spooky. Follow her on X @inkerley

If every ship were taken out of the water, would sea levels change?

New Scientist November 04, 2026

If every ship on the planet were hauled out of the water, how much would global sea levels change, and how quickly?

Mike FollowsSutton Coldfield, West Midlands, UK

If the world’s ocean-going commercial fleet were removed from the sea, global mean sea level would quickly fall, but by only a matter of micrometres.

Advertisement

By Archimedes’ principle, a floating vessel displaces enough water for the mass of that water to equal the combined mass of the vessel and everything aboard it. This means that a ship with a total mass of 100,000 tonnes displaces 100,000 tonnes of seawater, equivalent to about 97,560 cubic metres, given a seawater density of approximately 1.025 tonnes per cubic metre.

The ship itself is represented by its lightship mass: the mass of its hull, machinery and permanent equipment. Deadweight tonnage (DWT) is the maximum additional mass that a vessel is permitted to carry, including cargo, fuel, fresh water, ballast, stores and people. Ballast is used to provide stability, control draft and trim, and keep the propeller and rudder adequately immersed.

Removing the ships would buy us less than a day’s reprieve from the current sea-level rise of 4.5 millimetres a year

According to the UN Conference on Trade and Development’s 2025 Review of Maritime Transport, there are about 112,500 propelled seagoing merchant vessels of at least 100 gross tonnage (GT), with a combined carrying capacity of 2.44 billion DWT. GT is a dimensionless measure based on a ship’s size (specifically its enclosed volume), not its mass. Maximum displacement is greater than this because it also includes the vessels’ lightship mass. Using typical ratios of deadweight to displacement for different classes of merchant ship suggests that total maximum displacement is about 3 billion tonnes, equivalent to about 2.9 cubic kilometres of seawater.

Given that Earth’s radius is about 6400 kilometres and the ocean covers about 70 per cent of its surface, the ocean has a surface area of approximately 360 million square kilometres. Dividing the displaced volume by this area gives a maximum global mean sea-level rise of about 8 micrometres.

The actual figure would be somewhat lower than this because the entire fleet is never simultaneously carrying its maximum deadweight.

Herman D’HondtSydney, Australia

Here’s a back-of-the-envelope calculation. A quick internet search tells me that the carrying capacity of the global commercial shipping fleet is about 2.5 billion deadweight tonnes, or about 2.25 billion metric tonnes. Let’s assume a total of 3 billion tonnes for all ships and boats.

That mass equates to 3 cubic kilometres of water. On the other hand, the total ocean volume is 1.3 billion cubic kilometres.

Hence, removing the ships is going to remove less than half of one part per billion of the total ocean volume. The average depth of the ocean is roughly 3700 metres. Removing half a billionth of that drops the surface level by roughly 18 micrometres. Human hairs typically have a thickness of between 30 and 60 micrometres.

I don’t think anyone will notice a sea-level drop of half the thickness of a hair. It certainly won’t help to counter the effects 0f global warming.

Hillary ShawNewport, Shropshire, UK

The total global tonnage of ships is around 2.5 billion deadweight tonnes (fully loaded). Some will be in dry dock and many won’t be fully loaded, and a deadweight tonne doesn’t quite equal a tonne, or 1 cubic metre of water. There is also a long tail of countless tiny fishing boats on the sea. So, approximately 2.5 billion cubic metres of water are displaced by these ships. However, the world has 361 million square kilometres of ocean, so removing all these ships would result in a sea-level drop of just 7 micrometres, which would be almost instantaneous as the world’s ships are fairly evenly spread across the seas, outside Arctic circle latitudes.

That would buy us less than a day’s reprieve from the current sea-level rise of 4.5 millimetres a year. We might gain more by removing the 2.5 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions accounted for by shipping, but minus the extra CO2 from transport that shifts to road or rail, for instance in cargoes from East Asia to Europe. Also, a lot of oil is shipped by sea, so CO2 might fall even more as petrol and diesel gets very scarce and expensive in Europe and other places.

The DNA is backwards on The Selfish Gene’s cover – again

New Scientist November 04, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Feedback is not young. We have been here on the back pages for many years, endlessly pushing a boulder up a hill and trying to take joy in the effort. This means, every so often, we are forced to repeat ourselves – because the world repeats itself.

With a due sense of ennui, we turn our world-weary eyes to the cover of the new 50th anniversary edition of Richard Dawkins’s popular science classic The Selfish Gene. The title, written in all-caps, takes up most of the cover. The “I” in “SELFISH” has been replaced by a colourful little drawing of a DNA double helix.

Advertisement

Alas, something is awry. Geneticist Simon Fisher pointed it out on Bluesky: “You know a gene is selfish when its DNA twists the wrong way, as demonstrated by the left-handed double-helix proudly adorning the 50th Anniversary Edition of the multimillion copy bestseller on this topic.”

Yes, once again we have an example of a DNA molecule being drawn, essentially, backwards. In reality, it is a right-handed double helix, but the one on the book cover is left-handed. It’s twisting the wrong way.

Feedback’s mind’s eye immediately cast itself back to March 2025, when we covered a Lego model that included many scientific and technological objects, including a sadly left-handed DNA.

It turns out that The Selfish Gene‘s art has been wrong for at least a decade. Patrick Goymer, an editor at PLOS One, shared the cover of the 40th anniversary edition on Bluesky, and it has the same left-handed DNA in place of the “I”. Feedback notes that our own copy is the 30th anniversary edition, and the DNA is correct. At some point since 2006, the DNA on the cover has flipped into a mirror universe.

This little mistake would be doubly embarrassing if, say, the Nobel prize in chemistry had recently been awarded for research into these sorts of mirror molecules. Can you imagine?

Sometimes a scientific paper has a title so vivid, so immediate, that Feedback just has to write about it. Such is the case with a paper published in Cureus, titled: “Massive fecaloma dissolved by Coca-Cola: A case report”. It was sent to us by Australia reporter Alice Klein, who either has a truly terrible browser history or makes extensive use of a VPN.

A faecaloma, for those not yet blessed with the knowledge, is a large lump of impacted faeces trapped in a person’s rectum. In this case report, the faecaloma had a maximum diameter of 12.2 centimetres.

Readers anxious to see a dramatisation of such a condition are advised to try series two, episode five of The Pitt, in which one of the patients has impacted faeces that the doctors must manually dislodge. Based on our own personal experience, we do not recommend watching this sequence over dinner.

Back in the real world, the doctors reported that they tried “conservative management”, which apparently consisted of “polyethylene glycol, senna, mineral oil, and sodium phosphate enemas”. But the faecaloma didn’t budge, so they turned to a more drastic solution.

The authors tell us that “isolated case reports have described the use of Coca-Cola enemas for fecaloma dissolution with favorable outcomes”. This is because “Classic Coca-Cola acts as a mucolytic agent [it makes mucus less thick and sticky], a source of carbonic acid, and an effervescent solvent”. Hence the doctors administered two 1-litre Coca-Cola enemas, which shrank the faecaloma enough to resolve the situation.

Feedback has a number of thoughts, such as: would Pepsi work as well? What if the doctors had first inserted Mentos? We are also not sure we ever want to put Coca-Cola into our mouth ever again: if it can be used to destroy a faecaloma, we dread to think what it might be doing to our teeth.

Some weeks ago, Feedback began investigating unfortunate technology-induced truncations and abbreviations. These truncations have gone on for a long time and there is no end in sight.

Stuart Arnold was bemused to find Facebook recommending a post about an obsolete form of aircraft called a Rotodyne, which never made it past the prototype phase. It is best described as “a plane, but stick a set of helicopter rotors on top”. Unfortunately, due to the character limit in the Facebook feed, the post was cut off as follows: “designed to take off vertically, then fly faster and fart…” “It’s probably a good thing that the program was cancelled,” says Stuart.

Secondly, David Smith encountered a related problem: tech-induced rudeness. Because his name is a common one, he has long struggled to find unique identifiers for email addresses and such. Imagine his surprise when he joined a large organisation and found he was only the second person there with that name. This seemed like (minor) good news, but he swiftly discovered a downside to being the second David Smith. “The part of the email address corresponding to ‘2@’ has to be pronounced very carefully,” he says.

And finally, Andy Howe reminds us that Trinity Hall, one of the Cambridge colleges, “is colloquially abbreviated as Tit”. He tells us: “This was particularly unfortunate for an archaeology student who saw his name listed in a society’s membership records, followed by the descriptor ‘Arch Tit’.”

Why do people look better in a mirror than in a photograph? Part 3

New Scientist November 04, 2026

Why do people appear younger and better-looking in a mirror than in a photograph? (continued)

Kevin WoodingVia Facebook

Faces aren’t symmetrical and you become accustomed to the unique proportions of your mirrored impression over many years. A photograph shows your face without mirroring, and it can be unfamiliar and surprising with the two sides of your face swapped.

Advertisement

Of course, you could always spend a lot of time looking at photographs of yourself to get used to the non-reflected image of your face. Have fun with this.

Burcu AktenVia Facebook

I know the answer in my own case. I have a better relationship with myself than I do with others. I’m worried about how others see me, but I’m not worried about how I see myself. So, when my photo is taken, I tense up and look uncomfortable and distressed under the gaze of others. In the mirror, I am kind to myself. So, I see a confident and happy person in the mirror, not a scared one.

Kittens brought up in a box containing only horizontal striped lines couldn’t see vertical objects in a normal environment

Lisa Munroe-ShieldsVia Facebook

I look OK in the mirror. But I look like the love child of Hagrid and Worzel Gummidge in photographs! And the self-service cameras in supermarkets make me want to introduce a self-imposed ban on going in those particular shops!

Why don’t dogs look up when a low-flying plane passes overhead? Part 6

New Scientist November 04, 2026

Why don’t dogs look up when a low-flying plane or helicopter passes overhead? I’ve never seen one do this. (continued)

Liz HughesBath, UK

Referencing David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel’s work on the development of the visual cortex in animals, I believe the answer lies in the dog’s upbringing.

Advertisement

Hubel and Wiesel worked extensively on kittens, finding that if certain visual cues were removed from a kitten’s environment in the period when the animal’s brain was wiring its visual pathways, it wouldn’t be able to see those things once they had completed their development. In experiments, kittens brought up in a box containing only horizontal striped lines couldn’t see chair legs or other vertical objects in a normal environment.

So, if a dog wasn’t brought up in an environment that included objects at different heights, then its brain would potentially never be able to recognise that there is an aircraft overhead. And with the cacophony of other motorised and industrial sounds in our world, it is likely that the aeroplane would blend into the background.

Peter SeligmanMelbourne, Australia

We had a kitten that leapt up at a jumbo jet. It missed! And I have seen a cat catch a bird in mid flight. It began its leap in anticipation of the bird’s position.

There are jitters among some traders in financial markets over the prospect of a left-leaning Government worsening the cost of living.

The concern is that more unfunded, untargeted spending, as well as policies aimed at lifting wages without raising productivity, could put upward pressure on inflation.

Some observers are also worried Labour’s pledge to require the Reserve Bank to target employment as well as inflation could see inflation expectations rise, increasing the possibility of actual inflation rising too.

The finance sector hardly has a reputation for being a cheerleader for the left.

However, one participant believed the prospect of the Green Party playing a large role in a Labour-led coalition heightened the sector’s sensitivity to the election.

Read more of Jenée Tibshraeny's Premium piece below.

NZ First candidate Michael Laws says he supports Winston Peters' decision to hold a board meeting to decide his future with the party following comments made about the Opportunity Party’s female candidates.

Laws is also making unclear comments about his desire to become an MP, telling the Herald it would be a "misquote" to report he still wanted to be an MP, while also saying he was "dedicated to the aims and ideals of New Zealand First".

During a segment on his online radio show on The Platform last Wednesday, Laws compared some Opportunity candidates to primary school teachers, commented on another's hemline, called them "stern" and "princesses" and questioned what their face would look like "post-sex".

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said of the comments, it "makes my skin crawl" and Laws was not fit to be a politician.

Laws is sixth on NZ First's list and is essentially guaranteed to become an MP, given NZ First's current polling.

Peters this morning told the Herald it was still a "live issue" whether Laws would remain an MP, saying the party board would meet after the election to discuss the issue.

Laws was not aware of Peters' comments, nor the upcoming board meeting when contacted by the Herald this morning.

"If [Peters] thinks that's the appropriate thing to do then I'll support him in that particular endeavour," Laws told the Herald.

First asked whether he still wanted to be an MP, Laws replied: "I am dedicated to the aims and ideals of New Zealand First and its policies, otherwise I wouldn't have put my name forward."

Asked again to clarify whether he wanted to be an MP, Laws said: "I would not be continuing to campaign today and tomorrow for New Zealand First if I didn't believe that their ideals and their policies were the right ones for New Zealand."

Told by the Herald his comments suggested he did still wish to be an MP, Laws said reporting that would be a misquote.

"There is nothing that I have heard over the last 24 hours to suggest that if I am elected on Saturday night, I won't get to serve.

"All I'm saying to you is, you've provided me with information this morning that I will have to confirm and then, more importantly, process, but on any decision that is made by the board of New Zealand First, I'm going to accept."

Laws would not give a direct answer when asked repeatedly whether he had considered announcing before the election that he would resign if elected.

Hr reiterated how he had apologised for his comments, which he said were made in his "usual sort of stand-up comic/editorial routine" and that he deeply regretted causing offence.

Laws noted how Opportunity candidate Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, who was the primary subject of his comments last week, was the "only person who could possibly feel offended" and referenced a text message from Kingdon-Bebb, in which she said she wasn't offended.

"So perhaps at the heart of it, she understood too that I had no intention of being anything other than impish and puckish, which is the nature of my editorials on many, many, many occasions," Laws said.

Kingdon-Bebb's text, which was a reply to Laws' direct apology to her, also said Laws should "apologise for behaving like a creepy misogynist, for dehumanising and objectifying women who stand for different ideas than those you espouse" and encouraged him to rule out becoming an MP.

Peters this morning told Ryan Bridge TODAY there were women in NZ First who were "very annoyed".

However, Laws believed people would understand how his comments were intended.

"I think the average New Zealander knows exactly the context and the full content of my show.

"I think they understand that my aims were and continue to be both entertainment and enlightenment."

Asked how he thought this would impact NZ First in the election, Laws said: "I think that the overwhelming motivation for most voters at this coming election will not be this sideshow, that will be the cost of living and issues that affect them directly and their families."

Labour campaign chairman and Wairarapa candidate Kieran McAnulty said vote splitting would "distort the proportionality of Parliament and undermine MMP".

He told Ryan Bridge TODAY he didn't think vote splitting was right and believed a change of rules was needed.

Meanwhile, he said things were looking up in the Wairarapa electorate but were tight.

"Where the vote flows on the left, or the right for that matter – the Green Party candidate, the Opportunity Party candidate.

"Neither of those are seeking the candidate vote, they're only seeking the party vote, so I've been pretty upfront that 'well if you don’t want it, I’ll take it'."

McAnulty said it was the most door-knocking he had done in the five times he's run for Parliament.

"Feedback has been really positive, but we'll just have to wait and see."

When asked about train fares for longer haul trains within Wairarapa, he said Labour's $20 public transport fare cap policy would apply to those commuting within the region only.

Routes that crossed into other regions wouldn't be eligible for the cap.

He said he was mostly concerned about the areas that didn't have any public transport.

Labour List MP and campaign chairman Kieran McAnulty on Ryan Bridge TODAY. Photo / Jason Dorday

National leader Christopher Luxon began the day shaving the head of Sam, a member of the National Party's youth wing.

Sam arrived with his head half shaven.

Luxon, reminding everyone National's closing argument of the campaign is not to "leave the job half-done" began shaving the rest of Sam's head.

The shaving took a little longer than expected, with Sam's bar proving unexpectedly resilient to Luxon's clippers.

"What do you eat to grow your hair like this?" Luxon said.

Photos / Thomas Coughlan

All of the voters who were incorrectly asked to provide further information have now been told that they do not have to, says the Electoral Commission boss.

RNZ reported that up to 6800 residence class visa holders were asked to provide extra proof of their immigration status.

They have now all had it clarified they do not have to, said the commission's chief executive Karl Le Quesne.

"People have been pleased we've made the effort to contact them and clarify that with them."

Overall, voting has gone smoothly so far, he told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

"We know there's been a few hiccups, and we look into every one of those that are raised with us."

The Platform's founder Sean Plunket has accused the media of running a "hit job" on Michael Laws and using the story as a chance to promote Opportunity.

He said Christopher Luxon had ruled out NZ First candidate Laws in Cabinet because the PM was "inherently a woke suck-up", while it was "sad" to see Nicola Willis calling the comments disgusting.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong yesterday said comments from Laws about the party's female candidates made her "skin crawl" while the main target of Laws’ comments, Dr Kayla Kindon-Bebb, called them "creepy".

But Plunket claimed this morning that Opportunity were being hypocritical, given they were speaking alongside the party's campaign manager Iain Lees-Galloway, who was sacked as a Labour Government minister by then Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern over an affair with a staff member.

He had told NZ First leader Winston Peters that "whatever the political stuff you've got to deal with Michael that's nothing to do with The Platform, it's nothing to do with our relationship. Winston kind of smiled and said 'naughty boy, you better say sorry'".

Winston Peters told the Herald it wasn't possible for the party to meet ahead of the election, given the demands on the campaign.

Laws initially dismissed concerns about his comments when he saw the Herald's first report, laughing at claims the comments were sexist and accusing the newspaper of lacking a sense of humour.

Asked if Laws had shown poor judgment in his initial reaction, Peters replied: "Look, all those things are matters of judgment we're going to make when I have a chance to talk to my team, but we as a party democratically decide these matters. We don't just make a decision off the top of our head, and I haven't had time to do that, nor have I been able to assemble the people to do that at the same time."

A car has gone up in flames in North Canterbury after a firework was reportedly thrown through its window.

Emergency services were called to High St, Rangiora, after 9pm on Tuesday after someone reportedly threw a firework through a car window.

Fire and Emergency said the blaze threatened a nearby building but was contained before it could spread.

The fire is being treated as suspicious.

Email us

Police said they first received reports of a car fire on High St, Rangiora about 9.05pm on Tuesday.

They said inquiries are ongoing into the circumstances of the incident.

Fire and Emergency said the blaze was one of seven suspected fireworks-related fires this week.

The acting national manager for community readiness and recovery, Tom Ronaldson, said three vegetation fires involving trees and bushes appeared to have been ignited by fireworks in Papatoetoe, Kawerau and Fernside on Monday.

“On Tuesday, there were three vegetation fires in Rangitaiki, Ferrymead and Seddon, and a car fire in Rangiora, all likely caused by fireworks,” Ronaldson said.

“We haven’t seen as many fireworks-related fires as in previous years, but all of these fires are preventable. So it’s so important people who choose to light fireworks take responsibility and do it safely.”

Donaldson said while the forecast predicts possible showers across the country for Guy Fawkes celebrations, a low risk does not equate to no risk.

“The number of fireworks-related fires has been on the increase over the past two years.

“We would like to see that trend turn around this year.”

Donaldson advised people to check local fire conditions and restrictions at checkitsalright. nz before lighting them.

“Your fireworks are your own responsibility,” he said.

‘The system failed’: Ricky Kwok speaks out three years after parents’ murders

New Zealand Herald November 04, 2026

The Ministry of Justice first contacted Ricky three years after his parents' murders. Photo / RNZ, Nick Monro

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

Ricky Kwok was worried. His parents hadn’t turned up at his home in Hamilton to celebrate his father’s birthday before they would all return to Auckland and then head to Hong Kong together a few days later.

His messages to them weren’t being delivered and his calls weren’t being returned.

For hours he wrestled with whether to make the 90-minute drive to his parents’ home in Ellerslie, risking missing them “like two ships passing in the night”, or to wait.

Eventually, he decided to head to their home. But when he arrived, their car wasn’t there. He thought he must’ve missed them.

He decided to go inside and prepare dinner.

“We’ll just have a good laugh about all of it and how we missed each other,” he recalls thinking.

He opened the door and looked inside. The house was dark, with only fading sunlight making anything visible.

As he looked around he noticed what appeared to be a “heap of clothes” in the middle of the room. It wasn’t until a second glance that he realised it was his father Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok. He was dead, and Kwok’s mother, Mei Han Chong was missing.

Four days later, Chong’s body was found in a bush on the North Shore.

Three years on from their killings, Kwok speaks for the first time about their deaths, his quest for answers and how the system “failed”.

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong immigrated from Hong Kong to New Zealand in 1988 with their 3-year-old son, Ricky.

Ricky says his father, an orthopaedic nurse, “worked his backside off to support our family”.

After his death, several orthopaedic registrars and junior consultants told Kwok how much his father supported them in their careers.

“He was the cool, calm head. You’d see him and know things would be right somehow, one way or another. He’s that kind of guy.”

Chong had been a nurse and a midwife in Hong Kong. Once in New Zealand she felt the language barrier would make it difficult to be a nurse, and decided to focus on her family.

Ricky says his mother “wouldn’t hurt a fly”.

While living in Australia for his training he called his mother one evening. He was unwell, and he was homesick.

“I said, ‘Mum, I miss you, I need someone’.”

She was on the next flight and stayed with him for six months.

Ricky, who followed his parents by becoming a vascular surgeon, says his parents never pushed him into medicine.

“They didn’t want me to go into medicine,” he says. “They knew that this career was not going to be easy. This career has a lot of ups and downs. There’s a lot of pressure in this career …

“They always said to me, ‘Just follow your heart, follow your dream, and as long as you do something you enjoy we’re happy. We just want you to turn out to be a good person,’ and, at the end of the day, that’s all it was for them. It’s about being a good person.”

In November 2023, Ricky was living in Hamilton. His parents visited about once a fortnight, usually on a Monday, and the family would catch up for lunch.

On November 6, his parents were supposed to drive to Hamilton to have lunch with him to celebrate his father’s birthday a day earlier. They would then all return to Auckland ahead of a family trip to Hong Kong.

The couple were like “clockwork”, he says. Normally, the couple would arrive in Hamilton by 11am, and he’d receive a message to say they were in town and they would do their own thing until he’d finished work and then they would catch up.

But when he finished work about 12.30pm, there were no messages.

“I was like, ‘What’s going on? Maybe they’re just running late, maybe they’re packing’.”

An hour later there was still nothing. He tried messaging them on WhatsApp. His phone showed only one tick – the message had been sent, but it hadn’t been delivered for some reason, and it hadn’t been read.

He thought it was possible his father had forgotten to charge his phone, but it was unlike his mother to let her phone go flat.

“Something felt off,” he says. “I wondered if something catastrophic had happened, maybe a car accident on the Waikato Expressway - but that doesn’t make sense. Why would their phones not be working? Nothing made sense.”

Ricky says he sat in his Hamilton home for hours deciding what to do, struggling between staying or going to Auckland and potentially missing them.

“I didn’t want to leave, ‘Surely they’ll be alright, maybe if I go up now we will be ships passing in the night and I will miss them,’ that’s why I didn’t move.”

By about 4.30pm, still with no word from his parents, he called 105 and asked for a welfare check. He says the call taker suggested he go to Auckland to check on them.

He then drove to his parents’ home.

When he arrived outside their Celtic Cres home, he noticed their car wasn’t there.

“I’ve missed them,” he thought. “The ships passing in the night, exactly as I feared.”

He decided that, given he was there, he may as well go inside and prepare dinner for the family.

“There will be some story as to why this all happened. Mum or Dad forgot something, or Dad got lost.”

As he drove into the driveway he noticed the gate was askew, which was unusual. As he got closer, he saw that one of the two locks to the front door was unlocked. He didn’t think much of it and presumed one of his parents had forgotten to lock it.

“I need to mention it,” he recalls thinking.

He entered the home. It was dark, with the only light in the house coming from the fading sunlight.

“At first, I was like, ‘Why is there a heap of clothes in the middle of the room?’ Even when Mum is packing, it wouldn’t be so untidy.

“Then I look for a second time, and I realise it’s not a pile of dirty clothes. This is actually a person.”

Then it struck him: “That’s Dad. That’s his clothes. His head was covered, but I knew.”

There were no signs of breathing, no pulse; his father was dead. He recalls an “indescribable smell of death”.

His mind then switched focus to his mum.

“I’m frantically running around the house checking everywhere, I need to know what’s going on - maybe if I find Mum then it will make sense, but I need to find her first.”

As he ran downstairs, it dawned on him that she wasn’t there. He then called 111. The operator asked if he needed an ambulance, and his medical training kicked in.

“I suddenly realised that I had only checked a lack of pulse, a lack of response, but I hadn’t checked pupils.

“I carefully lifted the coat covering Dad’s head to be able to expose his head, and then I saw the blood-soaked towels. That was the point; there’s no point even checking for capillary response. That amount of blood is fatal.

“I said, ‘We need police, Dad is dead, Mum’s missing. I don’t know where she is.’”

Ricky was on autopilot. There was no time to take in the reality of what was happening.

While waiting for the police, he noticed a note on the front door. He ran next door and spoke to his parents’ new neighbours, hoping they might know something about the note.

“I said, ‘Dad’s dead, Mum’s missing, car’s missing, do you know anything about this note?”

The note had been left by the neighbours, who were hoping to speak to his parents about a shared wall.

“I broke down. I was still on the phone to 111, they were on the way and I just broke down.”

The neighbours invited him inside and made him a hot chocolate as he waited for the police to arrive.

Four police cars arrived, about seven minutes after they were called.

Ricky was taken to the College Hill police station. He was told they needed to take a statement from him, but it could wait if he wanted.

“I was like, ‘No, we do it now, whatever I can tell you, because I know that the sooner you start the better the chance you can find her and hopefully find her alive’.”

He left the station about 3am and went to a friend’s house. He struggled to sleep, and then he had to call relatives in New Zealand and Hong Kong to tell them what had happened.

He was trying to process the death of his father while still not knowing what had happened to his mother.

“Inside, I knew she was dead. There was no other rational reason why I wouldn’t have heard from her. It just made no sense.

“You’ve got to hold out hope, but I was very aware it was false hope.”

Then, four days after finding his father, police visited Ricky at his friend’s home.

“I remember them saying, ‘We’ve had a significant development. We found your mum, she’s passed’.”

Police would arrest Lok Fung Lorrence Li and Shu Man Poon – and charge them with murdering the couple as well as plotting to murder Li’s former landlord.

Poon would plead guilty to the charges on the morning they were due to go to trial in May last year. It would be more than a year later that Li would go on trial, with a jury finding him guilty of all charges.

A police review carried out after the killings, obtained by RNZ, says Li and Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok were involved in a crash in late December 2022.

Kwok’s insurer later sought resolution via the Disputes Tribunal. As part of the process, his insurer passed on to the tribunal that Kwok did not want his address disclosed to Li.

However, his request was declined by the tribunal because of “insufficient safety reasons”. Disputes Tribunal correspondence with both parties listed their home address.

The review said it appeared the disclosure of Kwok’s address to Li “has been a significant factor in Li and Poon’s preparations for the murders”.

The review also examined Poon’s visit to police in September 2023, where he told them he was being pressured to take part in the murder of Li’s former landlord.

While at the station, Poon appeared to be in “increasing psychological distress” and was crying in pain and clutching his head and said he wanted to kill himself.

The review said mental health and an ambulance were called. However, because of the delay, it was agreed Poon and his associates would travel to Auckland Hospital for treatment themselves, and they left the station.

The staffer who spoke to Poon sought advice from a police officer who advised her to report it, which she did, linking Li, Poon and other information to the file.

A staff member, whose name is redacted but is referred to as frontline station support team leader, was on leave at the time. When she returned to work on September 9, she reviewed the file and electronically filed it.

The review said police “missed an opportunity to investigate the matter further”.

“Critically, had police acted on the original information presented by Poon in September 2023, it could have alerted police to and possibly prevented the homicide.”

Ricky was informed of Poon’s visit to police not long after it was uncovered during the investigation. He says he was “disappointed”, but understood what had happened at the police station.

“The police are inundated by people who come with a lot of mental health problems, and in their judgment they made a call that he was having a mental health problem and they did the right thing and sent him on his way to receive medical care.”

However, what he didn’t understand was why the matter wasn’t followed up on.

Police have since made changes, including requirements for front-counter staff handling reports of serious or potential crime.

“When dealing with information that relates to violence or threat to property, this will immediately be assigned to the appropriate Criminal Investigation Branch team,” Detective Inspector Scott Beard earlier told RNZ.

In relation to the crash, Ricky said he didn’t know anything about it until several months afterwards when his mum briefly mentioned.

He was unaware of the Disputes Tribunal process.

“Knowing my parents, they would have just thought this is something the insurance company is tackling.”

He says the staff involved in declining his father’s request for confidentiality were “just following the systems and policies” and doesn’t fault them.

“But who thought this was a good idea? Who designed that system?” he says. “The Disputes Tribunal basically gave them the weapon.”

In response to questions from RNZ, Ministry of Justice chief operating officer Carl Crafar earlier said Kwok’s request for confidentiality was not granted as it did not meet the threshold under the Disputes Tribunal rules.

“Specifically, he did not raise any safety concerns, and the statutory threshold was not met.”

As a result of the couple’s killings, changes had been made to how personal information was shared.

“Physical and postal addresses are now kept confidential and are not shared with other parties. Only email addresses and telephone numbers are shared between parties.”

Ricky says he received a call from Crafar on Monday morning, after RNZ’s article on the police review was published. He says it was the first time he had been contacted by them since his parents’ killings.

Ricky made a complaint to the Ministry of Justice during Li’s trial about the disclosure of his parents’ address. He said Crafar told him they weren’t allowed to speak to him until after the court process was finished.

He believes the Ministry of Justice should have contacted him earlier and explained that to him, rather than waiting three years.

“There was nothing to stop them from actually being a little bit compassionate about this.”

He’s also “dubious” about whether they have made “meaningful changes” since his parents’ deaths and looks forward to meeting them in the future. He wants them to take accountability.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said Crafar called Ricky to ensure he was aware of RNZ’s article, and advised him of what he had said to RNZ.

“He also expressed his condolences for the tragic loss of his parents.

“Crafar also took the opportunity to acknowledge a complaint Kwok has made, and apologised for the delay in responding, and that no contact had been made in the meantime. We will contact Kwok again when there is an outcome to his complaint.”

Looking back at the lead-up to his parents’ killings, Ricky says “the system failed”.

“I came back to work in New Zealand to give back to the community that raised me, that looked after me. I feel I have been failed.

“It’s life-shattering. It’s devastating. I will never get my parents back.”

He admits he’s “conflicted” when it comes to how he feels about Poon and Li. He says that before his parents’ murders he was not a regular churchgoer, but he has started going back in the past three years.

“It’s helped to colour my perspective on things. But they talk about forgiveness in church. How do you forgive someone for this? I don’t know.”

In relation to Poon, Ricky says he saw his tears at sentencing as the details of his parents’ killings were read out, and hopes that if he is released from prison one day he can turn his life around and become a “good person striving to help society”.

He’s unsure about Li, but says that may change after sentencing next month.

Asked about the toll of the past three years, Ricky talks about the anxiety of the first few months every time he heard a knock on the door, and the worry walking down the street of who might be behind him while also struggling with flashbacks to the night he found his father.

He says he still finds it hard driving along the motorway in Auckland.

“It feels like you’re an inch away from an accident with the way people drive. And I’m always thinking … If there’s an accident, am I going to be the next victim?”

Ricky says he misses his parents every day.

“There are little things on a day-to-day and a week-to-week basis that I just think to myself, ‘What would Dad say? What would Mum say?’”

Thursday marks three years since his parents’ death. It’s also his father’s birthday.

Ricky tries to fight back the tears as he talks about a tradition his father had of visiting a bakery near their home and picking up cakes for the family to share every birthday.

He will do the same.

“I still do that just to remember them. You just got to keep these little traditions alive. They’re the little memories that make everything.”

Second-hand asbestos contamination leaves Tauranga property permanently listed as ‘hazardous’

New Zealand Herald November 04, 2026

A Greerton home has been permanently registered as “hazardous” after asbestos spread from a neighbouring property with 10 years of recorded and unremediated friable asbestos.

The house at 34 Kiteroa St was significantly damaged by a fire 16 years ago, and friable asbestos was first identified there in 2016.

Tauranga City Council bought the property for $500,000 this year and demolished it – but the problems have not ended for its neighbour at 32 Kiteroa St.

The asbestos was found in 2016, with the council told the surrounding ground was likely to be contaminated. An asbestos expert confirmed neighbouring properties were likely affected in 2017.

This was confirmed in November last year after the council tested the soil.

The Bay of Plenty Regional Council was informed of the contamination this year and registered both properties on the Ministry for the Environment’s hazardous activities and industries list (HAIL).

The owner of 32 Kiteroa St, who the Bay of Plenty Times agreed not to name, said she felt “punished” when she was notified about her property’s registration.

She bought her property in 2017, unaware the soil might be contaminated with asbestos.

The regional council sent her a letter in August, notifying her of the HAIL site registration.

A council spokesperson said the classification was due to hazardous substances migrating from 34 Kiteroa St in sufficient quantity to pose a health or environmental risk.

The Bay of Plenty Times asked whether the property’s HAIL registration could be downgraded, removed or amended.

The spokesperson said the council would not consider changing the classification unless further information was provided. The site’s history would remain on the regional council’s land use register.

Tauranga City Council has said the HAIL registration will be noted on the property file and available to future buyers who order a LIM.

Speaking to the Bay of Plenty Times, the owner said her family should have been able to find out about the potential contamination before they bought the property.

“I had a right, just as the next owner of my property would have a right, to know of any dangers or risks to themselves.”

She said her family’s full financial costs had not yet been realised.

“It’s the future cost, because the word asbestos is alarming to folks. The stigma on the land won’t be realised until we go to sell.

“It’s grossly unfair for our family to now have to bear the burden.”

Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell has been advocating for the neighbour.

He said the situation was unjust.

“[The owner] and her family have purchased a property where, if they had the full information that the council had, which wasn’t on the council LIM, then they would have made a different decision.”

Documents released by Tauranga City Council under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act (LGOIMA) revealed the council first initiated asbestos assessments at the fire-damaged house in 2016 after community members raised concerns.

A structural engineer confirmed the presence of asbestos in roof soffits on December 13.

A week later, the council was informed the soffit was “friable and a health risk, and that surrounding ground was likely to be contaminated and should be tested”.

A dangerous building notice served in March 2017 required the owner to remove and remediate the asbestos.

That same year, an asbestos specialist found adjacent properties were likely to be contaminated.

Council site visits in 2018 confirmed the property’s condition was “unchanged”, and asbestos remained present on-site in 2019.

No further inspections, records or actions related to 34 Kiteroa St occurred from August 2019 until July 2025.

The next asbestos-related record on council files was a WorkSafe complaint in October 2025.

Subsequent council assessments found the property owner had removed “some”, but not all, soffit linings in 2017.

The council said in 2025 that it had “no clear evidence” risks from 34 Kiteroa St were at a level to materially affect 32 Kiteroa St. Therefore, risks would not be included in a property file or LIM for 32 Kiteroa St.

In November 2025, the council and police inspected 34 Kiteroa St and found visible friable asbestos on soffits.

The Bay of Plenty Regional Council was not informed of asbestos contamination at 34 Kiteroa St or next door until February this year, prompting the HAIL registrations.

Firefighters described 34 Kiteroa St as uninhabitable after the 2010 fire.

Tauranga City Council issued dangerous and insanitary building notices, and a notice to fix various building issues, to the property’s owner between 2015 and 2017.

Building notices revealed “charred” structural framing, “buckled” roof cladding, smoke damage and broken windows.

An assessment found loose roofing and that exposed asbestos fibres could be “dispersed through the air”.

These notices were renewed this year, revealing many of the same issues persisted despite partial remediation work.

The council bought the property on June 22 to resolve the building issues.

Demolition and asbestos removal began a week later – a decade after asbestos was first identified.

The council previously acknowledged the community had been affected by the property for many years.

It defended its staged response to the issues over a decade and said public safety was paramount throughout.

Tauranga City Council referred new Bay of Plenty Times questions about the case to the LGOIMA process.

These include why HAIL registrations were not pursued when asbestos contamination was first identified, why the asbestos was not remediated until a decade later, and how the council assessed the risk to other properties identified in a 2017 report.

Bijou Johnson is a journalist based in the Bay of Plenty. She grew up in Tauranga and joined NZME in 2025 after studying communications at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Hillmorton Hospital patient threatened PM before 2022 murder of Christchurch woman

New Zealand Herald November 04, 2026

Christchurch's Hillmorton Hospital.

By Adam Burns of RNZ

A patient of Christchurch’s Hillmorton Hospital made a threat against the then-Prime Minister less than a year before he murdered a mother-of-four, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home on June 25, 2022, while Hussein was on unescorted leave.

Hussein was jailed for life, with a 13-year non-parole period, in November that year, and had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

The second phase of an inquest into Waka Tunidau’s death resumed in Christchurch on Wednesday before Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame.

A psychiatrist who treated Hussein between 2015 and 2022 continued giving evidence yesterday.

The clinician’s identity was suppressed.

Counsel assisting the coroner Stephanie Grieve, KC, asked them about a referral they made to New Zealand’s Fixated Threat Assessment Centre (FTAC) after Hussein penned several letters in late 2021.

The court heard that the letters – intercepted by Hillmorton’s clinical team – referenced multiple conspiracy theories, terror attacks in New Zealand and Australia, including the 2019 mosque shootings, and threats against then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and her family.

The clinician received an email in January 2022 from a fellow psychiatrist, explaining that Hussein was typical of the people who were referred to the FTAC.

They added that Hussein had a “serious mental illness” and his risk was primarily towards the community and himself and pointed to situations where his risk to public figures would increase.

The clinician told the court that Hussein during this period was experiencing “florid paranoid psychosis” and posed a significant risk which had extended to public figures.

This was, however, not the same symptoms he was presenting in the months before Waka Tunidau’s murder, they said.

The FTAC is a cross-agency partnership between police, Parliament and the Ministry of Health, which aims to manage risks posed by people who display fixations on public figures or causes.

“The key thing is that I contrast that with a presentation that was completely different through those periods of time when he was experiencing what we describe as sort of transient paranoid sort of thoughts about people being a snitch or that I didn’t think was psychotic in nature and that my colleagues from their notes don’t describe as being psychotic in nature.”

Lawyer for Waka Tunidau’s family Nikki Pender asked the clinician whether additional leadership roles they took on at the time took them away from their core duties as a psychiatrist.

“Looking back with hindsight, do you think you were trying to do too much,” she asked.

The clinician admitted it partially took a toll.

“I think I was a very hands-on, on the floor involved psychiatrist and I continued to be that, but I think I was there less.

“I think my one thing that was notable was that prior to taking on those roles, my paperwork was always done on the day, or released documents released straight away.

“And so that was one area where I can think back tangibly and think that I was a bit behind with that.”

Earlier in the day it was revealed that Hussein went to locations without permission while on unescorted community leave on June 6 and June 10, 2022.

More than 20 doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses involved in Hussein’s care were due to give evidence during the inquest.

The clinician would resume their testimony today.

- RNZ

Escaped Tāwharanui takahē may be searching beyond wildlife sanctuary for mates

New Zealand Herald November 04, 2026

A takahē mother and her offspring have breached a predator security fence at a Tāwharanui Regional Park sanctuary north of Auckland. Photo / Corelia Schulz, Dreamstime

A takahē and her breeding-age offspring have left a sanctuary north of Auckland, possibly in search of new mates, a ranger says.

The pair escaped Tāwharanui Regional Park’s open sanctuary sometime last Thursday by moving around the predator-proof fence line at the coastal boundary. The open sanctuary is bordered by farmland and coastline.

Auckland Council principal ranger Miranda Bennett said the mother, Heaphy, had lost her mate this year, while the younger bird, Tawhara, had recently reached breeding maturity.

“Takahē naturally roam in search of new territory or potential mates. Heaphy lost her mate earlier this year, while Tawhara has recently reached breeding maturity, so it is possible they were exploring beyond their established range,” she said.

Both birds are fitted with transmitters. Bennett said search teams had detected their signals more than 2km from the park and were still tracking them.

The council is working with conservation partners and neighbouring landowners to find the birds. Once located, they will be coaxed with food and guided into a container using large nets. They will then be transported back and placed in an enclosure in the open sanctuary.

Heaphy and Tawhara are two of the sanctuary’s four takahē. A male and a female remain inside the sanctuary.

The council is asking people to watch for the birds, drive carefully and keep dogs under control. Anyone who spots them should keep their distance and report the sighting immediately.

Bennett said plans would be made to move the birds to another protected population once they were caught, because birds that had learned to escape were likely to do so again.

“Due to the geographical nature of Tāwharanui Regional Park, there will always be a risk that birds find their way around the predator-proof fenceline at the coastal margins. The pest fence is regularly maintained and is fit-for-purpose,” Bennett said.

Two takahē escaped around the fence in 2019 and were safely returned 12 days later. They were subsequently relocated to Motutapu Island.

Takahē are classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and nationally vulnerable by the New Zealand Threat Classification System.

Report sightings to Auckland Council’s Courtney Davis on 027 382 9239 or email courtney. davis@aucklandcouncil. govt. nz.

New Zealand Herald November 04, 2026

Wellington City suffered the largest drop in population of any NZ city in the year to June 2026. Photo / Grace Symmans

Wellington is shrinking faster than any other city in New Zealand, with thousands leaving as jobs are cut from the public sector – but there’s a growing belief the tech sector could be the answer to stopping the exodus.

Latest data from Stats NZ shows that in the year to June, Wellington City’s population dropped from 210,800 to 208,300 people, a 0.6% reduction on top of last year’s 0.3%. It was the largest drop in the country.

Auckland meanwhile topped the list with 1.2% growth in population.

Wellington’s best year was 2020, with a population of 214,200 people.

Wellington hasn’t had an easy ride; early this year it was reported there were nearly 10,000 fewer jobs than at the last general election, and in May, Finance Minister Nicola Willis announced a further 9000 public service jobs were to be cut.

The public service makes up 23% of Wellington’s workforce.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little told the Herald, “The city has undoubtedly felt the impact of recent reductions in that workforce”.

He said there were other strengths the city could champion for growth, including the technology sector.

“The tech sector continues to grow, with companies like Revolut choosing to establish a presence in the city; one of our biggest success stories in recent years, Hnry, has put its name on the stadium, the biggest building in the city.”

Hnry chief executive and co-founder James Fuller has expanded his business to Sydney and London but still keeps the headquarters in Wellington.

He’s keen to invest back into the city which supported him and his wife in the business’ beginnings.

Hnry currently employs 105 people and Fuller is passionate about being an “in office business”; getting people in the city to support other businesses through what has been a tough time for the city.

He said that by investing in the stadium naming rights, he hopes to create a positive space for locals and a home where their sole traders feel like they belong.

“It’s great to see the sort of initiatives that are happening, not just businesses, but also community groups and people who are engaging to try and uplift Wellington in a positive way.”

He said there’s optimism about the capability of the local technology sector with the growing number of businesses.

“It’s exciting to see what’s going to happen with the tech sector in a way that maybe we haven’t seen for three or four years now.”

Fuller feels positivity has started to return to Wellington over the past six months.

“There’s a bit of self-confidence and maybe it’s coming from realising that central government is not going to solve Wellington’s problems and so maybe Wellington has to solve its own problems.”

Another fintech company with a Wellington base is Revolut, which this week became the first financial technology company to be officially registered as a bank in New Zealand. It has more than 80 million customers worldwide.

“A lot of those emerging and successful businesses choose to be based here in Wellington because of the attractive lifestyle and amenities that Wellington offers,” Little said.

Forté Recruitment works in both the public and private sector in Wellington and thinks the city’s co-dependency on the public service is a thing of the past.

Director Anita Murdoch believes the city’s turned a corner for employment after the “absolute worst” in 2024 and the private sector is creating its own opportunities to better the city.

“It’s been tough but there have been some really good things that have come out of all the hardship.”

The agency itself had to find 20% of its work outside Wellington due to the “terrible state” of the market a few years ago.

Murdoch said the mood has since changed, and Wellingtonians are not accepting the negative rhetoric anymore.

“There’s a greater sense of determination to help Wellington to remain positive and to keep moving forward.”

Murdoch said applicant-to-role ratios have levelled out, and they’ve seen a few months of “flurry activity”, particularly in the technology space.

The market is quieter now due to the election, but she expects it will be back to normal by February.

Murdoch is worried about younger workers and succession planning in the city, which she says “can be disastrous”. She says with limited graduate roles available, young people do head overseas.

About 1300 Wellingtonians left for overseas in the past year, according to Stats NZ – the largest loss in the country.

Murdoch thinks graduates are leaving solely for job opportunities, with it far easier to get a job in Australia according to the young people she speaks to.

She said people used to travel for one or two years, then come home and establish themselves, but if New Zealand is not careful, they could be gone for 10 or so years, impacting the entire market.

Murdoch now has to recruit Kiwis back from the Australian market to find people for experienced roles.

“One of the things that we’re trying to say to New Zealand employers is if you’ve got any opportunity to give a grad even a short-term contract for a piece of work or an internship or work experience.

“We’ve got to change our mindset a bit and be willing to give these kids opportunities so that we don’t lose them.”

Affordability is another challenge in the capital, according to the mayor; water bills have increased 13.3% this year under new water entity Tiaki Wai, with an average total annual bill of $2390.

This year Wellington City Council confirmed the lowest rates rise in six years at 5.9%.

“The council is focused on keeping rates increases as low as possible while making Wellington an attractive place to live, work, invest and do business,” Little said.

Seven cities nationally experienced growth in the past year, while Wellington, Dunedin, Nelson, Palmerston North, Napier and Porirua had losses.

This is a flip from 2024 when all cities had population growth, although Wellington City and Nelson were the lowest.

Auckland had the largest gain in international migrants at 13,000, followed by Hamilton (1900).

Wellington City lost the most people overseas, with a decrease of 1300, while Christchurch gained 1300, and the highest net number of Kiwis moving to the city.

After Auckland, Christchurch is home to the most people with 422,400, then Wellington at 208,300 and Hamilton at 193,300.

Over the past 10 years, Christchurch City grew by 12.76%, more than 11 times Wellington City’s 1.12% growth during the same time.

Latest figures show national unemployment has risen to 5.7%, the highest since 2015.

Wellington’s unemployment rate however is 4.9%, putting it below Auckland, Waikato, Gisborne/Hawkes Bay, Manawatu-Whanganui, Southland and Northland - which was the worst at 8.3%.

Little expects the completion of facilities like the redeveloped Town Hall in the new year, and the recently reopened central library, will help boost Wellington’s positivity.

“The new library Te Matapihi is bringing renewed energy and dynamism to the central city, bringing the beating heart back to the city.

“We will continue working to build on these strengths and ensure Wellington remains an attractive and dynamic city.”

Grace Symmans is a Wellington-based reporter who covers news in the capital. Grace joined NZME in 2025 as a producer for Wellington Mornings on Newstalk ZB. She can be emailed at grace. symmans@nzme. co. nz.

Breast density: Rotorua woman diagnosed with cancer 6 weeks after clear mammogram

New Zealand Herald November 04, 2026

Rotorua breast cancer survivor Denise Smith is encouraging women to self-check. Photo / Megan Wilson

Six weeks after Denise Smith had a “clear” routine mammogram, she was diagnosed with breast cancer.

The Rotorua woman believes having dense breasts may have had something to do with it.

She’s backing a call from the Breast Cancer Foundation for the next Government to fund alternative supplementary screening for people with dense breasts.

The foundation also wants BreastScreen Aotearoa – the national breast screening service – to be required to tell women how dense their breasts are in every mammogram result.

A petition urging the Government to take action on this has collected about 2000 signatures since October 23.

The foundation says about 10% of women have extremely dense breasts, meaning the breast is mostly fibrous and glandular tissue, with less fatty tissue.

For these women, standard mammograms may only detect about half of cancers. Dense breast tissue and tumours both appear white, potentially hiding tumours.

The foundation says supplementary imaging, such as contrast-enhanced mammography, can find 93–98% of cancers in dense breasts.

Health New Zealand says it is considering breast density reporting and exploring using AI technology to support “more consistent mammogram interpretation and improve cancer detection”.

BreastScreen Aotearoa provides free mammograms every two years to women aged 45 to 69.

Smith, 54, said she discovered she had dense breasts at her first routine mammogram. A lump was found, but a biopsy came back clear.

In 2019, her second routine mammogram at age 47 came back clear.

Soon after, she felt a lump on her breast when itching.

“I wasn’t checking because I thought my mammogram was clear … and luckily, it was near the front and I felt it.”

She initially ignored it because her father was sick but eventually went to the doctor.

“The doctor even said: ‘You’ve just had a mammogram. It should be all right’.”

“Luckily”, she was referred for a biopsy.

After the cancer was confirmed, Smith said she had an operation followed by four weeks of radiation in early 2020.

She took a hormone blocker for five years.

It was unknown whether the lump was fast-growing or had been missed on the mammogram, she said.

Smith wanted to see more information about breast density available at mammograms, such as a brochure, and funding for supplementary screening for those with dense breasts.

She encouraged people to check their breasts because “a lot can change” between two-yearly mammograms.

Smith was now in remission and volunteers for the Rotorua Breast Cancer Trust.

Her life was back to normal – she worked at a daycare and enjoyed gardening and walking.

Smith said the diagnosis had a “huge” impact on her life, especially because her father died during her treatment.

“There was just so much happening, but it made you realise – enjoy those moments, create those memories, take those photos, do those things, because it really throws you.”

The Breast Cancer Foundation asked Act, the Greens, National, New Zealand First, Labour, Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori if they would explore funding additional screening. The latter three responded.

A foundation statement said Labour would seek advice in its first 100 days on accelerating the introduction of breast density reporting, and was also open to advice on supplementary imaging.

Opportunity supported exploring funding, with eligibility and the type of screening determined by BreastScreen Aotearoa and clinical experts.

Te Pāti Māori said it would explore funding for supplementary imaging for high-risk women.

Foundation chief executive Vanessa Sorenson said women had a right to know about their breast density and information must be matched with access to screening.

“Breast density puts women at higher risk of developing breast cancer, while also making cancer harder to see on a mammogram.

“Yet women are not routinely told about their density through the public screening programme.”

Health New Zealand national public health service prevention screening director Alana Ewe-Snow said BreastScreen Aotearoa told participants of mammography’s “limitations”.

Mammograms detected “eight or nine” out of 10 cancers, she said.

Women should be aware of breast changes between mammograms and talk to their GP if concerned.

Ewe-Snow said higher breast density was one of several risk factors, including having a close relative with breast or ovarian cancer or inheriting a faulty gene.

She said introducing routine breast density reporting was “not simply a matter of adding information to a screening result”.

Health New Zealand was considering the requirements for introducing breast density reporting in a “safe, equitable, practical, and sustainable” way.

This included cost considerations, service impacts, workforce and imaging capacity requirements, and follow-up options.

Research to determine the proportion of women with different breast densities was also needed, she said.

No decisions had been made for this potential work.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Why it will be crime time (all the time) on Australian screens next year

Sydney Morning Herald November 05, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

If you could pick a trend coming to local TV screens next year, it’s easily summed up with one word: crime. Country crime, city crime, true crime, funny crime, crime adapted from a podcast and crime ripped from the headlines.

Everything from the first scripted drama about Erin Patterson and the infamous mushroom murders, to small-town crimes and a clutch of true-crime documentaries examining the murder of British backpacker Peter Falconio in 2001 to Sydney’s Hilton Hotel bombing in 1978.

Crime was the dominant genre at the recent upfronts, where broadcasters unveil their slates for the year ahead. The ABC led, with all six of its new scripted dramas being crime stories, while SBS, Nine and Ten also unveiled true-crime documentaries (Seven was the outlier, unveiling no new scripted dramas or documentaries).

It’s no secret crime pays for streamers and broadcasters. Crime dramas, true crime and investigative series have been a huge audience driver for Stan, for instance, with established series Scrublands and Travis Fimmel’s Black Snow leading the way, particularly with women aged over 40.

It’s a similar story at the ABC, with Anna Torv’s thriller Dustfall, which followed the investigation into the drugging and rape of a teenager, garnering a total audience of just under 1.5 million to date and claiming the title of No.1 adult show on ABC iview.

Speaking ahead of Paramount and Network Ten’s upfronts last week, where the streamer announced the Erin Patterson drama, Paramount’s vice president of content in Australia Tamara Simoneau said the appetite for crime was surging globally.

“Some really big docs on some of the streaming services that have just caught fire around the world, and people become intrigued. It’s one of those things people talk about, and then it just keeps getting life after that.”

So what’s the appeal? Simoneau believes the answer is simple.“There’s been a wrongdoing, and maybe that’s the attraction to it,” she says. “It seems macabre, but it’s justice. You’re watching in the hope justice will be served.”

Fortitude Valley (ABC): The inner-city Brisbane suburb has long had a shady history, and this contemporary drama aims to tap into that. Hunter Page-Lochard, who is also one of the creators and writers of the show, stars as a detective investigating human remains found at a building site. Kat Stewart and Wayne Blair are in support, while Brit actor Rupert Everett brings international star power.

John Bailey: The Enemy Within (ABC): Adapted from former ABC journalist Tim Ayliffe’s long-running series of novels, the political thriller stars David Lyons as (what else?) an intrepid journalist, with Homeland’s David Harewood, Anthony LaPaglia and Yael Stone in support.

Help Me! (ABC): Kate Box plays a journalist who returns to Sydney from New York to see her estranged mother, played by Sarah Peirse, when they are drawn into a plot to bump off wealthy old ladies. Can the sleuthing mother and daughter put aside their differences to help the vulnerable victims? Created by Sarah Lambert, the six-part series is directed by Fadia Abboud, and also stars Tilda Cobham-Hervey and Jai Courtney.

Who the Hell is Hamish? (Paramount+): Inspired by the hit podcast of the same name about real-life fraudster Hamish McLaren, the six-episode drama written by Adam Zwar and directed by Jeffrey Walker, stars Mama Mia’s Dominic Cooper as the cad who targets wealthy divorcee Bec (Claire van der Boom). It all seems rosy, until she notices gaps in his stories.

Mushroom Murders (Paramount+): It was only a matter of time before the Erin Patterson case made it to the small screen. Yellowjackets’ Melanie Lynskey will star as the convicted triple murderer, in this six-part drama that covers the 97 days between Patterson’s infamous beef wellington lunch in Leongatha and her arrest. Created by Anya Beyersdorf, Daina Reid and Deb Balderstone. Filming will take place in Victoria.

Pilli Sisters P. I. (ABC): Tasma Walton, who created and wrote the series, and Ursula Yovich play Marlee and May, a pair of Indigenous private investigators in Fremantle, who use “ancestor-given talents” to crack crime. Unfortunately, there is one case they haven’t been able to crack – that of their missing brother.

Rural Crime Unit (ABC): Filmed around Adelaide, the comedy-drama by Adam Zwar (who also wrote Who the Hell is Hamish?) and Darren Ashton follows local police officer Rita (The White Lotus′ Morgana O’Reilly) and city transplant officer Nick (Philip Lynch) as they tackle small-town shenanigans, with an assist from Rebecca Gibney and Cameron Daddo.

Two Birds (Stan): Set in Kalgoorlie, it stars UK actor Sheridan Smith as a police officer looking for a fresh start, but who is drawn into a web of intrigue. Jacki Weaver and Stephen Peacocke also feature, with the series written by Helen FitzGerald and Megan Palinkas, and directed by James Griffiths and Corrie Chen.

The Great White (ABC): Hugo Weaving stars as a disgraced barrister trying to stage a comeback by defending a dog. Set in Sydney’s eastern suburbs (above a panel beater’s shop, not the fancy part), the dramedy is created by playwright and screenwriter Ange Betzien, and comes from See-Saw films, home of Slow Horses.

Slander (Stan): Created by Rachel Griffiths and Marieke Hardy, this legal drama follows Griffiths, who plays Adelaide Craig, a defamation lawyer who returns to her hometown of Melbourne, where she assembles a crack women-led defamation chambers. Supporting cast includes Jessica De Gouw, Lincoln Younes, Roxie Mohebbi and Doris Younane.

Wentworth: Halfway Home (Binge): This sequel to the enduring hit prison drama Wentworth looks at what happens when the women have been released from prison. Katrina Milosevic returns as Boomer, who turns up at Sal’s Halfway House keen to get custody of her daughter. Unfortunately, a body turns up and staying on the straight and narrow outside is a lot harder than life inside.

Hedley Thomas Investigates (Paramount+): The journalist behind the award-winning Teacher’s Pet podcast, which helped bring down murderer Chris Dawson, takes his crime-cracking skills to the small screen in this six-part series. In it, he will investigate six cases, and promises to challenge assumed truths and go beyond the headlines.

The Hunt for Hamish and The Falconio Witness (Ten): 10News+ presenter Denham Hitchcock enters the true-crime arena, with two documentaries focusing on serial fraudster Hamish McLaren (see also Who the Hell is Hamish?) and the murder of British backpacker Peter Falconio in 2001.

Meeting a Murderer (SBS): Marc Fennell revisits the 1978 Hilton Bombing in Sydney, in this investigative docuseries in which he interviews the man responsible Evan Pederick.

Police (Nine): A six-part observational series that will follow frontline officers in Western Australia.

*Stan is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead.

UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 20:43:21 GMT

Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women

The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.

Kaur said: “The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.”

The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.

Kaur added: “Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.”

Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party who held Wednesday’s debate, said: “Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.

“To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.”

She said one of the selling points of the glasses in advertisements was that they could be used “to film discreetly”. Sabine said she did not want parliamentarians to “only regulate once it is too late”.

Kaur said smart glasses, which can come with built-in cameras, microphones and displays, could “be hugely beneficial” to some people. “For example, for those that are visually impaired, smart glasses have been a gamechanger, helping them navigate the world around them.”

A politician in the Senedd has defended his use of smart glasses in the debating chamber. Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, read a speech from an in-built teleprompter feature in his glasses last month.

He told the BBC’s Politics Wales: “One of the things I identified, a weakness of mine, was that my head was down looking at my notes a lot and I wanted to get away from that.”
