Valverde’s late winner breaks AEK Athens hearts as Real Madrid twice come from behind

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 20:04:07 GMT

Federico Valverde lashed home a stunning effort from distance to snatch Real Madrid a late 3-2 victory at AEK Athens on Wednesday in the Champions League and preserve their 100% start in the group phase.

José Mourinho’s side twice came from behind against the Greek champions before Valverde claimed all three points for his side.

Aboubakary Koïta sent AEK ahead after 12 minutes before Jude Bellingham equalised with a sublime flick for the record 15-time winners.

Stavros Pilios sent the Greek champions ahead with 15 minutes to go but Kylian Mbappé swiftly pulled Madrid level once again, setting the stage for Valverde’s late winner.

Madrid have now won seven straight games across all competitions.

Mourinho started with Vinícius Júnior on the left flank, after he missed the team’s previous two La Liga matches through suspension.

The hosts started with huge energy at the Agia Sophia Stadium and it was not overly surprising when they took an early lead. Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois saved well from former Los Blancos striker Luka Jovic before Koïta sent AEK ahead.

The Mauritanian winger shifted cleverly inside Marc Cucurella and thumped home at the near post, catching out Courtois.

The Belgiun goalkeeper saved again from Jovic as AEK tried to make their strong start count. However they inevitably began to tire and Madrid began to take the reins in the Greek capital.

Mbappé fired over and Bellingham netted from close range but was shown to be offside. But moments later the England international scored again and nobody could deny him that one. Cucurella fired in a low cross and Bellingham produced a brilliant flicked finish to beat goalkeeper Alberto Brignoli.

Former Chelsea defender Cucurella tested Brignoli and Bernardo Silva nodded off-target before the interval as Mourinho’s team controlled the game.

Brignoli pushed away Éder Militão’s long-range effort early in the second half and Lazaros Rota blocked superbly to deny the heavily-involved Cucurella.

after newsletter promotion

Mbappe bent a shot narrowly wide of the top corner with Italian stopper Brignoli at full stretch. The France forward was frustrated by the AEK defence when Vinícius turned sharply and found him with a high pass, but the striker’s shot was blocked.

AEK reclaimed the lead in the 75th minute when the impressive Koïta gently nudged the ball into Pilios’s path and the Albania international finished through Courtois’s legs from close range.

Madrid immediately responded with Bellingham playing Denzel Dumfries in down the right. The Netherlands defender rolled a low ball across the six-yard box and this time Mbappé was able to finish. It was the Frenchman’s fourth goal in four Champions League games this season, and his 16th across all competitions.

Madrid substitute Endrick sent Mbappé through on goal with five minutes remaining but Brignoli produced a sensational save to tip his strike against the crossbar.

However, Valverde refused to give up on the three points and in the 92nd minute he lashed home across Brignoli to keep up Madrid’s perfect record.

‘He was destined for this award’: China Miéville wins Goldsmiths prize for 1,200-page novel

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 20:00:43 GMT

The Rouse, which took its author two decades to complete, was praised by judges as ‘exuberant, overflowing’

China Miéville has won the £10,000 Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse, a 1,264-page epic that is part paranormal thriller, part historical saga moving through decades of British imperial and cold war history.

The win, announced at a ceremony in London on Wednesday, makes The Rouse the longest novel to take the prize since it was launched in 2013 to reward fiction that “breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form”.

The novelist Francis Spufford, who chaired the judges, said all the books on the shortlist were excellent, but “it seemed only right to give this year’s Goldsmiths prize to the one that, in terms of ambition, bold use of history, linguistic experiment and sheer scale, broke most explosively with expectation”.

Miéville has called The Rouse, which was 20 years in the writing, “the defining book of my life, that I’ve been writing for most of my adulthood” in an interview with the New Statesman, which co-founded the prize with Goldsmiths, University of London.

The novel opens in London in 1973 and follows Maur, whose son, Ewan, dies in an apparent suicide at an army barracks. As Maur tries to uncover what happened to her son, she finds allies among other bereaved families and a journalist, and gradually discovers the British state’s covert interest in the paranormal. Her search for the truth runs alongside the story of a soldier with experience of supernatural forces.

In a review for the Guardian, Stuart Kelly called it “maximalist, dense, disorienting and discomfiting”, arguing that Miéville deserves comparison with Roberto Bolaño and Mircea Cărtărescu, and describing the book as “affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frightening”.

The novelist Hari Kunzru, one of the judges, called the book “a monumental work” in which Miéville “sets himself the daunting task of describing phenomena that are indescribable, stretching language to its limits and pushing formal and genre boundaries”.

“In a time when much fiction is careful to colour inside the lines, this enormous, exuberant, overflowing book is a reminder that the novel is capable of containing multitudes,” Kunzru added.

Tanjil Rashid, culture editor at the New Statesman, said Miéville had spent his career giving “imaginative form to a distinctly weird vision of the world, deeply personal but also unashamedly political”. He added: “Of all the awards he has won, this is the prize he was destined for.”

Miéville, who grew up in London, is known for novels including Perdido Street Station, The City & The City and Embassytown. He has won the Hugo, World Fantasy and Arthur C Clarke awards, and is a recipient of a Guggenheim fellowship. His nonfiction includes Between Equal Rights, a study of international law, and October, a history of the Russian Revolution. In 2024, he co-wrote a novel with the actor Keanu Reeves, The Book of Elsewhere.

after newsletter promotion

Spufford was joined on the judging panel by the writer and translator Kate Briggs, Kunzru and the journalist and former Evening Standard literary editor David Sexton.

The Rouse beat five other shortlisted books: Polly Barton’s What Am I, a Deer?, Keith Ridgway’s Dooneen, Doireann Ní Ghríofa’s Said the Dead, Aea Varfis-van Warmelo’s Attention Seeking Behaviour and Missouri Williams’s The Vivisectors.

Now in its 14th year, the prize is open to novels by writers from, or resident in, the UK and Ireland that embody “the spirit of invention that characterises the novel genre at its best”. Last year’s prize was won by CD Rose for We Live Here Now. Previous winners include Rachel Cusk, Eimear McBride, Ali Smith, Isabel Waidner and Benjamin Myers.

The Rouse by China Miéville is published by Pan Macmillan (£35). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Muriqi caps Fenerbahce comeback to make Liverpool pay for defensive lapses

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:58:13 GMT

Andoni Iraola arrived in Istanbul hoping to plug Liverpool’s flaws in attack only for holes to appear at the opposite end of the pitch. Fenerbahce capitalised on a late defensive collapse to launch Dirk Kuyt’s interim spell with a tumultuous victory and end Liverpool’s 100% run in the Champions League.

Liverpool’s second successive defeat will infuriate Iraola as much as the manner of Sunday’s loss to Arsenal. It was careless and easily avoidable. The visitors led twice, through Trey Nyoni’s first senior goal and a header from substitute Alexander Isak, only for Fenerbahce to level swiftly on both occasions and snatch a late winner when Vedat Muriqi punished weak defending from several in red. Bradley Barcola’s anonymous display up front was an added headache for the Liverpool head coach.

Iraola’s team started strongly against an ageing home side and created two good openings in the first five minutes. Victor Muñoz and Barcola both fluffed shots from an inviting Kostas Tsimikas cross, while Jérémy Jacquet headed wide from the left back’s corner. Tsimikas’s deliveries were his strong suit. Defensively, he produced another uncertain display.

There was a Premier League feel to the contest given the number of recognisable faces in the Fenerbahce ranks. Kuyt’s starting XI boasted almost as much Premier League experience as Liverpool’s with Romelu Lukaku, Ederson, N’Golo Kanté, Nélson Semedo, Matteo Guendouzi and Mason Greenwood amassing 1086 appearances between them. The total of the visitors’s starting lineup came to 1241.

As expected, the Fenerbahce fans tested the ear-drums with their incessant whistling whenever Liverpool took possession. They were a test for structural engineers too with their constant bouncing in the upper tier of the home end. Liverpool sought to dilute the atmosphere by controlling possession in the early stages. Rio Ngumoha was prominent and Kanté should have been booked for halting one promising run by leaping on the teenager’s back. The referee, Clément Turpin, was in a lenient mood with both sides.

Fenerbahce had struggled to hold up play in the Liverpool half or create a chance of note when Archie Brown exposed the visiting defence with a superb ball from left back. The pass sailed over Tsimikas and was controlled well by Greenwood, before he was pushed over by the Liverpool defender. Neither Turpin nor the video assistant referee deemed it a penalty kick.

The decibel levels cranked up several notches as Fenerbahce’s penalty appeals were waved away. And even higher when Liverpool took the lead just seconds later. Ngumoha was heavily, inevitably involved with a darting run and shot that was charged down into the path of Szoboszlai. Brown, under pressure from Virgil van Dijk, headed the midfielder’s cross clear but only as far as Nyoni on the edge of the penalty area. The young midfielder swept a low volley beyond Ederson with the aid of a slight deflection off Kojo Peprah Oppong. It was a memorable milestone in the continued rise of Nyoni; the first goal of his career at the highest level.

It was also the cue for Fenerbahce to rouse themselves. The hosts almost levelled straight from the restart when Kanté released Brown on the left and his low centre was turned against Alisson’s crossbar by Irfan Can Kahveci, who may have been ruled offside. They did not have to wait much longer for the equaliser. After Dominik Szoboszlai was penalised for a foul on Kanté 25 yards out, Greenwood’s resulting free-kick took a huge deflection off Jacquet’s stomach and sailed past the wrongfooted Alisson. The Liverpool keeper did not hide his anger at Jacquet turning away from the free-kick and leaving a costly hole in the wall.

The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:22:43 GMT

Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same

On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability.

Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.

Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, been widely been described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.

Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.

Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama, and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.

“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.

The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “obvious to almost everyone”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.

“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”

Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipac pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.

The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.

“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

In Michigan, El-Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters, according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024..

This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.

For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said. “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”

Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.

“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

The great sleeping giant of the US has awakened

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:03:08 GMT

The real question in my mind is whether Democrats will take advantage of the new age of populism

The great sleeping giant of the US has awakened, taken a hard look at what’s become of the nation, and roared a thunderous “NO!”

What occurred on Tuesday was not – as some are saying – the inevitable midterm swing of the pendulum against the party in power. Texas hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988. The last time Kansas elected a Democratic senator was 1932.

Nor was it just the economy. Americans are unhappy with high prices, to be sure, but inflation isn’t out of control. The country is not in a depression or recession. Unemployment remains quite low.

Nor, finally, was it all due to Donald Trump. Despite Trump’s repeated efforts to get voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot, he was not. Most Republican candidates barely mentioned him and many Democratic candidates stressed local or statewide issues rather than fixate on him.

Something much larger is responsible for what occurred: anti-establishment populism. It’s burst forth against the mammoth corporations that have scored record profits while most Americans have had to pay more. Against the mega donors and super Pacs that have flooded US politics with more campaign money – legalized bribes – than ever before.

And against the big tech billionaires who have become the most powerful force in the US economy and society – as well as Trump’s and the Republican party’s most visible backers.

The irony is that anti-establishment anger propelled Trump into the presidency in 2016 and again in 2024. Many Americans had found his politically incorrect rants and “America first” nativism to reflect their own anger at being disrespected and left behind. “I am your warrior,” he told supporters when he announced his candidacy for the 2024 election.

But during his second term, Trump has morphed into the very establishment he had railed against. He gave tax cuts and subsidies to tech billionaires. He’s promoted their AI, pushed their datacenters, put Elon Musk in charge of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge), advocated their crypto, and went to war in the Middle East – not only causing gas prices to soar but making big oil billions (or, as Trump bafflingly boasts, “we’re making an absolute fortune in our country”) and enriching big tech weapons makers and investors, including his family.

Many who voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024 have now abandoned him because of this blatant corruption, crony capitalism and eagerness to be on the gilded side of the US’s new Gilded Age. According to CNBC’s late October poll, corruption was the top issue on voters’ minds.

Meanwhile, anti-establishment populism has taken firm hold in the Democratic party. “The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right,” said the newly elected Texas Senate candidate James Talarico. “It’s top versus bottom.”

Sherrod Brown regained his Senate seat from Ohio largely due to voter anger at datacenters and the big tech billionaires behind them.

Abdul El-Sayed never tired on the campaign trail of reminding Michigan voters that his opponent, Mike Rogers, was backed by big corporations and mega donors.

Even Kansas’s victorious Adam Hamilton – who during his run for the Senate adamantly rejected the leftist label his opponent wanted to impose on him – campaigned on making datacenters pay for their own energy, banning lawmakers from trading stocks, expanding Medicare drug-price negotiations, and cracking down on price-gouging.

Hamilton also rejected money from corporate Pacs, as did most Democratic candidates for the Senate.

The real question in my mind is whether, come January when they control Congress, Democrats will take advantage of the new populism to enact measures most Americans need, such as Medicare for All, and reforms most Americans want, such as tougher anti-monopoly laws and limits on campaign contributions (even if this requires a constitutional amendment).

Trump is likely to veto any such initiatives, of course, but at least they’ll lay down markers for the 2028 presidential election – which, judging from what we’ve seen in the midterms, is likely to be a populist doozie.

Both sides of the Atlantic sense more hope now: voters are drawn to the ‘politics of love’

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:35:18 GMT

Trump’s rout could be part of a democratic spring that began in Hungary. But will it extend to the French elections next May?

Hungary, Brazil, Serbia, and now the US. So far this year, when their hand has been held to the stove, voters have chosen what the Texas senator-elect James Talarico, the new face of the US’s Christian left, campaigned on as a “politics of love”: a society where we aren’t at each other’s throats, or a police state at ours.

Is it any surprise that when there is clarity about the choice on offer, voters have started to shrink away from a vision fuelled by billionaire wealth and runaway inequality? Away from oligarchic rule and unapologetic corruption, connivance with aggression, expansion, colonialism and war; environmental degradation and the surrender of the human spirit to a reality mediated by the algorithm.

Are we living, perhaps, through an extended “democratic spring” that began in Budapest in April with the overthrow of Viktor Orbán, and will continue all the way through to the arrival of the Élysée Palace’s next occupant in May?

That’s what it felt like to wake up on Wednesday morning, blanketed in an unexpected optimism sparked by a country that has fed my inner cynic for too long. In Michigan, voters chose a man who responded to a hate-filled question about sharia law with disarming, acerbic humour about shawarma law instead.

In neighbouring Ohio, where I grew up, voters refused to suffer the fundamental indecency of one candidate (the billionaire entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy) trying to weaponise the childhood abuse suffered by his opponent Amy Acton via Acton’s estranged mother. Acton defeated Ramaswamy to become Ohio’s first female governor and its first Democrat in two decades.

Farther south, New Mexico has the first ever female Native American governor; in Georgia, a Black woman will hold that office for the first time; in Texas, the first Latina.

There are dozens of stories like these that have temporarily transformed scrolling from an experience of doom to one of hope. Beneath them is something more structural; there is, as a French historian messaged me early Wednesday morning, a “Rooseveltian” quality to what has happened in the US.

For a decade, we have been dealing, across international borders, with the feeling that governments are no longer “in control” – not of starkly advancing inequality and growing corporate power, or the pace and direction of technological change and climate breakdown. The far-right response has been to try to assert control over the things within immediate grasp: immigration and identity.

Those of us who believe in democracy, environmental and social justice have a far more difficult task, both to sell to voters and to accomplish. That is to actually take back control (not superficially, as Brexit once proposed) of the forces that pose an existential threat to the type of society we want to inhabit. In Europe, this is all the more difficult because of an internal split – between those who think this is possible on a national scale, and those who, like me, think it obliges us to pool sovereignty.

In the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt recognised that liberal democracy, faced with an existential threat, had to evolve to survive. He knew that it would be impossible to defend an open society or the rule of law unless the state could guarantee economic progress in people’s lives, so he responded with the flurry of government actions that together comprised the New Deal.

In the US, the Democrats, who now control Congress, have a chance to rebuild democratic foundations after decades of self-inflicted destruction. In part because the youngest generation of voters, who have only ever known Trumpism, massively rejected everything Trump has birthed, and that rejection echoed down the ballot – all the way to state legislatures and school boards. That didn’t only happen because they were angry and the Democrats offered anger in return; it happened because they were angry and a slate of exceptional candidates said: “So are we, and it doesn’t have to be this way.”

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

In Europe, the rule of law and the institutions that maintain it have not bent as much in the US, but an equivalently forceful snapback of hope and relief is still incomplete.

For the past month, France’s high schoolers have crystallised the social and economic dilemma Roosevelt encountered, and there are candidates out there mirroring their justified anger. I worry, though, that this offer remains a politics of anger tinged with nationalism, and uninterested in defending European democracy; that it risks throwing away what Europe painstakingly constructed in response to its institutional shortcomings, rather than proposing a resolutely European type of renewal.

Or that France – where an overwhelming majority abhors Trump, but where huge numbers seem to want their own version of him – will stubbornly stumble into just what the US has been through, before coming out on the other side, in full rejection of the far-right National Rally.

Both sides of the Atlantic woke up with more hope on Wednesday, even if neither side has a clearcut and easy path forward. Europe’s path, though, now seems the more difficult one to navigate.

Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now

The Guardian view on the US midterms: joy for Democrats, a rout for Republicans and a reprieve for democracy

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:31:13 GMT

Voters have delivered a damning verdict on Donald Trump’s presidency with this Congressional landslide

Bitter experience made Democrats wary of believing that the blue wave predicted by polls would materialise. What arrived was not just victory but a rout: control of Congress and a Republican wipeout. It was an astounding humiliation for a president whose political brand is power. Donald Trump won it back in 2024 by promising voters lower prices and no foreign wars. He lost it by launching an illegal conflict that hit them in the pocket and imposing hefty tariffs too. He urged voters to pretend that he was on the ticket and they delivered a verdict that could not have been more damning.

Two years ago, retaking the House looked like a genuine fight for Democrats, and the Senate a long shot. On Tuesday, they needed to flip four more seats to gain a 51-seat Senate majority. Within hours of polls closing, they had 54, with two more races in the balance, and had easily passed the 218 seats needed for a House majority. This appears to be the biggest congressional landslide since 1976, in Watergate’s aftermath.

What was stunning was not only that Democrats claimed deep red states like Kansas, but that they did it so decisively. Mr Trump carried South Carolina by 18 points in 2024; Annie Andrews beat her rival for the Senate by almost five points. James Talarico won by 12 points in Texas, which the president carried by nearly 14 points. Democrats also flipped governorships, winning their first gubernatorial majority for two decades.

Two years after Kamala Harris’s crushing defeat by Mr Trump – and having watched even greater chaos and cruelty wreaked in his second term – Democrats are rightly rejoicing. Tuesday night delivered abundant new talent and a generational shift too. The first black and native American women and first out gay man will take their seats in the Senate. Yet the party remains unpopular and the battles over its future are just beginning. For progressives, Abdul el-Sayed’s senate win in Michigan is proof that they can win in purple states. But the scale of Democratic victory gives Hakeem Jeffries – poised to become the first black House speaker – a greater cushion against justified and necessary pressure from the left.

Simultaneously, a Republican faultline over whether to embrace Trumpism or move away from it is yawning. Mr Trump picked candidates (disastrously) and campaigned vigorously – yet seemed strangely detached. Republicans have genuflected to him because he wins. A growing number now believe that they can only win by facing him down – but fear being crushed in the process.

Strikingly, Democrats – notably the senator Jon Ossoff who was easily re-elected in Georgia – successfully tied the affordability crisis to corruption. They will use their newly gained power in Congress to pursue accountability, though Mr Trump’s executive overreach and refusal to accept legislative constraints are unlikely to shift. A vengeful and erratic president who is now wounded and wants to change the narrative may in some ways be more dangerous at home and abroad – notably on Iran.

At least, faced with results “too big to rig”, Mr Trump had to say that he would accept them. The Republican campaign hit new lows, but election officials (including Republicans) pushed back against voter-suppression efforts. Gerrymandering proved ineffective – with black voters turning out in response, and Latino voters whom Republicans counted on swinging back towards the Democrats. So did culture war attacks, vile bigotry and personal smears and a huge spending advantage. This was a bad election for Elon Musk and other big tech donors, with a voter revolt against datacentres and cronyism. It was not just a defeat for Republicans and a good day for Democrats, but a critical victory for democracy itself.

The Guardian view on EU ‘Made in Europe’ rules: a fatal blow to Brexiter delusions

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:30:24 GMT

It is getting ever harder for Eurosceptics to deny that it was an economic and strategic blunder for Britain to leave the single market

The EU is a constantly evolving institution. The rules keep changing and, since Britain is destined by geography to want a close economic relationship with the bloc, there will always be something to negotiate in Brussels.

Most of those discussions over the past two years have been uncontroversial, except in the eyes of dogmatic Eurosceptics. That doesn’t mean the talks have been easy. They never are with a club of 27 nations. But later this month, at a summit with the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham is expected to complete a treaty covering closer cooperation in a wide range of areas, including elimination of customs barriers to agricultural goods, a youth-mobility programme and integration with the EU’s carbon emissions trading scheme.

The agenda was set by Sir Keir Starmer as part of his intended “reset” of EU relations. Mr Burnham has since pledged to move further and faster towards closer ties, although he remains bound by his predecessor’s manifesto prohibition on membership of the single market and customs union this side of a general election.

What the prime minister can achieve in that space will be determined partly by his judgment of what domestic public opinion will allow, but more immediately by the terms of the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. This legislative package, more commonly called “Made in Europe”, mobilises public procurement rules to insulate continental industries from what many EU political leaders see as unfair overseas competition – chiefly from China. Industrial policy and protectionism on such a scale is a symptom of the way a once-globalised trading system has in recent years fractured into rivalry between continental blocs. China’s colossal trade surplus, causing panic among European car manufacturers, for example, is one side of that story. Donald Trump’s capricious tariff wars are another.

Britain looks perilously isolated in such a world, which is why Mr Burnham is keen to find some accommodation within the Made in Europe regime. That isn’t straightforward, given that the essential purpose of the new rules will be to benefit enterprises in the single market to the deliberate disadvantage of those on the outside, which includes Brexit Britain. Some compromise is available, with the UK recognised as a “trusted partner”, but that status won’t be accorded simply as a reward for pro-European vibes from Labour. Mr Burnham’s declarations of strategic intent are helpful, but there will be a lot of hard bargaining ahead on the terms of a deal. Without one, Britain’s carmaker and other industries would face crippling new trade barriers.

For that reason, the “Made in Europe” question has shot up the government’s agenda. The Eurosceptic opposition parties, meanwhile, are silent on the subject. To acknowledge the existence of a problem would mean recognising Britain’s disadvantaged status outside the single market, which is a refutation of the founding case for Brexit. Mr Burnham will not find it easy to negotiate the next stage of Britain’s reintegration with the EU, but those who resist his direction of travel will find it ever harder to pretend there is any alternative.

British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:18:37 GMT

Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit

A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.

A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.

Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”

Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.

There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency.

Trump’s billionaire-blue collar coalition has been smashed by class politics

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:18:34 GMT

As tech bosses get richer and ordinary Americans struggle, Democrats put the case against the US’s grotesque unfairness – and voters responded

Remember the “vibe shift”? Just last year, columnists and corporate boardrooms alike declared that the second coming of Donald Trump meant the old rules of politics and even everyday civility were roadkill.

“I feel liberated,” one top banker told the Financial Times. “We can say ‘retard’ and ‘pussy’ without the fear of getting cancelled … it’s a new dawn.”

Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, but to be a billionaire was very heaven. Because in Trump, the tech bosses had a politician who could work magic by forging a forever alliance between them and blue-collar America. This was the very core of Trumpism, the trick that wowed rightwingers around the world: how he could yoke together minimum-wage workers with the 1%; Latinos and black voters with those happy to dabble in a little light racism; the Epstein-haters with the Epstein class (who can forget Elon Musk’s email to Jeffrey: “What day/night will be the wildest party on your island?”). And he did it by alchemising class antagonism into culture war. Forget about that pay rise – have you have heard about those Haitians eating dogs?

Silicon Valley, Wall Street and east coast media owners all saw Trumpism not as a political strategy but as a turn in the entire culture: a vibe shift to the right. They were wrong. Tuesday night was a comprehensive rejection of the president. Before the midterms, ultra-wealthy donors such as Musk poured billions into Trump’s proxies, but the working- and middle-class base were not having it. The relatively new coalition that put the orange man in the White House has been smashed apart by old-fashioned class politics.

When election analysts observe that the struggle of ordinary Americans to afford the basics of life now “polls in a tier by itself”, that is class rearing its head. It is a response to the record petrol prices in a car-centred society, the huge swings in everything from eggs to mincemeat, the battle to meet the rent. The squeamish, including within the Democratic establishment, might euphemise these as “economic issues” or “affordability”, but remember that this time last year, the democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani turned affordability from a meme into a platform for winning elections. In late 2026, and going into the next battle for the White House, the New York mayor now wields national influence.

Among Mamdani’s achievements has been his reminder to ordinary voters that when they can’t afford the basics, it’s not just because prices are unreasonably high – it’s also because their pay is unfairly low. He has tied the cost of living to an argument about inequality, and rightly so.

Over decades – through Reagan and Clinton, Bush and Obama – Republicans and Democrats have changed the tax code to reward ownership rather than earning, so the richest 400 households now pay lower rates of tax than the bottom 50% of Americans. As the radical economists Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster show in their new book, Grand Theft Capital: What Workers Should Know About the Affordability Crisis, the share of national income going to ordinary workers has slumped from 30% in the 1960s to 20% today. This is the destruction of working-class lives and dreams in which Republicans and Democrats colluded. This is the American carnage that in 2016 helped propel Trump into the White House. But the most glaring feature of this era of Trumponomics has been its shameless inequality.

The “hottest country in the world”, as the president calls it, relies on AI for growth. For the first half of 2025, the Harvard economist Jason Furman estimated that spending on AI infrastructure made up 92% of GDP growth. These supposedly national gains are getting raked off by a tiny number of people and funds, based overwhelmingly in one strip on the west coast.

In October, the fund manager Apollo pointed out that, of the entire S&P index of America’s biggest 500 companies, only the so-called “magnificent seven” tech firms were flourishing. The other 493 were seeing flat revenues and flat profits. Torsten Slok, Apollo’s chief economist, wrote: “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America.”

Billions for Sam Altman and Dario Amodei and Jensen Huang; a pittance for those outside Silicon Valley. No wonder the most reviled candidate on so many of this week’s ballots was the datacentre: the energy-sapping, water-sucking, community-destroying datacentre that merely aids the processing of humans into appendages to chatbots. Analysis for the Economist showed that Trump supporters with a datacentre on their doorstep were flipping in droves to the other side.

The politics of this played out most clearly in Texas, which on Tuesday night flipped from red to blue, despite a quarter of a billion dollars for the Republicans in the state from one man: Elon Musk. Texas is the AI overlord’s home and a vital base for his businesses. Over the next few years Texas is expected to become the US’s centre for datacentres. In just two years, it is expected to provide over a quarter of all new computing power to the AI industry. James Talarico won on a squarely anti-datacentre agenda.

As he said after his win: “The real fight in this country is not left versus right. It is top versus bottom … The people at the top divide us by party, by race, by gender, by religion, by culture, so we don’t notice that they are picking our pockets. But tonight, we sent a crystal clear message to the people at the top, we will not be conquered.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The Democrats who caught the national and global imagination this autumn were those who most stridently put the case against the US’s grotesque, life-destroying unfairness and for a better politics – just as Mamdani did. Troy Jackson won Maine on a platform to abolish ICE. Abdul El-Sayed took Michigan (Michigan!) pledging Medicare for all.

These results suggest a new future for the Dems: anti-corruption, anti-war and anti-billionaire. In the days of Bill and Hillary, this would have been deemed impossibly leftwing. But mark my words: the Democrat who wants to get on the ticket in 2028 will sound more like Bernie Sanders.

For now, rejoice that a corrupt self-dealing bully is heading into two years of ignominy, of being treated even while in power as a back number. And remember that when politicians and journalists claim there is nothing better on offer than the same old rightwing rubbish, they’re usually wrong. “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters, OK?” Trump once said. “It’s, like, incredible.”

And truly, it wasn’t credible.

Husband who invited men to rape wife asked for an online review, court told

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:07:57 GMT

Nine men on trial in Manchester accused of either taking part in abuse or encouraging offending on internet

A husband who invited other men to rape and sexually assault his wife arranged for “more and more individuals” to visit his marital home as he resolved “to satisfy his own perversity”, a jury has been told.

The husband, who is in his 60s and from Stockport in Greater Manchester, has pleaded guilty to more than 60 offences against his wife. He cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim.

Nine men are on trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court accused of either taking part in the abuse of the victim, or encouraging the offending online while “hiding behind the screens of their mobile telephones and computers”.

One of the “non-contact” alleged offenders, Daniel Rayner, 42, of Whitstable, Kent, repeatedly sought imagery of the abuse of the victim, the court heard. He told the husband: “Passed out ones are obviously better,” and: “Hope she’s being used tonight.”

The husband had shared imagery of other men, Graham Brougham and Sean Peers, assaulting his wife, and when Rayner asked: “So I guessing she had no idea he had stripped and fucked her,” the husband confirmed she did not.

Rayner then asked him: “What did you give her … I’ve always used GHB.”

Rayner denies conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Setting out a timeline of the allegations, the prosecutor Louise Oakley KC told the court that by the start of January 2025: “[The husband] doesn’t appear to have had any new year’s resolutions to stop his offending on his wife.”

“If anything, his resolve to satisfy his own perversity continued,” she said. “With arrangements being made for more and more individuals to attend.”

Two of the defendants, Philip Wild, 59, and Mohammed Sabir, 28, both from Stockport, had sexually abused the woman one after the other in a single night in early 2025, the court heard.

Oakley said Wild was “fully aware” that the woman was not conscious and not able to consent to any sexual activity. “He’d been there before so that was no surprise, and certainly was no deterrent the state he’d seen her in before,” she told the court.

Wild has pleaded not guilty to sexual assault, attempted rape, assault by penetration and conspiracy to rape.

Oakley told the court that Sabir also “knew before he went into the bedroom” that the victim was not conscious, and “at no point” did he attempt to communicate with her, or seek her consent.

The husband later asked him to write a review on a swingers website, the court heard, and the jury was shown the review, which read: “Really easy to set up a meet. It was my first [experience] fucking someone’s wife in front of them, so thanks for that. Hope to meet again soon.” Sabir denies rape and conspiracy to rape.

In May 2025 the husband made contact with another stranger on the site, the court heard. Jordan Wallace, 31, a building supplies employee from Wythenshawe in Manchester, said he was “pissed” and asked the husband to pick him up.

He wrote: “13 mins if [you] wanna pick me up [and] me [and] [you] will get perverted with your wife.” When the husband declined to collect him, he said he would ride his bicycle over to the address.

Wallace was “fully aware” the wife was unconscious, and “because of her state of consciousness she was not able to consent to any sexual activity”, Oakley told the court.

She said the husband “recalls that at one point Jordan Wallace ‘got rough’ with [his wife] and he had to actually push him away, saying, ‘What the fuck are you doing?’ telling him he was going to wake her up”.

Wallace later apologised but asked the husband to send the videos he had taken, which he did, the court heard. Wallace has pleaded not guilty to rape and attempted rape.

In June 2025, the husband subjected his wife “to a humiliating, degrading and sustained sexual assault” over the course of three hours, and again invited two men in succession into their home to assault her.

The second man, Alan Keelan, 42, an industrial cleaning firm worker also from Wythenshawe, had climbed on top of the unconscious woman wearing a pair of black women’s knickers and attempted to have sex with her, the court heard.

When he was unable to, he sexually assaulted her before climbing off the bed, the court heard. Keelan denies attempted rape and assault by penetration.

In July last year, the husband again posted on the swingers website, and made contact with the sheet-metal worker Richard Townsend, 38, the court heard. Townsend was aware the woman was not conscious when he proceeded to sexually assault her, assisted by her husband, the jury was told.

The woman’s leg moved, and “it was clear she was restless and stirring, so together they decided enough was enough for that night and he left”, the court heard. Townsend, of Heywood, Greater Manchester, denies assault by penetration.

Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport, was described as “more cautious” than the other defendants, and first requested to meet the husband at his own house.

The husband visited Kirk at his house in August and showed him photographs of the woman passed out and being abused by him. He told Kirk he would consider drugging his wife, and Kirk, a paramedic, told him that “could be very dangerous”, the court heard.

Later, Kirk took a taxi to the husband’s house. “As a senior paramedic, he cannot have failed to notice she was not conscious. He is trained to spot that,” Oakley told the court. “The truth is, he knew and that’s how he wanted her to be.”

After having sexual intercourse with the woman, “Jonathan Kirk stood up and said, ‘fucking hell, wow’ and how great it had been before he left”, the court heard.

Kirk denies rape and conspiracy to rape.

Two other men are also on trial. Robert Stewart, 70, of Stockport, denies rape, conspiracy to rape and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

David Graves, 60, of Ilkeston, Derbyshire, denies “non-contact” offences of conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Peers, 38, from Stockport; Brougham, 74, from Cheshire, and another man, Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, have pleaded guilty to offences against the same woman.

Karl Lindsay, 56, from Somerset has also pleaded guilty to “non-contact” offences. All will be sentenced alongside the husband, at a later date.

The trial continues.

The pollsters had got it wrong on the US midterms, said Nige. That aged well

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:02:19 GMT

After his embarrassment of epic proportions, Farage turned up at PMQs – the last place anyone would expect to find him

In what counts as breaking news on this slowest of slow Wednesdays in Westminster – most eyes were on the US midterm elections – it was nice to be able to report that Nigel Farage was in the Commons for prime minister’s questions. Not something you can often say.

Despite Reform UK tanking in the polls, Nige still regards himself as the official opposition and considers it a major insult that he isn’t given six questions every week. Today he was happy not to get one. Not even Nige’s magic shield of narcissism would have been able to save him from hubris. An embarrassment of epic proportions.

On Tuesday night, Farage had used his GB News show to insist that the American pollsters had got it wrong. Sticking his neck on the line against what he dismissed as “the liberal consensus”, he was adamant that the Republicans would come good. How could they not, with Donald Trump as president and more than $400m of Elon Musk’s money behind them?

Only it didn’t quite turn out that way. The Donald had said “pretend I’m on the ballot” and Americans had taken him at his word. And they didn’t want to vote for a man who had said he would not get into any foreign wars and would protect his country against rising energy bills and had broken both promises.

Here in the UK, Nige was the last true believer left. His political judgment increasingly at fault, unable to conceive that Trump’s legacy was already in tatters. Along with his supporters. Even the Tories have now realised that a close association with Trump is toxic. Kemi Badenoch and her shadow cabinet are busily going through their social media accounts, deleting all Trump brown-nosing posts. They had always said Trump was a crook. A liability. Weird how none of that was a problem until he lost an election.

So you can just imagine how it would have played out. The speaker calls Farage. You can almost hear the derision. The loudest jeers coming from the very Tories who had previously praised Trump. It wouldn’t matter what the Reform leader asked, the response would have been the same. Nige would never live it down. One of the worst election calls of all time. The final piece of sycophancy from one fading politician to another.

In the chamber, it was a battle of the two deputies. Louise Haigh and Alex Burghart. Haigh was making her primetime debut and declared she was taking the place of Andy Burnham who was in Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth heads of government summit.

This was said mainly for the benefit of the absent Badenoch, who is suffering from severe memory loss problems these days. Only on Tuesday she had appeared not to know why she had called a press conference on a decommissioned warship from the second world war. If she didn’t know, how the hell were we supposed to? She had also been under the impression that the prime minister had gone to the Caribbean for a midweek break. You know what it’s like. You’ve got a plane waiting for you at Stansted and you can’t resist some late autumn sun.

The exchanges between Haigh and Burghart can safely be filed under forgettable. Neither made any major fuck-ups – the first rule of PMQs is not to make yourself look a halfwit – but there again, neither were particularly impressive. These were performances that will earn them future bookings from their party leaders. The last thing you want is a deputy who does better than you. Particularly Kemi. The myth around her renaissance of the Tory party – up one or two points from an all-time low – rests on her MPs and party members buying in to her talent. It’s amazing how good you can look when you surround yourself with mediocrity.

Not that this was Burghart’s fault. Alex is as Alex does. He’s more an academic, an intellectual rather than a showman. A slightly more obnoxious Oliver Letwin. Someone not really suited to the vulgarity of the Commons. A deputy who needs to stick to the script because he cannot tolerate spontaneity. So Alex merely read out his prepared questions in the order they were written. Seemingly oblivious to whether they had been answered or not.

There were clearly moments in his notes where his special adviser had written: “This next bit is meant to be funny. Try to smile knowingly as you say it.” Except he couldn’t. The wannabe gags died on his lips. He could have been a natural Malvolio at the National Theatre. A man who has no idea that the joke is on him.

All of this was supposedly building up to a signoff laced with anger and contempt. “If Labour doesn’t want to do the right thing, why doesn’t it just get out of the way?” This too got lost in translation. Alex is not a naturally angry man. And he’s bright enough to realise that his own party is largely culpable for the state the country is in today. The idea that the Tories are somehow a new party is delusional. So to land a barb like that, you’ve also got to be a bit dim. Richard Holden would be a natural for it.

Lou Haigh was not much better. She too relied on tightly scripted replies and point-scoring lines. Burghart had asked about the welfare bill and no one was any the wiser how Labour planned to bring it down, despite Lou insisting that everything was in hand. You would have imagined the Labour comms team would have come up with a better line on this by now. It isn’t a subject that’s about to melt away.

The kindest thing you could say was that this was incident-free. Apart from one Tory heckler who was called out by the speaker for “shouting a woman down”. I think you will find that Lou is more than capable of looking after herself. Though if she were honest about marking her own report card, she would put this one down as “could do better”.

Speaking for the Lib Dems, Daisy Cooper celebrated the Democrats’ victory in the US and wondered now if the government could help in releasing the rest of the Epstein files and putting the president back in the dock. Haigh was diplomatically restrained. Pleased at the turn of events but noncommittal about the prospect of British intervention. Several rows behind Cooper, Nige stared into the middle distance. Seeking divine help. Fearing the end of days.

‘Thrilled, scared but hopeful’: readers react to historic Democratic victory in US midterms

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:44:07 GMT

Excitement over midterm election results tempered by worry of return to ‘business as usual’ in Congress and US

Send us your questions about the midterm results

US midterms 2026 live – latest updates

Guardian readers from around the world have shared their reactions to the results of the US midterm elections on Tuesday night. Here’s what they had to say.

I am equal parts ecstatic and relieved! I feel like I can breathe again. The guardrails are back, to some extent, and people around the country are waking up to the greed, cruelty and hubris that have marked Donald Trump’s presidency. They see the cost of his impulsive war on Iran, his cozying up to tech billionaires and their drive for AI datacenters, the loss of health insurance, the rounding up of immigrants … I hope the Democrats can unify and move forward, taking this mandate seriously. Barbara Burkart, 75, psychotherapist, Massachusetts

I voted Democrat across the board. Woke up this morning to the news that we had taken back the House and Senate. I’m thrilled, scared but hopeful for the next few years that some solid changes will be made. I find that I have moved past my centrist-to-left stance, and would really love to see younger, much more diverse (in many ways, not just race) people in national leadership positions. But I am concerned that real changes cannot be made unless the status quo liberals start working with the progressives more than they have in the past. Trying to not be cynical, because I know that conservatives will not follow the rules, and will not go quietly.

My greatest hope is that we start digging in and sowing some seeds of love and change. And that the newly elected leaders find creative ways to govern. But given the puritanical, corrupt and greedy roots of this country, I am not entirely convinced that can even happen. Pamela, Virginia

My own state of Utah is one of the reddest there is, and I have been happy with our Republican governor and with John Curtis, one of our Republican senators. (I do not like Senator Mike Lee.) However, in this election, I feel that there was only one viable party for any national office.

I hope the Democrats try to undo every single thing the GOP has done for the last two years. I hope our support for Ukraine stabilizes. I hope we impeach a bunch of officials for the good of the nation and the world. I hope economic policy can be brought back to sanity. I doubt it’s within Congress’s capabilities to do this, but I really hope some international relationships can begin to be repaired.

Domestically, I just want to see ICE off of American streets. I wouldn’t mind if the immigration enforcement arm of this agency were entirely disbanded and … I’d like tariffs to be dropped. I want the federal government to approach AI with appropriate skepticism, and to regulate phone and social media use, particularly among young people. And we should revive the Green New Deal. Buttressing up the coal industry isn’t just bad for the environment, it’s also stupid. Electric is the tech of the future and China is eating our lunch in this domain. S, Salt Lake City, Utah

It will be good to have a bit of our southern neighbor back. Over the past two years, it has often felt like we were in a political standoff with the US. In response, our Canadian leadership seemed willing to sacrifice environmental protections and climate commitments in the pursuit of new economic partners and trade opportunities. I hope this election opens the door to a more constructive relationship, without losing sight of the importance of protecting nature and addressing climate change. David Roy, executive director of the NGO Workshops for Biodiversity, Canada

I lived for more than 10 years in Los Angeles attending the University of Southern California. Half my family currently lives in the US. These midterm results represent a seismic shift, a tidal wave of public sentiment and a powerful reminder that democracy ultimately belongs to the people. I was genuinely joyous watching these historic results unfold. Against the backdrop of a deeply polarizing, tough and self-centered presidency, voters have sent a message that cannot be ignored: leadership must be accountable, power must have limits and arrogance must never replace public service.

Michigan made history with Abdul El-Sayed becoming America’s first Muslim senator. Texas delivered another stunning moment, with James Talarico defeating Ken Paxton for the Senate. And Georgia made history by electing Keisha Lance Bottoms as America’s first Black female governor. These are not simply electoral victories; they represent changing political attitudes, greater representation and the determination of citizens to make their voices heard. The Democrats’ victory in both chambers of Congress adds another historic dimension. This is democracy speaking loudly. Jayjay Epega, entertainment publicist, London

I’m an independent in Arkansas, a ruby red state. I voted Democrat across the slate. I value democracy and rule of law. The Trump administration has subverted the rule of law, put us in an unnecessary war, worsened the economy, frayed international alliances that protect and defend the western world. I’m elated. My state stayed ruby red, but it was closer than the past 20 years. Oversight and accountability. Investigation of corruption. My concern is the Democrats being too to complacent, resting on the results and not doing what we elected them to do. Crista, 61, restaurant manager, Arkansas

I was just so worried that somehow people would not turn out to vote. I had hope because of some of the positive messaging from key candidates across the country. I hope that they spend time not as much on finger-pointing and investigations but on stopping the military overreach and getting food, gas and housing for average Americans. I hope that we can return to kindness and quality of life as our measures of success. My biggest concern is that we forget to get rid of big dark money and also the electoral college in politics. They make it harder for the public’s voice to be heard. Monica DeLaTorre, 64, educator, New Mexico

after newsletter promotion

I hope the newly elected leftwing Democrats continue their work shifting the Overton window in the US leftwards, making leftwing economic and social policy and human-rights centered foreign policy more viable options in the national debate. This election was not a vote of confidence for the Democrats, but a vote of no confidence for Trump. The Democrats have to earn the confidence Trump lost.

I’m hoping the Democrats work to mitigate the chances of anything like the Trump administration happening again. Democratic control of Congress will surely do much to rein in Trump’s dangerous politics, but to what degree will remain to be seen. I should hope the Dems are able to force Trump’s hand in working to bring about peace in the Middle East. The US should also work to give Ukraine more support, something which Trump has cut back on, as well as working more towards real concrete results at the negotiation table with Russia.

I’m slightly afraid some European policymakers might return to ‘business as usual’ if the blue shock allows Uncle Sam to get his act back together and return to the usual level of international participation and soft power. Pietari Wishart, 18, student, Finland

Everybody is talking about the results as a landslide and a strong rebuke of Trump and the Republican party. But almost half of voters were still happy to vote for the people in charge. I feel a sliver of hope, but not much. I’ve followed US politics for years because of its enormous impact on the rest of the world. America used to be seen as a pillar of democracy, but we’ve seen how easily that can be undermined. Here in Europe, we’re having to think about how we can manage without relying so heavily on the US. I’m hopeful that change was possible in so many states. But the Democrats need a plan beyond simply saying they want to save democracy. How are they actually going to do it? Joep de Vries, test engineer, the Netherlands

As a young woman I am thrilled at the number of women who have been elected. I feel more represented and I really crave the change I feel women could properly execute. I really hope America continues to wake up and realizes we have a choice. It is time we take better care of ourselves, our loved ones, our planet. Enough is enough.

Every party has its downsides, my hope is that intelligent, empathetic people gain more power and can right the ship. Less polarization is a must. We need to talk to each other. We can’t hate everyone on the other side of the line. If you’re Republican, talk to a Democrat, understand what they need. If you’re a Democrat, talk to a Republican, understand what they need. We need to understand why we make the choices we do in order to develop a plan to unite us. Compromise, like a family. We have to. Emma Carroll, 24, MEP engineer, Manchester, New Hampshire

The Democratic wins are incredibly good news. Since the beginning of this presidential term it’s seemed as though the incumbent has operated with unfettered power and no accountability with disastrous implications for the entire world. We now have hope that sanity, normality, pragmatism and decorum will be restored to what was once an esteemed office (now widely maligned and ridiculed).

The recurring theme in commentary over the past few months has been ‘where is Congress?’ These results hopefully bring back an era of accountability and democracy in the US, which has implications for the rest of us. From the outside it’s looked like only the courts have been able to curtail what was increasingly looking like a slide from democracy into authoritarianism. Hopefully this will mark the end of foreign policy decided on a whim (and with personal interests at the fore). Vusi, self-employed, South Africa

I moved to the UK when Obama was still president and have watched what’s happened in the US over the past decade from afar. When Trump first announced his candidacy, my husband found it amusing, but I grew up in Texas and knew how easily politicians could use the demonization of others to gain power. I stayed up to watch the results, even though I hadn’t intended to. It’s a good day, but I see it as a momentary reprieve. We’ve got here after years of attacks on democratic institutions, human rights and the rule of law.

The consequences have been felt around the world, particularly in the global south, so it’s a relief but these results don’t undo the damage. What troubles me is that the Democratic victories seem to have been driven largely by Americans’ concerns about their own cost of living, rather than a rejection of the wider injustices we’ve witnessed. There’s still a lot of accountability needed. I hope the Democrats use this opportunity to start anew, with a progressive agenda that connects issues such as healthcare and human rights to people’s everyday economic concerns. This is a step in the right direction, but it’s not a silver bullet. They’ve squandered opportunities before and I hope they don’t do so again. Victoria, author, London

Rory McIlroy backs claim that LIV tried to ‘destroy’ DP World Tour

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:23:54 GMT

McIlroy: ‘LIV turned pro golf into an arms race’

DP chief executive: ‘We pay everyone on time’

Rory McIlroy voiced his support on Wednesday for the DP World Tour chief executive’s claim that LIV Golf’s goal was to “destroy” the European golf circuit.

The six-time major winner and former world No 1 spoke ⁠with the media on Wednesday before the Abu Dhabi Championship and was asked about Guy Kinnings’ recent interview with the Scotsman.

As LIV Golf struggles to move forward without funding from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Kinnings has ⁠said any golfers who sign up ⁠for “LIV 2.0” will not be ​eligible for the DP World Tour in 2027. He said the DP World Tour is drawing a line in the sand: play on one tour or the other, but not both.

“But we also have to ⁠protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7bn, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour’. I have heard that from so many different people they talked to, who I have known for ⁠over 30 years within the game and who I trust implicitly,” Kinnings said.

“Clearly, when you are faced with statements like that, and then ​people then ask why we are doing what we are doing with ‌our membership and invite policy for 2027, then ‌I think the answer becomes pretty obvious. Myself and everyone at the DP World Tour have a duty to our members to protect our tour. ‌We are proud of that and are proud that we treat everyone who works for the tour, whether that be staff, suppliers, contractors, everyone, with respect and dignity. We pay them and pay them on time. We look out for everyone.

“Our tour has been in existence for over 50 years and it stands for everything that is good, right and proper in the game worth fighting for and that is precisely what we have done and what we will continue to do.”

McIlroy, 37, was asked about Kinnings’ remarks after his practice round on Wednesday at Yas ‌Links, where the Northern Irishman is chasing a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title.

“I agree with everything that Guy said,” McIlroy said. “They took players; they took sponsors; they turned professional golf into an arms race. They were going around Augusta saying ​they wanted to destroy the European Tour.”

As it attempts to shore up funding to continue, LIV Golf has suffered an exodus of top players since the end of this season, including Spain’s Jon Rahm and Sergio García.

“It was always going to be good for a few years until something like this happened, or they realised they weren’t going to get any return on investment, or they were going to leave the golf space and go invest in something else ⁠and invest in something that would actually make them money,” McIlroy said.

McIlroy, who plays on the PGA Tour and ​DP World Tour, believes men’s golf needs a reset. “I ​think we’ll look back on it as a ​very strange time,” McIlroy said. “It gave players a lot of leverage over the tours, and I don’t necessarily think that’s a ​good thing for the overall health ‌of the professional game. ​I think there has to be a ​balance there. There has to be a bit of give and take.

“You know, I’ve said this from the start, like there’s never been a better time to be a professional golfer. Talk to Jack Nicklaus or any of these older guys, they would have loved LIV to come around in their day. They would have made more money, and we are all making more money because of it. But I do think there has to be a bit of a ‌reset.”

Billy ‘The Kid’ Loughnane can be new ‘face of racing’ and next Dettori after Godolphin deal

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:22:05 GMT

The combination of prodigious talent in the saddle and an easy likeability out of it is a perfect fit for Dubai operation

“I want to ride more Group One winners,” Billy Loughnane said last month when asked to name his main ambition for 2027, and Britain’s new 20-year-old champion jockey seems all but certain to achieve his aim, following Wednesday’s news that he has signed a retainer to ride in the royal blue colours of Sheikh Mohammed’s global Godolphin operation next year.

Loughnane will be contracted alongside William Buick as one of two retained Godolphin jockeys next year, and not as an outright No 1, but even if Loughnane does not claim the lion’s share of the best rides as soon as next year, his trajectory within the operation seems clear.

That, in turn, can only add to the hopes within the sport that Loughnane is a potential successor to Frankie Dettori, Godolphin’s first and most successful No 1 rider, as a “crossover” talent with the charisma to build a public and media profile beyond the confines of the racing bubble.

Loughnane has been swatting away comparisons with Dettori, who was a relative veteran when he won his first title at 23, almost since his earliest days as an apprentice.

He is engaging and articulate, has the same showman’s instincts and ability to engage with the crowd, and takes as much obvious pleasure from a big-race winner as the fans cheering him back to the winner’s enclosure. For a racing operation conceived as a soft-power advertisement for Dubai around the globe, it is a combination of prodigious talent in the saddle and an easy likeability out of it that fits the brand ideally.

At the same time, though, he is not the next Dettori, he is the first Billy Loughnane, and the racing, sporting and media landscapes have also changed completely since “Frankie” managed to achieve the same first-name status with the wider sporting public that “Lester” enjoyed a generation earlier.

Dettori, after all, not only rode all seven winners on the card at Ascot early on in his career. He was also a familiar face for around eight million BBC viewers each week as a team captain on A Question Of Sport, where the fact that, at the time, he had never won the Derby was a running joke. It was, in effect, a priceless – and free – weekly advertisement for Dettori, racing and the Derby on the national broadcaster, and in the fragmented world of social media and YouTube, such platforms no longer exist.

But there is still potential, perhaps, for Loughnane to be the first racing star of the Tik Tok era, and his new contract with Godolphin should soon enough see him competing aboard runners with a leading chance in all but a handful few of the season’s showpiece events.

He has already progressed through the ranks at extraordinary speed since riding his first winner shortly after his 16th birthday. He set the seal on an exceptional season in 2026, which also included his first Classic success on Bow Echo in the 2,000 Guineas in May, by riding his first Breeders’ Cup winner, at Keeneland in Kentucky, five days ago.

He has also been riding for Godolphin since his apprentice days, and notched his first Group One success on their stalwart Rebel’s Romance in Berlin in August 2025. A formal contract with the operation, though, elevates him towards the elite group of riders – including Buick, Ryan Moore, Oisin Murphy and Colin Keane – who can expect to ride Group One winners on a regular basis.

Whether it is possible to split those winners between two different riders, or for how long, remains to be seen. Buick had 32 rides in Group One races in Britain alone in 2026 – only Ryan Moore, with 34, had more – and his six winners started at 5-4, 3-1, 4-9, 9-4, 11-10 and 2-1. Even Godolphin, in other words, is not blessed with such a wealth of top-class horses that the best Group One chances can be easily shared around.

Plumpton 12.33 Bond Broker 1.08 Sweet Caryline 1.43 Jenny France 2.15 Ferret Jeeter 2.47 Central Command 3.22 Bel Ombre 3.55 Crest Of Arms

Newbury 12.42 King William Rufus 1.17 Merlin Allen 1.52 Princess Day 2.25 Kilwaughter 2.58 Percy De Courcy 3.33 Manu Du Noyer 4.05 Newgrove

Newcastle 12.59 Brace For Landing 1.34 Evaluation 2.07 Thorneylands 2.40 Looking Splendid 3.15 Tom Creen 3.50 That Guy

Chelmsford 1.57 Jenson Benson 2.30 Makes Me Wonder 3.05 Chaise Longue 3.40 Pyleates 4.15 Havana Touch 4.45 Galimix 5.15 Marhaba Ya Tayib 5.45 Missmisfortune 6.15 Fuseboard

Southwell 2.20 Ten Cuidado 2.53 Oneforthegutter 3.28 Dovey Moon 4.00 Fenaroli 4.30 Enola Grey (nap) 5.00 Pride’s Queen 5.30 Celestial Fire 6.00 Modern Times 6.30 Infinity Blue (nb)

But for the moment, this will be of little concern to Loughnane as his whirlwind career continues on an upward curve. Having achieved his first grand ambition of a jockeys’ championship in double-quick time, fancied horses and favourites in races like the Derby and Arc lie ahead.

The pressure and scrutiny will also ratchet up another notch or two, of course, not least when Charlie Appleby next has a fancied runner in a Classic or Group One and needs to decide who will ride. Loughnane’s ride on Libertango after sweating down to 8st 5lb, though, was just the latest confirmation that he has the big-race composure and mentality to thrive at the very highest level.

Never mind Dettori, in fact. The win on Libertango had more than a touch of Ryan Moore about it, as Loughnane steered a confident path from off the pace aboard the hot favourite, and the prospect of regular head-to-heads between these two generational talents, in the colours of Flat racing’s twin superpowers, is one to savour on the Flat next year.
