Why the UK settlement rule changes are unjust

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:01:02 GMT

Readers question the motives and fairness behind Shabana Mahmood’s new immigration proposals

This week, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced that many migrants on skilled worker visas earning below £50,000, outside the social care sector, will have to wait for 10 years to “earn” settlement (Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash, 2 November). This blatantly overlooks the contribution of those whose work cannot be measured in high salaries.

I arrived in the UK in September 2022 to pursue a master’s degree, for which I paid more than twice the fee that domestic students pay. Since then, I have worked for two organisations, including the Institute of Development Studies, a leading institution for development research. I have paid my taxes and met the financial requirements of successive visas, paying substantial fees twice, first for a graduate visa and then for the skilled worker visa, including the immigration health surcharge. I would like the government to explain what more I must do to demonstrate that I have “earned” the right to settle.

These proposed changes raise urgent questions about which professions the UK values. People working in development, social sciences, academic research and public policy often earn considerably less than those in finance or technology, despite contributing to research and policymaking, and addressing some of the world’s most pressing challenges. So just because I don’t make £50,000 or work in social care, I have no contribution to make?

Britain wants to retain its position as a global centre for research and development expertise while introducing immigration conditions that could make it harder for international researchers and professionals to build long-term lives here. An income-based settlement system undermines those whose contribution cannot be measured by salary alone.

The government needs to stop mistaking higher salaries for contribution and take a more holistic view of the wider social, intellectual and public value of people’s work. Jigyasa Agarwal Hove, East Sussex

Despite saying that she wants a fair migration policy, Shabana Mahmood’s statement on “earned settlement” contains many examples of unfairness beyond those in the headlines and your editorial (The Guardian view on a migration U-turn: it still leaves unfair changes intact, 2 November.

Here is just one example that has received little attention. Under “no recourse to public funds” rules, most migrant families are not eligible for child benefit or universal credit even if they are working and paying tax. If the rent goes up, a partner leaves or the main breadwinner falls ill, the remaining partner ends up working long hours of overtime to try to earn enough to pay the rent and feed their family. Sometimes that is not enough, and a family faces the grim prospect of eviction and homelessness.

It has always been possible to apply to the Home Office to change the “no recourse to public funds” condition if a family would otherwise become homeless. But under the new immigration rules, a migrant family that has claimed public funds at any time in the previous five years will be ineligible for permanent settlement, or will be required to wait an extra 10 years to settle.

Waiting an extra 10 years will mean renewing the family’s permission to stay every 30 months, each time paying thousands of pounds in fees. Either option will mean deep poverty, debt and mental distress.

The children in these households – over 380,000, according to one recent estimate – already face severe deprivation, with long-term effects on their health and wellbeing. The government’s changes will push these families into even deeper, more grinding and Dickensian poverty. Lynn Sloman London

Having worked with asylum seekers and refugees while running a charity for 10 years, I was horrified to read of the home secretary’s recent proposals, and I am glad they have been reviewed and changed somewhat.

But they are still an unjust punishment for people who take low-paid jobs, as so often they have little or no choice. It is important for Shabana Mahmood and the government to realise that having to wait for 30 years for settlement will not deter those crossing the channel in small boats. First, because there are hardly any safe routes, and second, because those attempting the crossing will not know of this restriction.

They will come anyway as they are encouraged to by people smugglers. The answer is to provide safe legal routes for all those fleeing danger and persecution that is beyond what we can imagine. Dr Elizabeth Hare Former chair, RAIS Lancaster (Refugee, Advocacy, Information and Support)

As a UK visa holder, I would hardly call the few concessions in the earned settlement plan a “U-turn”. A crucial aspect is that from now on, vast proportions of present or future skilled worker visa holders will be on a 10-year route rather than a five-year route to settlement (indefinite leave to remain, ILR). Something that not everyone is aware of is that this visa type is linked to a specific job and employer, placing visa holders in a fragile position of dependency for 10 years.

For example, if your employer is downsizing and laying off staff, you not only lose your job, you and your family will lose your UK visas and will have to leave the country unless you rapidly find a new job with another registered sponsor, which is unlikely. Think of being in this fragile position for 10 long years.

To resolve this, the government could have stipulated that after five years on a skilled worker visa you would be eligible for an “open” work visa that isn’t bound to a specific job and employer. But the fact that the government hasn’t done this shows the true nature of this reform. Fearing massive reliance on benefits once on ILR, the government is trying to push out of the country most of the people who entered thanks to the lowered criteria in about 2022-24. Therefore, not only have the ILR goalposts been extended by five years, but the pathway to get there has been made even harder by relying on the skilled worker visa, a clearly inadequate tool.

This suggests no “fairness” ethos in the earned settlement reform, but rather the intention of making life as hard as possible for a specific population group. While the Home Office estimates the number of affected people at 500,000, independent estimates have suggested up to 2 million. Name and address supplied

I came to the UK in February 2021 as an international student. I studied, followed the rules, secured a permanent role as a software engineer in 2023 and moved on to a skilled worker visa. Like thousands of others, I made major financial and personal decisions based on the settlement pathway that existed when I arrived.

What troubles me most about the government’s earned settlement proposals is not that immigration rules can change. Governments have always had that power. It is that people who came here lawfully, in good faith, could find the goalposts moved years into their journey.

The Home Office argues that settlement should reflect contribution. Yet contribution is not measured only by salary. A person earning below £50,271 who pays taxes, works full-time, obeys the law and never claims public funds contributes meaningfully to British society. Suggesting that someone earning £50,271 deserves settlement five years earlier than another law-abiding taxpayer risks creating a two-tier system of belonging.

Britain’s reputation has long rested on fairness, predictability and respect for legitimate expectations. When migrants make life-changing commitments based on published rules, those commitments should matter. Trust works both ways.

The government’s retreat on care workers is welcome, but it highlights the wider problem. If retrospective changes are unfair for one group, why are they fair for others who also followed every rule asked of them?

Integration is achieved when people can plan their futures, buy homes, start families and put down roots. Security encourages commitment. Uncertainty discourages it. Srujalkumar Patel Watford, Hertfordshire

The £10,000 refugee tax must be scrapped

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:51 GMT

Such a punitive measure will leave people at risk of exploitation and severe poverty, says Mark Joselin of the Refugee Council

Cabinet ministers are right to be worried about the potential impact of the new asylum bill (Mahmood infuriates fellow ministers by failing to reveal impact of UK migration shake-up, 30 October). The proposed refugee tax unfairly punishes refugees by threatening to slap most with a £10,000 tax once they are granted refugee status, a clear breach of the UN refugee convention.

It is aimed at those who arrived with nothing and were not allowed to work while their claims were being assessed, and it ignores the reality that refugees already contribute through the tax system.

Requiring these refugees to pay an extra tax of £10,000 will leave them at risk of exploitation and severe poverty, with some risking homelessness to avoid becoming liable for the tax. It will also damage work incentives and undermine integration, making it harder for people who have fled war and persecution to rebuild their lives. And it undermines progress that the government is making on poverty, community cohesion and homelessness.

We urge readers to support the Refugee Council’s campaign on this vital issue. Mark Joselin Public affairs adviser, Refugee Council

Airbnb can be positive for the community

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:43 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Arwa Mahdawi on some self-catering hosts calling for a strike in response to new guidelines

Regarding Arwa Mahdawi’s article (Airbnb feels like a soulless rip-off – and its hosts are revolting, 28 October), I’m really sick of being scapegoated. I’m aware that Airbnb has negatively impacted some urban communities, but without the income from the two self-catering cottages on my family croft, I couldn’t afford to live in Wester Ross, raise my kids here, spend my money in the village stores and volunteer as a community councillor for the last 25 years.

There may be tyrannical hosts with 90 pages of house rules, but the new guidelines are nonsensical. If self-catering guests are now not expected to wash up, am I supposed to provide them with enough crockery and cutlery for each day of their stay? They’ll then have to live with a growing pile of dirty dishes.

And if I’m expected to wash their dishes after they leave, that is not “charg[ing] hotel-like fees without providing hotel-like services”. On the contrary, it’s expecting hotel-like service for a self-catering fee. I’ve just taken a booking from a group of five for next February – at that time of year, they’ll each be paying £25 per night.

There is an assumption that hosts are necessarily rapacious capitalists with an extractive attitude to the community.

As part of my community work, we’re applying to the Scottish Land Fund so we can build some affordable housing for locals.

We asked some housing associations for an average annual rent on a two-bedroom house. The figure we were given is 20% of the income achievable from the same property as a short-term let. That’s an economic fact that we all share. Anyone offered five times the money for the same work would take it. Alasdair Wright Poolewe, Highland

For 20 years my partner and I have been letting our spare room through Airbnb. Originally, the idea of Airbnb was to have locals host visitors, and this is what we think it should revert to. Anything we read about Airbnb takes no account of locals who rent rooms, and just dwells – understandably – on the evils of the encroaching apartments.

We are both now in our 70s, and the stream of people through our house in Belfast has been a joy to us and keeps us young at heart. Some of our guests have become friends and return regularly to stay. We are not well off and our extra income, within tax limits, is used on occasional holidays and treats. We get to meet so many people, young and old, from all parts of the world who give us heart, and we get to share with them our enjoyment of our house and our city. We have looked for alternative platforms to use, but unfortunately we cannot find one that works so smoothly. Mary Blair Belfast

Indeed it is hard to feel sympathy for many Airbnb owners, especially those with multiple properties, out to make a fortune. However, as a single traveller, I find that few hotels these days have single rooms, with the result that I end up paying the same or almost as much as a couple for a double room. So staying in an Airbnb room in a house where the owner lives and is raising money from letting out one or two rooms to partly finance their mortgage or help with care costs (both of which I have experienced) is an affordable alternative.

In addition, as a single female older traveller, chatting to the host, sharing the occasional meal and getting tips about local sights and events can make the trip much more entertaining. I believe that this was the original aim of Airbnb – as the name suggests, the idea was to offer an “airbed and breakfast”. It is a shame that it hardly reflects those ideas these days. Jill Cadorath Exeter

As a host who has let out rural gîtes in France for 15 years, the blanket changes to Airbnb’s checkout policy give me serious pause. I would never ask a guest to scrub floors or do other heavy cleaning. I am sorry that Arwa Mahdawi’s first Airbnb experience left her so traumatised, but we are not all money-grabbing corporate landlords running meagre city spaces.

I understand that cities have been inundated with mass tourism as Airbnb became a massive commercial business, but that is not the reality of rural getaways. Some of us are level-headed people offering an excellent escape in nature for a modest income. I meet my guests personally, clean up after them and expect a basic level of common sense. Most stay for weeks, not days.

Is it really unreasonable to ask them to take out their rubbish? The hamlet bins are just 50 metres away. Yet under the new rules, removing rubbish off-site is banned. Consequently, I’ve had to order a general waste wheelie bin and three recycling bins, ironically resulting in even more plastic products. Expecting them to do their own washing up is apparently now considered an onerous chore too.

I am not a hotel. I do not collect rubbish daily or provide dishwashing services. I offer a clean house and garden for families to enjoy nature safely. Whatever happened to the traditional self-catering holiday where common sense prevailed? Paula Chatlani Davidson Castelnau-Durban, France

Arwa Mahdawi’s article on Airbnb misses the positive side of the business model. Guests and hosts build a reputation within the app that grows in value with every positive review. Our personal experience over more than 20 years is that a well-reviewed guest is quickly accepted all around the world and a well-reviewed property can be relied on to deliver location, amenity, and in many instances a personal touch like a great coffee machine or sharp kitchen knives, as promised.

We are both hosts and guests in the system. The occasional misrepresentation of the property or failure to leave our premises in a reasonable condition has been quickly and efficiently dealt with by Airbnb. Our reputation once again comes to the fore in any dispute.

Compared with a hotel, we enjoy the location, a price discount, being able to prepare locally sourced food in the accommodation and being able to relax in a private lounge/dining area. Bruce Hartican Bega, New South Wales, Australia

Borthwick given RFU backing for World Cup even if England flop in Nations Championship

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:39 GMT

RFU chief Bill Sweeney offers full support to Borthwick

England boosted by fly-half Fin Smith’s return to training

Steve Borthwick has been given the Rugby Football Union’s unequivocal backing to lead England into the World Cup next year even if the team flop this autumn.

Borthwick’s contract was extended in September to end after the 2028 Six Nations – despite England posting their worst Six Nations performance this year – to avoid speculation in the buildup to the tournament next year. But the head coach remains under pressure on the back of five defeats in the past seven matches.

England have, however, been boosted with the fly-half Fin Smith coming through a key training session on Wednesday before an autumn campaign that features matches against Australia, Japan and New Zealand as well as a rankings match on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend.

Nearly four years ago, Eddie Jones was sacked after an autumn that featured a defeat by Argentina, victory against Japan, a draw with the All Blacks and defeat by South Africa, which was greeted with a chorus of boos by the Twickenham faithful. But the RFU chief executive, Bill Sweeney, said he could not see a scenario where Borthwick would be replaced, irrespective of results this month.

“We’re committed to Steve, we’ve extended his contract to the middle of 2028,” Sweeney said. “We believe in what he’s doing. We had a difficult Six Nations this year, we accept that, but we just want to see continued progress and we’re backing him to get that done.

“We just felt that going into a World Cup is a tough enough challenge anyway. We wanted our coaching team just to be focused on the World Cup, not be thinking about: ‘Oh, I don’t have a role lined up,’ and be thinking about that in the buildup. It was to take away any distraction around that, and take that same coaching team through into the transition into the Six Nations in 2028. That was the sole intention. It was the same process with the women’s team.”

After England’s first defeat by Italy in March, the RFU took the unprecedented step of offering conditional support for Borthwick, backing the head coach but calling for improvements in summer Tests against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina. Sweeney offered further qualified backing after the Six Nations before Borthwick was again endorsed by the anonymous post-championship review.

England proceeded to lose heavily against the Springboks, thrash Fiji and edge past Argentina to sit third in the northern hemisphere Nations Championship pool but discipline – one of the few areas in need of improvement identified by the review that was made public – remained a problem with Borthwick’s side receiving 14 yellow cards and one red in 2026 to date.

“It was a really thorough in-depth review,” Sweeney said. “It happens after every competition. The mini version happens virtually after every single game, but we have a review after every comp. We were clearly very disappointed about the Six Nations this year. Nobody wanted to see that performance. It did highlight some areas that required action that happened, were followed up on, and we’re confident that’s had an effect.”

Smith is primed to line up against the Wallabies after completing Wednesday’s training session. The 24-year-old fly-half has been nursing a calf injury but remains on track to give Borthwick a timely fillip.

“Fin trained today and got through all right so we are cautiously optimistic that he’s available for selection,” said England’s defence coach, Richard Wigglesworth, who revealed the 200-metre world silver medallist and five-time European champion sprinter Amy Hunt visited the squad on Wednesday. “We’ll need to see what the next 24 hours are like in terms of his reaction but he did well today. We’re training Friday, so obviously he’s got to train then, but we’ll know before then the state of availability. We’re pretty optimistic.”

Smith has emerged as an integral part of Borthwick’s side, having started the past five England Tests and cemented his position as Borthwick’s first-choice fly-half.

“He looked good,” the back‑rower Ben Earl said. “Obviously, we know Fin, he’s a class, class player. He’s been in unbelievable form for a number of years. Six Nations and Sanzaar agree to sell global broadcast rights together in unique deal

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:39 GMT

Rugby’s biggest unions aiming to grow revenues

New rights management agency to oversee sales

The Six Nations and Sanzaar unions have agreed to sell all their media rights and commercial deals collectively for the first time in a new revenue-sharing model.

In an innovative arrangement that is the first of its kind in sport, the southern hemisphere nations will receive a share of the profits generated by the Six Nations and British & Irish Lions tours, while the European countries will benefit from broadcast and sponsorship deals generated by the Rugby Championship and the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series between New Zealand and South Africa.

The sales process will be managed by a new rights management agency to be set up by a 10-person board that has been created to run the Nations Championship, which resumes this weekend.

Commercial and media rights for the Nations Championship are already sold collectively and the revenue shared between the 10 founding members – the Six Nations plus New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and Argentina – with Fiji and Japan given much smaller appearance fees. Having worked together to create the Nations Championship the 10 biggest unions have moved to pool rights for international rugby outside the World Cup in the hope of achieving growth, particularly in a difficult media market.

The new strategy represents a global extension of Project Light, through which the four Home Nations unions have collectively sold Six Nations rights since 2019.

“In effect, we are creating a commercial rights agency which sits underneath the 10 Nations Championship founding unions,” the Rugby Football Union chief executive, Bill Sweeney, said.

“We think that will result in a much better and more efficient approach to the market, obviously with the intention of increasing overall valuations and growing the commercial side of the game.”

The new arrangements are expected to affect sponsorship and commercial deals from 2028, which coincides with the second edition of the Nations Championship, but will not have an impact on TV rights sales until two years later, as all the Six Nations and Sanzaar’s broadcast rights are secured until 2029.

Jeanette Winterson’s point about AI brings to mind an Isaac Asimov story

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:00:30 GMT

Ed Kelsey and Arthur Gould respond to an interview with the author in which she discussed AI and the future of humanity

I thoroughly enjoyed the interview with Jeanette Winterson (‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity, 28 October), particularly her quote from Jill Lepore that we are living out the sci-fi books that tech leaders read when they were 13. I was one of those 13-year-olds, and my favourite author was Isaac Asimov.

Many of his stories accurately predicted our modern world, from mobile technology to AI (through his fictional supercomputer Multivac). However, it was Winterson’s closing point – that “of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists, but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people” – that really made me smile.

It immediately brought to mind an Asimov story that has stuck with me for 50 years: Profession (published in Nine Tomorrows in 1959). It depicts the future specialist needs of highly specialised, automated worlds and the absolute need for some of those specialists to be “well-rounded”, which reflects Winterson’s view so exactly it is uncanny; I would encourage her to read it.

Admittedly, I didn’t read it under the covers with a flashlight, nor did I grow up to be a ruling “tech-bro” – but I did become a computer programmer. Ed Kelsey Maresfield, East Sussex

At last, someone who is not pessimistic about AI? Thank you, Jeanette Winterson, for making us think about the possible benefits of AI. As she says, “there is no inevitable dystopia”.

If the examples of AI we are experiencing at the moment show intelligence superior to Homo sapiens, might it not be a force for good in the future? If it becomes more out of our control yet better at making decisions, surely it will see what many of us cannot? It might see a way out of the climate catastrophe we are heading towards. It might see the senselessness of bombing whole cities and people into oblivion. Far from pressing the nuclear button it might prevent us from doing it.

Not only will important decisions be removed from humans, they will be made by a superior intelligence. They might not always be easily palatable, but they might be in the long-term interests of the planet. Arthur Gould Loughborough, Leicestershire

Goalkeeper Jesús Owono experiencing ‘hardest days of my life’ after De Miguel’s death

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:23:02 GMT

Owono says he feels ‘huge pain’ over tragedy

Investigation into medical attention De Miguel received

The FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after he was involved in the collision that led to the death of the Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel.

Owono had raced out of his goal and crashed into De Miguel in added time at the end of the Spanish second division match on Monday afternoon, causing the striker to experience a cardiorespiratory arrest. De Miguel was taken to hospital in Santa Cruz de Tenerife but never regained consciousness and died on Tuesday morning.

“These are being the hardest days of my life,” Owono said in a statement published by Andorra. “I find it hard to find the words and very difficult to assimilate what has happened. I feel a huge pain, the loss of Jesús. I am thinking about him, his family and all the people who loved him.

“I know that there will be many questions to address and I will face up to whatever comes with respect. But right now, sincerely, I cannot think about anything other than Jesús and the pain that we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

Andorra’s statement said that the club remained “deeply affected” by De Miguel’s death and demanded “the greatest respect and sensibility”. The homicide division of the Spanish national police opened an investigation, which is standard procedure in Spain whenever there is a death not by natural causes. Santa Cruz de Tenerife’s chief prosecutor, José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui, told the Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings against the goalkeeper were “very unlikely”.

The investigation will focus on the events that preceded De Miguel’s death, including the attention he received after medics sprinted on to the pitch. De Miguel was treated on the field for five minutes before being taken off on a stretcher and to an ambulance that waited in the corner. Tenerife had reported that medics were able to recover a pulse in the ambulance before he was admitted to intensive care.

“We can’t say if they acted correctly or incorrectly, but we can demand that all the emergency procedures follow international standards of correct practice,” Elvira González, the president of Spain’s Association of Nurses, Emergency Medics and Caregivers, told the Associated Press. “There is contradictory information. The first thing we need to know is where and when he supposedly recovered a pulse. The first minutes are critical. You can only move a person once a pulse is restored.”

Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García, told Cadena Ser radio: “There are those who say that the impact caused his death, and that later they were able to stabilise him artificially even though it was very difficult to bring him back. I prefer to wait for the autopsy and then we can take steps. I would like to see [the results of] the investigation to know if there is something to ensure this doesn’t happen again, something that could have prevented this tragedy.”

Owono had earlier been defended by his teammate Lautaro Spatz, who wrote on social media: “I also ‌want to say a few words about my teammate, goalkeeper ‌and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened. Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment, and that he ‌would never intentionally hurt anyone. In football, unfortunate incidents can happen, but no one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences.”

The Equatoguinean Football Federation expressed its support, saying that Owono, who has 47 caps for the country, was going through a situation of profound sorrow and grief.

Owono was sent off for the challenge and immediately walked towards the touchline, only to turn back as staff began running in the other direction. The goalkeeper deactivated his Instagram account on Tuesday after receiving abuse online, with some users commenting “murderer” on his posts. Andorra said they were offering psychological support to anyone at the club who needed it after De Miguel’s death. The Tenerife president, Felipe Miñambres, had said they would need “professional help”.

De Miguel, 30, was married and had an 18-month-old child, both of whom were in the stadium when the incident happened. Flowers have been left at the stadium by gate nine, his shirt number, and a minute’s silence was held at the Canarian government building.

De Miguel’s body laid at the Tanatorio Santa Lastenia funeral parlour in Santa Cruz before being flown to the Spanish mainland on Wednesday afternoon. Tenerife’s players and staff will fly to Madrid on a charter on Thursday morning and go from there to the village of Navahermosa in Toledo province, where De Miguel’s parents are from, for the funeral. A final homage will be held at Tenerife’s Heliodoro Rodriguez López stadium on Saturday evening.

The knuck: how to wear trousers and boots – without looking like a pirate

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:02:38 GMT

Forget the French tuck. This year, the fashion press has another style move in mind – and it will at least keep your jeans clean

Name: The knuck.

Age: A brand new term for an enduring look.

Appearance: How you’ll all be wearing your trousers this winter.

Please no. I just want to be able to wear trousers normally. Oh ye of little faith. Just because the knuck has an objectively stupid name, it doesn’t mean that this is an impractical trend.

Come on. It’s called the knuck, for God’s sake. Yes, but there’s a very pertinent reason for this. “Knuck” is a portmanteau of “knee” and “tuck”.

Then why have they added a definite article to the start of it? Was it very important that this trend had to sound as if it could be the name of 2008’s eighth-worst indie band? Listen, do you want to know what the knuck is or not?

Reluctantly: yes. Good. The knuck is where you tuck your jeans into your boots. It’s what Sienna Miller did in the 2000s, and Diana, Princess of Wales did in the 1980s, and several buccaneers did in the 1650s.

Seriously? That’s it? Wearing trousers welly-style? This isn’t a case of gen Z taking something that people have done for decades and then bunging a new name on it. The knuck is its own distinct thing.

Please tell me how. The key to achieving the knuck lies in how much of your jeans hangs over the top of your boots.

Are you telling me there’s actually a way of doing this wrong? Oh heavens, yes. If you tuck the whole of your trouser leg into your boots, you’ll look like a pirate. But if you don’t tuck enough of it, then you’ll look all floppy and weird. You’ll be a laughing stock.

What is the acceptable middle ground? According to Grazia, which seems to have coined the term, “the sweet spot is a soft gather of fabric just above the boot shaft, rather than a perfectly smooth tuck or an enormous mound of material”.

But why? Grazia again: “Aesthetically, it gives denim a more considered silhouette, adding shape around the leg while letting your boots take centre stage.”

That’s me told. There is a practical element to consider, too, which is that applying the knuck before yomping around a field will keep the mud off your jeans.

That is something. Yes, but make sure you do it in an aesthetically pleasing way. Otherwise you might as well just roll about in animal cack and be done with it.

Surely something as fussy as this cannot possibly catch on. You’re wrong. The knuck has taken centre stage at autumn/winter fashion shows by Isabel Marant, Acne Studios and Dries van Noten.

So there’s no getting away from the knuck. None at all. Get good at it quickly, or risk humiliation – at least until it goes away six weeks from now.

Do say: “The knuck keeps mud off your jeans.”

Don’t say: “So does staying indoors.”

‘Jimi Horsedrix brought me so much joy’: the comic drawing a horse a day – and day 69’s is unsuitable for children

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:01:45 GMT

On day 58, he did a boxing Ali horse. On day 67, he did a howling horse. So what made Andy Field suddenly decide to draw 100 equines? And what made day 48’s so phallic?

Andy Field was midway through his standup run at this year’s Edinburgh fringe when he was struck by an unusual urge – the urge to draw a horse. “I hadn’t sat down to draw anything since I was at school,” says the 34-year-old comedian. “Drawing was a skill I didn’t have.”

He’s not lying. The subsequent horse Field posted to TikTok and Instagram was rather naive, with its four identical straight legs and cartoon eyeball. But the project he announced alongside it – Drawing a Horse Every Day Until I’m Really Good at Drawing Horses – immediately captured people’s hearts. Over a million people watched the minute-long video of him drawing that first horse with a four-colour ballpoint pen. By day three – an undeniably terrible effort in which the horse appeared to have sprouted a platypus’s bill – more than two million, by his estimation, had tuned in. “People were willing the series to continue,” says Field. And so he did.

Field is now approaching day 80 of his horse drawing series and it’s been quite a journey. We’ve had howling horses (day 67), an Ali-style boxing horse knocking out an equine Sonny Liston (day 58), a skateboarding horse (day 29), a horse turning the tables and drawing a portrait of Field (day 24), and a horse on its knees playing a guitar solo (day 21). If some commentators were hoping Field was going to draw the same horse every day and gradually work on his understanding of proportion and perspective then they were left disappointed. Because Field’s project is really a joyful celebration of drawing for fun – of following a daft idea and seeing where it takes you.

Sometimes, that’s not a place anyone intended. On day 48, Field decided to focus in on a horse’s face, but ended up sketching something that – to his evident horror – became increasingly phallic. “I was picturing those shots in a Ren & Stimpy cartoon, where it’s so grotesquely zoomed in and you’re getting all the warts and sweat and veins. But I didn’t draw a great shape of head, and, well …”

As part of his droll commentary on each day’s effort, Field likes to name each horse. The one resembling male genitalia was given the moniker Gentle Brian. The guitar-shredding horse was Jimi Horsedrix. Often, the less traditional Field’s horses are, the more impressive they turn out. He might have visited the National Gallery (day 19) to take tips from the master of horse drawing, George Stubbs, but he’s more at home doing horses wearing shades (day 64) or horses infused with the spirit of his new kitten, Toast (day 56).

“I get dozens of comments every day with tips on how to draw horses – but if I sat down and felt as if I had to follow them it wouldn’t have the same joie de vivre about it,” he says. “Prioritise what brings you joy – and a horse playing an electric guitar brought me so much joy.”

Field says that his love of horses started ironically: whenever someone asked what he wanted for his birthday, he would request a framed picture of a horse. “It was just a funny thing to ask for,” he says. How many horse pictures did he receive? “Oh, a bunch.”

This equine interest has undeniably served him well. The series has inspired some viewers to pick up a pen and draw their own horses, whereas some have said they watch each day with their children. “They’ve said it’s a good example of someone not worrying about making mistakes and just enjoying themselves,” he says. “That’s been one of the most gratifying things.”

Said parents are best advised to avoid day 69’s image of horses observing oral sex. Field has also launched a merch range: the day three catastrophe makes an appearance on a T-shirt, as does his colourful swirl of horses eating each other (day 27, given the name Seabiscuits).

There have been notable landmarks. On day 50, Field redrew his first attempt, to show how far he’s come. The difference was vast. “I now have a more segmented view of a horse,” says Field. “I go through it, like, the ears are their own thing, then the little bit of hair between the ears that connects to the mane ….” Many videos show his dedication to the curve that joins the neck with the front legs, a section of horse that Field refers to as “horse cleavage”. “Don’t even be gross,” he says on one video. “It’s a normal part of horses.”

Field promised that, when he hit 100,000 followers, he would do an oil painting of a horse (Day 54), despite some viewers warning him off the idea. “They said it would be too messy,” he says, “and they were right.” But learning from mistakes is part of what Field is embracing. “What’s the downside of doing a bad oil painting of a horse? I mean, it’s not life or death, is it?”

Sticking to his promise of one horse per day hasn’t always been easy. Soon after Edinburgh finished he spent a weekend at the End of the Road music festival on the Wiltshire-Dorset border, and was forced to film himself drawing from a windy campsite (days 14-16). “People were criticising me for not taking the pen off the paper – but I had to keep the pen down to stop the paper blowing away!”

It was at that festival that he saw one of his favourite bands, Geese, perform their song 100 Horses. Field thought that seemed like a decent number of horses to end his project on. “I have a plan for how I’m going to finish the series,” he says. “Everyone in my life is telling me that it’s a bit elaborate, but we’ve got to go out with a bang!”

The big question, though, as we head towards day 100: does Field think he will have made good on his desire to get “really good at drawing horses”?

“I mean … I almost regret calling the series that,” he says with a laugh. “Because what’s ‘good’? To me, being good means being able to sit down and do art and feel fulfilled, regardless of the outcome. So in my head, I’m already good!”

Cambridge asks Post Office inquiry barrister to lead review into death of Jason Arday

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:54:19 GMT

Jason Beer KC will examine university’s handling of claims against Arday and protection offered to academics in spotlight

The lead barrister for the Post Office Horizon inquiry has been appointed to head an independent review into the death of the Cambridge academic Jason Arday.

Jason Beer KC will examine the handling of allegations of research and other misconduct made against Arday before his resignation as well as the university’s recruitment and support for him as its youngest ever black professor at the age of 37.

Beer said he would consider whether wider institutional changes were needed at Cambridge after looking into the protection it offered to academics facing significant public and media scrutiny and the procedures around the appointment of Arday.

The professor of the sociology of education died at his home in south London while facing widely publicised allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but Cambridge said on 5 August it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. He resigned hours after this was announced and was found dead nine days later.

Beer said Cambridge had asked him to conduct an independent, thorough and searching examination of its institutional arrangements and the decisions it made over Arday.

He said: “I will look not simply at what the university’s policies and procedures required but also at whether they were themselves reasonable; how they operated in practice; who was responsible for making decisions; what information was reasonably available to them; whether relevant concerns were recognised and properly addressed; and whether the university’s various structures and functions worked together effectively – all in the case of Prof Arday, and more broadly.

“I hope that those who have relevant knowledge or experience will feel able to contribute to the review. Their perspectives may be important in understanding not only what happened in Prof Arday’s case but whether there are wider institutional changes to be made.

“I will take seriously my responsibility to treat participants with sensitivity, to respect confidentiality and to ensure fairness to anyone whose actions may be examined.”

Beer’s review is the second of two independent reviews of Cambridge’s involvement with Arday. The first, announced by the university in September, asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death.

A veteran of public inquiries, including working for NHS England in the Covid-19 inquiry, Beer is best known for his role as lead counsel to the Post Office Horizon IT statutory inquiry that investigated the wrongful criminal prosecution of nearly 1,000 post office operators.

Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said: “Jason Beer is an eminent legal expert who will bring vast experience of leading complex reviews and inquiries. We are equally thankful to the distinguished panel of independent experts he has convened to assist him in this important task and look forward to receiving their findings and recommendations in due course.”

BBC attempts to reassure Jewish staff after ex-producer says she faced antisemitism

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:52:03 GMT

Deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies meets staff group after case of Lucie Kon prompted calls for inquiry

The BBC has attempted to reassure Jewish staff that discrimination against them will not be tolerated, after a former producer said she had faced antisemitism while employed at the corporation.

Rhodri Talfan Davies, the BBC’s deputy director general, met representatives from the broadcaster’s Jewish staff network on Tuesday after coverage of the case of Lucie Kon.

The former commissioning editor for the BBC’s Storyville documentary series was paid £400,000 by the corporation after her departure. Kon said she had faced antisemitism after the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas. The BBC said its internal processes did not uphold her antisemitism claims, but has acknowledged “shortcomings, and the personal impact” on her.

The staff group is understood to have asked for a meeting after Kon’s claims. She stated in an interview: “The BBC isn’t full of antisemites, but it does have a problem with antisemitism.”

Her case has prompted calls for an independent inquiry from some MPs and former BBC figures including the ex-home affairs correspondent Danny Shaw.

While Talfan Davies did not accept an independent inquiry was needed, he pointed to new staff training on antisemitism, as well as internal attempts to build an inclusive culture inside the BBC. He is understood to have written to some Jewish staff members after media coverage of Kon’s case.

The issue has provided an early test for Talfan Davies, who was handed the deputy job to spot the kinds of crises that eventually led to the resignation of the previous director general, Tim Davie.

Those crises included several disputes over the BBC’s Middle East coverage. The corporation apologised last year after a documentary about children in Gaza failed to disclose that its child narrator was the son of a Hamas official. It was also criticised for dropping another documentary about medics in Gaza after concluding it “risked creating a perception of partiality”. The programme was later shown by Channel 4.

Talfan Davies said at an event this week that he did not think an independent inquiry into potential antisemitism at the BBC was necessary as “we have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly”.

Responding to questions from journalists at a Broadcasting Press Guild lunch in London, the deputy director general said: “Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.”

He added: “I don’t believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done.”

Talfan Davies said the BBC had “taken enormous steps” to improve its workplace culture, such as introducing mandatory training and implementing the results of a recent review that focused on “calling out bad behaviour”.

“I don’t recognise a description of the BBC as in any way institutionally discriminatory,” he said. “But I also understand that the coverage of the last two weeks will have been difficult for our Jewish colleagues within the BBC and we need to talk to them and work with them to support them. But I think that’s different from believing that you have some sort of deep-rooted issue in the organisation.”

While the BBC has said complaints about antisemitism were not upheld in Kon’s case, it has not explained the size of her payout. Talfan-Davies said he was unable to comment further for legal reasons, but said: “It didn’t relate to findings of antisemitism in the investigation.”

Spain’s deadly train crashes have damaged public confidence in the system

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:40:37 GMT

Pedro Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are racing to rebuild trust ahead of a snap election, but the task they face is immense

Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

A week ago today, for the second time in nine months, I got in my car and drove south from Madrid to cover a deadly train crash.

At 8.53am last Wednesday, a high-speed train operated by Spain’s state-owned rail company, Renfe, smashed into the back of a stationary train run by the private rail company Iryo, on the outskirts of the small town of Urda in Castilla-La Mancha. Sixty-nine people died in the accident, more than 100 were injured, and Spain’s already depleted confidence in its treasured rail network plummeted.

As I drove to Urda, I – along with much of Spain – was feeling a grim sense of deja vu. On 18 January, an Iryo train on the same line from Madrid to Seville had derailed near the Andalucían town of Adamuz before being struck by a Renfe train coming from the opposite direction. Forty-six people died, scores were injured and public trust in Spain’s trains was badly shaken.

The things I saw and heard in Urda mirrored those I’d seen and heard in Adamuz: local people rushing to the train tracks to help the injured; the rapid repurposing of municipal halls into emergency triage centres; and all manner of spontaneous acts of selflessness, bravery, practicality and compassion.

Some of the passengers whose journey south had come to a violent and premature end near Urda stood in line, many still with their wheelie cases and rucksacks, waiting for the coaches that had been chartered to take them onward. The queues looked almost normal until you noticed the odd bandaged head, torn trouser leg, or bloodstained top.

Josimar Medina, a young Peruvian who was travelling with his Brazilian girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, told me the blood on his brown T-shirt belonged to an American called Austin. Medina had helped free Austin from the wreckage and had managed to get him out of the train.

Although the young American was badly hurt, Medina had seen far worse injuries as he clambered off the train. “I saw … people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” he said. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

The shock and sorrow has echoed around Spain as the country tries to come to terms with what has happened, and to accept that its extensive and modern speed rail system – long a source of national pride – may not be the safe and reliable network it once seemed.

As the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, put it last week, “public trust in the high-speed system has been broken”.

Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are now racing to rebuild that trust, but the task they face is immense – especially given the current circumstances.

How will this play out in the elections?

The anger and grief are still raw and, with a snap general election now less than a month away, the political atmosphere is explosive. The prime minister’s critics point out that 115 people died at Adamuz and Urda, and Sánchez and his ministers have had eight years to focus on, and invest in, rail safety. On Tuesday evening, the transport minister, Óscar Puente, accepted the inevitable, announcing his resignation, with the acknowledgment that “neither the country, nor I, can bear 100 deaths in less than a year”.

With the election drawing closer, the language from opposition parties is becoming more strident.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which is expected to finish first in next month’s vote, has accused the Sánchez administration of failing to keep Spaniards safe and of trying to use the latest tragedy to political ends.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

“It’s not just obvious that they’re not good at being in charge,” Feijóo said on Monday. “It’s that I’m also not sure that they’re good people, either.”

The far-right Vox party, with whom the PP could form a national coalition government, has been even more scathing, accusing the government of “killing” the train crash victims and of “incompetence, corruption, cronyism, and a lack of investment in maintenance and infrastructure improvements”. It is also urging the supreme court to investigate Puente on suspicion of manslaughter and causing bodily harm through gross negligence. Puente has rejected allegations of mismanagement, and has insisted that Spain’s railway system is “safe and reliable”.

Despite signs of a modest resurgence in support just before the latest crash, Sánchez always faced a tough road to re-election. Corruption scandals have bedevilled his inner circle and his government was much criticised for its response to the mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta over the summer. That road now looks even more impassable.

But with disasters, emergencies and deaths so frequently politicised, especially in Spain, the worry now is that solutions to the failings at Adamuz and Urda may be missed amid all the campaigning and point-scoring.

As the politicians bicker and Spain prepares for its fifth general election in 10 years, the long process of recovery is just beginning for some of those who survived last week’s crash.

On Saturday afternoon, I got an email from the family of Austin Hartman, the young American pulled out of the train by Josimar Medina. They told me that Austin, a Cal Poly State University student who had been studying in Madrid, was being treated in a Spanish hospital for multiple fractures to his pelvis, hip, femur, humerus and rib, and was unlikely to be well enough to return home for at least two months. GoFundMe pages have been set up for Austin and his friend Leah Silver-Fajardo, who was also badly hurt in the accident.

His family had seen the photo I took of Josimar and Vitoria in Urda and wanted to know if there was any way of contacting them so that Austin could say thank you. By the following day, Austin and his family had video called the couple.

“It was so helpful for us to … thank Josimar for treating Austin with such loving care when he needed it more than anything,” Austin’s stepmother, Sandi, told me in an email on Tuesday. “Austin credits him with saving his life. As we know, beautiful things are born of tragedy and it’s usually in the relationships that are formed out of it.”

Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:33:31 GMT

The cost of checking your coat or bag is galloping ahead of other – also rising – prices at venues. We explain the surprisingly complex reasons why

Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues.

At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and if you want to retrieve something, you’ll need to pay again. At north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 (though they’re reusable with no extra fee). At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised?

The price rises are helping to push average spending per head on a night out from £20.95 in 2020 to £28.06 in 2026, according to Night Time Industries Association. “For years, nightlife businesses have faced relentless increases in the cost of operating, from energy and employment to taxation, business rates and supply chains,” says chief executive Michael Kill. “Many have had no choice but to pass some of those costs on to consumers simply to keep their doors open. But the reality is that consumers have now hit an affordability ceiling.”

With consumers spending less on alcohol, locker systems and cloakrooms offer premises a way to make some of that money back, but, Kill says, “the consumer cannot be the industry’s financial shock absorber indefinitely”.

UK storage policy changed after the 2017 attack at an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester Arena which killed 22 people and injured more than 1,000. “Martyn’s law” legislation requires “appropriate public protection measures” at public events to reduce the risk and impact of terror attacks. It led to many venues – including the nationwide network of 18 Academy Music Group sites – banning bags over A4 size entirely and offloading them to external lockers or storage partners. In London, these are often kebab shops, restaurants and barbers.

Carrie Wang, a London-based spin instructor, was buzzing to see Hot Chip at O2 Academy Brixton until she learned her near-empty tote bag had to be stored in a kebab shop round the corner. “I was fuming,” Wang says. “They charged me £10 and it wasn’t a proper facility, it was just a random storage room – it’s not like they had lockers and my things were actually safe there.” Academy Music Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Ahmed Khan is the owner of Kentish Delight, a kebab shop in Kentish Town. He says that in 2022, O2 Kentish Town Forum’s management asked if he had any spare space in the takeaway. “They had a look and said my premises are perfect and secure for the customer – and I said yes, why not?” Khan charges £5 per bag and says nothing has ever gone missing. “Although the bag people never buy kebabs.”

The high costs and added logistics mean that some people are taking risks with their belongings. At an AEW wrestling event at Wembley Arena, fans were directed to a nearby Premier Inn to stow their bags, at £10 a pop with long queues.

Soul singer Danny Toeman decided to stuff his rucksack behind a carpark vending machine. “I could stuff most of the valuable contents into my pockets,” says Toeman. “So I thought: let’s just stash it somewhere and if it gets stolen, so what?”

That in itself is a security risk – if staff had seen Toeman’s backpack, the venue could have been evacuated. But it’s become commonplace. One Reddit user opted to hide their bag outside the O2 Academy in Southampton. “They will literally not let you in,” they wrote. “I was forced to leave it outside the building entirely and it was stolen when I came out.”

Willem Pelle is head of sales at eLockers, a Dutch company working with many UK nightclubs including Drumsheds, Fold and Warehouse Project. “When we expanded into the UK, we saw that many venues were facing staffing challenges following Covid, making traditional cloakrooms increasingly difficult to operate,” Pelle says.

London is their main UK market, with Manchester a close second. Pelle says there is typically no upfront cost for the venue, which gets to share the takings with eLockers, adding: “It’s important that the pricing works for both the venue and its customers, while creating a sustainable additional revenue stream.”

Some clubbers have reported benefits to lockers, such as those at Drumsheds, where you can put stuff in and out – allowing for outfit changes during an event. But not all venues opt to install expensive locker systems. At Hackney Bath House, the cloakroom is free. Sneaky Pete’s in Edinburgh installed lockers in 2012 and still charge £2 per locker. Peckham’s 200-capacity club the Carpet Shop charges £3 per item: “No need to charge more, it’s a tiny bit of space and a rail,” says general manager Cam Prentis.

He sees the cloakroom as a valuable part of the club experience in its own right. Upstairs and away from the bustle, it’s where staff and punters can have a break and a chat. “Whoever’s on the cloakroom has their own music playing,” Cam says. Unlike at an unstaffed array of lockers or the back room of a kebab shop, “it’s a vibe up there”.

After Martha Stewart’s Halloween homeless costume disaster, I have to know: celebrities, why do you risk it?

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:22:16 GMT

Cynics might say it’s about courting controversy, but I think these fancy dress faux-pas hint at a bleaker truth

It’s not easy being an optimist these days. It requires practice, like exercising a muscle. It’s why I like to think of reading the news as a kind of challenge, batting away the miserable updates with optimistic mental rebuttals. Global heating on track to exceed the 2C threshold? “But we have the technology to turn this around!” I think. A well-funded global fascist network? “People have overcome worse!”

And so it is that this week I find my optimism being put through its paces by the news of US superstar homemaker Martha Stewart and her offensive Halloween costume of a homeless person, complete with a dirt-smeared face and a sign reading “I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!”.

How’s this for a more upbeat interpretation: she is preparing for her next chapter as an edgy, anti-humour one-woman act known as Martha Stewart Lee. I can see it now: her Fringe show – which I am calling Laundered – receiving rave reviews. “After decades of perfect tablescapes, Martha Stewart serves up something truly unpalatable: herself.” Five stars!

Before influencers made “being a Pinterest board made flesh” a viable career, there was Stewart. Arguably the US’s national authority on doing domestic things properly, Stewart, now 85, built an empire of cookbooks, magazines, TV shows and homeware. In 1999, she took her company public and became a billionaire. Then, in 2004, she was convicted of conspiracy, obstruction of an agency proceeding and making false statements to federal investigators, and served five months in prison.

Back to the photo. The negative response was immediate – “what in the ‘let them eat cake’ is this costume?” asked one user – and even though the post was quickly deleted, screenshots had already secured the veteran lifestyle guru a place in the Famous People in Tone-Deaf Fancy Dress hall of fame. Stewart is in illustrious company: Bill Maher as the bloodied body of the beloved conservationist Steve Irwin, weeks after he was killed by a stingray; Chloë Sevigny as the corpse of Diana, Princess of Wales; and the depressingly long list of celebs in blackface, or apparently having a laugh referring to genocides (see: Prince Harry in a Nazi costume, or any celebrity wearing a Native American costume).

As celebrity apologies go, Stewart’s was a real doozy. It had all the hits, such as the “I’m so shocked everyone is upset by the objectively upsetting thing I did” classic – to quote Stewart, she was “distressed” that the costume had offended people. You see, dear readers, it turns out she was just raising “awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness”. A noble cause, which she pursued by using the post to promote her candle range, with the caption: “My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!”

Let’s just take that at face value for a second. Maybe it was meant to be provocative. Maybe, just maybe, it’s a kind of Halloween jumpscare that leaps out at you precisely when you’re indulging in pointless candle shopping to remind you consumerism is not working for everyone. Yep, definitely that, and definitely not a mistaken upload providing a snapshot into the dehumanising ways the rich and powerful can come to see ordinary people when they think we’re not looking. As costume, as gimmick. As punchlines.

Say what you like about Martha Stewart Lee, but her work sure does make you think.

Jokes aside, how do these incidents keep happening? How do people whose entire brands depend on public approval – with teams of staff and social media to test the water – get it so wrong? Some, like Maher, court controversy and dine out on the notoriety. I doubt Stewart is one of them, though she has form in turning scandal into success post-prison. But if every costume-to-cancelled incident was just intentional marketing strategy, then surely there’d be less apologising after? Perhaps it’s the yes-man culture that surrounds the wealthy so that no one dares say: “Heidi, darling, Klummy-pops, love the Halloween party, but dressing as a Hindu goddess might read more ‘disrespect’ than ‘hot and wrecked’, you know?” And of course, there’s the algorithms that reward shock.

But I can’t help but feel that fundamentally it’s the result of being in the ivory tower: the strange, insulated life that comes with sustained wealth and only ever mixing with people at your level, and the inevitable disconnection from the levels of decency the rest of us possess. So potent is the effect that even five months in prison, among women who’d likely have experienced homelessness, didn’t give Stewart pause as she dirtied her face this Halloween.

But there is one reason for cheer. The whole episode did raise awareness of homelessness. Coverage of the row reminded readers that more than 700,000 Americans are homeless. And at a time when many Americans are being squeezed by the cost of living, a multimillionaire was told in no uncertain terms that poverty is not a punchline. For any atrophying optimism muscles, consider that one rep done.

Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UK

‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:18:46 GMT

It’s 20 years since Jo and Richard Hill bought anything in Rotherham town centre. Why have they and so many locals abandoned it for the nearest retail park – and what would it take to change their minds?

On 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.

Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.

Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost half of Britons don’t visit their high street weekly. Instead, shoppers are opting for retail parks. Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even paying extra to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, sit at 13%, reports Savills.

Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.”

Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard.

A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, are vacant, far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street.

The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would drain jobs from the high street, “disembowel towns and villages” and disadvantage those unable to drive.

Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent.

The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a government analysis found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time. Recent police data shows there were 1,105 crimes, including 356 violent and sexual offences and 188 instances of shoplifting recorded in central Rotherham in August of this year alone. Nearby Sheffield city centre recorded 836 crimes in the same period. Donna says drug users also hang around her shopfront. “They sleep in my doorway sometimes. There’s needles and all sorts left. We’re not getting anybody into the shop because it looks bad.”

For Saj, the lack of affordable parking is another problem killing the high street. Car ownership has soared since the advent of the retail park. In 1971, 52% of households in Britain owned a car. A decade later, this had jumped to 60%, and by 2022 nearly three-quarters of households had a car. On its website, Parkgate touts its “over 2,000 free parking spaces”, all in one concentrated area.

Within Rotherham town centre, there are 1,610 spaces, which, until fairly recently, were all paid – though the council has recognised parking as a challenge. In 2016 it cut long-stay charges from £6.50 to £3.50 a day, and last year, it introduced free parking for one hour on weekdays. At the weekend, some spaces are free all day, but many, while acknowledging the council’s efforts, say it is not enough.

Sitting on a bench and lapping up the sun on Rotherham High Street are Leo Lopez and Claire Mercer. “I’ve seen a massive change,” says 50-year-old Lopez, a support worker. Mercer, also 50, a road safety campaigner, agrees. “You don’t come here to do general shopping after 3.30pm. It’s aggro caused by drugs mainly. People are more out of their head by that time. It’s an unfortunate truth, but it’s everywhere.”

The state of the town centre “deteriorates the morale”, says Lopez. And it may be contributing to the rise of rightwing populism: research by the thinktank Power to Change published last year found higher support for Reform UK in areas with run-down high streets that have high vacancy rates. Mercer says a part of town filled with ethnic minority shops and restaurants has been disparaged by some as “a foreign bazaar”. “Would they prefer the shops were empty? It’s much better to have busy shops, but people don’t like change.”

The town centre isn’t totally devoid of good news. Days before I came to town, Yella Brick Road – a quirky clothing and homewares shop – was preparing to close its doors, a decision it reversed after loyal shoppers flocked to keep the business afloat. Owner Dannii Paston has been trading in the town centre for 17 years. “Recently, people are just careful with money. We’re a shop where you don’t need anything in here – it’s all treat spends,” she says.

Surprisingly, it was the relocation of Primark, the supposed big, bad clothing behemoth, that Paston believes cost her the most business. “I didn’t think they were our customers, but actually, people would go to Primark for certain things like pants, tights or a cheap dress for the 10-year-old, then come to us for themselves,” she says. Even when the chains were in the town centre, their limited stock couldn’t compete with their warehouse-sized counterparts in Parkgate, says Paston. “It’s a societal shift on how people want to shop. Why would you go into a tiny high-street shop that’s got a quarter of the selection?

She believes supermarkets were the first to pull customers from town. In many large Morrisons branches, for example, you can take your passport photo, wash your clothes in an on-site launderette and even have keys cut while doing the weekly shop. Sainsbury’s has closed 420 Argos high-street shops since 2020, after acquiring its parent company, and shifted them inside its larger stores. “It’s like a little high street,” says Paston.

The out-of-town shopping destination – whether it’s a retail park, mall or outlet – hasn’t always been part of British life. The UK’s first such complex, Gem Superstore, opened in West Bridgford, Nottingham in 1964. Operated by an American company, Government Employees Mart, it brought US-style shopping to Britain – and demand was through the roof. The Goldfinger star Shirley Eaton was brought in for the official opening day, when 30,000 people rushed down its aisles. At 110,000 sq ft, fairly paltry compared with the sprawling shopping complexes that followed, it was more akin to a modern-day large supermarket. Two years later, Asda, then still a fledgling chain of small grocers, bought the site for its first superstore.

London’s Brent Cross Shopping Centre, which opened in 1976, took things to the next level. Traders feared that the 800,000 sq ft behemoth – boasting air conditioning (unheard of at the time) and the triple threat of Fenwick, John Lewis and Marks & Spencer under the same roof – would hammer local trade, and the Labour government tried to thwart the development. But Barnet council, in a Tory stronghold where Margaret Thatcher held her parliamentary seat, gave it the enthusiastic thumbs up. The indoor shopping centre opened the year after Thatcher’s ascendancy to leader of the opposition in 1975. Already there was consensus among local authorities that out-of-town shopping centres would destroy high streets but, after the Tories entered Downing Street in 1979, planning rules were eased. “There is a change of attitude in the 1980s which begins to allow these out-of-town locations,” says Alistair Kefford, the chair of urban studies at Leiden University in the Netherlands. In 1981, there was one out-of-town retail park in the UK. By 1988, there were 90 and at the end of 1996, there were 385.

In the end, the critics were right. “There’s only a certain level of consumer demand within a regional economy,” says Kefford. “If you build a wonderful, shiny, exciting new shopping mall or retail park, it doesn’t create a lot of new shoppers. They just stop going somewhere else.”

The bruising figures bear this out. In 2024, 13,479 shops across the UK closed their doors. While retail accounts for 5% of the UK economy and less than a tenth of employment, an area’s former glory is often starkly highlighted by its decrepit high street. “Dying high streets make people feel ashamed of their place, that their life is falling apart,” says Eddie Blake, a director at the architecture practice Studio Weave.

How to save the high street has become fertile political territory. Parkgate lies within John Healey’s constituency. In 2019, the now-chancellor scolded M&S for shutting its branch in the shopping complex, about a decade after relocating from Rotherham town centre, meaning the retailer would “disappear from the town for the first time in 125 years”. Since entering No 11, Healey has said “blighted” high streets will soon be “on the up”. Last month, Andy Burnham announced £210m in funding to regenerate down-on-their-luck high streets. But Kefford is sceptical. “Retail is a barometer – it’s not an engine. Where you see retail doing well, it’s a sign that the regional economy itself is doing well, but retail by itself won’t make a place wealthy. It’s not an engine of growth because it relies on people spending their disposable income,” he says.

Efforts to turn the ship can often be futile. “Once a location has set off down a particular path, it’s very hard to get out of it. In fact, everything leads further and further down that path. The narrowing range of shops, the growth of empty properties – these are things that snowball and get worse and worse,” says Kefford.

So, are UK high streets doomed? Shops “are probably not going to come back”, says Kefford, but there’s still hope. “In the 1950s and 1960s, town centres sustained loads of uses. There were many more houses and social activities: churches, working men’s clubs, community associations, charities, theatres. We need to think more fundamentally and creatively about what is the point of a town centre,” he says.

This may be good for society, too. Blake says the retail parks and shopping centres, and the cars we use to get to them, contribute to an “atomised culture that makes people feel alone”. A multifunction high street can better facilitate social interaction: “The small-grain interactions of social life are better, higher quality, and more frequent.”

Until then, many of us will be drawn to these bland, uninspiring shopping pens on the fringes of town. On my way to the train station, the No 8 bus pulls up on the high street, having just stopped at Parkgate. Sure enough, the passengers who alight are carrying bags from Primark, TK Maxx and Sports Direct.
