Cocaine overtakes heroin as leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:09:24 GMT

Charities say government ‘must act now’ with cocaine-specific deaths eight times higher than in 2010

Cocaine has overtaken heroin as the biggest cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, figures from the Office for National Statistics show.

The government “must act now to reverse this deadly trend”, charities have said, with 1,233 deaths caused by cocaine last year.

Though drug deaths fell slightly in 2025 compared with the previous year, they “remained historically high” at double the rates of 10 years ago, with cocaine-specific deaths four times higher than a decade ago and eight times higher than in 2010.

The Guardian revealed last week that police were recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving.

Wastewater analysis shows consumption of the class A drug is surging, becoming a more common sight in pubs, festivals and workplaces. It is linked with a rise of 10% in crime associated with cocaine since 2019.

For the first time, cocaine was the drug most involved in drug-related deaths, the figures show, amounting to 22%. This included its use as a powder and deaths caused by injecting the drug or smoking it as crack cocaine.

A total of 64% of cocaine deaths registered were of people over the age of 40, a trend also seen among people seeking help from drug treatment services.

Overall, 5,519 deaths related to drug poisoning were registered last year, 46 fewer than in 2024.

The north-east of England had the highest rates of drug deaths, at 135.2 deaths per million people in 2025, while London had the lowest rate at 58.3 deaths per million. Deaths were five times higher in the most deprived areas than the least deprived.

The statistics also showed rates of deaths from ketamine had risen dramatically from a very low base a decade ago. Ketamine was mentioned in 115 deaths in 2025, compared with 27 in 2020 and seven in 2015.

Niamh Eastwood, the executive director of Release, the UK’s national centre of expertise on drugs and drug laws, said cocaine deaths were “a direct result of policy failures both in the UK and internationally”.

She said: “Cocaine production is at an all-time high; it’s more available, cheaper and purer than ever, despite billions spent on trying to disrupt or eradicate the trade.”

The NGO said the UK’s focus on punishing drug use prevented drug services offering harm-reduction interventions, “meaning there is literally nothing practical on offer for people who use [cocaine]”.

after newsletter promotion

Mike Trace, the chief executive of the social justice charity Forward Trust, said the overall drug-related death rate was “a national scandal” that needed urgent attention.

He said: “That cocaine has risen to the top of the statistics for drug-related deaths should come as no surprise. We’re facing the perfect storm of record levels of production in South America leading to falling prices combined with increasing purity, which means increasing potency and risk.”

Will Haydock, the chief executive of Collective Voice, a drug treatment campaigning charity, said that improvements previously made were “now at risk due to government inaction”.

“For over two years the government has been largely silent on addiction, and has paused the planned investment programme, freezing funding at year-three levels rather than continuing to follow the path laid out by the independent review of drugs, which has amounted to a real-terms cut at a time when we are trying to support more people in treatment than ever before,” he said.

The independent review led by Prof Carol Black was commissioned by Boris Johnson’s government and published in 2021, and recommended an overhaul of drug treatment services.

Haydock said: “If the current prime minister is to achieve his ambitions on a whole range of policy issues – including violence against women and girls, the crisis in the criminal justice system, homelessness, and young people’s employment and mental health – then we must talk about drugs, and specifically treatment and recovery services.

“We urgently need a new drugs strategy with clear priorities, including reducing drug-related deaths. If we get our response to alcohol and other drugs right, we can save and improve hundreds of thousands of lives.”

The best Christmas gifts in the UK for mums, grannies, aunties and friends

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:00:37 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Fancy stationery, cashmere knits and truly beautiful ceramics … we’ve handpicked 61 thoughtful gifts to spoil the mother figure in your life for Christmas 2026

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

A lot of stuff gets marketed as perfect for mums. But be careful, she really doesn’t want a kegel exerciser in her stocking, nor anything that makes washing up easier, unless you just do it instead of her. Also, beware of joke presents – they end up in the bin.

The perfect present for a mother figure of any age – be that a cherished aunt or beloved granny – is, I think, something either personal (which is where personalisation options can be useful) or an elevated version of something you know she likes that she may not treat herself to. Both take a little time and research, which I’ve done for you here.

Whatever your budget, go for quality over quantity. Size does not matter here, so don’t worry if it looks small, as long as it’s chosen with love. If you can rope in others to pool resources – siblings or cousins, perhaps – it can be worth clubbing together to buy one special thing. Whatever you wrap up, the most important bit will always be a handwritten note telling her just why you value her; that will mean more than anything on this list.

If you’ve been forwarded this by someone – as I heard a lot from my Christmas gift guide for mums last year – take note. They like where this is heading …

Martini glass, 220ml x 4

The cool mums have moved on from spicy margs and now are all about at-home martinis. I asked the barman at the Dover in Mayfair, London, what glasses were used for its signature martinis, and it’s these Luigi Bormioli ones (they use the Optica fluted style).

Toast flannel dressing gown

This is on the expensive side but, as with everything from Toast, I find the quality is exceptional, and you know it will last a lifetime (if it does need repairs, Toast has a free mending service). The brushed cotton feels incredibly soft, and the cheery pop of orange makes dark mornings a little brighter.

Glug Glug jug

My glug glug jug is a real party piece – named because it actually makes that sound when you pour it. I’ve had my Villa Bologna Pottery one, handmade in Malta, for years, and it looks lovely on the shelf or table.

Scented candle

For a down-to-earth, nature-lover, the environmentally conscious Cornish-made candle and perfume brand St Eval is a great port of call. My favourite fragrance is the bay and rosemary, and I love that it comes in a little tin, which you can of course reuse.

Merino slipper boots

I’ve worn the Small Home slippers for 10 years: they hug your feet like two tiny blankets. I take them when I go away for the weekend, and even when popping to someone’s house for coffee. I had to replace the pair I wore to hospital when my daughter was born, but I can’t blame the brand for that; my new pair are still going strong five years later. The sizing options make them easy to gift, with small (EU 36-37), medium (38-39) and large (40-41).

Monoware incense holder

A striking incense holder becomes a sculptural presence on a shelf. This one by Monoware in collaboration with London-based designer Byron Friesem is hand-carved from solid aluminium and looks like a piece of jewellery. I love the ritual of lighting the stick and watching it burn down.

Ceramic mug

A well-crafted mug is a thing of pure beauty: I have a hodgepodge collection in my cup drawer and love each one. This piece by Bristol-based ceramicist Nicholas Dover is finished in a soft grey glaze, big enough for a proper cup of tea, and is shaped to fit snugly into a cupped hand.

Scented candle, 312g

If she loves premium candles, like Diptyque, surprise her with a brand she won’t already have. Nette’s Sunday Chess is a really musky, incense-y number that I think smells phenomenal (I don’t love anything too floral), and the simple jar will ultimately make a great pen pot. There are big (£70, linked above) and little (£30) versions to choose from according to budget.

Red gingham eye mask

I love the ethos behind the nightwear brand Siân Esther (I own several pairs of its lovely PJs); it’s a female-run, B Corp-certified brand using responsibly sourced cotton and ethical factories in Portugal. It also gives back through profits (and donated pyjamas) to the Luminary Bakery, which trains women from disadvantaged backgrounds to bake. The sizing of this mask is very generous, totally covering your eyes, and not too tight on the head.

Alphabet brush pot

My husband and I have monogrammed alphabet brush pots with our initials on, and have at times used them on our desk or just on the kitchen shelf to add a pop of colour. They’re fun, personal and useful.

Faux flowers

Letterbox flowers were a great invention, but I find they often arrive looking tired and don’t last that long. Instead, I’ve been building up a collection of Ett Hem London’s realistic faux flowers. I love this (50cm) sprig of white foxgloves for the winter months, and they come in an elegant box that makes them feel special.

For more, read our guide to the best flower deliveries in the UK

Photobooth frame

I came across the brand Mora Interiors, which has fun options such as frames for a strip of photo booth pictures, or a mount that slightly off-centres the photo, meaning they look more statement than bog-standard (you can also create bespoke frames). I like the colour selection too: I’ve paired a pink mount and a burgundy frame on the wall (next to a frame and mount in the reverse colours) and love the combination.

Hand cleanser, 270ml

Pelegrims makes luxurious soap using waste products from the wine-making process from a family-run winery in Kent. This soap has English Ortega grape extract, which helps repair and hydrate the skin, but also smells delicious – rose and tomato-y. You can buy refill pouches so the glass bottle doesn’t go to waste.

Serra ceramic talisman

This is the most intriguing little gift: a lovely jar to store trinkets in with a ceramic lid that you drop fragrance on to. I’ve found one drop lasts a couple of weeks: every time I walk into my living room, I’m met by the most delicious scent, created by Reia and designed with Sister by Studio Ashby. Each talisman, which comes with a 30ml scent refill, is made to order and arrives hand-drenched, so when she unwraps it, she’ll smell it immediately. It’s expensive, I know, for something that perhaps on first glance looks just like a box, but honestly gorgeous.

Hardcover photo album

I have longstanding photo guilt that nine years of my children’s lives are stuck as memories on my phone. I’ve started to tackle the problem, creating a book a year with Popsa, but what a gift it would be if someone else were to do that for me. The app is easy to use; it can lay the photos and book all out for you using AI, though I prefer to arrange as I want – which takes longer. Hardback looks nicest, and more permanent, but even a softback is a joy to receive and flick through.

Photobooks are from £22, but use the code GUARDIAN50 for 50% off until 1 Feb

Kaweco classic sport fountain pen

On a mission to write more letters, I recently bought a Kaweco fountain pen from Choosing Keeping, a wonderful stationery shop where you can get lost for hours (though I have since found it cheaper online). It’s a lovely thing to hold and use – and has definitely encouraged me to write more. I recommend a cheery red.

Personalised leather notebook

This personalised leather notebook from the British brand Priestleys is up there with my ultimate Christmas gifts; it’s thick and substantial-feeling, hand‑cut and hand‑finished in its studio. You can choose initials (up to three is free) or a name, date or short phrase to emboss on the outside for £5. You can also select charms from £2.99. The presentation box makes it feel even more deluxe. I’ll be buying this for everyone.

How to Make a Woman by Marie Darrieussecq

A little blue Fitzcarraldo book poking out of a bag is always a good sign. How to Make a Woman tells the story of two friends, Rose and Solange, growing up in the Basque region of France in the 1980s, from teenage years into adulthood. It’s a brilliant portrait of the complexities of female friendship, and feels akin to Elena Ferrante’s writing.

A5 canvas pouch

Stationery addicts and neat freaks will get excited for this: an A5 cotton canvas pouch designed to store notebooks in (but works just as well for travel documents). As someone who has a pouch for everything (purse, keys and iPhone cable, for instance, in my daily handbag; a bigger one for gym kit), I love this. The brand, Mark + Fold, is a serious IYKYK: founded by Amy Cooper-Wright because she couldn’t find the perfect diary for herself. I already buy a diary and wall planner from it every year, but am adding the pouch to my wishlist.

Wildness, Myth, Mystery and Mischief by Anna McCracken

For a mystical mother, this is a “witchy field guide” to the hidden world of birdsong, moon cycles and stargazing that gently suggests ways to reconnect with nature, even if you live in the middle of a city.

Kiltane necktie

A wool necktie is one of the most useful pieces for a winter wardrobe: it can transform an outfit in seconds. I have several Kiltane cashmere versions – a cheery red, a brown and this burgundy – and they are so soft I find I can wear them all day. You could add in the matching fingerless gloves (£35) to make a complete package.

Wrist warmers

If she’s a fan of Claudia Winkleman’s style on The Traitors (and who isn’t), then these luxurious, knitted wrist warmers are a nod to the trend. All the wool from Herd pieces is traceable to Bluefaced Leicester sheep from the north-west of England, made into yarn within 150 miles of the farms and knitted in England. These wrist warmers are one size, soft and durable (I’ve had a pair for two years).

Hooded scarf

While I couldn’t pull off last year’s knitted bonnet trend, this hooded scarf is a more wearable and flattering take. It’s not wool, but it is soft and chunky. Navy is the most flattering colour to pick.

Chunky wool socks

I’ve got several pairs of chunky, knitted socks from Rock and Ruby. They are lovely and sturdy, in a range of joyful colours (I’m particularly into the red), and will be a welcome upgrade to your mum’s sock drawer.

Ada crewneck cardigan

This is a splurge (unless there are siblings to divvy it up between), but it will be a lifelong gift. I had & Daughter’s Ada cardigan in my mental basket for two years until I bought it in cherry red in January, and I don’t regret it for a second. The Ada cardigan is a lovely crew neck style, but with a roomier fit than most and works with everything in my wardrobe.

Scrunchie

A big blousy scrunchie looks just as good on the wrist as in the hair; this by the cult nightie brand If Only If is made from cotton voile to match its oak floral print, but is perfectly acceptable as a gift in its own right.

Hair claw

The speedily assembled “mum bun” is often an essential hairstyle, and a pretty claw clip makes it look more intentional. This collaboration between Shrimps and Tort brings together the creativity of its two female founders. The brown claw is my favourite for a subtle, go-with-anything piece, and the matching slides catch stray hairs, which make me look more polished on the school run than I often feel.

Glasses case

This is a premium update for something a glasses-wearer uses every day. I have a Stow London bag, and love the quality of the leather (I’ve really thrown it around in a thorough test). This case is handmade in its Spanish workshop and can be personalised with up to three initials, which makes it feel like a special gift. Carol Lovell helped to start Stow London with a Kickstarter campaign in her 40s. I always love a midlife reinvention story.

Antler overnight bag

If the mother in your life loves travelling, this is an excellent overnight bag: sturdy and chic in its own right, with enough space for all her packing needs for a weekend. Plus, it has the most ingenious strap on the back, which allows you to hook it on to a wheeled suitcase (any size, any brand). It’s one of those gifts whose true value may not be fully realised upon unwrapping, but I honestly couldn’t travel without it.

Shearling hot-water bottle cover

For those who feel the cold, this shearling hot-water bottle cover is total luxury. Handmade from soft New Zealand wool, it’s cosy, and the quality is excellent. I have one attached to my lap from November to February.

Apothecary Warmth eau de parfum, 50ml

With its notes of cardamom, cinnamon, cedarwood and sandalwood, M&S’s Apothecary Warmth is an impressive dupe for the far pricier Le Labo Santal 33 fragrance, which I love.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Rocco undereye masks, pack of three

Lots of the eye masks you see influencers wearing on Instagram are budget-busting, but these by the new beauty brand Rocco are more affordable, and instantly perked up my eyes. Founder Laura Jackson says they have special non-slip formulations, so I did what I tell my children not to do and hung upside down off the sofa with them on – I can confirm, no slippage.

Emma Lewisham hand crème, 75ml

A hand cream at Christmas is always a welcome gift; whose hands aren’t dry and cracked? There are lots of hand creams to choose from, but this from Emma Lewisham is particularly lovely. I’m already a fan of her skincare, and this promises to treat hands and nails, plus it smells of tomato leaves and geranium, which are two of my favourites. It sinks in immediately, leaving no greasiness but just a light scent.

Hair pudding, 75ml

I didn’t know I needed pudding for my hair, but this tub has transformed my locks. You use the tiniest amount to smooth flyaways (which get worse as you develop greys, I’ve discovered), while a bigger blob works as a mask, leaving your hair smooth and shiny for days. Plus, the tub is an extremely pleasing shape and colour.

Bath salts, 400g

These restorative bath salts are a serious treat, with magnesium and lavender among other relaxing botanicals; I’ve found the ritual of pouring them into a hot bath deeply soothing. A big tin lasts a long time, can be refilled, and looks chic on the side of the tub.

Victoria Beckham mascara

Few of us can splash out on Victoria Beckham’s clothes, but her beauty line is a more affordable treat. The Vast Lash mascara is particularly good – it glides on smoothly, lifts your lashes naturally, and feels like a luxe present.

Magnesium butter, 120ml

If she struggles with sleep, I can recommend Dreem Distillery’s CBD drops, which make you feel kind of spacey and relaxed. But a more budget-friendly gift is the magnesium butter. It’s a lovely nightly ritual (which I’ve also used on my kids), and smells divine.

Horseshoe ring

This ring brings a bit of statement, but can be worn every day and looks a lot more expensive than it is. I’ve got several pieces from reasonably priced L’Atelier 73, including three of its Talisman Amours – little bracelets handmade in Jaipur – which I bought for me and my daughters to wear.

Charm earrings

Laura Vann is a wonderful jewellery designer based in Birmingham whose collections are art-deco inspired – her newest is an ode to her city – and look elevated and polished. While her fine jewellery pieces are an investment, she has a lovely line of more purse-friendly gifts, such as these sculptural mixed-metal earrings which were, touchingly, inspired by the ridged lids of vintage perfume bottles on her mother’s dressing table.

Gold bracelet with personalised disc

A simple gold chain bracelet suits everyone, and can be personalised with initials engraved into the pendant. I’ve got this in a necklace version, with the initials of my first daughter on the first disc, with another disc added for my second child. I absolutely love them – and still wear them 10 years on – but am now eyeing up this 18k gold vermeil bracelet.

Cord bracelet with initials

I love the sister-founded British jewellery brand Otiumberg and have built up a collection over the years. One of my favourite pieces is this simple cord bracelet with my daughters’ initials on it, which I stack with other jewels or just wear alone.

Silver and gold ear cuff

An ear cuff makes you feel cool, at any age. Scrape your hair back on a bad-hair day, slip one on and suddenly feel put together. This mixed-metal one from Astley Clarke looks more expensive than it is (gift nirvana), and is comfortable enough that you forget you’re wearing it.

Birthstone earrings

I previously bought these birthstone earrings for a November birthday, and they went down exceptionally well. There’s something special about personalising your gift, and birthstones are a great alternative to letters on a chain or inscribing something on a pendant. These are subtle, made from 18k gold, and could be worn every day – reminding her of you.

Fingerprint signet ring

This is so charming, and perfect for a mother or grandmother of small children: a 14k gold vermeil signet ring with a little person’s fingerprint on. For dog mothers, there’s the option of a snout print, too. Get a wiggle on if you want it by Christmas, as it takes 6-8 weeks to make. Otherwise, there are lots of other charming and reasonably priced jewellery options by the brand.

Mini T-bar chain

Tilly Sveaas’s T-bar designs – inspired by her great-great-uncle’s pocket watch chain – have garnered a celeb fanbase (Taylor Swift, Kylie Jenner, Elle Macpherson among them), but because of their historic reference, they don’t look like a trend piece. This lighter version of her chunkier styles is a great size for someone who doesn’t want it to be a big, blingy statement; it’s more budget-friendly than others in the collection, too.

Coffee

I start dreaming about my morning coffee the night before, and I love trying new blends. Spring Valley Coffee is among Africa’s few B Corp-certified coffee producers and also one of the few coffee brands in the world to keep everything from cultivation and farm management to cherry collection, processing, roasting and packaging all in Kenya, which equals traceability … and money going to those on the ground. Plus, it’s delicious. I particularly love Masara because it tastes almost chocolatey.

Cocktail picks, set of four

A friend bought me these cocktail picks for my birthday, and they not only look like little gems individually but are also sweet to have out when you have guests over. I’ve used them a lot.

Brew flask, 350ml

This 350ml hot drinks flask is ideal for commuting, is made from recycled plastic and steel and funds the collection of “ocean‑bound” plastic. It’s also great for holidays or just taking a cuppa out into the garden. There are 13 colours to choose from, along with three exclusive Liberty prints, and you can add engraving (from £6). I’ve got several Ocean Bottle bottles and cups at home, and they really feel made to last.

Ottolenghi x Citizens of Soil extra virgin olive oil, 500ml

Olive oil is having its wine moment, and a fine bottle of it is a treaty gift. Citizens of Soil, founded by olive oil sommelier Sarah Vachon, sources traceable oils directly from regenerative farmers across Europe. In an olive oil she developed with Yotam Ottolenghi, the flavours are ones he remembered from childhood summers spent in Tuscany and Umbria. Utterly delicious.

Sapling climate-positive vodka, 70cl

Sapling’s “climate positive” vodka is made in the UK using organic winter wheat that’s grown slowly through the seasons, and the brand plants a tree for every bottle sold. It tastes good, with a silky smooth finish ideal for martini lovers.

Mother Root aperitif, 500ml

There’s now a wide range of alcohol-free drinks available but, to my tastes, many are too sweet. Mother Root’s ginger switchel gives you a spicy kick, is deliciously bitter and looks handsome on the shelf. If you want to give extra, wrap it up with a small bottle of soda water, an orange and a sprig of rosemary so that it’s ready to serve.

Anna Jones online vegetarian cookery course

To me, Anna Jones is a total kitchen legend, and while your mum may already have her recipe books, this online video course might be a welcome gift for vegetarians and those wanting to expand their repertoire. I’ve taken this – and other Create Academy courses – before and it’s excellent.

The Kitchen Book by Ella Risbridger

This is a gorgeous book filled with more than just recipes, but oh boy, will you want to cook them all. Risbridger cleverly divvies up ideas into categories for when you might need them – a night on the sofa, for instance, you might fancy sticky-crispy Korean tofu, pistachio chilli, pumpkin and raisin roasted rice, while if you’ve got a big group of hungry friends coming around, it could be sheet-pan leek latkes, pig cheek and queen bean burritos, paired with smoky rosemary palomas. I enjoyed reading and bookmarking, then making her creations.

Tinned fish selection box

There has been an outpouring of love for luxury tinned fish among foodies and, from my extensive research, I think a selection from the Tinned Fish Market is the best: the fish tastes amazing, the producers have thorough sustainability credentials and the packaging is so pretty you want to display it. A one-off hamper is a brilliant way to explore its products, though personally I’d be thrilled with a monthly box of anchovies (£38, subscription).

Garlic crusher

For the enthusiastic home chef, this hand-crafted garlic crusher is so handsome it deserves a spot on the kitchen shelf. It’s made from stainless steel, solid walnut and brass in Katto’s Sheffield workshop. Having just invested myself, I love the ritualistic rocking motion and that I’m no longer in danger of slicing my fingers when chopping garlic.

Twinkling lights chocolate selection, box of 10

Every chocolate from Irish brand Grá is handmade and individually hand-painted using ethically sourced Valrhona chocolate, Irish cream and butter, and local touches like Achill Island sea salt and Irish honey. I loved the Twinkling Lights selection: 10 beautifully coloured chocolates peeking out from their pink box, each with a delicious filling.

Beats 360 over-ear headphones

This is a spendy pick, but could be one to club together on. For those who prefer over-ear headphones (I’m increasingly seeing women in the weights rack at the gym in them), I’ve tested the Beats 360, and they are really very good. They have Beats’ active noise-cancelling technology, but what I really like is the interchangeable ear cushions because I’ve found it’s always those that get damaged first.

Nano power bank portable charger

No, this isn’t a glamorous present, but it could end up being MVP of the Christmas season. I take my power bank around with me daily – despite being the latest model, my phone doesn’t manage to make it through the day – but this is an even smaller version that would fit in the smallest of bags.

Brick app blocker

If she is concerned about her phone usage, this could be a helpful present. It’s a little device you programme via an app to help you block certain websites. You tap the phone on the device to turn on the block and have to physically tap it again to unblock it – creating a small friction against mindless scrolling when you just picked up the phone to look at a recipe. I’ve found my Brick – which is stuck to my fridge – really helpful.

Earphones travel pouch

AirPods are easy to lose, so for the woman who keeps shelling out on replacements (like me), this cute case for your pods would make a sweet gift. It also clips on to a bag.

Personalised leather iPhone case

A new phone case is always a welcome update: they all get tatty eventually. I’ve stumbled across this husband-and-wife Cambridge-based brand that sells beautiful leather tech accessories – such as this case, which can be personalised.

For more, read our guide to the best homemade Christmas gifts that anyone can make

Christmas shopping can be tough, but the Filter is here to help. We’ve been testing Christmas presents all year to help you find thoughtful, creative and genuinely brilliant gifts for everyone on your list. Browse our other gift guides for hundreds more tried-and-tested ideas, from gifts you can make yourself to toys for every age group.

Jessica Salter is a lifestyle journalist who covers fashion, food, interiors, tech and wellness. Along with writing serious stories about company founders – often women – and brands – particularly those that do good in the world – she’s often asked for tips on the best gifts. As a mother of two herself, she is also in the ideal position to help you pick the perfect present for your mum

The worst two words in the dead of night? ‘Motorway closed’

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:00:37 GMT

You are shunted into side streets, crawling along, united with your fellow drivers in wordless despair. Last week, at 2am, my spirit broke

The worst three words in the transport lexicon are often said to be “rail”, “replacement” and “bus”, in that order. But there’s worse. “Motorway closed” is worse. At least with rail replacement buses you get fair warning, on booking apps and whatnot. You can resolve to embrace the pain or, more likely, abandon the journey. Motorway closures, in the dead of night, invariably come as a nasty surprise.

Waze, Google Maps, Apple Maps, etc can reliably get you from a car park in Penzance to a cul-de-sac in East Kilbride, but often can’t tell the difference between an open motorway and a shut motorway in the middle of the night. Football fans know all about this. You travel across the country for an evening match, and you lose. The prospect of a long drive home blackens your mood further, but as you slope away from the ground you cling to one consoling thought: at least there won’t be much traffic on the road. And this is true, but light motorway traffic looks rather like heavy traffic once it’s bullied on to side roads. Out of nowhere come the sign, the cones, the arc lights, and off you go, ushered with the other hapless nightbirds into the slow, black void. Dispossessed, demoralised, you crawl along unfamiliar roads, united in wordless despair.

To be fair, you can do some pre-planning on the National Highways, Traffic Wales and Traffic Scotland sites – if you have a knack for navigating not-especially-intuitive internet offerings. But as for satnav, often as not, when you need it most it lets you down.

Last Thursday night, for reasons too complex to go into, I had to get from Malta to Gatwick to the West Midlands and thence to Liverpool by Friday morning. The flight was an hour late and, deliciously, there was then a half-hour wait for a bus to the terminal. Bowed but not yet beaten, while my suitcase took its sweet time reaching the carousel, I checked all the map apps available to me and they all gave my route a clean bill of health. No closures. Great.

It had gone midnight when I set off. As soon as I got on the M23 an electronic sign came leering out of the mist: M25 closed after Reigate. Surely not. Please let it be just a rogue sign on the blink, which has been known to happen. But no. Off the motorway I was firmly ushered into deepest darkest Surrey, ignoring persistent entreaties from two different satnavs to stop being so silly and return to the M25. I yelled at the screens, something along the lines of, “I’d love to get back on the bastard motorway, you useless morons, but they won’t let me!”

If AI is so clever – and I assume it has a hand in the operation of satnav services – then how come it doesn’t know the M25 is shut overnight? Come the zombie apocalypse, with AI warrior goons on the rampage, we should entrust our defence to the people who execute these night closures. Truly, it is miraculous how they can muster a battalion of heavy machinery, an army of hi-vis’ed workers and a million cones, all without AI seeing any of it. Now that’s what I call a stealth operation.

Relations with my satnavs now having broken down, I had no choice but to trust the signs advising me to follow the yellow triangle. Or was it a circle? Or a square? I’ve always wondered what those things were for. It was at 2am, lost and alone, groping my way around Epsom, that my spirit broke. At a filling station I bought pastries and crisps, ate them, felt a lot worse, and soldiered on into the night.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Where Trump and Republicans lost the midterms – a visual analysis of the key states

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:34:12 GMT

The Democrats have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives. These charts and maps reveal the key trends and races behind this result

Live results from all 50 states

Send us your questions about the midterm results

The Republicans have lost seven Senators, 25 House districts and five governor races.

As of 9.25am Eastern Time (ET) on Wednesday, more than 1,900 of nearly 2,500 counties with Senate elections had returned more than 90% of their votes. Americans did not turn out in significant numbers for the Republicans amid high fuel prices and dissatisfaction with the president.

This allowed the Democrats to pick up a number of seats – and take back control of the US House of Representatives and Senate. Here’s how it happened.

In the Senate the midterm results have given Democrats the ability to put a serious check on Trump's agenda – including blocking any new appointments to the supreme court or his cabinet.

Republicans had previously held a majority of 53 seats out of 100 – but this has now been emphatically overturned.

Thirty-five seats were on the ballot. Senators serve six-year terms, with a third facing voters at each two-year election cycle.

In practice, the battle for the Senate was fought across a very small map.

The Cook Political Report – a prominent US election forecaster – had listed six seats as tossups: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas.

Democrats had to flip at least four seats that were held by Republicans to gain a majority. They surpassed this target.

In an early sign of the Democrats’ momentum, the party won the Senate race in Texas, a longstanding Republican stronghold. In the run-up to the election, polls had shown a razor-thin lead for the Democratic candidate.

The actual result was, in fact, record-breaking – with James Talarico winning the seat by more than 10 points. No Democrat had won a Senate seat in Texas since 1988.

Texas has voted Republican in presidential elections for decades. The last Democratic presidential candidate to win the state was Jimmy Carter in 1976. In 2024, Trump won 56% of the vote to Kamala Harris’s 42%.

Kansas has elected its first Democratic senator since 1932. The state was classed as a toss-up before the vote, and the Democrats ended up securing it with a 21-point swing compared with the 2024 presidential election.

Adam Hamilton's victory was a seismic defeat of outgoing Republican Senator Roger Marshall in a deep-red state.

The Republicans are used to regularly achieving winning margins in the double digits in Kansas, and the state only became a toss-up later in the campaign as Donald Trump's approval ratings slid further.

Roy Cooper became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from North Carolina since 2008.

It recorded one of the biggest swings to the Democrats, with a swing of 22 points since 2024.

Every single county in North Carolina swung to the Democrats in the election.

Several House districts in North Carolina were still too close to call at the point of publishing this article. However, the Senate race flipping to the Democrats indicates that they are likely to take several of the remaining House races in this state as well. This would be despite Republicans successfully redrawing the state's boundaries in their favour before the vote.

James Talarico’s focus on billionaires in Texas was echoed in Michigan where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won. His victory came despite a controversial endorsement of the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, by the Democrat Haley Stevens prior to the election.

At the presidential level, Michigan remains a swing state. Trump won it in 2016 and 2024, but lost it to Joe Biden in 2020. But El-Sayed’s win extends the Democrats’ long run of Senate victories in Michigan: no Republican has won a seat there since 1994.

Of the 2,500 counties in states with Senate elections, just over 1,900 counties had enough votes to be accurately analysed. The vast majority of these swung to the Democrats, when comparing against the 2024 presidential election results.

The biggest state swings were recorded in Texas, Rhode Island, North Carolina and Mississippi.

On a county level, several counties in Texas - such as the Starr, Webb and Duval counties - and Kansas's Seward county saw swings of more than 45 points from the Republicans to the Democrats.

In terms of demographics, counties with a high proportion of urban residents swung towards the Democrats.

In the metropolitan area of New York, New Jersey's Passaic county recorded a tight Trump win with 49.8% of the vote in 2024. In the 2026 Senate race, the Democrats won 62.3% of the vote compared with the Republicans' 34.3%.

Another driving factor in the election was the number of younger voters in an area. When there was a greater share of people aged under 30, the Democrats enjoyed larger swings.

A key example can be seen in Riley county in the swing state of Kansas, home to Kansas State University and the US army's Fort Riley, where 42% of the population is under 30.

Harris carried the county with a very fine margin in 2024, but after a 19-point swing to the Democrats in 2026, they managed to win 59.1% of the vote.

One of the most important trends in the early results was how areas with higher proportions of Hispanic voters swung away from Trump in comparison with the 2024 vote.

Starr county in southern Texas, where about 97% of residents are Hispanic or Latino, demonstrates this trend. Trump won in this county in 2024 with 58% of the vote, but this year it returned to the Democrats in the Senate election, with Talarico taking 77% of the votes.

The House of Representatives will now be controlled by the Democrats after they gained more than 25 seats in the midterm elections.

The House of Representatives was controlled by the Republicans before the elections. Every seat was up for election, as members only serve two-year terms.

The Democrats managed to win the House by claiming almost a clean sweep across the 40 races ranked as competitive by the Cook Political Report before the election.

As the campaign developed, more races moved against the incumbent Republican party, meaning that the Democrats were even able to win seats that the Republicans had held for over a decade, such as Kentucky's 6th and North Carolina's 11th district.

An exit poll conducted by the Associated Press and US broadcasters provided a first look at how different groups of voters shifted nationwide. It indicated that young people, urban voters and households with lower incomes had swung most heavily towards the Democrats.

These swings helped Hakeem Jeffries' Democrats claim seats including three out of four of Iowa's districts, four districts in Pennsylvania and two counties along the Texan border with Mexico.

The incumbent Republican Ann Wagner lost Missouri's second congressional district, with 46.2% of the votes against the Democrats' 51.1%.

This is despite the district being redrawn by Republicans ahead of this election, to give the party a further advantage. While the county voted for Trump with a margin of eight points in 2024, the new boundaries would have given him a margin of 11 points.

A former ambassador under George W Bush, Wagner held the seat from 2013. Her race was ranked as "likely Republican" before the vote.

The Republicans also lost Indiana's fifth district, a seat they had held for more than 30 years. The Democrats' JD Ford beat incumbent Victoria Spartz with 51.7% of the vote to 48.3%.

The differences in the total number of votes cast for the House candidate between the 2024 presidential year - which always has higher turnout - and this year is revealing. The Republican candidate's votes dropped from almost 203,000 to 134,000, while the Democratic candidate's votes held steady, changing from 136,000 to 134,000.

Marcy Kaptur won re-election in north-western Ohio, extending the longest tenure of any woman in Congress. She has held her seat since 1983 and is one of nearly two dozen Democrats representing districts Trump won in 2024.

Her victory was also in a district with newly redrawn boundaries that increased Republican lean, showing that some voters were still willing to split their tickets between parties.

Nationwide, a record number of Democratic women were elected to the House of Representatives.

Across the nation, there was an unprecedented level of politically motivated redistricting in the run-up to the 2026 midterms.

Nine states redrew congressional boundaries, some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Analysis suggested that Republicans would gain more seats overall.

This redistricting has been subject to several legal challenges. A Democratic gerrymander in Virginia was struck down by the state supreme court, and the US supreme court rejected a Republican attempt in Missouri.

Democratic victories in redrawn districts in Florida, North Carolina, Alabama and Texas all presented proof that Republicans' gerrymandering did not yield the gains they had hoped for.

The Democrats look set to finish the elections enjoying a “blue wave” of wins, even in districts that Trump won by wide margins in 2024. It leaves them with a double-digit majority in the House and a larger than expected majority in the Senate.

This follows a historic precedent: all recent presidents have lost control of a chamber in midterm elections, including Trump in the 2018 election.

However, the scale of the defeat – with the president's party losing seats they have held for decades – by far surpasses results from recent elections.

There are still other potential losses for the Republicans in the Senate, but as things stand, the president's party has already lost seven seats, making it already the worst performance in the Senate since 1994.

The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP calls the winner in a state when they determine that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.

Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days as more data on voter turnout becomes available.

Official results can take days or weeks to be fully finalised. This is often because of the verification process of absentee, mail-in and provisional ballots. In some states, mail-in ballots can be received and counted several days after election day.

County results are only included in the interactive if more than 90% of precincts within the county have reported ballot data.

The shift in margin compares county-level results for the 2026 Senate election against the 2024 presidential election. It only assesses the change in margin between the two major parties, and discounts votes for third-party candidates.

Demographic data used has been sourced from the US Census American Community Survey 2024 five-year estimates. Urban and rural classification is sourced from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Congressional District Health Dashboard. Historical election data is sourced from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Redistricted boundaries are sourced from the Redistricting Data Hub and All About Redistricting.

‘He lent me his RSC Oberon cape for my school play’: Patrick Stewart remembered by readers

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:15:47 GMT

From coaching youth community theatre to supporting Huddersfield football club and delighting sci-fi fans at graduation ceremonies, the actor is fondly remembered

Patrick Stewart – a life in pictures

On Star Trek, Patrick Stewart could make anyone feel hopeful for humanity

Patrick Stewart brought gravitas and complexity to the screen

‘He stood for the best of us’: William Shatner and more pay tribute

What I always loved about Patrick was that he genuinely seemed connected to where he came from despite his global success. Once a Yorkshireman, always a Yorkshireman. I was lucky enough to see him at the Royal Shakespeare Company performing Hamlet, Merchant of Venice, and in Godot at the Haymarket, which is the only time the play has been so brilliantly performed as to make sense to me. I loved that he supported causes he clearly believed in, such as tackling domestic violence. He remained a good old-fashioned socialist. Got to applaud that. Shirley, 55, West Yorkshire

I managed to secure front row tickets to see Matilda in Stratford-upon-Avon for my daughter’s ninth birthday. Throughout the first half of the show, a huge booming laugh that was strangely familiar kept grabbing my attention and, when we got up for the interval, there was Sir Patrick a few rows behind us and we walked together to the bar. Completely starstruck, I asked him if he wouldn’t mind me taking a photo of him with my daughter to keep as a memory of her birthday, and he happily agreed. Instead of leaving it there, he stayed chatting with us for much of the interval, asking her about how she was enjoying the show, telling her what it was like to be on that very stage and making us both laugh. That photo is brought out every year on my daughter’s birthday – she’s now 24, and it’s as special a memory as ever. It was such a joy of an encounter, meeting someone you think is special, only to find out that they are everything they seem and more. Emily, 55, Henley

I grew up eating lunch in Stewart hall at Mirfield Free grammar school almost every day, the same secondary school Sir Patrick Stewart once attended. He would often return to give talks, fondly recounting how a teacher first encouraged him towards the stage. His humility, warmth and genuine passion always left an impression on me. Growing up where we did, struggling at school, the idea of achieving something extraordinary often felt like a distant fantasy. Yet here was someone who had walked the same corridors, proving that your beginnings need never define your future. His portrayals of Picard and Professor Xavier helped ignite my lifelong love of science fiction and the possibilities beyond our own world. But perhaps his greatest inspiration was simply showing a young lad from Yorkshire that even the most distant stars were worth reaching for. Thom, London

Star Trek and Jean-Luc bind me to my sons. With a four-year age gap, finding things they both enjoyed was a challenge, but without fail, every week on Mondays from 6.10-7pm, my boys and I would gather on the sofa to watch Star Trek. It was a time of closeness I have never forgotten. Not only the stories but the moral imperatives behind them, including challenging stereotypes and doing what was right, which Patrick Stewart portrayed with such conviction. Both sons, now aged 40 and 44, texted me last night before I’d even seen the news. We shared in the sadness of the end of an era. Shared memories of childhood. I shed some tears. Ann, St Albans

Sir Patrick showed the world that working-class men from forgotten towns like Huddersfield could be cultured, intelligent and loved around the world. He never forgot his home town, despite living in California, and would regularly be back in England supporting his beloved Terriers. And what a versatile actor who could move between sci-fi and Shakespeare. Colin, 44, Tameside

I was at the Bristol Old Vic theatre school a few years after Pat. I was the assistant stage manager at the Old Vic Company at the Kings theatre. Our paths crossed regularly and we were at the Royal Shakespeare Company together. When he became a millionaire during Star Trek, I used to pitch him ideas for his company Flying Freehold. He would always respond to my messages. He gave donations to struggling theatre companies. He was a kind and generous man. Roger, 82, retired stage manager, Catalonia

Patrick was one of the incredibly generous actors who gave his time to coach us at Chiswick Youth theatre in the mid-80s. It was a free community group for local kids drawn mainly from our failing comprehensive. Patrick and his then wife Sheila, a renowned choreographer, helped us with our production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. I was Oberon and he coached me one-to-one for weeks. We bonded over my strong ideas of how to play the part. He would smile quietly, with a slight twinkle in his eye, listen to my adolescent certainties and then we’d move on. I had no idea who he was; he was just Patrick, a nice bloke who was an actor with this VOICE! His warmth, support, energy, insights into speaking Shakespeare, and exacting standards made it all uniquely memorable. Just before our first night, he brought in an incredible diaphanous cloak, which he lent to me – a 15-year-old kid. He’d worn it as Oberon at the Royal Shakespeare Company. I wore it every night for the duration of our week’s run at our school. Daniel, Cambridge

During Covid, Patrick Stewart read and posted on Facebook a Shakespeare sonnet a day for 100 days. I eagerly waited for those posts. They helped us all get through that dark time. His voice was unforgettable. And he will always be Captain Picard to me. Anonymous, Washington, US

Just under 20 years ago, I graduated from the University of Huddersfield. Patrick Stewart was chancellor of the university at that time, and as fresh-faced 18-year-olds we converted the cleaning cupboard of our first year halls into a dedicated shrine to all things Patrick Stewart. As chancellor, he often made an appearance at the graduation ceremonies – but usually for the drama department, and because we were graduating in music production from the department of computing and engineering, we thought little about it. However, while we were all seated, waiting for the ceremony to start, a ripple spread through the auditorium. Patrick Stewart had been spotted outside!

Lo and behold, we were going to receive our degree from Captain Picard! Excitement buzzed around the room as we all tried to decide if we should say “Make it so” while shaking his hand, or give a Vulcan salute while walking across the stage. He was so kind and gracious, he even gave the “captain’s log” speech in a thick Yorkshire accent. He took each “Make it so” and “Earl Grey, hot” in his stride, and I’m pretty sure he made the entire computing and engineering department’s day – we were all nerds. Sam, 40, climate resilience practitioner, Vancouver, Canada

Kemi Badenoch says Africans should apologise for slavery. She should read a history book

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:01:27 GMT

Enslavement’s devastating impact on Caribbean and African nations means that cross-diasporic solidarity has become central in addressing its legacy

Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Despite reports that the UK attempted to keep reparations off the formal agenda for the Commonwealth summit attended by King Charles and the UK prime minister, they are in the air. British Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch is among those detractors who have argued that it is African nations who should apologise for the transatlantic slave trade. It may seem like a spectacular case of whataboutery (it is) but it also touches on an enduring tension in some Black communities surrounding African involvement in capturing and enslaving people. This week, I speak to two historians to sort fact from fiction.

When discussing slavery, we should be “honest about the whole history”, Kemi Badenoch wrote in a recent post on X. Her statement comes after months of mounting pressure on Britain’s monarchy and politicians to formally apologise for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, and offer reparations to affected Caribbean nations. Badenoch continued: “If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?”

While the question was asked in bad faith, many within Black communities are unable to confidently answer it. In conversations with African and Caribbean colleagues at the Guardian, plenty of us experience division within our communities around the subject of African people’s participation in enslavement. The topic can be incredibly sensitive and difficult to tackle without a firm grounding in the history and political economy of the transatlantic slave trade. Yet, the experts I spoke to made it clear why African nations should not be held to the same standard as European countries and the US when atoning for their historical crimes.

Slavery was a system created by Europe and the US

Writer and historian Panashe Chigumadzi says that in understanding enslavement and who should be held to account, it is crucial that we see it as a system. Chigumadzi – who was the architect of the continental African Union’s landmark reparations framework – tells me that the trade was a structure that legally positioned all Black people as enslaveable property. No one was safe from this, whether on the continent or in the diaspora, king or commoner. She says: “[Badenoch] assumes Africans are ‘co-defendants’ and not ‘co-plaintiffs’ in prosecuting the case for a crime that fundamentally restructured the world as we know it, and created what we now know as the modern world racial capitalist system.”

Bayo Holsey, an associate professor of African American studies who specialises in west Africa at Emory University, agrees. She emphasises the overarching system that created a slave economy: the colonisation of the Caribbean and the Americas. “Europeans created the demand for enslaved labour,” the academic tells me. “The Atlantic slave trade would not have existed without this demand.”

In the latter part of the 17th century, demand for African captives on plantations had grown so much that capturing enslaved people was only possible through raiding and warfare. Given this, UK reparations would not only help repair the harm that the descendants of enslaved people have inherited, but would redress what Holsey describes as “the ill-gotten wealth of western nations”.

African people were victims of enslavement, too

We must also look at present day wealth – the economic growth of many European nations and the US was facilitated by enslavement. “The slave trade shaped the economic advantages that these countries enjoy today,” Holsey tells me. The case is fundamentally not the same in Africa. “Much of the wealth that select African individuals gained from the slave trade evaporated with the onset of colonial rule,” she says.

Africa was victimised by the slave trade too. Holsey tells me that while a small number of African people engaged in slave trading and accrued wealth, many more were victims of the trade. “They experienced fear, social instability, and the loss of loved ones as a result,” she says. Estimates based on the Slave Voyages database suggest that approximately 12.5 million enslaved Africans were forced aboard ships bound for the Americas, of whom 10.7 million survived the crossing. These figures exclude those who died before embarkation.

This depopulation destabilised the west and west-central coasts of the continent, devastating entire societies. Chigumadzi argues that the “scramble for Africa” in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the continent was invaded, divided and colonised, was a “structural continuation of the original crime of racialised chattel enslavement”.

Holsey tells me: “Today, most African nations face economic precarity as a result of historical and present-day inequities within the global economic order”. “So, unlike European nations and the US, African nations do not enjoy ongoing benefits from past participation in the slave trade. Therefore, they should not be targeted to repair the harm done by this vile system.”

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

Many African nations have made efforts towards repair

“Britain has already paid reparations for racialised chattel enslavement,” Chigumadzi says. “It paid them to the enslavers.” After the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, the British government agreed to pay 40% of the national budget in compensation to 46,000 enslavers, a sum that wasn’t paid off until 2015.

Passing the buck to African nations ignores the fact that many have attempted to meaningfully address their role in slavery and its ongoing legacy. In recent decades, leaders from Libya, Nigeria, Benin, Ghana, Cameroon and Uganda have apologised for enslavement – and a number of countries offer citizenship to diasporans. But these gestures are still either symbolic or individual, and fail to make a dent in the ongoing economic impacts of enslavement. “Addressing this issue is a much more difficult task,” Holsey tells me.

It also requires genuine unity across the diaspora. This shouldn’t revolve around a story of winners and losers, but rather an understanding of the slave trade’s devastating impact on African and Caribbean nations. March’s historic UN resolution, which declared the trade as the “gravest crime against humanity” and called for reparations, was tabled by Ghana and coordinated by the African Union – representing this kind of cross-diaspora solidarity.

“The question we should ask is not, ‘What do African nations owe to the African diaspora?’” Holsey says. “Instead, we should ask: ‘How can African nations and the African diaspora work together toward the creation of a more just world?’”

US midterms voters said: enough is enough. Is this the beginning of the end for Trump?

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:48:50 GMT

With Democrats in power, Trump may be under siege and lose his dominance over the Republican party – but his id will relish the prospect of fighting

US midterms 2026 live – latest updates

Tell us: what do you want to know about the midterm election results?

Donald Trump posted a document on social media this summer by a supposed historian that compared him with, among others, Napoleon Bonaparte and Adolf Hitler. That now seems fitting: the US president has himself fought one battle too many, and appears to have brought about his own destruction.

Tuesday’s US midterm elections were a thumping, shellacking and extinction-level event rolled into one. Ruby-red Republican strongholds once deemed safe toppled like dominoes. Democrats won Senate seats for the first time in Kansas since 1932, in Texas since 1988 and in South Carolina since 1998.

The House of Representatives and Senate had flipped from one party to the other in the same midterm just three times since the second world war – in 1946, 1994 and 2006 – but now it has happened again, ensuring that the US Congress will be a bulwark against Trump’s expansion of executive power.

The president, who swiftly noted he was not on the ticket on Tuesday, is the architect of his own lame duck status. Indeed, having spent months repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ticket, he could hardly have done any more to sabotage his own party. In 2024 he won the presidency promising to lower prices and end foreign wars; his tariffs added to upward pressure on prices, and his ill-starred attack on Iran pushed them higher still.

Then there was Trump’s wild and bizarre campaign, which consisted of long and rambling speeches about architectural projects, outbursts of vile Islamophobia and musings about the “ass” of a Republican senator from Ohio. It culminated at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he declared victory in the war on algae.

The voters said: enough is enough.

Now for the Republican postmortem. According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. Trump, who was purported to be an economic populist, had flaunted his self-enrichment and fancy ballroom even as people struggled to put food on the table. It was too much even for some in his supposedly rock-solid base.

How will Trump cope with this new political reality? Is this the beginning of the end?

From January, Democrats will have the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments. Life could suddenly become uncomfortable for the likes of Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, or big tech leaders such as Elon Musk. Democrats might even consider impeaching Trump for a third time.

That potentially leaves the president under siege – a diminished figure mired in Washington gridlock and reduced to wielding a veto pen, which he had already starting threatening to use on Tuesday evening.

However, it must be said that Trump paid little attention to Congress during his first two years in office, apart from the passage of his Big, Beautiful Bill Act of tax and spending measures. He has acted unilaterally on tariffs and military strikes on Venezuela and Iran. Like his predecessors, he will surely continue to pursue foreign policy as a legacy project, an alarming prospect for the world.

He will also push on with his other obsession: giving Washington a radical makeover with a new White House ballroom, a triumphal arch and more gold. Congress might take the view that this is a relatively harmless activity to keep him occupied compared with the havoc he could be wreaking elsewhere.

More threatening to Trump than any Democratic investigation is the inexorable march of time. The race to succeed him in 2028 begins now.

This president is psychologically ill-equipped to deal with the prospect of the national spotlight leaving him to focus on JD Vance, Marco Rubio and other potential candidates.

That shift could also eat away at Trump’s cult-like dominance of the Republican party and the Maga movement. He has shaped the party in his own image for a decade and it will not easily snap back. But members of Congress picking through the wreckage of Tuesday may well conclude that Trump is a creature of the past – and their survival depends on placing the right bets on the future.

Every swing of the electoral pendulum gets over-interpreted. Trump’s two presidential election victories were seen as a fundamental shift in America, even though he never achieved 50% of the national popular vote. His defeat in 2020 was hailed as the end of the Trump era, only for him to rise from the political dead four years later.

Anyone re-proclaiming the end of that era after Tuesday’s landslide should remember that the president is not yet halfway through his second term, and that his id will relish the prospect of fighting Democrats.

A wounded Trump who feels he has nothing to lose over the next two years might turn out to be the most reckless and dangerous of all.

Want to know what all your co-workers earn? Be careful what you wish for

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:42:27 GMT

A new proposal for openness about pay could have unexpected downsides – if workers become demotivated, resentful and more likely to quit

Would you like to know what your colleagues are paid? If the Equality and Human Rights Commission gets its way, you will be able to find out. Under its proposals, workers will be able to request detailed information about the pay, bonuses and other perks received by their co-workers. The government agency argues that if we increase pay transparency, we can also reduce the pay gap between men and women. But countries that have tried this model have discovered that there are downsides to it too.

The gap between men’s and women’s pay had started to close when equal pay legislation was introduced in Britain in the 1970s, and then more women moved into previous male-dominated occupations in the 80s and 90s. Today, women in the UK earn on average about 6.8% less than what men earn.

This has left policymakers asking what else can they do. One intervention that dozens of countries have adopted is some form of pay transparency. The idea is that allowing people to understand what others are paid will help to shine a light on blatant inequalities, ultimately creating social pressure to remove them.

Many countries have introduced some version of these transparency laws. Since 2010, organisations in the UK that employ more than 250 people are required to publish their gender pay gap. In sectors such as higher education, employers must publish a report of the gender makeup of all those who are paid more than £100,000 a year.

These kinds of transparency laws have brought progress. One US study found that instituting gender pay reporting in the UK led to a 19% reduction in the gap between men’s and women’s pay. However, it also found that this reduction came largely from curtailing the growth of men’s pay, rather than stimulating the growth of women’s. In the UK university sector, meanwhile, a slightly different picture emerges. Following the 2007 requirement to report people paid above £100,000 a year, there has been a small increase in women’s earnings relative to men’s. However, this has mainly benefited highly paid women who have used pay transparency to help negotiate better packages. Outside the UK, increased pay transparency has also led to a notable improvement in women’s mental health. A Danish study found that following pay transparency laws, there was a decline in the number of women prescribed antidepression medication.

There are some things transparency laws have not changed. One is occupational sorting. This is the tendency for men to enter higher paid occupations, such as engineering and finance, and women lower-paid occupations, such as nursing and teaching. The introduction of transparency laws has allowed people to clearly see the average wages for different occupations. But this information does not seem to have changed people’s decisions about which occupations to enter. After Danish pay transparency laws were put in place, wages overall declined, because men’s wage growth slowed while women’s grew slightly. Another thing pay transparency laws did not change was overall levels of productivity in the economy: people produced a little less, but were also paid a little less to do it.

Given the success of gender pay laws in moving the needle on inequality, UK policymakers now want to push for even greater levels of transparency. Instead of just asking employers to publicly share their gender pay gap, the EHRC is now suggesting that employees be given the right to request details of other individuals’ pay, bonuses and performance reviews.

This kind of individual-level transparency has already been tried in a few sectors around the world. Canadian universities, the Californian public sector and Nordic countries have all made individual income levels publicly available. And it has helped to further increase pay equality: a study of the Canadian university sector found that individual-level pay transparency resulted in a 20% to 40% reduction in the gender pay gap; a study of 100,000 US scientists found that individual wage transparency led to reductions in gender inequality in pay; and the introduction of individual transparency in Norway also helped to narrow the pay gap, but it mainly benefited women changing jobs who were able to use pay information to search and negotiate for better-paid jobs.

But individual-level pay transparency can also have some less positive outcomes. The study of US scientists found that it broke the link between pay and performance: scientists who were significantly less productive than their peers were more likely to end up earning about the same as their more productive colleagues. A study of top managers in the Californian public sector found that pay transparency led to a drop in overall wages of about 7% – and a 75% increase in quit rates.

Another study of US universities found that when faculty members were made aware of the pay of their colleagues, those who earned less than the average became more dissatisfied with their jobs and more likely to look for another role. The same information had no impact on how better earners felt about their jobs. A recent modelling exercise has suggested that increasing pay transparency can lead to a rise in unhealthy social comparison, which can trigger feelings of anger and envy among co-workers.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

More stringent transparency pay laws involve a real trade-off. These laws are likely to make the pay of women and men a little more equal. However, they are also likely to dent the link between performance and pay, stoke resentment among those on lower pay, drive up staff turnover rates and potentially drive down overall pay. Salary ranges in job ads along with published gender gap data gives employees what they need to spot unfairness. But there is a difference between being able to challenge an unfair system and being able to see what every colleague earns. Some sorts of openness actually reduce trust. Open pay books may be one of them.

André Spicer is professor of organisational behaviour at the Bayes Business School at City, University of London. He is the author of the book Business Bullshit

French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:22:28 GMT

Temperature and defrosting thresholds raised to ‘very high levels’ at three cold stores stocking vital blood products

France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.

The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.

The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.

The attack, which EFS said had occurred overnight on Monday, came as the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in almost a dozen European countries soared as high as 50C (122F), causing millions of euros of food damage.

Retailers in Italy, Germany, Romania and the UK were targeted on Tuesday, after Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems the previous day.

In a wave of attacks in France last month, hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets. A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank said on Wednesday it had been the victim of a cyber-attack.

Something similar may have happened in the US in early August, when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries in at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.

After Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence officials on Tuesday, Thomas Regnier, an EU spokesperson, said the bloc’s agencies were holding urgent discussions with national authorities to formulate a collective response.

“These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said, declining to name any potential culprits. No motive for the attacks is known and no one has claimed responsibility.

A growing range of devices, including commercial refrigeration systems, can be monitored and controlled remotely. Without patching to repair emerging vulnerabilities, internet-connected software can leave code open to hackers.

Sign up to Headlines Europe

after newsletter promotion

Some authorities and experts fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in the aftermath of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Western intelligence officials say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that is taking many forms.

Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos, told the Guardian this week the most plausible attribution scenarios were a “state-based signalling and demonstration of capability” or a lone-wolf hacker.

EFS said it was not directly targeted, with the attacks hitting cold stores run by its contractors. Products stored in the affected rooms, which included plasma bags for transfusions and medicine manufacturing, had been moved to other sites.

It added that France’s national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the health ministry had been alerted, and monitoring of all its equipment had been reinforced.

All’s Fair season two review – am I delirious … or is this getting good?

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:06:48 GMT

From Glenn Close in pleather to naughty rumours about Bruno Mars, this legal drama is still absolutely ludicrous. But squint hard enough and it has slightly improved since its zero-star debut

On the one hand, Trump and the Maga movement have been routed in the midterms. On the other, the second season of All’s Fair is out. Truly, the lord giveth and the lord taketh away.

For those of you who have blanked the first season from your mind, All’s Fair is the existentially terrible offering from Ryan Murphy’s increasingly manure-filled stable, starring Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts and, absolutely unaccountably, Glenn Close as the super-duper lawyers of an all-female California divorce firm. Sarah Paulson plays their bananas enemy lawyer, Carrington Lane. And if you think that is some rum work pulled at the font, the other characters labour under the monikers Allura, Emerald and Liberty. Close gets off lightly with Dina, which I hope suggests she has at least some clout left in this strange business we call show.

I would catch you up on what happened in the first season, but the second season doesn’t seem to care much, so why waste time when there’s so much nonsense to get through? Carrington and Dina have a head to head in which the former (dressed to indicate her evilness in a sort of pleather gabardine, unless mine eye deceives) recaps as much as is needed. “I did plant the dementia drug, but I didn’t frame you for the murder.” And on we go.

There is a lot happening and yet nothing at all. Since the end of her marriage to Chase (Matthew Noszka), Allura has moved home. “I’m still getting used to an all-glass house,” is a thing she says to explain to her fellow legal she-eagles why she is not spooked by the sight of a hooded male figure looking in at her as she cleans her teeth one evening. “I don’t think it’s anything to be worried about.” Dina disagrees. “You have to remember, you girls, how risky life can be for divorce attorneys. I know from experience. Vengeance is a savage game.”

This is the first sign that someone has been trying to improve things since season one. If you squint and hope, this could be a metatextual pop reference spoken by the star of perhaps the most famous revenge movie in film history – and the kind of camp, self-aware flourish for which Murphy was once famed. When Allura later makes a reference to failing to pass the California bar exam on her first attempt, as happened to Kardashian last year, the suspicion that a human has been introduced into the pool of script-typing monkeys hardens almost into delirious certainty.

Allura’s inaugural plotline is … throwing a ball. A scorpion ball, to be precise, à la Grace Kelly’s famed 40th birthday celebration in which Elizabeth Taylor stole the show by turning up in a velvet and silk cape by Tiziani Roma, embroidered with diamante scorpions. Allura has bought the cape at auction and hired Adele and Bruno Mars to play at the ball; Liberty says she has heard that he is well-hung, everybody laughs and I think I am losing my mind. Onward!

Liberty and Emerald have this week’s legal case to solve. A new client, Aphrodite Lovesong, has come to them after her husband served divorce papers a month before becoming liable for perpetual alimony and after nearly 10 years of banging every cover girl they met as he and – uh – Aphrodite built a magazine empire together. She also has an unsigned prenup. “It appears we have ourselves a case!” says Liberty, sharper always than a tack. The twist involves invisible ink. I check again whether I am losing my mind.

By the time it all kicks off at the scorpion ball, I must have. By then, I’ve heard Carrington call her rivals “Black Mae West, Fat-ass and Dry Vag” and “Dina-saur”, Liberty has come out as gay (“Deep down, I think I am a power lesbian”), astrology has been inflicted on everyone and Dina has been hit on by a waiter younger than Allura’s acrylics, because “you radiate power and that is incredibly alluring”.

However, at some point – although not one I can specifically locate – you realise that you are having fun, instead of, like last time, holding your jaw off the ground and wondering how television could be this bad. It has started groping its way towards “so bad it’s good” territory. Like the US, it is not fully on course yet, but this is a journey that deserves encouragement. And so, unlike last year’s offering, I award it a full one star. I wish this clattering bag of preposterosity well. For the sake of us all, but especially Glenn Close.

All’s Fair is on Disney+
