Jodie Burrage offered support by WTA after death threats and online abuse

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:55:19 GMT

Briton received abusive messages after defeat in India

WTA says ‘staff in Chennai offering Jodie support’

The WTA has offered additional support to Jodie Burrage after she received death threats and online abuse following a first-round defeat at a tournament in India on Tuesday.

Burrage shared a raft of abusive messages sent to her Instagram account after a gruelling 3-6, 6-3, 7-5 defeat against India’s Vaishnavi Adkar at the Chennai Open. The 27‑year‑old, who was playing her first WTA Tour match since last summer, accompanied the messages with the caption: “Nice welcome back to the tour. I remember why I left.”

It is three years since the WTA – in partnership with Wimbledon, World Tennis and the United States Tennis Association – launched the AI-led Threat Matrix service, which aims to identify and tackle online abuse against players and officials.

A WTA spokesperson said in a statement: “Protecting players and the wider tennis family from online threats and abuse is a key priority for the WTA. We have WTA staff on the ground in Chennai offering Jodie support, along with our wider player welfare and Threat Matrix team.

“As much of the abuse players receive comes through direct messages, the WTA has offered Jodie additional support, including a private channel to report abusive direct messages, and moderation that hides abusive comments on public channels before she sees them.

Alexander Zverev made a losing start to his reign as world No 1 on Wednesday as the two-time Grand Slam champion went down 7-6 (5), 6-2 to an inspired Lorenzo Musetti at the Paris Masters.

Playing his opening match in the round of 32, Zverev went ahead 5-2 in a first-set tie-break but Musetti rallied to string together a run of five consecutive points and take a one-set lead.

The Italian failed to convert a break opportunity in the first game of the second set but made no mistake two games later as he capitalised on an error-strewn display from Zverev.

Musetti continued to deploy a sliced backhand to devastating effect as unforced errors mounted on the 2024 Paris Masters champion’s side of the net, culminating in a second break which allowed the Italian to serve out the match.

Novak Djokovic also crashed out of the tournament on Wednesday as the 24-time Grand Slam champion lost 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 to Australian qualifier Rinky Hijikata.

The shock defeat to the world No 83 ended the 39-year-old Serb’s hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals later this month.

After the loss, Djokovic told reporters his plan for the next few weeks was "just rest". "I’m looking forward to it," he added. Agencies

“Threat Matrix is also reporting the abuse Jodie received to the platforms, and investigations are under way to identify those responsible. Where the abuse is linked to betting, they will be added to the Bad Actor programme so betting operators can act against their accounts.”

Burrage is one of a number of players to have spoken out previously about the level of abuse received and a failure of the governing bodies and social media companies to tackle it effectively. She spoke out on the abuse after her first-round exit from Wimbledon in 2025.

Callum Turner emerges as James Bond favourite as Pierce Brosnan endorses actor: ‘He’s so strong’

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:34:54 GMT

Bookmakers’ odds have shortened to 8/13 for the British actor, seen sipping martinis with his wife Dua Lipa at the weekend

Ten days after final screentests for the most coveted role in British cinema, one actor has emerged as a strong favourite to don the 007 tux for Denis Villeneuve’s forthcoming film.

The bookmaker William Hill has cut the odds of Callum Turner being named as the next James Bond from 3/1 to 8/13, with previous favourite Jack Lowden now at 2/1. Josh O’Connor, who also auditioned recently, is now at 9/2, with Richard Madden, Robert Pattinson and Joe Alwyn at 16/1.

The flurry of activity has been prompted by news over the weekend that Turner had resigned as director of his own production company, Twentytwo Films Ltd, which he founded last August with his wife, the musician Dua Lipa. Some took this as an indication that Turner’s movie priorities may now lie elsewhere.

On Saturday, the couple also posted to social media photographs of themselves dressed for Halloween sipping martinis – the signature cocktail of the British spy.

And in a new interview, former James Bond actor Pierce Brosnan also endorsed Turner, who played his son in 2017 drama The Only Living Boy in New York. “Callum is someone I’ve worked with,” Brosnan told Vanity Fair, “and he’s so strong.”

Brosnan added: “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men.”

Turner, Lowden and O’Connor are all 36-year-old white, heterosexual film stars, suggesting that whichever of them wins the role, the approach adopted by incoming owners of the brand Amazon MGM will not stray far from Ian Fleming’s template.

Speaking to GQ, Lowden said the rumours linking him to the role were “all very flattering. It’s nice to be mentioned – for any role – and I’m just not really going to add to the noise.”

Meanwhile, on Tuesday O’Connor also sought to simultaneous embrace and play down the speculation. “To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary,” he told the BBC. “It’s an incredibly bizarre pinch-me moment ... even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that.”

It is not known how imminent an announcement by the production company behind the 26th film in the series is, but producer Amy Pascal has said that the news is likely to be revealed “by the end of the year”.

Turner began his career as a model before breaking though in films such as John Boorman’s 2014 drama Queen and Country, and the second and third Fantastic Beasts films, The Crimes of Grindelwald and The Secrets of Dumbledore, in which he played Newt Scamander’s brother.

More recent films include George Clooney’s rowing saga The Boys in the Boat (2023), and love triangle romcom Eternity (2025) opposite Elizabeth Olsen and Miles Teller. Turner also appeared in the satire Rosebush Pruning, which was released earlier this year, and will shortly be seen in cyberpunk series Neuromancer, due to debut on Apple TV in January. He is currently in production on two films: Possession, a horror from the director behind the Smile franchise, and Marielle Heller’s The Comebacker, a sports comedy with Tom Hanks.

If named, Turner will take over the role from Daniel Craig, whose last outing as 007, No Time to Die, was released in 2021. The narrative for the 25th film in the series lent the franchise a sense of closure, with Bond apparently dying, before a title card promised: “James Bond will return.”

In February 2025, Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, heirs to producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films, sold the rights for “creative control” over the franchise to Amazon MGM Studios in a deal worth more than $1bn.

Pascal and David Heyman were then brought on as producers of the new film, followed by Dune’s Villeneuve as director and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight as screenwriter. It is said to be scheduled for release in 2028.

Broccoli, who retains some ownership rights to the character, said last year that the new Bond would be “a man”, adding: “He’ll likely be in his 30s. Whiteness is not a given.”

The hiring of Villeneuve has led many to suspect the new Bond film will be gritty, serious and cinematic, unlike some of the more tongue-in-cheek instalments led by Roger Moore and Sean Connery.

Speaking after the announcement of his involvement, Knight said: “I will be able to produce something that’s the same but different, and better, stronger and bolder.”

Craig’s announcement of his intention to retire from the role, as well as the considerable delay in the release of his final Bond film because of Covid, meant many actors have had their names linked to the role over the past four years.

Tom Hiddleston, Tom Hardy and Idris Elba were long considered frontrunners, but all three aged out of the running the longer production on a new film was delayed.

Since then, other names in the running have included Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland, James Norton, Damson Idris, Henry Cavill, Theo James, Jacob Elordi, Paul Mescal and Jamie Dornan.

The first actor to play the role of Bond was Scottish star Connery in 1962’s Dr No. So successful was the film that he returned to make four further films over the next five years, which are considered by many as some of the franchise’s finest: From Russia With Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball and You Only Live Twice.

Fleming’s choice for the role, the English actor David Niven, starred in the non-canonical original Casino Royale (1967), while the Australian star George Lazenby joined for one outing, 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, before Connery rejoined for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).

Moore then lent the series a more ironic spin for his seven films between 1973 and 1985, including Octopussy and The Spy Who Loved Me, with Connery coming back in 1983 for Never Say Never Again.

The role then went to British actor Timothy Dalton for two films in the late 1980s; a five-year gap preceded Irish actor Brosnan’s debut in 1995 with GoldenEye. He shot four films as 007 before Craig’s tenure began.

The official James Bond films have so far made a total of $7.8bn, making the franchise the fifth highest-grossing in history. Proceeds from merchandise and sponsorship deals are estimated to far exceed that figure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:03:18 GMT

Nintendo Switch 2; NintendoThis ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains

It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time.

Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true.

Let’s start with what hasn’t changed. This is a clever, challenging game about a lonely boy who travels back and forth through time to save the world, and its flow and structure remain the same. We visit all the same places in the same order, emerging from misty Kokiri Forest into the expanse of Hyrule Field, onwards to the active volcano Death Mountain with its good-natured rock people, to Lake Hylia and its sunken treasures, through Kakariko Village and Castle Town and their small but memorable cast of strange inhabitants. Intimidating dungeons and temples still hide in plain sight in these places, and the solutions to their ingenious puzzles remain the same, whether you are lighting a stick on fire and rolling over cobwebs to burn them up inside an ancient tree, or searching with a magic lens to find invisible gaps in the crumbling walls of a crypt. If you played this game as a child you may find, as I did, that the solutions to these smart spatial and logical conundrums rise unbidden from the very depths of your memory, and you will feel suddenly compelled to shoot an arrow in the direction of the rising sun for reasons you can’t quite recall.

What has changed is how all of this is framed. Ocarina of Time’s story was once told through necessary understatement: you could not fit reams of dialogue and hours of cinematics onto a Nintendo 64 cartridge in 1998. Text chatter with Hyrule’s denizens has been spruced up and expanded here, so that the world feels more alive: it’s funnier and more colourful. But more importantly, pivotal moments in this story play out in fully voiced cutscenes (don’t worry, Link himself remains silent) that recall 2023’s Tears of the Kingdom.

I anticipate that these scenes will prove divisive – this is a good time to remind Ocarina of Time purists that the original is still there, if you want it – but I found that they brought out the latent epic drama in a previously sparse tale. They really boost the pathos. First encounters with important characters are now more impactful; there are pre-battle face-offs with temple bosses that keyed me up for the action. The desert king Ganondorf in particular comes off as thrillingly evil. An entirely new scene at the story’s most vital juncture, when young Link pulls the Master Sword from the stone in the Temple of Time and is frozen in time for seven years, had me close to awestruck. I found that knowing what was going to happen enhanced my anticipation of these moments: I was excited to see how each would be remade.

Ocarina of Time used to look like a dream: angular, fuzzy around the edges, full of evocative but simple colours and textures. It now looks like very detailed theatre scenery. Link is doll-like, with glassy eyes; his clothes are richly embellished with decorative stitching and his tools – boomerang, sword, bombs, a bow – look exaggerated and prop-like. Other characters are less detailed; something about this aesthetic choice speaks to how the important details of a story stand out in the memory. There are some changes that I didn’t like – I was disappointed to find that the warrior Sheik had lost a lot of his androgyny – but nonetheless I was won over by this art style, reminiscent of puppet shows and handmade toys. It is not so much realistic as hyperreal. The places, meanwhile – Hyrule Field under the setting sun, atmospheric dungeons filled with menacing lizard soldiers and scowling skull-spiders that curl up and evaporate in puffs of blue-purple smoke when you defeat them – are straightforwardly beautiful. There are an abundance of visual flourishes here, such as the glowing red eyes of the awful zombie creatures that can freeze Link in place with a shriek.

A couple of important but less obvious changes make Ocarina of Time easier to play. Link can jump anywhere now, with the press of a button, where previously he could only leap over predetermined gaps. All of his trinkets and tools are quickly accessible via quick-select buttons and a horizontal selector like Breath of the Wild’s, rather than buried in menus. (You will be extremely grateful for this when you enter the sunken Water Temple, and find that you can take Link’s iron boots on and off with blessed ease.) Fighting feels a little faster, more dramatic, as you draw Link’s sword and circle an armoured skeleton. And the all-timer of a score, redone with a full orchestra, is newly powerful and portentous. There are playful touches, too: irresistibly, you can now play Link’s ocarina with your voice rather than your controller, humming those familiar tunes into the Switch 2’s microphone.

Despite all of this new sheen, Ocarina of Time retains its understated melancholy. There is an essential tragedy to this tale about a boy hero whose childhood is stolen by an evil king. It is a dark fairytale that begins with a nightmare and the death of a forest god, sometimes scary and, like all children’s tales that stand the test of time, totally unpatronising. It is preoccupied with the sadness and inevitability of the passage of time, and the alignment now between that story and the real-world circumstances of this remake is impossible to ignore. The first time I stepped into the Temple of Time and pulled the Master Sword from its stone, I was myself a child. Re-entering that place as an adult gave me shivers I can’t quite describe. It got me thinking very deeply about how we pass down our cherished stories to the next generation.

I cannot make any pretence of objectivity about Ocarina of Time. It was one of the most important games of my childhood and indeed my life; a game that showed me the possibilities of the form when the rules of video games were still being written, and cemented my love of games. I cannot play it without the influence of nostalgia, and like Link, I often felt returned to my child self as I played. But even without that powerful attachment, I think anyone would be moved by this game. Nintendo’s modern Zelda team have turned one of the best games of the 1990s into one of the best games of the 2020s, and made time-travellers out of us all.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is out on 5 November; £59.99

‘Democrats need to not blow it’: our panel reacts to the historic midterms

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:30:26 GMT

Democrats should take the right lessons from their great night – but will they?

Trump has been a disaster for our country. His economic plans are incoherent, the Iran war is making inflation worse, and his complicity with Israel’s crimes in Gaza and other acts of lawlessness, from the extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean to the kidnapping of Maduro, have been combined with a continuing coarsening of American culture.

We live in a country with more casual racism, with more speculation and moral depravity, more selfishness than at any point in the recent past, and the rot starts in the White House with a man who’s the personification of vice.

Voters are making him pay. But the fact that even a victory like this leaves Republicans with so much support tells us about the extreme polarization of the country and the limits on how much electoral punishment a disastrous administration can expect.

To break through, Democrats need to do better in rural and semi-rural areas, and they need to reverse the trend of class dealignment in a more systematic way by making their party the party of working-class concerns and interests. That means fighting for higher wages, stronger unions, affordable housing and healthcare, and giving working people a reason to believe that Democrats will make their lives better.

They can’t rely on having Trump gift them elections through his erratic rule. A normal Republican administration can be almost as dangerous to working-class interests but will present nowhere near these opportunities. Democrats need to give voters something to support beyond their opposition to the man in the White House.

Fundamentally, we need a durable popular supermajority for progressive change in this country. And we need a wider coalition to do that. Winning back the House and Senate gives Democrats an opportunity to build it. But I have no confidence they’ll even attempt to build one.

Bhaskar Sunkara is the president of the Nation, the founding editor Jacobin, and the author of The Socialist Manifesto: The Case for Radical Politics in An Era of Extreme Inequalities

It hasn’t been at the front of most minds as the results have come in, but one of the biggest victors of the night has been the polling industry.

For a decade, since Donald Trump’s surprise victory in 2016, the field of opinion research has been placed under a tremendous amount of scrutiny ⁠– partly as a consequence of misses that suggest pollsters have systematically been undercounting Trump supporters.

Those critiques pointed to real challenges facing survey science but also an underlying anxiety ⁠– that Trump and Republicans under him have been able to defy gravity thanks to a standing reserve of disaffected, previously marginal voters willing to show up and back the right through thick and thin. Given that, the wild margins predicted for Democrats ahead of tonight couldn’t possibly have been real.

Well, they were. An ailing economy and high prices, an idiotic war abroad, a war being waged, here at home, against American cities and immigrant families that in no way resemble the criminals and vagrants the right has been ranting and raving about for years, naked corruption in Washington in the service of adding filigrees to the president’s fascism ⁠– these things did mater, it turns out, even to voters who’ve been willing to give the Trump circus multiple chances at the ballot.

A blue Texas would have set the mind reeling at the extent of the backlash alone ⁠– what’s happened on top of that is the most consequential midterm result in decades, big enough that this is already being discussed as a realignment election.

But a realignment to what? The majorities Democrats have won comprise candidates on both sides of the party’s internal divide ⁠– both the left and the center will have victories and near misses to crow about and parse.

The question of where the party should go in the broadest sense will remain unanswered in all of this; it’s not altogether obvious how Democrats will collectively decide to handle even the next two years of this administration, pulled, as they’ll inevitably be, between camps rightly demanding a crusade against Trump and rightly insisting that Democrats will need to prove to voters that they are attentive to the policy concerns that sent so many voters their way.

It will take bold, but shrewd political leadership to bridge those two tasks. We’ll find out very soon if there’s any of that to spare in the freshman class.

Osita Nwanevu is a Guardian US columnist

The Democrats swept Tuesday’s midterm elections, and the Republican party has no one but itself – and its leader – to blame.

Democrats took the House, winning seats that had been blood-red just two years ago. They took the Senate, grabbing formerly Republican seats in the Republican strongholds of South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa, all states Trump won in 2024 with significant margins.

Voters didn’t seem to be particularly enamored with the Democratic candidates. They did, however, seem fed up with Republicans.

And who can blame them? As they worried about the cost of gas and ground beef, Trump obsessed over his new ballroom and the presence of algae in the reflecting pool.

Many people who voted for Trump did so in part because he promised to bring prices down and to refuse to enmesh America in messy wars in the Middle East; he has instead decided to go to war with Iran, which has sent prices soaring at the pump.

While Americans on the left and the right have made clear that they don’t want datacenters in their backyards, those AI behemoths have been built anyway, even in the face of intense community opposition – and Trump has essentially told people to get over it.

The Republican party talks about “freedom” and scaremongers about Muslims taking away the rights of Americans, and yet across a significant chunk of the country, women can no longer get safe abortions – largely thanks to conservative Christians.

As Americans see their real spending power decrease, the Trump family and friends have used their power to make billions in corrupt deals.

There were, of course, some very bad Republican candidates in the race. From Lindsey Graham’s unqualified sister in South Carolina to the charisma-vacuum Ken Paxton in Texas; and Georgia’s Mike Collins.

And there were some excellent Democratic ones: the competent doctor Annie Andrews in South Carolina; the let’s-all-get-along seminarian James Talarico in Texas; the future president Jon Ossoff in Georgia.

But while candidate quality may have taken Democrats across home plate in some of America’s reddest states, it was Trump who got them to third base.

And as Republicans consider their party’s future two years from now when Trump is leaving office for good, they should take this as a clear lesson – the president has made their brand toxic. They should do their best to excise him from their systems now.

Jill Filipovic is an American author

Republicans used to have a saying – that a government big enough to give you everything you want is a government big enough to take from you everything you have. It turns out that this saying applies equally to Donald Trump.

In 2024, Republicans gave Trump unprecedented and almost dictatorial control over the party, and he delivered victory on a scale that suggested populist majorities for decades to come. But returned to the White House without any restraints on his worst instincts, Trump brought misery to his working-class base through tariffs and the kind of forever war in the Middle East he had specifically promised to avoid. Now he has almost singlehandedly led the party into its worst defeat since perhaps the 1930s.

Unfortunately for the country, the Democrats’ victory was impressive in its dominance yet unlikely to determine the future direction of either party.

Both moderate and leftwing Democrats will claim that their victories showed why their faction should lead the party, and they seem likelier to spend as much time attacking each other as trying to find solutions to the country’s political dysfunctions and broken institutions.

Trump, who cares nothing about the party he leads, will punish any Republican who dissents from his ruinous and erratic course.

In any case, the Republican party has no positive program, only the negative hope that voters who are perpetually frustrated with the party in power will turn against the Democratic Congress in 2028. The 2026 midterms were a political earthquake but not a political realignment.

Geoffrey Kabaservice is Niskanen’s Vice President for Political Studies. He is also the author of Rule and Ruin

I guess we can all kiss that $5,000 goodbye.

I’m referring of course to the so-called Trump dividend, where the president promised every adult voter a cool $5,000 if the Republicans held on to both the Senate and the House. Who knows how many people believed him, but the election results are now in. These midterm elections are a total and complete repudiation of the Trump agenda.

Not that Trump didn’t try to control the outcome of these elections from the get-go. He was behind the move to gerrymander election districts to be favorable to him across the country. He pushed to weaken key elements of the Voting Rights Act. He sought to have the federal government “take over” running the midterm elections from the states by “nationalizing” the elections. He tried to change the rules for voter registration, and he sought to destroy mail-in voting.

And yet, it didn’t work. This midterm elections prove that maybe it’s not so easy to manipulate American democracy, after all. (Some gerrymandered districts still went for the Democrats!) This fact is a huge relief, especially under the historic failures of years of Maga politics.

But this election also brings extraordinary responsibility to the Democrats. And yet, this is a party that seems far too comfortable in being perpetually divided over what it believes in beyond being anti-Trump. Impeachment hearings alone do not constitute a political agenda.

The next few months may witness some (hopefully non-violent) tumult, as Trump may challenge the certification of some elections and exaggerate both noncitizen voting and voter fraud. And Trump, who excels in blaming others for his own failures, will no doubt now exploit Democratic control over Congress as the reason for all his future failures.

But let’s be clear what happened in these elections. The American people are rejecting foolish and expensive wars, rebuffing inhumane immigration enforcement, refusing self-enrichment of the few as economic policy, and, I think, maybe even showing that full-throated American support for Israel is no longer a given in Washington. I’m relieved by this result. More than relieved. In fact, I’ve never been happier to lose money I’m sure I never would have received in the first place.

Moustafa Bayoumi is a Guardian US columnist

It was a wave election as predicted. Today, tribunes of every progressive faction will explain how Tuesday night’s results demonstrate a clear mandate for their wing. In important ways, each faction will be right.

The progressives are right that the electorate is hungry for new, bold solutions to their problems. The moderates are right that most voters don’t want to be hassled over woke moral citizenship tests. And the so-called #ResitanceLiberals are right that people are fed up with Trump’s corruption and want Democrats to do something about it. Fair enough.

Taking a step back, however, the biggest lesson of the election is not that voters were enamoured of this or that flavor of liberalism, but, rather that they ferociously rejected Trump’s party. And the historic scale with which the masses swung from Trump in 2024 to the Democrats in 2026 is more a story about a long-term crisis than about the success or failure of a given election strategy. The truth is voters are increasingly losing patience for party politics; they want someone, anyone, to address the stagnation in wages, the rising cost of living, cost of housing, insecurity in healthcare, and overall increasing difficulty of life in America.

They want someone to restore the old social compact where the promise was, if you worked hard, and played by the rules, you’d be rewarded with a comfortable life. Saying you’ll address the slow-roiling economic challenge, as Trump did in 2024, isn’t so hard, but governing in a way that actually makes life better for most working people is a different story. Similarly, for Democrats, “affordability” is a good slogan, but it’s not an economic program nor is it a political roadmap. To hold their majority in 2028, Democrats need to embrace the populism of the age and redouble their efforts to win the loyalty of working-class voters. That means being willing to break with the professional-class “woke” social values and with the donor-class’s pro-corporate economic agenda at the same time. The party has been given a precious and fragile gift, another bite at the apple with frustrated voters. They have two years to earn their trust.

Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623

As it happens, it was not smart for the Republicans to fashion themselves into the party of pedophiles and tech oligarchs aligned behind an illegal war that is driving up the cost of gas, fertilizer and just about everything else.

Democrats won massively across the board on Tuesday night. Even races where progressives weren’t polling especially well – including Angie Nixon’s Senate bid in Florida – came in much closer than expected.

Even my Trump-leaning home district in South Jersey kicked out a four-term incumbent, a Republican convert, who was expected to win big over a relatively uncharismatic Democrat. The question now is who claims victory: Normie Dems won big. The Democratic Socialists America won big, too. Democrats will control the House and the Senate. What will they do with their newfound power?

Even riding high, Democrats will have relatively limited control over how to govern. They can exercise some leverage with their congressional oversight powers, but asking questions of this cycle’s enemies – namely, big tech – will only get them so far.

To set themselves up for success, Democrats will need an answer for what the economic future of the United States looks like that doesn’t revolve around the hugely unpopular datacenter spending that now accounts for roughly a third the country’s GDP growth.

These answers aren’t hard. And in an election where most voters’ primary concern was affordability, democratic socialists have real answers. This was an election about the cost of energy, which is currently being driven up by datacenters and a disastrous war in Iran.

And it was an election about Trump. Voters want Medicare for All, affordable housing and monthly bills that aren’t tied to volatile energy markets. Democrats should take the right lessons from their great night: the future means delivering a better, cheaper quality of life for working people, and holding the people making their lives more expensive accountable.

Kate Aronoff is a staff writer at the New Republic. She is the author of Overheated: How Capitalism Broke the Planet–and How We Fight Back, and co-author of A Planet to Win: Why We Need a Green New Deal

The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded

The Guardian Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:31:55 GMT

The electorate voted decisively to curb the president’s power

There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.

Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.

It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.

Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.

In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.

His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.

But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.

The next two years will look nothing like the previous two. In the first several months after his return to power, when he controlled a unified government and was said to have won a restoration in 2024 on the heels of widespread cultural discontent and anti-“woke” sentiment, Donald Trump seemed momentarily as if he might succeed in his efforts to consolidate an authoritarian regime in America.

He purged the federal bureaucracy, eliminating hundreds of jobs and stuffing thousands more with his loyalists and incompetent cronies. He imposed his will and social agenda on non-governmental institutions, from large tech companies to major universities, which complied in part because they feared retaliation from a strong Trump regime if they refused.

He snatched the power of the purse away from Congress like a thief yanking a pocketbook away from an old lady, and reappropriated taxpayer money as he saw fit, disregarding the intentions of the people’s elected representatives.

And he did all this – he was able to do all this – because he seemed powerful, and his opposition seemed weak. For the first year of his second term, he bet that he could get people to obey him because he could threaten consequences for refusal, and because the Democrats could not credibly threaten consequences for complicity.

That credibility has flipped. Donald Trump’s re-election in 2024 seems, now, less like a broad cultural realignment and more like a product of material factors, namely inflation. Those same material factors have come back to bite Republicans now, as staggering gas prices, consumer disempowerment, persistent unemployment and visible, egregious inequality outrage voters.

Donald Trump, meanwhile, seemed indifferent, if not oblivious, to these concerns – that is, when he was not actively making them worse. His reckless and needless war on Iran is broadly blamed – largely correctly – for driving up gas prices.

Meanwhile, Trump busied himself by draping large banners of his own face over federal buildings, remodeling the White House in gold, and making bizarre diatribes on rally stages about male politicians’ backsides. He seems frivolous and out of touch, like Marie Antoinette in a bad toupee.

Donald Trump will enter 2027 with a hostile Congress, noticeably diminished cognitive power and physical stamina, a cratering approval rating and a term limit.

Moreover, he will enter the new year with a fractured coalition: his decision to pursue a war with Iran has split his inner circle and destroyed his credibility with the Republican rank-and-file for whom his “no new wars” pledge in 2016 had signaled a break with the neoconservative establishment.

Ambitious Republicans – younger Republicans – will sense blood in the water. They will begin to turn on him in an effort to shore up their own prospects; he will rage at their betrayal and rally his base against them, like some sort of stupid King Lear. But his efforts to crown kings and exact revenge may be severely diminished after tonight.

Trump’s strength was always the hold he seemed to have over the Republican base, the degree to which his charisma could compel voters to follow him anywhere. If the margins of the Democratic victories on Tuesday night are any indication, they are not following him any more.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX Tumble After Republican Losses

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The world’s richest person has antagonized Democrats, some of whom have signaled their intent to investigate him when they take control of Congress.

By Ryan Mac and Jack Ewing

Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections, especially in his home state, Texas. After Democrats won sweeping victories, gaining control of both houses of Congress and capturing other important state races, shares of SpaceX and Tesla, which are both run by Mr. Musk, fell sharply on Wednesday.

Tesla’s stock dropped when markets opened, and later traded down more than 2 percent. SpaceX, which conducted a blockbuster public offering in June, followed a similar pattern, before settling at a loss of closer to 3 percent. The declines stood out among tech stocks, as Meta, Microsoft, Google and the wider stock market rallied at the start of trading.

SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger, which could be complicated by a Congress controlled by Democrats, some of whom have already signaled their intent to investigate the world’s richest person and his companies. In recent years, Mr. Musk has antagonized Democrats, spending heavily to elect President Trump, involving himself deeply in firing federal workers and shutting down government agencies while aligning his companies’ interests with those of the administration.

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Edward J. Markey, Democrat of Massachusetts, posted on X on Tuesday night about potential hearings for technology executives.

Investigations could also complicate plans by SpaceX’s Starlink division, which offers satellite internet access, to expand into mobile telecommunications. Qualcomm Technologies said Wednesday that it would supply Starlink with equipment for base stations that would be part of a nationwide cellular network.

Mr. Musk spent at least $474 million on the midterm elections, the most money of any donor in a U. S. election cycle, apart from candidates who have funded their own runs for office. About $224 million was spent on races in Texas, particularly in support of the losing campaign of the Republican Ken Paxton for a Senate seat against the Democrat James Talarico.

Both SpaceX and Tesla have their headquarters in Texas. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Mr. Musk moved there after declaring that California had become too liberal for his taste. He also complained about overbearing regulations.

Both companies are developing extensive infrastructure in Texas, including a joint effort to build a more than $100 billion chip manufacturing plant in the state, though those efforts could now face greater scrutiny. Texas is set to have a Democratic governor after the election of Gina Hinojosa, as well as a Democratic attorney general and lieutenant governor.

Ms. Hinojosa campaigned on promises to rein in development of data centers. That could create problems for Tesla, which is testing autonomous driving technology in Austin that relies on a data center there.

“Texas welcomed data center companies who were unable to get permits in other states,” Gary Black, managing partner of the Future Fund, an investment firm, said on X. “Its status as a data center hub may now be over.”

Mr. Musk was also attracted to Texas by corporate law that limits shareholders’ ability to sue. Tesla shifted its corporate domicile to Texas from Delaware after a Delaware judge voided his pay package in response to a shareholder lawsuit. The decision was later overturned. SpaceX is also domiciled in Texas.

Democrats also appeared poised to take control of the Texas State House and the court that hears appeals from the Texas Business Court, which would hear any lawsuits stemming from the merger of SpaceX and Tesla. Judges on the appeals court are elected.

But the law that shields company managers from shareholder lawsuits has bipartisan support and is unlikely to change, said James Spindler, a law professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

“It was seen as a way of bringing business here,” Mr. Spindler said. “Everyone wants more tax revenue. Everyone wants more jobs.”

Mr. Musk, 55, did not return a request for comment.

Mr. Musk’s midterm spending, while substantial, will have little impact on his overall wealth. As of Tuesday, he was worth $898 billion, according to Bloomberg, meaning that his political contributions amounted to a tiny sliver of his net worth.

In relative terms, it was akin to a 55-year-old with the median U. S. net worth of about $411,000 spending a little more than $217.

Mr. Musk, who avoided posting on X for most of Tuesday night as votes were being counted, returned to his social media platform in the early hours of Wednesday to joke about his political losses and his companies’ prospects.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote, referring to SpaceX’s goal to put A. I. computing clusters in orbit.

Mr. Musk also appeared to be deleting old posts. On Tuesday, he told his more than 240 million followers on X to “vote red today!”

On Wednesday, that post could no longer be found on his account.

Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

Ryan Mac is a Times reporter who covers corporate accountability across the global technology industry.

Jack Ewing covers the auto industry for The Times, with an emphasis on electric vehicles.

Appeals Court Hands Win to Mamdani in Fight Over Second-Home Tax

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The court reversed a judge’s order that had said New York erred in its rollout of the tax, granting Mayor Zohran Mamdani a victory over a key piece of his agenda.

By Mihir Zaveri

An appeals court on Wednesday ruled that Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration can proceed with efforts to collect a new tax on high-end second homes in New York City, handing the mayor his first major legal victory over a core piece of his progressive agenda.

Uncertainty had clouded the tax for weeks, after a Staten Island judge ruled in September that the city had mishandled the rollout and ordered it to start over. The city immediately appealed, and continued rolling out the tax as the lawsuit proceeded. The decision on Wednesday, from a panel of appellate judges in Brooklyn, reversed the judge’s ruling.

The tax still faces other legal challenges. But the ruling is a win for the mayor, whose lawyers are also defending other policies he campaigned on, including a rent freeze on rent-stabilized apartments.

Mr. Mamdani had embraced the tax as a way to make good on his campaign promise to “tax the rich,” as well as a way to help close the city’s budget gap.

The mayor said in a statement on Wednesday that he was “heartened” by the ruling.

“From Day 1, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city,” he said.

Randy Mastro, a lawyer representing the group of homeowners who brought the lawsuit, did not say whether he planned to appeal. But in a statement, he said that the tax rollout, which he called “lawless and chaotic,” would “go unremedied.” Mr. Mastro said he believed that challenges to the constitutionality of the tax itself — the core argument in the other lawsuits, including one he brought — would succeed.

The process of introducing the tax on second homes, also known as pieds-à-terre, has been turbulent.

The tax was unveiled by Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring with Mr. Mamdani’s support, and passed in the state budget. It must be paid by people who live outside New York City most of the time while also owning a high-value home in the city.

Levied as a surcharge on property tax bills, the tax applies to condos and co-ops that are used as second homes and have a “market value” — a complicated metric determined by the city’s Finance Department — of at least $1 million. It also applies to one-, two- and three-family second homes with a “market value” of more than $5 million. (The tax does not apply if the home is being rented to someone, or if a relative of the owner lives there most of the time.)

It is expected to raise some $500 million annually for the city.

The lawsuit that led to Wednesday’s ruling did not challenge the legality of the tax. Instead, it argued that the city had sowed confusion by sending out notices to about 17,000 New Yorkers informing them that their properties might be subject to the tax, without first making sure that they were not full-time residents.

The suit also took issue with the city’s publishing an online list of nearly one million “properties that may be subject to the charge” that included the owners’ names.

The city has maintained that it acted in accordance with the law that established the tax.

The notices asked property owners to provide proof of residency, such as a driver’s license, or a copy of a lease to show that the home was being rented out. As of Oct. 28, the city had approved around 8,800 applications from homeowners who said they were primary residents and should not be taxed.

The city has said in recent days that even as that figure has grown, it remains confident that the tax will yield the anticipated $500 million in annual revenue.

In a six-page decision, the appellate court said that the homeowners who sued had not demonstrated “that any bad actors have misused the information” on the published list of properties, “or that the publication itself subjected them to any crime, harassment or defined public ridicule.”

The court also said that the mailed notices did not constitute harm, concluding that the homeowners lacked the standing to sue.

Despite the ruling, two separate pending lawsuits are seeking to overturn the tax itself. Both of those suits argue that the law establishing the tax violates provisions of the state constitution that limit how much the city can collect in real estate taxes every year. Among other claims, they also argue that the tax is discriminatory under the U. S. Constitution because it applies only to residents of states other than New York.

One of the lawsuits was brought in September by former Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, his wife, Hilary Geary Ross, and the casino mogul Steve Wynn, all of whom live in Florida but own second homes in New York City.

The other was brought by the corporation that owns an Upper East Side co-op building known as the Montclair, as well as a handful of homeowners, including some who live in Florida and in Suffolk County on Long Island. That lawsuit is backed by the Real Estate Board of New York, an influential lobbying group.

Mihir Zaveri covers housing in the New York City region for The Times.

Trump Has the Democrats Right Where He Wants Them

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Cottle

By Michelle Cottle

Ms. Cottle writes about national politics for Opinion.

Talk about a thumping. After months of struggling to overcome brutal political fundamentals, most Republicans awoke Wednesday to the fresh pain of getting kicked to the curb by the American people, along with a fat dollop of dread about what comes next.

But not President Trump. I suspect he greeted the morning with a tingle of anticipation, if not outright excitement, for what lies ahead: two years of nonstop, bare-knuckle brawling with a Democratic-controlled House and Senate. In other words, Mr. Trump’s idea of heaven.

Yes, the president is a sore loser, as Jan. 6 illuminated in blood and chaos. He got busy early in this election rigging the playing field in his team’s favor, then spent the final months of it pleading with followers to pretend he was on the ballot.

But he wasn’t really on the ballot, meaning he can now tell himself this electoral humiliation had nothing to do with him. And he has never given two flips about the fortunes of the broader G. O. P. So, in his mind, Republicans belly flopping without him probably just confirms his singular importance.

Mr. Trump cares only about developments that affect him directly. As such, he might feel a whisper of unease about his lap-dog Republicans ceding control to crusading Democrats with subpoena power and two years of pent-up rage. After all, one of his go-to campaign pitches to Republican voters this year was that, if the blue team won the midterms, Democrats would immediately revive their unfair persecution of him. Maybe even impeach him a third time!

But, deep down, a Democratic win was surely what he was rooting for all along.

Conflict is Mr. Trump’s jam. The nastier the better. For all his self-aggrandizing talk about building stuff, his true talents lie in combat and destruction. He long ago shattered the spine of the G. O. P., so humiliating its members now is a minor thrill at best. But facing off against Democratic majorities in both chambers still buzzing from their electoral win? Now that is something to live for.

Expect Mr. Trump’s relations with Congress next year to make the partisan hostilities of his first term look like a meditation retreat. The incoming chairmen of the House Judiciary and the Oversight Committees have likely been protein loading and drawing up subpoena lists for months in preparation for their coming investigations into Trump & Company. At least, I sure hope so.

Not that Mr. Trump has ever cared much about congressional authority. Which means we can look forward to rampant stonewalling of Democrats’ requests for documents and witnesses. If at least a couple of administration officials aren’t held in contempt of Congress by the end of next year, it won’t be for lack of trying.

For Mr. Trump, this pandemonium is doubtless much more fun than the thankless tedium of trying to govern. The guy has never been much for policy, unless you count whipping up fear of immigrants and imposing a tariff scheme that seems to have been drawn up on the back of a napkin. And his second-term “accomplishments” thus far have been about as popular as a root canal without sedation.

True to form, Mr. Trump has responded to his failures by whining about the public’s refusal to appreciate everything he has done for them. Pre-election, members of his administration pleaded with voters to just be a little patient, to allow more time for the positive results of the administration’s policies to manifest. Maybe buy their spoiled kids fewer toys in the meantime.

That’s all over now. Going forward, Mr. Trump can simply redirect the blame for all of his incompetence onto Democratic lawmakers. High gas prices? A disastrous war in Iran? More expensive health care coverage? Rural hospitals shuttering? Pfft. If only the radical Communist extremist Democratic majorities would let Mr. Trump work his magic, all those problems and more would have been resolved by now.

Will his blame shifting work? Maybe with the Trump Kool-Aid drinkers. But it is the natural condition of the president to be blamed for most of what goes down on his watch, and a growing portion of the electorate has grown wise to his game.

There has been some speculation about whether, saddled with divided government, Mr. Trump will make an effort to cut a few bipartisan deals. Perhaps pursue populist tax changes or reduce prescription drug costs or … you know, something.

It is indeed pleasant to imagine that the president cares enough about, if not the welfare of Americans, at least his own legacy to get serious about helping people other than his rich cronies and grifter family. I wouldn’t hold my breath. Mr. Trump has never displayed much interest in or patience for working out knotty bipartisan deals. Rather than waste time on policy negotiations, he seems more likely to sit around binge watching Fox News and noodling over how to annoy his Democratic nemeses with yet another monstrous monument to himself.

The closing years of a presidency can be a drag. Especially if, like Mr. Trump, you have done a lousy job. The electorate is tired of you. Your congressional team is increasingly focused on the future beyond you. Worse, people expect you to own the problems you once railed against, along with the failed policies you have rammed through. Where is the joy in that?

Instead, Mr. Trump can now spend his waning days in office wallowing in perpetual combat and chaos. That has always been his happy place, no matter the cost for the rest of us.

Source photo by Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images.

With Democrats’ Sweep, Congress Is Set to Reassert Power to Check Trump

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

President Trump usurped power from the legislative branch with Republican help for two years. Democrats are now positioned to try to claw back some of Congress’s prerogatives.

By Carl Hulse

Carl Hulse has covered Congress for more than four decades.

The Democratic sweep of the House and Senate that has upended the balance of power in Washington has also given an atrophied Congress an opportunity to reclaim its relevance and constitutional role as a check on the president after two years of Republican compliance.

Since President Trump was elected in 2024 along with G. O. P. House and Senate majorities, Republicans on Capitol Hill have defined their role mainly as empowering him and beating back Democratic resistance. That has allowed the executive branch to act with near impunity, steamrolling Congress on spending, tariffs and war powers.

Now, with Democrats set to take firm control of both chambers in a rebuke to Mr. Trump and the Republicans who ceded much of their power to him, the legislative branch is poised to reassert itself in multiple ways — notably on spending and oversight. Democrats say they are determined to investigate and push back against the president and his administration.

“We are going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country,” said Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is in line to become speaker.

On Wednesday in Washington, as the scope of Democratic victories came into sharper focus, he declared, “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over.”

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, also vowed that Democrats would bring about the an end of an era: “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over,” he said.

Despite their aggressive intentions and the scope of their electoral victories, Democrats may be limited in their ability to restrain the president. Mr. Trump has demonstrated a disregard for the power of Congress and the traditional norms that govern the relationship between the legislative and executive branches.

Mr. Trump told Fox News before the elections that he intended to be “Mr. Veto” if Democrats seized control. But as the results — and the obvious backlash — poured in from across the nation, the president struck a more conciliatory tone, saying he would be willing to cut some deals.

It was reminiscent of his first term, when the president, embracing his art-of-the-deal persona, seemed open to bargaining with Democrats on big issues. But partisanship has hardened considerably since then, and Democrats, bolstered by the reach of their victory, are going to press for any deals to be made more on their terms than his.

It is also likely that the administration will put up fierce resistance to attempts by Democrats in Congress to demand answers from executive branch officials, which could spark major conflict and poison efforts to work together legislatively.

In their appearances before Congress over the past two years, Trump administration officials have been dismissive and confrontational with minority Democrats sitting on panels run by friendly Republicans. Democrats will wield those gavels beginning in January, with the accompanying subpoena power to pursue what they see as a target-rich environment of activities and people that merit thorough investigation. Senate Democrats will also have veto power of their own and will be able to delay or block confirmation of Mr. Trump’s judicial and executive branch nominees if they choose.

Top Democrats say they hope the election defeat attributed in many respects to the president will persuade more Republicans to break with Mr. Trump — even at the risk of angering the now weakened president — and join them in pushing back against the White House and even undoing some of its actions.

But Senator John Thune, the South Dakota Republican and current majority leader, took a combative stance as the losses piled up Tuesday night, saying Republicans would not let “fringe” Democratic positions become mainstream. Even with their gains, Democrats remain short of the 60 votes needed to overcome the filibuster, allowing Republicans to retain some leverage.

“Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” Mr. Thune said. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”

Democrats say they intend to give Republicans the chance to show whether they took any lessons away from the drubbing by forcing votes on reversing cuts to health care and other safety net programs that hurt rural areas where voters rejected Republicans.

“We are going to challenge them,” Mr. Schumer said. “We are going to put some easy things on the floor and see if they vote for them.”

Democrats will have some challenges of their own. Their members have sharp ideological differences that could be difficult to bridge, lessening the party’s ability to reach consensus. And despite Mr. Trump’s sudden impulse to cut bargains, legislative agreements could be hard to come by, frustrating voters who demanded sudden change.

Spending fights could be particularly thorny. Democrats will want to reclaim congressional spending authority after Republicans used a special party-line process to fund Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown after Democrats balked, leading to an extended shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security.

The administration also refused to spend some money Congress had allocated and shifted other money to pay for Mr. Trump’s pet projects in ways lawmakers have not approved. The administration has also applied its “rescission” authority to strip out money in a way that lawmakers in both parties say breaks budget laws.

Democrats will be eager to restore Congress’s spending prerogatives and could look for help from some Republicans on the House and Senate Appropriations Committees who were quietly unhappy with the president’s spending decisions.

The congressional obeisance to Mr. Trump was clearly a factor in the election outcome, as Democratic candidates skewered Republicans on Capitol Hill for standing on the sidelines while Mr. Trump neutered them and took actions detrimental to their states and districts.

“We’ve got a Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who in essence is a ‘yes man’ to the president,” Adam Hamilton, the Democrat who defeated Mr. Marshall in Kansas, said on MS NOW. “Instead of fighting for the people of Kansas, he comes back as though he’s a spokesperson for the White House.”

In his remarks after the results, Mr. Jeffries said the outcome was the beginning of the “great American comeback.” It could be a comeback for Congress as well.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

On the Democrats’ Agenda: Investigations of Trump and His Family

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

When a new Congress is sworn in, it will have the power to hold hearings and issue subpoenas, prompting one representative to advise White House officials and others to “lawyer up.”

By Ben ProtessMichael Gold and Andrew Duehren

A $1.4 billion cryptocurrency windfall. Well-timed stock trades. A wedding after-party bankrolled by a Kremlin-connected businessman.

For nearly two years, congressional Democrats were powerless to probe these potential scandals and conflicts looming over President Trump and his family businesses. But after pulling off a landslide midterm election victory that amounted to a sweeping rebuke of the president, they will soon seize control of Congress — and with it, the power to open investigations, hold hearings and issue subpoenas.

Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, summed up the threat succinctly in a statement late Tuesday: “Lawyer up.”

In an interview on Wednesday, Mr. Garcia said that his warning was meant chiefly for people at the White House who “engaged in corruption” and enriched themselves. “The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities,” he said.

Subpoenas, though, do not guarantee a fruitful investigation.

Some of the president’s business associates and allies are expected to fight some of the subpoenas in court, which could become a lengthy process. And even if the Democrats shed new light on moneymaking ventures, there is no indication that the Trump family violated the law — potentially complicating any effort to pursue impeachment proceedings against the president.

Still, Mr. Garcia and other congressional leaders believe they will find a target-rich environment.

After winning back the White House two years ago, Mr. Trump abandoned his first-term pledge to rein in his family’s deal making, enabling new ventures that enriched the president, his sons and some of his advisers. He shrugged off concerns about conflicts of interest, contending that he “found out that nobody cared.”

He turned out to be wrong. An AP exit poll found that government corruption was a crucial issue for many voters, and that roughly seven in 10 voters said Congress was doing “not enough” to provide checks and balances on the presidency.

In the House, the Oversight and Judiciary committees will lead the investigative efforts, which will not be limited to the Trump family business. Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat in line to chair the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, is expected to conduct her own investigations as well.

“We need to zero in quickly on the forms of systemic pay-to-play corruption that are destroying the rule of law and have cost the public huge amounts of money,” Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, said in a statement.

Here are some of the main issues that Democrats are expected to investigate.

Mr. Trump’s financial returns have multiplied during his second term, largely thanks to his crypto businesses. Those ventures pulled in at least $1.4 billion in revenue last year, a windfall that posed unparalleled potential conflicts of interest.

Congressional investigators will most likely focus on the Trump family’s main crypto company, World Liberty Financial. Last year, an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought a huge stake in World Liberty. Four months later, the Emiratis struck a deal with the Trump administration — over the objections of some national security officials — for the export of valuable computer chips.

Mr. Trump also collected hundreds of millions of dollars from sales of his $TRUMP memecoin, a type of cryptocurrency that is typically treated like a collectible, and World Liberty’s sale of its own digital tokens. The buyers included foreign entities and businesses seeking relief from the Trump administration.

The activities of the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., are another top priority for Democrats.

Mr. Trump Jr. has not made things easy for himself. He allowed a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars to help finance his wedding after-party in the Bahamas this year, drawing outrage from congressional Democrats. The president has said that his son repaid the businessman, Umar Kremlev, but Mr. Garcia has flagged it as an investigative target.

Mr. Raskin has also begun investigating 1789 Capital, a venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a senior partner. Several of the companies that 1789 has invested in have received government funding while others benefited from Trump policies.

In a statement, a spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. said that he “is a private citizen who holds no position in government and has broken no laws.”

The statement added that Mr. Trump Jr. “has never sought to influence government policy or official decision making for the benefit of his personal business interests and has every right to pursue lawful and legitimate business and investment opportunities.”

Jared Kushner, a son-in-law of the president, is also on the Democrats’ radar.

Mr. Kushner is not a formal member of Mr. Trump’s government, but he has operated as a top envoy in negotiations to resolve President Trump’s war with Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine. Mr. Raskin has called for Mr. Kushner to recuse himself from those negotiations, partly citing potential conflicts arising from Mr. Kushner’s private equity firm, Affinity Partners, which has received investments from foreign nations that have a stake in those conflicts.

“Partisan politics aside, no one has ever pointed to a specific legal or ethical guideline that Jared or Affinity has violated,” Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Mr. Kushner, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Unlike his first term, when the Trump family real estate business swore off all new foreign deals, the president imposed few restrictions on deal-making in his second term. That omission opened the door for the Trump Organization to announce new international property deals in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, among others, licensing the family name in exchange for payments.

There is no indication that the Trump Organization linked these deals to foreign policy. And although real estate projects are potentially lucrative for the company, they represent a small fraction of what the president earned last year, meaning they will likely draw less scrutiny.

In the first three months of this year, President Trump’s brokerage accounts placed more than 3,600 trades, and some of those trades appeared to be well timed.

In February, nine days after Mr. Trump’s account executed a purchase of more than $1 million in Dell stock, the president praised the company and its founder, Michael Dell, at an event in Georgia. The Pentagon later announced a $9.7 billion contract with Dell.

There is no indication that the contract was related to the president’s stake in the company, and the trade represented a small fraction of his overall investment portfolio. The Trump Organization has said that the president and his family have no ability to direct the trading, all of which is controlled by outside brokerage firms.

Democrats nonetheless seized on the timing. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the Massachusetts Democrat in line to lead the banking committee, has previously pushed for an investigation into Mr. Trump’s trades.

Democrats might also examine the protection Mr. Trump’s own administration provided him from Internal Revenue Service scrutiny.

In a stunning order this spring, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told the I. R. S. to halt any ongoing investigations into Mr. Trump, two of his sons and their businesses. Mr. Blanche’s order also barred the I. R. S. from starting any new audits of the tax returns that the Trumps had, at that point, already filed.

Historically, the I. R. S. has audited the sitting president’s tax returns every year, as a way to signal that even the occupant of the Oval Office has to comply with the nation’s tax laws.

A congressional investigation would most likely focus on the circumstances and legality of the Justice Department granting Mr. Trump this protection, which came after Mr. Trump sued the I. R. S. over the leak of his tax returns.

The Trump family is hardly the only area of interest.

Democrats made it clear during the campaign that they planned to use their newfound congressional oversight powers to look at corruption allegations across the Trump administration.

Mr. Garcia has said he plans to investigate “corporate corruption,” including looking at whether donors to projects such as the White House ballroom may have leveraged their contributions to benefit from Trump administration decisions or government contracts.

He also plans to continue the House’s investigation into the government’s handling of its criminal case against Mr. Epstein, who died in prison in 2019, and his potential links to Mr. Trump. Mr. Garcia has pushed to subpoena Mr. Blanche, who oversaw the release of the Epstein files, a move that Republicans have resisted.

Mr. Raskin also has vowed to investigate the lucrative pardon industry that has sprung up around the Trump administration.

Ms. Hassan said she planned to investigate the Trump administration’s use of no-bid contracts to donors and other allies of the president. Several deals, including a lucrative contract for deportation planes that was approved under Kristi Noem’s tenure as homeland security secretary, have come under intense scrutiny.

In both the House and Senate, Democrats will also seek to use their subpoena power to investigate the killings of Americans by federal immigration officers, including two shootings in Minneapolis at the beginning of the year.

As they sought to make the war in Iran a focus of their campaigns, Democrats also signaled plans to investigate Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is already facing an impeachment effort.

So far, Democratic leaders have demurred when discussing an impeachment effort against the president, with many lawmakers wary after their two efforts to remove him from office in his first term came up short.

Madeleine Ngo contributed reporting

Ben Protess is an investigative reporter at The Times, covering President Trump.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

Stocks Rise as Democrats Flip Control of Congress

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Markets traded higher as investors foresaw gridlock in Washington, typically a bullish signal.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Sui-Lee WeeAruni SoniEshe Nelson and Joe Rennison

Stock markets gained on Wednesday, as it became clear that Democrats were set to seize control of Congress in a resounding midterm election victory that surpassed the party’s most optimistic expectations.

The S&P 500 rose 1.8 percent in afternoon trading, putting the benchmark index on course for its biggest daily gain in months.

For investors, perhaps the most important takeaway from the midterms is that they are over. Uncertainty over what might happen on Election Day has historically weighed more heavily on the market than the clarity of a result, regardless of what that result has been.

The Democrats’ sweep is likely to produce gridlock in Washington. That can cause political problems in some areas, such as when it comes to approving government spending. At the same time, an extended stasis for policymaking tends to be a bullish signal for investors, allowing them to focus on the fundamentals of their investments more than the political maneuverings behind new rules and laws.

Another reason that markets tend to respond positively to elections is that money parked on the sidelines to avoid any potential tumult re-enters the market, helping to lift stock prices.

“Stocks are breathing a big sigh of relief this morning, as the midterms are finally done,” said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, an advisory firm. “Markets hate uncertainty, and now with the election out of the way, we are seeing buyers step in across the board,” he added.

Notes: All times are Eastern. Data is as of 2 p. m. Japan is the Topix index, Europe is the Stoxx 600 index and the United States is the S&P 500.

Source: FactSet.

Jason Karaian/The New York Times

When early results on Tuesday night pointed to a landslide victory for the Democrats, Asian stocks initially tumbled, as investors fretted about the artificial intelligence trade that has lifted markets to new heights. Before the midterms, the theory was that a Democratic sweep would slow the A. I. build-out, potentially derailing the prolonged rally in technology stocks.

But such concerns appeared to be pushed off and a broad rally in European and U. S. markets followed, with most sectors posting gains.

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at the investment bank Natixis, said that she did not expect the Democrats to “kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.”

The Democratic sweep, according to a research note from Allianz Global Investors, “ultimately brings greater political tension than fundamental policy change.”

The stocks of some key “hyperscalers” at the forefront of the A. I. build-out — companies like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — rose once exchanges opened in the United States.

Attention homed in on some of the A. I.-linked companies that investors deemed to be riskier, either because of large debt loads, runaway spending or a lack of revenue to justify such aggressive expansion. Oracle fell slightly and CoreWeave, a company whose data-center dealings have worried investors, lost nearly 10 percent.

Tesla and SpaceX, Elon Musk’s companies that both make heavy use of A. I., tumbled in a choppy trading session, pointing to the probable congressional attention to come on Mr. Musk roles as a political megadonor, former government cost-cutter and as a business leader who has aligned his interest closely with those of the Trump administration.

More defensive parts of the market that investors typically move into during periods of upheaval also saw selling on Wednesday. Industrials and energy stocks were the two sectors of the S&P 500 to fall, while the other nine rose.

Several analysts said the election result could increase President Trump’s focus on foreign policy, specifically the war in Iran. In a social media post, Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republican wipeout squarely on the war with Iran. Later, Mr. Trump said the assertion was “largely true.”

Oil prices fell sharply on Wednesday, with Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, sliding to around $94 a barrel, extending declines in recent days as negotiations took place between the United States and Iran.

Government borrowing costs, which have closely tracked the price of oil for much of this year, also fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which underpins interest rates for consumers and companies, dropped on Wednesday to 4.89 percent. The dollar, which tends to move in line with the path of interest rates, fell against other major currencies.

According to the Franklin Templeton Institute, the S&P 500 averaged a 14.9 percent gain over the 12 months after the 10 midterm elections under Republican presidents since 1954, with similar market moves regardless of whether Republicans or Democrats took control of Congress.

But some analysts have warned that a conventional post-election rally may not hold for long, given the potential for renewed conflict in the Middle East and still-high borrowing costs and government spending.

“Shutdowns, debt-ceiling brinkmanship and budget gridlock under a Democratic Congress are greater risks,” strategists at the research arm of Amundi Investment Solutions wrote in a pre-election report. “In prior cycles, gridlock was a relief trade. At current yield levels, it may not be.”

River Akira Davis and Alexandra Stevenson contributed reporting.

Sui-Lee Wee is the Asia business correspondent for The Times.

Eshe Nelson is a Times reporter based in London, covering economics and business news.
