CVS to Split Off Drugstore Business, Ending Its Bigger-Is-Better Era

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a breakup planned for 2028, CVS Health intends to keep together its insurance and pharmacy benefits divisions and create a separate company for its pharmacies.

By Rebecca Robbins and Reed Abelson

CVS Health plans to split in two, in a major unraveling of one of the country’s largest health care conglomerates after decades of rampant expansion, the company announced on Wednesday.

Under the breakup, expected in the first half of 2028, a spinoff company, to be called CVS Pharmacy, will house the conglomerate’s approximately 9,000 retail pharmacies, in-store medical clinics and a warehouse-based operation that sends prescriptions through the mail to consumers.

A second company will retain the name CVS Health and include Aetna, the major insurer; Caremark, the giant pharmacy benefit manager; and other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.

CVS Health and its peers, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have been under mounting scrutiny from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers, regulators and others because of the companies’ dominance over nearly every aspect of consumers’ health care services.

Critics say the three have long exploited internal conflicts within their web of businesses to increase profits, stifling competition and helping to drive up medical costs.

Within the past two years, Arkansas and Tennessee have each passed laws that aim to prevent the conglomerates from both managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.

Smaller pharmacies claimed the companies favored their own drugstores in determining which stores patients could use and how much the stores were reimbursed for the prescriptions they dispensed. In Washington and other states, lawmakers from both parties have proposed similar legislation, which the giant companies have fiercely opposed.

CVS Health, which mounted aggressive advertising and legal campaigns to try to block the state laws, warned repeatedly that splitting off pharmacies would force it to close drugstores and raise costs for consumers.

The company sometimes offers patients a financial incentive to use its pharmacies, rather than fill their prescriptions elsewhere. But in practice, consumers may not notice a difference from the breakup, because those kinds of arrangements could still exist.

In an interview on CNBC on Wednesday morning, David Joyner, chief executive of CVS Health, said that the political and regulatory pressure is “one of the external things that we assessed” in making the decision to split the company.

During a call with analysts, he said that having two separate public companies will allow the distinct businesses to “innovate and move faster.” He added, “We are doing this from a position of strength.”

Mr. Joyner will run the business that includes the remaining insurance and pharmacy benefits divisions. Another longtime CVS executive, Prem Shah, will head the pharmacy spinoff.

CVS Health generated over $400 billion in revenue last year. That ranked seventh among U. S. public companies, according to FactSet, a financial data provider.

The Financial Times on Tuesday reported the company’s plans to split itself up.

The planned breakup would end an era of enormous growth, which began nearly 20 years ago when CVS, the drugstore chain, coupled with Caremark, the pharmacy benefit manager hired by employers and government programs.

In 2018, CVS merged with Aetna, one of the nation’s largest health insurers. That same year, Cigna bought Express Scripts, the pharmacy benefit manager.

Since then, CVS, UnitedHealth and Cigna have become increasingly prevalent in how Americans receive health care. Each company now encompasses a major insurer, a giant pharmacy benefit manager and a mail-order pharmacy, along with a vast array of other businesses.

The mergers were originally justified as a way of better managing patient care less expensively, and the company was allowed to proceed with the combination. That hasn’t happened as hoped.

“The split is a belated acknowledgment that the synergies between CVS pharmacy and Caremark were oversold from the start,” said Adam Fein, a consultant who writes a popular industry blog. “Owning a pharmacy chain has done little to strengthen Caremark’s market position or make it a more competitive P. B. M.”

Arielle Trzcinski, an analyst for Forrester, a research and advisory firm, said in a statement: “Now, CVS Health is effectively acknowledging that bigger isn’t always better.”

For CVS, the merged businesses have struggled in recent years and have not met Wall Street’s demands for growth. At the end of 2024, the company’s market value fell to its lowest level in over a decade, though it has since rebounded.

On Wednesday, the company announced higher-than-expected financial results in the third quarter, swinging to a profit from a loss for the same period of 2025.

Many investors see CVS’s pharmacy benefit manager as the shining jewel of the portfolio. But prospects have dimmed for the retail pharmacy business, which has lower margins and is vulnerable to changing consumer habits and industrywide challenges that shuttered Rite Aid.

CVS Health will also retain its lucrative specialty pharmacy business, which provides patients with expensive medications, like cancer drugs, that are not available at a drugstore or through traditional mail-order pharmacies.

Existing shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction. CVS’s stock was down 12 percent by early Wednesday afternoon, even as the broader market rose after Democrats gained control of Congress.

Rebecca Robbins is a Times reporter covering the pharmaceutical industry. She has been reporting on health and medicine since 2015.

Reed Abelson covers the business of health care, focusing on how financial incentives are affecting the delivery of care, from the costs to consumers to the profits to providers.

The American Southwest Is Parched. Can the Recent Floodwaters Quench It?

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A series of storms has added to reservoirs in the Colorado River basin, but the long-term water outlook remains bleak.

By Scott Dance

Reporting from Washington

Floods have overwhelmed parts of the parched American Southwest in recent days and weeks, pouring water into critically low reservoirs.

But the deluge did little to ease worries over the water crisis that required significant limits on usage across the Colorado River basin earlier this year.

Instead, it exemplified a sort of weather whiplash that is becoming more common as the climate warms, making it harder to maintain a stable water supply for the West. Right after enduring one of its driest stretches of spring and summer on record, the Southwest is now experiencing one of its wettest autumns.

“It gives us a little bit of breathing room, but we’ve just got to see how much it snows this year,” said Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

Here’s what to know about the floods and what they mean for the Colorado basin, which supplies water to 40 million people and 5.5 million acres of farmland across parts of seven U. S. states, as well as about two dozen Native tribes and two Mexican states.

Water levels have risen sharply in Lake Powell, the nation’s second-largest reservoir, which straddles the Utah-Arizona border. The lake’s surface rose by nearly 16 feet from mid-September through the end of October. Lake Powell is expected to continue to rise once floods that hit parts of Colorado and Arizona last weekend flow downstream.

Along with Lake Mead, Lake Powell provides a stable water supply for the Colorado River’s populous and growing lower basin, including parts of Arizona, Nevada and California.

Both reservoirs had hit record lows in August.

Lake Powell remains less than 26 percent full, so it would take years of rainy and snowy weather — along with continuing water use cuts — to replenish it. Even with the recent precipitation, on Sunday the lake was only at 41 percent of its average for this time of year, dating to 1963.

The Colorado’s flow has diminished by about 20 percent over the past two decades, as the Southwest has endured a stretch scientists say is its driest in 1,200 years.

Nevertheless, the wet weather could provide some medium-term benefits, Ms. Sorensen said.

The rain has saturated soils across much of the Southwest, causing more precipitation to run off rather than percolate into the ground. While that is making the floods worse, it could also mean that more of any precipitation that falls in the coming months will make it into reservoirs, Ms. Sorensen said.

It may also prevent many farmers from drawing water from the river, she said, easing the strain on reservoirs.

There is no observed link between wet fall weather and the snowy winters needed to ensure a stable year-round water supply, said Cody Moser, a senior hydrologist at the Colorado Basin River Forecast Center.

A year ago, the Southwest received similarly heavy autumn rains, but a record snow drought followed in the winter. That led to drastic water use cuts this summer in states that rely on the Colorado. Melting snowpack is responsible for roughly 80 percent of the river’s flow in a typical year.

It’s definitely contributing. The climate pattern that is strengthening in the Pacific Ocean is increasing the amount of moisture reaching the Southwest, Mr. Moser said.

El Niño is tied to unusually warm waters across the central and eastern Pacific, where it has been increasing hurricane activity. That tropical moisture is fueling storms affecting the Southwest.

The phenomenon is known for delivering heavier-than-normal winter precipitation to Southern California and, to a lesser extent, the Southwest.

Climate change is also adding to the intensity of the rain, as well as the whiplash the region is experiencing between drought and floods.

As temperatures warm, the air can hold more water. That means storms can carry greater amounts of precipitation and deliver more intense rainfall than in the past.

That increased capacity to hold water vapor means the air can also suck more moisture out of the landscape. So during dry seasons, vegetation and soil can become parched more quickly — counterintuitively, exacerbating drought.

“We are seeing a higher frequency of more extreme events on both ends,” Mr. Moser said. “Unfortunately, the drier events have been outweighing the wetter events over the past 25 years.”

Recent water extremes on Lake Powell demonstrate the challenging trend.

The lake received record inflows in October of about 1.6 million acre-feet, Mr. Moser said. One acre-foot of water is enough to supply two or three households for a year.

Compare that to the 1.1 million acre-feet that flowed into the lake during a key stretch from April to July, when winter snowmelt typically refills the reservoir. That was the second-lowest inflow on record for that period.

Such extremes are becoming more common, Mr. Moser said: “They both happened in the same year.”

It can be counterintuitive to learn that climate change is influencing both the intense droughts and floods the Southwest has experienced this year. In this article, I wanted to help readers understand that connection, and why deluges like this latest one aren’t exactly a reason for optimism.

Scott Dance is a Times reporter who covers how climate change and extreme weather are transforming society.

Trump Has Been Thumped. That Doesn’t Make Him Any Less Dangerous.

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Jamelle Bouie

By Jamelle Bouie

Opinion Columnist

There are two basic stories to tell about the 2026 midterm elections.

The first, obviously, is the political collapse of President Trump and the Republican Party in the wake of authoritarian repression, economic mismanagement and a failed war of choice. That story explains the results of Tuesday’s elections, in which Democrats swept to victory across the country in a total repudiation of the president’s vision for American life. In addition to Congress, Republicans lost state legislatures and governor’s mansions, losing power up and down the ballot in the most stark rejection of a political party since 2010.

Those results are so striking that the second story might go by the wayside — dismissed as immaterial to the bigger picture. But that would be a mistake, because the second story is ultimately the most important one.

The core of the problem is that Trump turned the federal government against American democracy in a relentless effort to challenge, subvert and undermine the nation’s election infrastructure. All in an effort to disrupt the conduct of free and fair elections and hold onto power in the face of popular discontent.

Trump has always rejected the idea that he could legitimately lose an election. In 2016, he insisted that illegal voting by noncitizens had given Hillary Clinton her winning margin in the popular vote. In 2020, he blamed fraud for his defeat at the hands of Joe Biden and then started a monthslong attempt to overturn the election, culminating in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. There was, unsurprisingly no such complaint of fraud or illegal voting after the 2024 election, which he won. But that just proves the point.

Direct control of the election system was, along with mass deportations, border security, tariffs and an attack on civil society, a top priority for Trump at the start of his second term. In March of last year, claiming extraordinary authority over Congress and the states, Trump issued an executive order purporting to overhaul — and seize control — of federal elections. His decree would have required proof of citizenship to register to vote, decertified voting machines used in dozens of states, penalized states that count timely ballots received after Election Day, opened voter files and registration lists to both the Department of Homeland Security and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency and conditioned federal grants and awards on whether states had worked with the Department of Justice to prosecute election crimes.

The president’s order was, from top to bottom, a lawless exercise of executive authority and a blatant violation of both federal law and the Constitution, which delegates the power to run elections to the states, with the caveat that “Congress may at any time by Law make or alter such Regulations.”

Following a lawsuit, a federal court enjoined the executive order and in a final decision issued later that year, the court permanently blocked the president’s attempt to take control of American elections.

But Trump is nothing if not persistent, and he continued to look for ways to commandeer the voting system. He pressured Republicans to pass the SAVE Act, which would have codified his executive order into law. He pushed the Department of Justice to validate his election conspiracies. In January, the F. B. I. raided the election office of Fulton County, Ga., a frequent target of Trump’s claims of voter fraud. The Department of Justice made repeated attempts to try to get access to state voter files, ultimately losing each time. “Put simply,” as the Federal District Court for the District of Columbia put it in League of United Latin American Citizens et al. v. Executive Office of the President, “our Constitution does not allow the President to impose unilateral changes to federal election procedures.”

And still, Trump was not deterred. In late March, he issued another executive order, this one aimed at the United States Postal Service, in which he ordered the postal service to determine who can vote by mail and deny ballots to anyone not deemed eligible. He also ordered the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of eligible voters.

The ultimate aim of this order was to undermine mail-in voting — a frequent bête noire of the president — and effectively block millions of eligible voters from casting their ballots. To try to compel compliance, Trump also ordered the attorney general to investigate and prosecute state and local election officials who issue mail ballots to voters deemed ineligible by D. H. S.

As this order made its way through the courts, Trump administration officials also tried to put their thumb on the scale, threatening state and local election officials for not following the president’s dictates. In July, the Justice Department sent letters to all 50 states and Washington D. C., threatening criminal prosecutions if election officials counted ballots cast by noncitizen voters. In a similar move, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin alleged that over 250,000 noncitizens were registered to vote in four states, a claim that rested on a flawed system for seeking out noncitizen voters. Analysis by independent groups as well as the states themselves has found that noncitizen voting is practically nonexistent.

In September, the Supreme Court blocked the president’s attempt to use the postal service to undermine mail voting. But still Trump pushed forward. In a set of last-ditch efforts to undermine the midterms, the Justice Department has tried to make hay of ballot stacking in Alaska, using reporting from The Times to argue that the Democratic Senate nominee, Mary Peltola, broke the law when her campaign worked to recruit an independent candidate, Dan Sullivan, who shares a name with Peltola’s Republican opponent (an accusation that Peltola denies). It has also tried to force California to segregate suspected noncitizen ballots from the rest of the pool. In both cases, courts have smacked down the administration for overstepping its authority.

Most Americans who voted had a normal Election Day. Some, often those in majority Black or Hispanic precincts in states controlled by Republicans, faced the usual challenge of long lines and limited places to cast a ballot.

But the long effort to subvert the elections and keep the Republican Party in power, against the will of voters, fell flat. And while there are still avenues for chaos and disruption, the scale of Trump’s defeat at the ballot box makes it very unlikely that he’ll have anything more than token support from his party. For his part, Trump said on Tuesday that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of the elections.

That is no reason to breathe easy. What we know is that, if he thinks he might lose, the president is opposed to free and fair elections. He is opposed to the idea of electoral accountability. He rejects the fundamental republican principles of self-government and popular sovereignty. If he could act unimpeded, he would make the United States a Potemkin democracy.

This election cycle may be over, but as a threat to our freedom to govern ourselves, Trump still looms.

Jamelle Bouie became a New York Times Opinion columnist in 2019. Before that he was the chief political correspondent for Slate magazine. He is based in Charlottesville, Va.

Connections Coach

Millions viewed Lisa He’s post about her mother’s struggling business in Edinburgh. But internet fame created its own complications — and obscured bigger questions.

Credit... Video by Robert Ormerod For The New York Times

Supported by

By Isabella Kwai

Reporting from Edinburgh

Sophie Li wiped the tables and swept the floors every day at China Star, even though few customers came through the door.

For nearly 20 years, Mrs. Li’s Chinese restaurant in Edinburgh has been both her life’s work and her cross to bear. In better times, business was steady enough to support her and her two daughters and help send them to universities.

But early this year, the restaurant was almost always empty. Still, Mrs. Li, approaching 70, scrimped and toiled seven days a week to keep China Star open.

“I am a person who can endure hardship better than humiliation,” she said.

Down in London, her younger daughter, Lisa He, worried about the toll on her mother’s health. She traveled up to Scotland and posted a plea on social media.

“My mum’s Chinese restaurant is dying,” Ms. He, 29, said in a video on Instagram in April. She had decided to put aside several months to try to save it.

“Follow the journey and let’s see if I can turn this around,” she said.

Within days, the post had been viewed millions of times. Influencers and sympathetic locals suddenly flocked to China Star, overwhelming the modest 13-table restaurant.

Neither Ms. He nor her mother had been ready for internet stardom. She wondered whether she had made a mistake.

“It was absolutely awful,” Ms. He said. Going viral “doesn’t help when your restaurant’s already broken.”

Sitting in China Star’s dining room can feel like taking a trip back in time.

An aquarium filled with shy fish welcomes diners, and lucky cat figurines sit in the window. Decorations from a long-ago wedding still hang on the back wall. Dishes are washed by hand.

Mrs. Li was born Wei Li but took the name Sophie after emigrating to Edinburgh in 1993 from mainland China with her husband, a doctoral candidate at the University of Edinburgh. She liked the regal sound of her new name, and hoped to live up to it. To support the family, she worked as a dishwasher and waited tables.

But she didn’t feel at ease in her new home. She worried that Lisa and her older sister, Emma, would not assimilate. In 1997, with loans from relatives and friends, she opened a restaurant, then a decade later moved to her current location, on busy West Maitland Street, beneath a large red sign with “China Star” in gold letters.

“I felt like my standing wasn’t as high when I first came,” she said. She wanted her children “to hold their head high.”

Her chefs were from Hong Kong and southern China, and they cooked a version of Chinese food that had been shaped in postwar Britain into a cuisine of its own: salt-and-pepper stir-fries, sweet and sour chicken, fried noodles and curries. Mrs. Li eventually kept two menus: one for Chinese visitors and one for locals.

She worked 15-hour days, sleeping only a few hours per night. Mornings were for cleaning and ingredient prep. Then came lunch service. She waited tables and delivered takeout orders herself, keeping the restaurant open until midnight, even on Christmas.

Time passed. Her husband returned to China. Her daughters moved to London. Mrs. Li paid off the mortgage on China Star.

But as newer Chinese restaurants opened in Edinburgh and competition grew, the restaurant began to feel more like a burden. Foot traffic ebbed, and more of her business shifted to internet orders, whose commissions ate into their margins. Online ratings for the restaurant dropped.

Mrs. Li does not consider herself tech-savvy, so she didn’t see the customer reviews that complained about small portion sizes or bland fried rice. Arthritis was slowing her down. And she felt lonely.

“I didn’t think there was much hope,” she said. “But I had to keep going. There’s no other road to walk.”

In London, Ms. He, who was making a living as an actress and paralegal, kept tabs on China Star by logging into its CCTV camera. She saw how tired her mother looked. Early this year, she booked a trip home, hoping to give her a break.

“I came back out of a desperation to save my mom, rather than save the restaurant,” she said.

Ms. He has complicated feelings about restaurant life. When she was a baby, her mother brought her to work, putting her in a makeshift crib in a side room. After school, she felt guilty watching her work so hard.

“I often felt like I had to give up my social life to help out at the restaurant,” she said.

Before April, Ms. He’s social media account consisted mostly of images of her dancing or in film rehearsals.

But in this video, she turned the camera on her mother and China Star and gave her own, raw assessment of something many businesses may prefer to hide: what wasn’t working, from the uninviting facade to the outdated menu. And she invited people to follow her own journey as she tried to turn their fortunes around.

Perhaps it was Ms. He’s candor, or the video’s documentary style. Or perhaps it was the feeling, for watchers online, that they could still stave off the loss of yet another family-run business in a world of corporations and chains.

Ms. He’s comments lit up with offers of help, from improving the design to revamping the menu. Diners promised to visit. Restaurant owners encouraged them to rethink the business. “Don’t give up,” one said. “It isn’t over until it’s over.”

Ms. He posted the video on a Sunday. On Tuesday, she found herself back in the kitchen, trying to manage a situation for which they were entirely unprepared.

Food bloggers and new diners filled the restaurant in the days after that viral post. Mrs. Li, who learned of her daughter’s post only after it blew up, was shocked.

Suddenly, daughter and mother were racing up and down stairs to take orders as their two cooks, used to a scattering of orders each day, suddenly had to pump out dishes.

Tensions boiled over when one frustrated chef walked out in protest during lunch as a full house waited for meals. Overwhelmed, the mother and daughter decided to shutter the restaurant temporarily.

People following China Star’s struggles online replied to Ms. He with thoughts about what the restaurant needed to survive, and she decided to act on some of the advice.

She convinced her mother to slim down the menu and add Chinese wines, hired more servers and installed an electronic system for orders. They reopened after about a week with earlier hours and they closed on Mondays.

She shared updates on Instagram, where more than 200,000 accounts are now following her.

Five months after going viral, Ms. He was still working in the dining room, taking orders and mixing drinks. On a Thursday this September, the tables were filled with people who had seen her videos, drawn as much by the story of filial devotion and small-business survival as by the food.

“Usually the second generation — they don’t want to do the restaurant work,” said Wing Cheong, a visitor from Canada. “I think she is a good daughter.”

Mrs. Li, energized, could not imagine giving up China Star, and was hopeful that her daughter would take it over one day. Revenues this summer more than tripled from the year before, and the online attention has led to sponsorships.

But Ms. He wasn’t sure.

She was struggling to balance it all — the social media posts, the long days, the physical labor. There was a leak in the storeroom; a bathroom toilet seat needed fixing.

Beneath it lay a familiar generational dilemma: She had put her own career, and her ambitions to act and dance, on hold to keep her mother’s business afloat.

In one post this summer, she asked whether going viral had made their lives better, or just busier. In her mind, maybe it was time to let China Star go, for her mother to retire and for her to go back to London.

Her video had succeeded. But it had also revealed how differently mother and daughter imagined what should come next.

“If I’m tiring myself and my mom to death every day,” she said at the restaurant, in a quiet moment before lunch, “I don’t really see that as a success.”

For now, decisions on the future would have to wait. For the first time in a long time, the restaurant had large bookings for the holidays in December, and there was plenty of work to do: folding napkins, sorting prawn crackers and washing glasses. They would be back the next day to do it all again.

In April, I saw a video from Lisa He about her mother, and their struggling family-run restaurant. The restaurant, China Star, reminded me of a lot of businesses run by an older generation — once local institutions, but facing closure in an increasingly competitive industry.

What interested me most was the clashing of both an old and new world. Seemingly overnight, strangers were invested in the fate of a small, largely unknown restaurant in Edinburgh. It appeared, on the surface, a dream outcome for any business owner. But what comes after sudden internet fame, and can it really change everything?

Isabella Kwai is a Times reporter based in London, covering breaking news and other trends.

Five Things to Know About Hakeem Jeffries

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The New York Democrat who is in line to be the first Black speaker was raised in Brooklyn, is a moderate who is cautious by nature and loves a hip-hop reference.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

On the frigid evening of President Trump’s inauguration last year, after the vindicated president swept back into power and immediately pardoned nearly all of the Jan. 6 rioters, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, gathered his top lieutenants for a quiet dinner in Washington.

In a private back room at Osteria Morini, an Italian restaurant on the Anacostia River, Mr. Jeffries, the relatively untested Democratic leader, and his team strategized for hours about how to use their limited power in the minority to check a newly empowered president who now had control of both houses of Congress.

Mr. Jeffries, according to a person who attended the dinner, was preoccupied with a single imperative.

“We just have to win,” he said firmly. “If we don’t win in 2026, it’s over.”

On Tuesday, Democrats did just that, claiming the House majority and putting Mr. Jeffries, 56, on the precipice of making history as the first Black speaker of the House. He presided over historic victories for his party that exceeded even their own expectations. Now, his actions will determine how effective Democrats can be in checking Mr. Trump’s power, and help set the agenda for the 2028 presidential campaign.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Jeffries.

Mr. Jeffries grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, when the now-gentrified neighborhood was a hotbed of Black activism but also overrun with crime and unrest associated with the crack cocaine epidemic.

The son of a social worker and a substance abuse counselor, who became a high-powered litigator, Mr. Jeffries grew up in a house that was described by longtime associates as teeming with Black nationalist ideas. His uncle, Leonard Jeffries, a professor at the City College of New York, was associated with the Afrocentrism movement and often expressed extreme views on the subject.

Mr. Jeffries and his brother, Hasan Kwame Jeffries, a history professor at Ohio State University, were pushed by their churchgoing parents to excel above all else.

“When Hakeem was growing up, Myrtle Avenue was known as Murder Avenue,” recalled Lupe Todd-Medina, one of his longtime political advisers. “It was not a place white people wanted to go. He grew up in this bubble of love, with lots of aunties around him. That also helped shape who he is.”

His mother and his aunt joined the Cornerstone Baptist Church, a Black house of worship, in the 1960s, and the congregation and its pastors became an important force in shaping Mr. Jeffries’s early life. Growing up, he served as an usher there. His grandmother predicted that he would one day become a pastor.

Mr. Jeffries has said that he has been motivated since entering law school by fights over racial justice. If all goes as expected and he is elected in January as the first Black speaker, he would be second in line to the presidency.

“That might be the thing that matters the most to him — breaking the glass,” Ms. Todd-Medina said.

At a victory party on Tuesday night, he ended his remarks with a note of hometown pride.

“We made it, Brooklyn,” he said. “We made it.”

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi never exactly groomed her mentees, but she had a small circle of loyal House Democrats around her whom she viewed as potential successors. Mr. Jeffries was never one of them. But when he was elected by Democrats in 2018 to be the chairman of their caucus, essentially their chief messaging official and No. 5 leader, he was widely seen as having the potential to be the first Black speaker.

And four years later, when Ms. Pelosi acceded to calls to relinquish her role as the top Democrat, Mr. Jeffries quickly emerged as his colleagues’ top choice to take her place. He was elected House Democratic leader by acclamation after the 2022 midterm elections.

Still, while he is not expected to face a challenge for the job of speaker, Democrats are not unanimously thrilled about his elevation to become the most powerful man in Congress.

Though he is seen as a fresh face compared with the octogenarians who led Democrats in the House until recently, Mr. Jeffries is substantially more moderate than Ms. Pelosi and the progressives who are the largest bloc in the caucus. He is viewed as an establishment figure at a time when many Democratic voters are rejecting their party’s entrenched power structure.

Mr. Jeffries is known for his stentorian speeches and statements and his sharp-tongued attacks on Republicans. But he is a careful politician who avoids public confrontations and prefers lengthy private deliberation to quick moves. That has led some Democrats to view him as overly cautious, according to interviews with a half-dozen officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer an unvarnished view of his standing.

They questioned whether he had the instincts to sustain the kind of fights that Democrats will need to show voters they can wage and win, now that they have swept into power in Washington.

Some House Democrats also said they had been surprised over the years when they did not hear much directly from Mr. Jeffries, even after successes or struggles. They had grown accustomed to Ms. Pelosi, who would constantly work the phones to keep her finger on the pulse of the caucus, often congratulating or commiserating with lawmakers as she quizzed them about what they were hearing. But Ms. Pelosi effectively operated as both the speaker and the whip.

These days, the duties are more divided, and it is Representative Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 who is in line to become the first female majority leader, who takes on the member management tasks that typically come with the job of chief vote counter.

Some of Mr. Jeffries’s allies said they expected him to act more aggressively and decisively in his new job.

“When you’re the speaker, you become the engine of the vote,” said Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Democrat of New York and one of Mr. Jeffries’s most trusted lieutenants. “Hakeem is ready to do just that. In the minority, your role is not as commanding.”

Many democratic socialist candidates elected this year view Mr. Jeffries with particular aversion, regarding him as an establishment politician who has held back some of their progressive goals.

They also see him as too closely aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group that has come to be seen by many Democrats as politically radioactive. The radio host Charlamagne Tha God has mocked him as “AIPAC Shakur.”

Mr. Jeffries bristles at the notion that he is beholden to any outside special interest group.

“Nobody can point to a single instance of me taking a vote that had anything to do with being influenced by any outside group,” he said in an interview earlier this year.

Still, Mr. Jeffries will face a major test next year from a progressive bloc of lawmakers who want Democrats to unite around ending military aid to Israel, which has bitterly divided the party. He will face competing pressure from more centrist Democrats, who have privately warned him that the party will get flattened if he goes too far in appeasing the left.

Mr. Jeffries is already cognizant of a need for Democrats to recalibrate their position on Israel. The question is how far he will be willing to go.

Earlier this year, he opposed a measure that nearly half of House Democrats backed that would have terminated U. S. aid to Israel. But in a letter announcing his position, he conceded that there were good reasons to back the measure and asserted that “a meaningful change in direction is needed” in the relationship between the United States and Israel.

Mr. Jeffries, a Generation X leader in a Congress still filled with baby boomers, has made hip-hop culture a central part of his public persona, often peppering his speeches with rap lyrics.

During Mr. Trump’s 2020 impeachment trial, Mr. Jeffries ended his somber presentation with a lyric by the rapper and fellow Brooklynite Biggie Smalls: “And if you don’t know, now you know.”

At a news conference in February, he quoted the rapper Jay-Z while railing against redistricting in Texas.

“At what point will Republican extremists come to the conclusion that your reach ain’t long enough and your peeps ain’t strong enough?” he said.

He turned again to inspiration from Jay-Z in March, at a news conference related to the government shutdown.

“But for us, difficult takes a day, impossible takes a week,” Mr. Jeffries said, quoting a Jay-Z guest verse on Kanye West’s “Diamonds from Sierra Leone.”

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Israel’s President Holds Crucial Cards in Breaking Post-Election Deadlock

The New York Times November 04, 2026

Israel’s Election

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

President Isaac Herzog has tried to avoid controversy and heal rifts in his largely ceremonial role. But his skills as a savvy mediator could be instrumental after an inconclusive election.

By Isabel Kershner

Reporting from Jerusalem

For five years, Isaac Herzog has tried to avoid controversy and heal rifts in his largely ceremonial role as the president of Israel. Now, following last week’s inconclusive election, he must make a decision that is likely to roil one half or the other of a fractured country.

One of the president’s few powers is the ability to grant a party leader the mandate to try and form a government. Typically, this is assigned to the head of the party that has won the most votes or appears to have the best chance of building a coalition that would command a majority in Parliament. But the law is vague, giving the president a lot of leeway over the process.

Mr. Herzog, the scion of an illustrious Israeli family who is expected to remain involved in the backroom talks throughout the process, will have to draw on his skills as a savvy negotiator and mediator — expertise he honed over his years as a lawyer and politician, including as leader of the center-left Labor party.

After working in law, he served as a government secretary under Prime Minister Ehud Barak and as a minister in multiple governments. He ran a credible but unsuccessful campaign to replace Mr. Netanyahu in the 2015 election and went on to lead the Jewish Agency, an organization that serves as a bridge between Israel and the Jewish diaspora.

A longtime advocate of national unity, he will most likely work to enable as broad a government as possible, analysts say, to try to get Israel out of what many call the political “plonter,” a Yiddish word to describe a mess, like an intricate knot that is hard to unravel.

“This is his big moment,” Nachman Shai, a former Labor minister and lawmaker, said of Mr. Herzog. “He is a polished, creative politician,” he added. “Not everyone will like his ideas, but I’m sure he will be looking for solutions to build a coalition that are out of the box.”

Starting on Wednesday, representatives of the 11 political parties elected to the new Parliament will troop through the presidential residence in a leafy neighborhood of Jerusalem to consult with Mr. Herzog and to recommend their candidate for the premiership.

Most party leaders are expected to back either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the longtime right-wing leader, or his main center-right rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief.

Note: Parties must win at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter the 120-seat Knesset.

Source: Israel’s Central Elections Committee

Neither man’s political bloc won an outright majority of 61 seats in the 120-member Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud took 27 seats, making it the largest party, but his hard-right, religious coalition’s tally fell to 53 seats.

Mr. Eisenkot’s main bloc of Jewish opposition parties secured 48 seats. If the Arab-led parties that oppose Mr. Netanyahu and won 19 seats also recommend him to Mr. Herzog, the president may well grant him the first opportunity to try and form a government. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s Jewish allies, however, have balked at the idea of a government relying on Arab support.

Mr. Herzog cannot take political sides and must remain a unifying figurehead above the fray. He has called for a “stable” government without specifying how it should be formed and has called on the parties’ representatives to consult with him with open minds and hearts.

The law allows the assigned candidate 28 days to try to form a government, though the president can extend that period by up to 14 days. If the first attempt fails, the president can give another candidate a chance or refer the efforts to Parliament. If no party leader is able to form a governing coalition, new elections would be held — an outcome that Mr. Herzog has urged them to avoid.

The kind of broad unity government that Mr. Herzog may envisage would likely require some kind of power-sharing deal between Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Eisenkot — a prospect that faces huge obstacles.

Mr. Eisenkot says that Mr. Netanyahu must be replaced and has ruled out serving under him. Mr. Netanyahu, who has been on trial for six years following corruption charges in three separate but interlocking cases, cannot serve in a government as a minister. According to Israeli law, only a prime minister can serve under indictment.

Mr. Herzog has a potentially valuable, if highly contentious, card to play to try to bring Mr. Netanyahu on side with a unifying coalition, analysts say.

The president has the authority to issue pardons, generally for people already convicted of crimes. Mr. Netanyahu, who has denied any wrongdoing, submitted a pre-emptive request for a pardon during his trial a year ago.

Mr. Herzog has instead offered to try to initiate a mediation process to reach a plea deal and invited the attorney general and Mr. Netanyahu’s lawyer for talks. Mr. Netanyahu’s team never replied.

“A pardon can be part of a package deal,” Mr. Shai said. “It could be a way for Mr. Herzog to come to a compromise with him. Everyone is tired of the trial by now, and nobody knows how it will end.”

“Herzog is energetic, super active, primed for action,” he said. “People forget he is one of the most experienced people around,” he added.

Mitchell Barak, an analyst who worked as an aide to Mr. Netanyahu and later for President Shimon Peres, a former Labor leader, said Mr. Herzog’s history with the prime minister and the “ace” of a potential pardon could be viewed either as a conflict of interest in negotiations or as an advantage.

“He is holding a get-out-of-jail-free card for Netanyahu,” Mr. Barak added. “Or you could call it leverage,” he added.

The president’s office dismissed suggestions of a conflict of interest, saying the pardon and the efforts toward forming a government were two different tracks based on separate laws.

As president, Mr. Herzog oversaw negotiations that tried, and failed, to reach a compromise over the Netanyahu government’s plans for a judicial overhaul that caused turmoil in Israel. Mr. Shai said many Israelis had expected Mr. Herzog to take a stronger stand against the government’s moves and that the episode harmed his public standing.

Mr. Herzog also appears to have tried to build confidence on both sides of Israel’s political divide.

He has spoken out against what he called “a terrible process of brutalization” creeping into Israeli society, citing a surge of “mob” violence by Jews against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the abuse of detainees in Israeli custody.

Mr. Herzog also recently expunged the criminal record of Elor Azaria, a former soldier who fatally shot a severely wounded Palestinian man at close range while he lay on the ground a decade ago. The man had earlier been seriously injured after he attacked an Israeli checkpoint. The president’s move baffled and angered many liberal Israelis but fulfilled a long-sought demand from Israel’s right.

Mr. Herzog also has his family legacy and reputation to consider. His grandfather, Rabbi Dr. Yitzhak Isaac Halevi Herzog, was the first Chief Rabbi of the state of Israel. His father, Chaim Herzog, served as the sixth president of Israel.

After the 1984 election, when Mr. Peres and Yitzhak Shamir, then the Likud leader, were in a deadlock, Mr. Herzog’s father played an active role in promoting the formation of a unity government, resolving the political impasse.

Mr. Herzog “is part of the country’s old guard and political elite with a storied tradition of excellence,” said Mr. Barak. “There’s a certain responsibility that comes with that.”

Isabel Kershner, a senior correspondent for The Times in Jerusalem, has been reporting on Israeli and Palestinian affairs since 1990.

‘Dune’ Reunion: Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya and Friends Can Take the Heat

The New York Times November 04, 2026

What to Watch

As Denis Villeneuve’s blockbuster series concludes, the cast recalls dealing with desert shoots and wrestling with the story’s moral implications.

As Denis Villeneuve’s blockbuster series concludes, the cast recalls dealing with desert shoots and wrestling with the story’s moral implications.

Credit... Charlie Gates For The New York Times

Supported by

By Eleanor Stanford

Reporting from London

Back in 2018, when Timothée Chalamet was announced as the star of Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune” series, filming a blockbuster adaptation of one of science fiction’s most complex stories did seem like “a little bit” of a leap, the actor said.

After all, David Lynch’s 1984 attempt hadn’t resonated at the box office, and Villeneuve’s three-part vision would cost hundreds of millions of dollars at a time when some superhero vehicles had struggled to make a profit.

But that little leap has paid off. Together “Dune: Part One” and “Part Two” have grossed more than $1 billion worldwide. That’s especially noteworthy given that the first one arrived in the wake of Covid theater shutdowns and the sequel was delayed by the writers’ strike.

“Part Three,” which is based on the subsequent novels in Frank Herbert’s “Dune” series, arrives in theaters Dec. 18. “The anticipation of this one has been really, really awesome,” Chalamet said in an interview with several castmates.

The third installment jumps ahead nearly 20 years, with Chalamet’s Paul Atreides now an interplanetary emperor under threat and estranged from his former love, Chani (Zendaya), who continues to fight fiercely for her Fremen people. Robert Pattinson joins as a new villain, intent on taking Paul down. He called the series “one of the only franchises where I’m like, ‘oh I’m a full fan.’”

Filmed in Hungary and the deserts of the United Arab Emirates, “Part Three” reunited the stars, castmates like Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy and Jason Momoa, and crew members, including the same costumer (Lori Harris), Zendaya said. “She’s watched me grow up, and I feel like now she’s an auntie.”

In October, Chalamet, Zendaya, Momoa and Taylor-Joy gathered in a studio space in London to discuss working together, being directed by Villeneuve and why fans of the books shouldn’t be concerned by how “Part Three” diverges from its source material. (Pattinson and Pugh spoke via video call a few weeks later.)

Here are edited excerpts from our conversations.

Zendaya and Timothée, you were both 22 or 23 when you filmed “Part One.” Does it feel like you’ve grown up with these films?

TIMOTHÉE CHALAMET Absolutely. I was thinking about it with Z, usually you grow up with people over your childhood or your adolescence, and it was special with Z to kind of begin working with each other at the end of youth, and at the beginning of adulthood.

ZENDAYA If I look back at the version of us then, it is like a child to me now. Which is a beautiful thing. Because we were all anxious and really coming into it, back then at least, bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, and wanting to do a good job. I think there’s no better home to have been learning and growing. Because of his kindness and his generosity, Denis is a great leader.

Denis’s kindness is something that people who’ve worked with him talk about a lot.

ANYA TAYLOR-JOY It can’t be understated how magical it is to be in the presence of somebody who leads with love and who commands this enormous ship of people to do this thing, and they’re not doing it because they’re afraid of him.

CHALAMET It’s a really wholesome instinct that everyone has to try to make him satisfied, basically.

FLORENCE PUGH Totally, everyone is teacher’s pet. Oh my God, I am an ultimate teacher’s pet. We certainly wouldn’t follow anybody into battle, but we do with him.

That makes me think of the notoriously tricky desert shoots the “Dune” films require. How were they for you all this time around?

ZENDAYA The hardest thing is to just meditate through the heat. There’s scenes where the sun is so bright that I am trying to give another facial expression other than [Zendaya scrunches up her face as if in pain] and I physically can’t. [Laughs] I was just pouring sweat, trying to focus, keep my eyes open as much as I can.

You’ve got to get ready and set up before the sun starts coming up, while it’s still cool, and also we had to get into the prosthetics of it all. No one earlier than Rob.

ROBERT PATTINSON The desert is just another level. There’s this one sequence where I’m in this spaceship, on a gimbal, on the edge of a sand dune, and we had this 350-foot-long model of a sandworm. The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you’re having your own “Dune” theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all. There are no negatives.

Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn’t even really notice them. He’s so easy to work with, Denis, it’s never really a stress.

Anya, you were on set briefly for a cameo in the second film.

TAYLOR-JOY I mean, barely. [Laughs] I was part of a rogue team that went to Namibia, but it was one of my favorite shooting experiences of all time.

Your character Alia, Paul’s sister, is born with knowledge from previous generations of women and is a much bigger part of this movie.

TAYLOR-JOY At the end of the movie, Denis and I talked, and I was like, “Whoa, I’m the bad guy. That’s crazy.”

But I really understood where she was coming from. What a gift of a character to play somebody that has one connection to one person, and nobody else matters at all.

That kind of straightforwardness felt almost animalistic in a way. I’ve never really done animal work before, but she was definitely my most feral creation.

Herbert wrote a sequel to his first “Dune” novel in part because readers in the 1960s hadn’t understood the message of the first novel.

TAYLOR-JOY This has kind of happened with the movies, too. Paul is a very charismatic character and you have to have the third movie to be like, hold up, this is not the moral of the story.

Making the film, how pertinent did Herbert’s intended warning about the dangers of a messianic, totalitarian leader feel?

CHALAMET Well, it definitely feels personal because of how many of these themes have stood the test of time from the ’60s to now, and the scary world we live in.

The more I worked on “Dune,” the less I felt it was my more local responsibility to be thinking about the greater themes at large. That Denis was perfectly handling them, and, especially in this one, thinking what would it actually be like to be in that kind of situation, thinking of world leaders, good and bad, present and past, and how exhausting and diminishing it is to always be making decisions of importance.

PUGH I think we are witnessing a lot of the way that people feel right now through their art, and that hasn’t been lost on me for a long time. For the last 10 years of filmmaking — other than “Barbie,” which was brilliantly upbeat — I feel like we have been feeling that in art.

Jason, your character Duncan Idaho was killed in the first movie. In “Part Three,” you play a character who looks just like Duncan and was created from his genetic material but has none of Duncan’s memories or personality.

JASON MOMOA It’s probably the weirdest character I’ve ever had to navigate, because I know I was hired to play Duncan for a certain reason, then I had to figure out how to play a guy who doesn’t know who the guy is.

I also didn’t have Denis, like I had on the first one. They were already shooting and I came in, and I was not going to call and ask a bunch of questions.

It was very challenging. I’m not the most subtle actor, or human, so it was probably my most subtle performance. I haven’t seen it yet. I don’t know which takes he used.

And another thing too, working with Tim, I have to fight him. [His character Paul] is at a whole other level, and better than me as a fighter. And you know, realistically, how do we put that together?

CHALAMET That was a very polite way of saying that.

[All laugh]

MOMOA He’s a better actor. I’m better at fighting. But he’s really fast. I was super impressed: Just because you’re a great actor, it doesn’t mean that you’re able to dance. Ultimately, it’s a dance.

For those of you who have seen the film already, how was watching the conclusion of these characters’ stories? How different is it from the novel?

ZENDAYA There’s a lot in this film that is very true to the source material, and there are departures.

TAYLOR-JOY Denis is literally the biggest “Dune” fan of all time, so for that to be the person who’s steering the ship, you feel pretty good about it.

PATTINSON You got to be kind of crazy if you’re going to be picking fault with this one.

The script was really cool, but it was quite complicated. And watching the film, it’s not about what I thought it was going to be about at all. It reads as much more of a grand political, moral fable, and the movie is so much more emotional. A lot of it is about parenting, and I just thought it was so moving.

MOMOA Are you satisfied, when you watch the end?

CHALAMET Absolutely. It didn’t feel like the bar dropped at all, Denis just changed the location of the bar. This movie is its own thing.

MOMOA I have butterflies in my belly. I’m going to watch it tonight with my kid [Nakoa-Wolf Momoa, who plays Paul and Chani’s son] and it’s going to be special. That’s his first movie he’s ever been in.

TAYLOR-JOY What a great first movie!

In 2021, when “Part One” came out, Covid had hit and ticket sales were really down. Today, Hollywood is in a very different place, with a recent boom at the box office. How big a part do you think the “Dune” movies have played in this resurgence?

PUGH I think they brought back moviegoing. What an event the second one was. It was just so lovely to be a part of something that we know is our generational kind of “Star Wars.”

CHALAMET Hopefully it’s had a big part in it. I think everyone here has humbly had a big part in it.

ZENDAYA Any opportunity that we have that we can hopefully contribute to the moviegoing experience and keep that alive, because it’s so much a part of my life, my childhood, so many people’s lives — it’s the reason we do it.

Key Part of Jet in Deadly Florida Crash Found Far From Impact Site

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Florida Learjet Crash

Advertisement

Supported by

The mechanism that controls the vertical angle of the plane was found in three pieces, including one nearly four miles away. All nine people aboard were killed.

By Karoun Demirjian and Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs

A crucial part of the private jet that crashed in Florida on Sunday was found in fragments far from where the aircraft slammed into the ground in Palm Beach County, federal investigators said on Tuesday.

The fiery crash killed all nine people aboard, and the part, a mechanism that controls the angle of the plane, was found in three pieces, including at a spot nearly four miles from the crash site.

The discovery of the part, known as the left tail elevator, was a “very important piece of evidence,” Thomas B. Chapman, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, said at a news conference on Tuesday.

But it was not yet clear whether the tail part broke off before the plane began to plummet or during the aircraft’s plunge to the ground.

Still, the recovery of the part was a bit of progress in an investigation that has been hampered by a host of complications, including the powerful storms that investigators believe were a factor in Sunday’s crash. There were severe thunderstorms in Palm Beach County on Sunday afternoon when the plane, a Learjet 60, crashed nose first on a road, erupting into a fireball that was captured in harrowing video footage.

Mr. Chapman said much of the wreckage remained in a crater, still off limits to investigators, who hope to have access by Wednesday once public works teams finish clearing the site of water and other damage caused by the crash.

The extreme force of the impact, Mr. Chapman said, meant that most of the physical evidence the N. T. S. B. team had been able to recover was in very small pieces.

“We don’t even know in most cases what we’ve found,” he said on Tuesday, adding, “Even the elements of the aircraft that are in the crater are going to be very likely in smaller pieces.”

Among the missing and potentially critical pieces of evidence is the aircraft’s cockpit voice recorder, which investigators often rely on for insights into pilots’ decision-making leading up to an accident. On Monday, N. T. S. B. officials told reporters that the plane had been outfitted with such a recorder, but that they could not confirm whether it was present on the aircraft when it crashed.

The pilots were Jeff Gregory, 55, and Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who had earned her pilot’s license at 17, her mother said. Ms. Filgueiras, who was talking to air traffic control during the plane’s descent, was certified as a commercial pilot earlier this year, according to records.

Among the passengers who were killed were Adam Robinson, a technology executive; his wife Helen Sharp, who worked in public relations; the couple’s two children, Emma and Charlie; and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny for the children.

The plane was flying from Austin, Texas, where the family lived, to the Bahamas, when it plunged from the sky, eventually reaching a rate of 22,000 feet per minute.

According to the pilots’ exchanges with air traffic controllers, they initially sought permission to fly across Florida on a course that would have led them straight through a large thunderstorm system. A controller warned them that the weather was bad in the area, and flight maps show that they subsequently changed course to fly south of the worst storms.

Several minutes later, Ms. Filgueiras reported to another controller that they were encountering turbulence she described as “moderate,” what she called “manageable” problems with icing on the plane, and precipitation. But shortly after that, the pilots appeared to lose control of the plane, prompting Ms. Filgueiras to issue a mayday call as the aircraft began to plummet to the ground.

It was not immediately clear to investigators what condition the aircraft’s radar and anti-icing systems were in leading up to the accident.

In an interview, Michael McCormick, a former director of air traffic operations at the Federal Aviation Administration who now teaches at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said the Learjet 60 has three complementary de-icing mechanisms, but stressed that they work best when activated in advance of encountering bad weather.

“Any one of them could fail and you’re in trouble,” he said.

Investigators will also be trying to determine what caused the plane’s left tail elevator to break off the airplane before impact — though Mr. Chapman cautioned that it would not likely have been able to save the aircraft from disaster, even if it had remained intact.

“The function of the elevator is to control pitch up and down,” he told reporters Tuesday. “At those speeds, I don’t know if it would have been effective, even if attached to the aircraft.”

Billy Witz contributed reporting, and Georgia Gee contributed research.

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs reports on stories across the United States, including natural disasters, protests, unsolved mysteries, high-profile criminal cases and more.

The Biggest Pro-AI Super Pac Network Didn’t Really Impact the Midterms

Wired November 04, 2026

Leading the Future, the biggest pro-AI super PAC network, is walking away from the midterm elections with just over $20 million still in the bank and a roster of dozens of successful congressional candidates from both sides of the aisle.

At first glance, that looks like a win. The details tell another story, though. The donations went overwhelmingly to safe candidates, and the results in the small handful of riskier races that Leading the Future got involved with indicate that its plans to shape the election fell flat.

When Leading the Future first entered the scene in August 2025 vowing to “oppose policies that stifle innovation," it had a war chest of around $100 million thanks to some of Silicon Valley’s biggest tech billionaires—including Andreessen Horowitz, Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman—and was led by major political strategists.

Designed as a “structured ecosystem,” it set a goal of having ”maximum flexibility to engage in the 2026 election cycle and beyond.” The network is made up of 501(c)(4)s, and federal and state super PACs catering to both sides of the aisle: American Mission largely gives to Republicans, while Think Big largely gives to Democrats. Its structure and overlapping strategists quickly drew comparisons to Fairshake, a massive, well-funded pro-crypto super PAC network that dominated in the 2024 election.

“They came out guns ablazing, saying be afraid, we are going to spend our millions to influence not only how lawmakers legislate us but also against you in your primaries and in your re-election,” Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, tells WIRED. ”The purpose of that was to bully lawmakers into acquiescence, intimidate them into not sticking their necks out on AI safety or tech industry regulation at all.”

Leading the Future did not respond to requests for comment.

Late last year, Leading the Future took on Democrat Alex Bores, a former Palantir engineer and state lawmaker running in New York’s 12th congressional district on an AI safety platform, spending millions of dollars in attack ads against his primary bid.

“They fully expected to bury him, put his head on a spike and parade it around as proof that they could,” says Haworth. Instead, Bores’ candidacy became a high-profile proxy war between competing AI philosophies, boosting his profile and platform. The pro-AI safety network Public First, which has significant financial backing from Anthropic, spent $15 million boosting Bores’ candidacy. Though Bores didn’t win, he came second in a crowded primary field to another candidate, Micah Lasher, who campaigned on tech accountability and AI safety.

Leading the Future spent about $26 million in independent expenditures on the primaries alone. But spending tapered off as it headed into the general election, as the network dropped about $10 million in total while overwhelmingly backing candidates in safe races. Its funding also dropped off, with the network reporting zero donations in the second and third quarters.

The strategy seems to have shifted around the same time that stark polling began coming back showing widespread distrust of Big Tech and cronyism in Washington, DC. (An NBC exit poll found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers played a “major” role in their vote.)

Backing safe candidates was, simply put, “an influence play,” says Haworth. ”They're trying to ingratiate themselves with incoming members of Congress.”

The co-founder of Public First Action says that the midterms marked a victory for AI safety. “Voters in both parties delivered the same verdict tonight,” says Brad Carson. “This is a crushing blow to the AI industry’s anti-regulatory efforts to buy a Congress that would look the other way.”

Results weren’t great in the riskier races that Leading the Future jumped into.

One of its biggest bets was on Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, who was an incumbent running to serve a full term in South Carolina. Graham earned the moniker “Data Center Darline” from her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews due to her enthusiastic support of AI and data center expansion. American Mission donated more than $2 million to Graham, who ultimately lost with 46.5 percent in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1998.

Of the other toss-up House races that Leading the Future weighed in on, almost all were in support of Republican candidates through the American Mission super PAC. The exception was Democratic Florida representative Jared Moskowitz’s re-election campaign, which it funded through Think Big. Moskowitz won by 13,000 votes against challenger Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton.

In North Carolina’s 1st congressional district, Leading the Future through American Mission backed Republican Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel who served as an assistant secretary of defense working on cyber policy under president Donald Trump in 2025, in her primary. Guardrails Alliance, another player in the AI safety network, backed her opponent, Democrat Don Davis, who previously co-sponsored a bill which would limit tax giveaways for data center development. Davis won.

Leading the Future also backed Aaron Flint, a retired combat veteran, conservative commentator, and former state director for Republican representative Ryan Zinke, who was running in Montana’s first congressional district. Flint conceded to his Democratic opponent Sam Forstag, a Democratic wildland firefighter who landed endorsements from major progressives including Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez and advocated for strict federal oversight of AI. (The Associated Press has yet to call the race.)

American Mission Florida, a state-level super PAC in the Leading the Future network, got $3 million in support of Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds. While both Donalds and opponent David Jolly took nuanced approaches to the AI safety issue, they diverged strongly on the issue of data center expansion, with Donalds opposing statewide bans or moratoriums on data centers.

After Tuesday night, Silicon Valley will be bracing for what’s expected to be a reckoning over the expansive power and freedom they’ve enjoyed thus far during Trump’s second term. Democrats have vowed to bring Big Tech bosses to Capitol Hill for hearings. Senator Ron Wyden signaled what's to come in a pithy statement on X. “Subpoeanas,” he wrote.

Blade Runner 2099 Shows the ‘Silver Linings’ of a Replicant Takeover

Wired November 04, 2026

Ridley Scott’s 1982 film Blade Runner casts a long shadow. In some ways, literally.

It defined what noir sci-fi would look like for years to come: the rain, the dramatic lighting, the trenchcoats. Denis Villeneuve delivered a worthy sequel in 2017 with Blade Runner 2049, but for some fans nothing will ever touch the original.

Silka Luisa tries not to think about these things. “If I didn’t love Blade Runner this would’ve been way too hard,” the showrunner of Prime Video’s limited series Blade Runner 2099 said Wednesday during the WIRED World Fair event in Miami.

Luisa’s show differs quite a bit from its forebears. It still has the humanoids known as replicants, but in 2099’s future, they’re the ones calling the shots, giving humans the grunt work they used to do. Set 80 years after Blade Runner and 50 years after 2049, it focuses on a replicant Blade Runner, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), on the search for rogue agents. Along the way she gets teamed up with Cora, played by Hunter Schafer, a human pretending to be a replicant to survive. (We’d say more, but the show doesn’t premiere until November 25, and, you know, spoilers.)

If this vision of dystopia sounds too familiar for comfort, Luisa hears you. When asked about how she chose to tackle the franchise, she noted that in the last couple of decades, “the present caught up to the films” as megacorporations and environmental collapse became realities in ways they weren’t in 1982. The point of her Blade Runner is to show what happens in a post-revolution world and “not focus on the fears we’re living with right now.”

That doesn’t mean that Blade Runner 2099 is entirely a dystopian tale. For Luisa, it’s about showing the “silver linings” of a world run by replicants. To do that, she picks up on some of the environmental themes touched on in Villeneuve’s movie, which showed how Earth had been wrecked by human activity. Blade Runner 2099 depicts a world that replicants are trying to bring back from the brink of ecological collapse using the skills they gained when they were working for humans. “They’re able to rehabilitate the planet,” Luisa says.

Blade Runner 2099 also gave Schafer a chance to flex some action-hero muscles—something she’d never done before and something her costar, Yeoh, has been doing for decades. Schafer jumped right in, running and diving across the screen from the pilot onward. For the fight scenes, though, she got some help from Yeoh.

“It was really physically demanding,” Schafer said during WIRED’s conference. “I felt so lucky to have Michelle Yeoh, who is the fucking master, as a scene partner.”

But back to that shadow cast by Scott’s original adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? In addition to being a sci-fi classic, it also created a whole new template for what dystopian fiction could look like. It broods.

Luisa insists there’s a little more hope in hers—and hopes audiences see that, too. She also wants audiences to know that replicants aren’t the same as the AI bots humans are fixated on in 2026. “They’re more akin to us,” she said. “AI, I just don’t have that same sympathy for.” Hear that, Claude?

Google Is Forcing AI Overviews in Classrooms. Schools Are Searching for a Way Out

Wired November 04, 2026

Two weeks ago, an IT administrator for an elementary-middle school took to Google’s support forums requesting a way to block students from seeing AI Overviews—the chatbot-generated answers at the top of search results.

“This seems counterproductive to what we're trying to teach,” the administrator wrote. “Students need opportunities to navigate search results, examine sources, and draw their own conclusions rather than being handed an AI-generated synthesis before they've even started.”

No one from Google responded to the concern, which has been bubbling up for years. But counterparts from three districts voiced similar frustration and pointed to workarounds they were employing or considering to block AI Overviews in lieu of an official “off” switch. Their expertise is about to be in demand.

Google announced on Tuesday that it is declining to provide schools an option to disable AI Overviews. Instead, starting next year, schools will have to block access to search altogether to get rid of the feature. The decision has stunned educators, parents, and technology researchers across the US.

“We were flabbergasted,” says Dominique Johnson, part of an Oregon community group called Lake Oswego Parents For Responsible Technology. “This move makes things even more difficult for school districts that have determined AI is harmful to foundational learning.”

Google didn’t respond to a request for comment. But in a public response to the controversy shared on X, the company contended that schools will now have “more choice, not less” because search, its Gemini chatbot, and Gemini Notebook tool will be off by default starting next year. Administrators can enable one, two, or all three services.

The issue for schools and parents, though, is that Google considers AI Overviews and a companion feature called AI Mode inseparable from the traditional search experience. Respectively launched in 2023 and last year, they bring the functionality of AI chatbots, such as Gemini or ChatGPT, directly into search results.

“Kids are already using these search-bar summaries to skip real effort, pulling instant math answers and letting AI write their essays,” Johnson says. “To make matters worse, these AI snapshots frequently make mistakes and output false facts, which younger students take as absolute truth.”

The AI-generated responses are tempting to read and often good enough to trust, triggering headaches beyond classrooms. Wikipedia, news websites, and education tools have lost human visitors as people rely on overviews. Google uses the same bots to crawl the web for its search and AI products, making it impossible for publishers to opt out of their content being used for the latter.

Google’s push to make AI Overviews a prominent part of search has already come at a cost. Last week, shares of parent company Alphabet suffered their worst single-day selloff, erasing half a trillion dollars in market value after the company reported weaker-than-expected search ad sales. A big cause? Increased usage of AI Overviews and AI Mode, which aren’t packed with many ads yet—although some experts believe the slump will only be temporary.

For schools, the dilemma over search may be just beginning. While several districts WIRED contacted didn’t respond to requests for comment, Los Angeles Unified says it is still reviewing the potential implications of Google’s announcement. Some education technology experts argue that schools should abandon Google search altogether, or at least do a better job teaching students to question the validity of AI answers.

“Under-resourced districts will grit their teeth and say, ‘we don’t have the capacity to dig in our heels and not use Google,’” says Stephen Aguilar, who coleads University of Southern California’s Center for Generative AI and Society. “A lot are likely going to accelerate plans they already have to teach students about this new digital literacy.”

Parent advocates also plan to push districts to look elsewhere. “This move just continues a well-established pattern of big tech companies pushing products into classrooms,” says Karolle Rabarison, a policy and communications strategist who helps lead Schools Beyond Screens in Washington, DC. “It’s not going to work any more.”

Tech industry veterans disagree about how difficult it would be for Google to let schools disable AI Overviews without affecting the rest of Search. “It’s a question of whether they’re committed to maintaining two versions of search in the long run,” says Nicole Kerson, a former senior Google Search product manager who runs the AI strategy firm Collected Company. “It's very hard to maintain a forked product like that.”

Microsoft offers a Google Chrome extension that lets users turn off AI-generated summaries in Bing search. Adeel Khan, a former teacher and principal who now runs MagicSchool, which provides AI chatbots for students and teachers, says it is “infuriating, insulting, and ludicrous” that Google isn’t doing something similar.

Without an official way to disable AI Overviews, schools have turned to technical workarounds, including modifying search URLs and adopting browser extensions that change how Google results appear. Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia recently developed its own extension. But these loopholes could stop functioning if Google changes how its search results are delivered.

Smaller search engines, such as the privacy-focused DuckDuckGo, see an opportunity to win business from schools frustrated with Google. “I wouldn't expect to see a Google-style ‘DuckDuckGo Classroom’ anytime soon, but ideally, we'll have special resources just for educators looking to make a switch,” says spokesperson Allison Goodman.

Following a federal ruling in 2024 that Google illegally maintained its search monopoly, the company was ordered to share certain search data and services with rivals and loosen restrictions on how its products are distributed. But the effort is well behind schedule, thanks to ongoing legal disputes slowing the independent committee meant to oversee the remedies. The AI Overviews issue could prompt fresh scrutiny as several lawmakers, including US Senator Bernie Sanders, criticized Google’s stance toward schools.

Studies examining the effects of the new AI tools entering schools have raised concerns about whether they are eroding opportunities for students to develop skills such as critical thinking, according to a Stanford review of the research as of a year ago. According to a survey conducted by Google itself, three in four teenagers report using AI weekly, but only about half say they double check its outputs for accuracy. A recent study by Washington University in St. Louis, meanwhile, found that only about 42 percent of AI Overviews could be fully verified using the citations they contained. Google has said overviews undergo rigorous testing and are continually improving.

In its response to the recent furor over AI Overviews, Google said it plans to launch a new feature for students in the coming months called Guided Learning. The idea is to coach users to find information rather than provide them with an immediate answer. “We believe AI products should support ‘productive struggle’—enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president for education wrote in the company’s Tuesday blog post.

Some researchers are already questioning how effective Guided Learning will be, arguing it won’t be as natural as working with a human tutor. Aguilar views Guided Learning as another attempt by Google to maintain the position it already occupies in American classrooms, where Google-powered Chromebook laptops, Google Classroom learning software, Search, and YouTube are commonplace.

“There’s a kernel of truth in saying we have to prepare students for a world where AI is ubiquitous,” Aguilar says, “but it shouldn’t be through a company making a very self-serving pronouncement because it’s heavily invested in AI.”
