What’s the Difference Between an Ebike and an E-Moto?

Wired November 04, 2026

Ebikes are in a weird place.

The good: US sales are way up from the start of the decade, after the pandemic sparked interest in two-wheelers and helped riders go farther, faster, and with less effort. More people also see ebikes as viable transportation options and as more affordable and accessible alternatives to increasingly expensive cars. The bad? Sales are down from two years ago, and bike manufacturers and sellers have suffered. Riding injuries are up, notably among children, and lawmakers are looking for ways to control them.

Part of the issue is that people struggle to understand the difference between types of ebikes, and between ebikes and their faster cousins, e-motos. This often isn’t their fault. Lawmakers and vehicle retailers themselves have blurred the edges of the product categories, even though many places require riders of the most powerful ebikes and e-motos to meet age, licensing, and registration requirements.

Today, a kid might see a targeted ad online for an electric dirt bike capable of speeds exceeding 40 mph and ask their parents to buy it straight from the internet—neither understanding that no one, much less a minor, is legally allowed to pilot them on public streets without a license.

Here’s a handy guide to the different types of electric micromobility vehicles available, to help you keep them straight. Local laws vary, so buyers should research and understand what’s allowed on their local roads before whipping out a credit card.

The electric bicycle industry uses three “classes” to differentiate product capabilities. Class 1 ebikes have motors that kick in when the rider pedals—the assist stops at 20 mph. Class 2 ebikes also have this “pedal assist” functionality, plus throttles, so riders can travel up to 20 mph without pedaling at all. Class 3 ebikes have more powerful pedal assist that stops helping at 28 mph. (In some places, this limit is 25 mph.)

Thirty-nine US states incorporate these three-class systems in their laws. In general, they require Class 3 riders to wear helmets and be at least 16 years old. Some states require riders to be at least 14 or 15 to ride any ebike at all. Outside of the laws, ebikes are mostly regulated like standard bicycles, and riders must follow the same rules of the road.

Most states don’t require a license or registration to ride ebikes. As of 2026, New Jersey and Alaska are the two exceptions. New Jersey requires registration and licensing for all ebikes, and insurance for Class 3 ebikes. Alaska, meanwhile, has no statewide ebike laws, and some locales, including Anchorage, require licenses for ebikes with sustained output over 750 watts, which can generally hit between 20 and 28 mph.

When shopping for an ebike, buyers should keep an eye on motor wattage levels. Entry-level ebikes typically have 250-watt motors and are great for commuting and flatter leisure riding. Upgrade to 500 watts to reach about 20 mph with a throttle and ride up moderate hills; 750 watts is generally the legal limit for street-appropriate ebikes and is great for bigger hills and heavier loads. Vehicles that are 1,000 watts and over aren’t considered ebikes and are usually sold for off-roading and riding on private property.

Those 1,000-watt devices? Despite some manufacturers’ marketing claims, they aren’t legally bikes but e-motos or mopeds. E-motos don’t need to have operable pedals—in fact, sometimes manufacturers or riders add fake ones to make them appear as ebikes. They are throttle-dependent rather than pedal-assist. They can have between 1,000 and 6,000 watts of motor power and can reach top speeds of 60 mph.

Because these vehicles are more powerful, many states require riders to register them and obtain a license and insurance—just like motorcycles. In most places, the process for getting one of these licenses looks a lot like getting a car license. Riders can get permits or junior licenses at 16 or 17 years old and often must be legal adults to get a full license.

Beyond looking at a two-wheeled vehicle’s specs, e-motos have other visual tells. Ebikes have a classic slender bicycle-like frame; observers should be able to see clear “daylight” through the body of the device. They have slimmer tires and rear fenders that hug their back tires. E-motos are chunkier, with wide midsections and substantial battery packs, which block most “daylight.” They have substantial coil shocks to absorb road impacts. They usually have wide, knobby tires and big rear fenders that sit high above their wheels. E-motos often have fixed foot pegs, like motorcycles, versus classic pedals.

There’s a final, tricky twist. Many ebikes are electronically speed-limited and can be hacked to go faster via (often easily available) software modifications. Some can be modified physically, by strategically moving sensors or cutting wires. These changes can turn a once-legal ebike street-illegal. That can not only void a device's warranty but also strain other components, risking failure.

PeopleForBikes, a US trade organization, warns that some manufacturers enable this sort of dodge by putting pedals on e-motos and calling them ebikes. These vehicles can be easily “unlocked” or come with “off-road” modes that let them travel much faster.

“E-motos are motor vehicles,” the group says.

Chernobyl’s Dogs May Be Evolving, but Scientists Don’t Know Why

Wired November 04, 2026

The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction remained unclear.

The explanation that’s perhaps most tantalizing to a sci-fi author is that the persistent radiation at the nuclear site has caused mutations to accumulate in the dogs’ genomes. But there are other ways a population’s genetics can change over time, such as random drift or natural selection. A recent study published in the scientific journal Genes revisited these pups, searching for genetic patterns pointing to one of these processes.

The researchers compared the DNA from dogs living in the area right around the nuclear plant with genetic material from dogs living in the city of Chernobyl, about 16 kilometers away. They also compared these canines to other global dog populations. The contrast alone was extreme. The dogs in Chernobyl city “are more genetically similar to dogs in the Galapagos Islands than they are to the dog population” at the nuclear plant, said Megan Dillon, a postdoctoral researcher at North Carolina State University and first author of the study.

But more striking still, the comparison revealed that random chance alone could not explain the differences between the dog populations. Instead, it seems the dogs at the nuclear site have been experiencing natural selection.

“When I was first doing those analyzes, I had to kind of pause and was like, ‘Wow, I have to make sure I'm doing all of this right,’ because this is very interesting, very surprising,” Dillon said.

Not only did the dogs seem to be evolving, but some of the genomic regions under the highest selective pressure were associated with functions such as DNA repair, immunity, and cell survival. In other words, certain genetic differences in the dogs from the plant could be relevant for coping with environmental stress.

Instead of being mutations, these genomic variants likely already existed among local dogs but became more common in the population over the past 40 years. “These dog populations already had this high degree of genetic diversity,” Dillon said. “Maybe this founding population at the power plant had the kind of genetic toolkit to endure and survive in these harsh conditions. It’s not necessarily that they were being bombarded with new mutations.”

Taken together, the results support the hypothesis that natural selection contributed to the difference seen in the dogs at Chernobyl compared to other populations. What remains unclear is which environmental factors favored these variants and whether they provide any specific advantage. “Even though we found this evidence of selection and it is around these biologically relevant genes, we still cannot say that this is tied to the exposures that the dogs have faced,” Dillon noted.

Radiation at the disaster site might seem like the easiest explanation to point to, but there are many other selective pressures this dog population has faced since nuclear meltdown. Chernobyl’s dogs are descended from pets left behind during the evacuations. Since then, they’ve persisted through Ukraine’s harsh winters and weathered other pollutants including heavy metals and pesticides also deposited in the area. “A lot of these contaminants have similar signatures and similar pathology,” Dillon said. “There are just too many different things to really be able to tease apart a single variable.”

The researchers also don’t have access to longitudinal samples that would show exactly how this population has changed over time. “It's almost like looking at a single still image and trying to figure out what came before it,” said Matthew Breen, a professor of genomics at North Carolina State University and the study’s senior author. “Those first few years were probably the most critical period—if they were selected, that's when that selection process would have happened.”

It’s not possible to go back and get samples from the dogs who lived there in 1986, a time when no organism—not even a bacterium—had its full genome sequenced. Breen was a graduate student in England then. “I was involved in a project driving around the Welsh mountain hills, collecting sheep from the pastures because the radioactive cloud had blown over Western Europe,” he recalled. There wasn’t anything to see in the data gathered then, but the technology has evolved, and those sheep had also not been living at the center of a nuclear meltdown for generations.

Nearly four decades after the accident, the Chernobyl exclusion zone has also become a refuge for wildlife. Wolves, deer, wild boars, and lynx now roam the area—a return that researchers largely attribute to the decline in human activity. Among some of these residents, such as the wolf population, researchers have also observed similar genomic distinctions to those seen in the dogs.

“It really demonstrates the resilience of nature to catastrophic events caused by humans,” Breen said. “You push something in one direction, it can respond to that and either push back or deviate its path going forward. I think this is what we're seeing here.”

The Motley Fool is the O. G. stock and investment advice website, dating back to the early days of the Internet, when WIRED’s website was still called hotwired. com. It started as a tip sheet in the early ‘90s by brothers Tom and David Gardner, and it rode a wave of hype to become a cult phenomenon, viewed with equal interest and skepticism by the established investment class. Thirty years and a whole bunch of books later, The Motley Fool now feels like the established investment class, with a Stock Advisor subscription service offering stock tips that were shown in a 2017 study led by Penn State to consistently beat the S&P 500.

Subscriptions to the basic Stock Advisor tips are quite reasonable on a weekly basis, but more sophisticated analysis is also available for professionals and high-volume investors at premium prices. Luckily, new subscribers can usually access Motley Fool promo codes and introductory pricing. Be sure to check out our regularly updated Motley Fool discount codes and Motley Fool coupons to save big now for your future.

The Motley Fool is not a single service. Rather, it’s a suite of stock-tips and analysis services, packaged in different bundles. The three main tiers are Stock Advisor ($199), Epic ($499), and Epic Plus ($1,999). Each higher tier offers more stock tips per month, more comprehensive data and research on potential investments, and more sophisticated analysis tools. The Epic Plus tier also offers access to “moneymaker” investment portfolios that are touted to follow Warren Buffett’s investment strategy. Generally, the site advises beginning investors with smaller portfolios to stick to the basic Stock Advisor tips to start out. The Fool also tends to recommend buying at least 50 stocks and holding them for at least 5 years, so it’s not a day-trading tool. Anyway, it’s often hard to find the right links to receive Motley Fool membership discounts. Go to this Motley Fool subscription discount page here for as much as half off the Stock Advisor, Epic, and Epic Plus Bundles for the first year only.

The website tends to offer a wide range of Motley Fool subscription discounts, depending on what URL you reach. Honestly, it’s a little confusing (and maybe infuriating, if you accidentally paid too much.) Motley Fool’s most popular option, Stock Advisor, offers the fabled market-beating “Top 10 Stocks to Buy Now,” plus portfolio analysis, analyst news, and monthly stock rankings. The best Motley Fool Stock Advisor discount I’ve seen at the moment comes by locking in your subscription for two years at $149 (as opposed to the nominal price of $199 per year.) Note that if you lock in a one-year subscription, Stock Advisor is yours for $99 a year, or $100 off.

As a premium service, The Motley Fool offers an “Epic Bundle” designed to address the heavy concentration in current markets on AI and AI infrastructure, robotics, drug discovery, and all that we’re currently calling “the future.” The Fool also claims to have a more defensive balance than competitors going all-in on the AI zeitgeist and the probable AI bubble. Subscribers can choose among cautious, moderate, and aggressive risk profiles. This is a more expensive service than the basic Stock Advisor, priced at $499 a year. But with the introductory Motley Fool promo code EPICSALE, you can try it for a year at $200 off. It’ll renew at $499, though.

If you want to begin investing but aren’t sure where to start, I’d recommend reading Motley Fool’s “Best Stocks to Buy Now: Our Buy-and-Hold Picks,” which is updated monthly. With thousands of publicly traded companies to choose from, many investors don't know where to start. That, along with this year’s stock market volatility due to the Iran conflict, tariff uncertainty, and fears of a weakening economy, makes things even shakier. But with this updated article, folks can gain insider knowledge to make the best financial decisions for their specific needs.

For better or worse, I’ve become a podcast person. Like so many people, I find them a great way to passively learn while doing other tasks. Motley Fool offers a variety of podcasts to help you achieve your goals or find financial stability. There’s the Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing podcast, which releases new episodes daily at 4pm (Eastern time). This podcast is for stock investors, offering a “long-term perspective on business news with The Motley Fool's investment analysts,” and weekend episodes feature a mix of personal finance advice and longer-form interviews. There’s also the Rule Breaker Investing podcast, which airs on Wednesdays and features David Gardner, co-founder of The Motley Fool. During the show, Gardner shares his insights into “today's most innovative and disruptive publicly traded companies” and offers advice on how everyday people can profit from them using unorthodox methods.

It can be difficult (and scary, TBH) to determine which retirement plan is right for you and your financial situation. Your retirement plan determines how much you contribute annually, how it's taxed, how withdrawals work, what you can invest in, and how much you pay in fees. Motley Fool offers a wide range of content to help you decide which retirement plans work best for your financial situation, including: 401(k) plans, IRA, Roth IRA, Nondeductible IRA, Keogh plan, and more. With this valuable tool, Motley Fool lays out all the information you’ll need, including employer-sponsored plans, individual retirement accounts, and plans for self-employed individuals and small business owners.

Democrats Sweep Republicans in Nearly Every Race That Matters

Wired November 04, 2026

Democrats stormed through key battleground races across the US in their battle to capture the House and Senate on Tuesday night, marking a decisive repudiation of President Donald Trump’s second term.

The scale of victory for Democrats—in some races, the party flipped seats that Trump won by double digits just two years ago—marked a historic night that exceeded the party’s highest expectations.

Democrats pulled off arguably the greatest upset in Texas, where James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton and where Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott for the governorship, despite the millions and millions of dollars spent by billionaire Elon Musk on behalf of the Republicans. No Democrat had won a statewide seat election since 1994.

Democrats also seized other critical Senate races on election night, including in Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, and North Carolina, while retaining control of seats in Georgia and New Hampshire, according to the Associated Press.

At the White House, stunned Trump officials tell WIRED that high gas prices and the increased cost of living brought on by the Iran war were the principal reasons for widespread GOP losses.

“If any good comes out of tonight for the Republican party, it’s that no Republican president will ever listen to imbeciles like Mark Levin and Marc Thiessen again,” one source close to the White House said of two commentators who had urged Trump to prolong the Iran war.

Exit polling showing massive defections from other parts of the 2024 Trump coalition show there was more to the losses than that, with Latino voters turning to Democrats as the administration pursued brutal and unpopular immigration policies.

Some officials, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly, privately laid the blame at the feet of the president for taking the nation into the Middle East conflict, which he wrongly assumed would be over in a matter of weeks and has continued with no clear end in sight.

“President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” a White House official said in a statement, even as Trump had implored his base on the trail to pretend that he was on the ballot.

“Also, candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves,” the official added.

Many of the losing candidates were hand-picked by Trump, who forced out incumbents like Texas senator John Cornyn and blessed candidates like Darline Graham (sister of late senator Lindsey Graham), who ran a dismal campaign in South Carolina.

Still, other Trump officials have cast about for other scapegoats, blaming a failed redistricting effort as well as candidate quality.

Republicans embarked on a strategy earlier this year to redraw numerous congressional maps as part of a gambit that White House aides thought could yield 10 to 15 House seat pickups if Trump voters turned out. The downside, political scientists pointed out, was that it made seats harder to defend, as while there were more Republican districts, each was less Republican.

On election night, the strategy failed to yield results. Democrats won at least three House seats in Florida that Republicans had redrawn, as well as the seat in North Carolina.

The closest thing to a bright spot for Republicans came in the Senate race in Florida, which became abruptly competitive in the final days of the midterm campaign. In the end, Ashley Moody barely fended off the progressive candidate, Democrat Angie Nixon.

As the likely control of the House and Senate became clear, top House Democrats separately ended the night relishing the prospect of mounting an aggressive oversight campaign against the Trump administration.

Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word statement: “Lawyer up.”

It's become harder than ever to find a high-end laptop under $1,000 that doesn't have any significant compromises. That's an even bigger challenge if you're after a laptop with a larger display. For example, the Dell XPS 13 sells for $900, which is another good option around this price, but it's a tiny device focused on portability. The IdeaPad Slim 5x has a much larger 15.3-inch screen that's great for those who plan to actually sit down at a desk or table and work entirely off it without using an external monitor. At 0.61 inches thick, it's not overly chunky either—matching the thickness of the 14-inch MacBook Pro, for reference.

The chip inside, the Snapdragon X2 Plus, is another reason this laptop deal is so special. This is Qualcomm's latest PC processor, but because of how rocky pricing has been this year, it's rarely shown up in laptops you could call affordable. That's a shame, because it's a very capable processor that's in the same league as Apple's M5 in terms of CPU performance. I wouldn't buy this laptop for full-time video editors or 3D animators—or if you're a serious gamer. The graphics performance just isn't there. But in terms of everyday tasks, whether for office work or schoolwork, the X2 Plus won't skip a beat, no matter how many browser tabs, open applications, and background tasks you have going. It even has plenty of ports onboard, including two USB-C, two USB-A, HDMI, and a microSD card slot.

And last (but not least), the IdeaPad Slim 5x has a touchpad that's nice to use. I mention this because so many budget-oriented laptops cut corners on the quality of the touchpad. That might seem minor, but unless you're a mouse-only person, the touchpad is something you're constantly interacting with and goes a long way toward making a laptop feel premium. The IdeaPad Slim 5x doesn't have a haptic feedback trackpad that more expensive laptops use, so the click is a bit loud. But I can vouch that it doesn't make me feel clumsy when using it.

Mobile Carriers’ iPhone Duo Deals Promise $1,200 Off. Here’s How They Work

Wired November 03, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Don’t expect Apple to offer a sale on the iPhone Duo. The company almost never discounts its products, especially new ones that are selling like hotcakes. (It’s back-ordered.) With the Duo starting at $2,000, it’s very expensive for most people to buy Apple’s first foldable, and the best way to get a deal may be through a carrier.

Of course, there are stipulations, but if you qualify, you could “save” significantly on an iPhone Duo—as much as $1,200, knocking the price to $800. (Keep reading, there’s a catch.) Here are some of the potential deals we found.

Shipping times are stretching into January, so it may be a while before you can get your hands on an iPhone Duo, even with one of these offers.

Apple

Apple

AT&T

Verizon

T-Mobile

If you sign up for an Experience Beyond plan, T-Mobile will credit you $1,200. To qualify, you need to purchase the iPhone Duo and sign up for the Experience Beyond 2.0 plan for 36 months if you’re a new customer, or sign up for the Experience Beyond 2.0, Experience Beyond, or Go5G Next plans if you’re an existing T-Mobile customer and not already enrolled in another payment plan.

Here’s how the deal works.

You don’t get $1,200 upfront. Instead, T-Mobile spreads that amount across 36 monthly credits on your bill. For the 256-GB base model, for example, you’ll pay $22.22 a month for the phone on top of the monthly plan; those payments total about $800 over three years, plus the Experience Beyond 2.0 plan is $100 a month, excluding taxes and fees. The deal doesn’t apply when you pay in full or choose a cheaper plan. If you hate expensive contracts, this isn’t for you.

T-Mobile offers several other incentives for the iPhone Duo, including $1,200 off with trade-in or $1,000 off for seniors, military personnel, students, and first responders. To see what you might qualify for, click on the “see promotions” link on the T-Mobile iPhone Duo purchase page.

If you’re not clamoring for the iPhone Duo, T-Mobile’s incentives also apply to the new iPhone 18 Pro and other models.

AT&T and Verizon are also offering incentives on the iPhone Duo. AT&T has a trade-in plan similar to T-Mobile’s: You’ll pay $22.23 a month for the phone for 36 months, which is equivalent to $1,200 off after you’ve fulfilled your contract. AT&T also has a “contract-breaking” deal that will get you an $800 reward card when you switch to AT&T, but you’d still have to pay the full price of the iPhone Duo.

The same goes for Verizon. You can get $1,200 off a 36-month Unlimited Ultimate plan, with or without a trade-in, as a new or existing customer. As an extra incentive, Verizon is including your choice of an Apple Watch Series 12 or iPad.

Whichever company’s deal you pursue, you’re entering into what is essentially a contract. The phone will also be locked to the carrier until you’ve made your final payment. You’ll also pay more after fees and taxes are added, although there’s no monthly interest. When you factor everything—the cost of a particular plan and the discounted phone—it could be what you're currently paying for a premium plan, or possibly much more.

We usually don’t recommend cell phone contracts; it’s best to get a phone unlocked, even if it means paying full price. However, if you plan to stay with a carrier long-term and want to lower the cost of the iPhone Duo, it’s still worth considering. But do the math before committing.

The Internet’s Conspiracy Theorists Are Desperate for Voter Fraud

Wired November 03, 2026

Voting had been underway in the US for only a few hours, and polls hadn’t even opened in some parts of the country, but Republican strategist and pro-Trump influencer Joey Mannarino had apparently seen enough.

“MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF VOTER FRAUD BEING REPORTED ALL OVER THE COUNTRY!” Mannarino asserted on X at 9:02 am EST, offering no evidence to support his declaration. “The Democrats are stealing our country right out from under us!”

As in any other election year, as polling places opened, people began showing up to vote, and voting machines started whirring into action, some jurisdictions ran into problems.

Severe flooding along Florida’s Space Coast meant about 20 polling places had to be moved. Bad storms over the weekend likely caused brief power outages in Arizona’s Maricopa County, forcing the temporary closure of several polling places. Pennsylvania’s Luzerne County was missing a scanner box. And in Westchester County, New York, voting in the hotly contested House race between incumbent Republican representative Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley hit a roadblock early on Tuesday morning when machines stopped accepting paper ballots.

Voting machine malfunctions—much like bad weather and power outages—are fairly common during elections. While typically attributable to some mundane problem like aging components, these malfunctions are often the source of rumors or conspiracy theories.

And like other election years in recent memory, there’s a network of MAGA influencers, Republican lawmakers, pro-Trump trolls, and administration officials with enormous online audiences who are waiting for anything—literally anything—that they can claim is evidence of voter fraud. The Trump administration has also been laying the groundwork, priming its electorate to believe that the American voting system is rigged against them.

Within minutes of reports that ballot scanners in Westchester weren’t working, some of the biggest proponents of election conspiracy theories seized on the countywide glitch to claim that Democrats were sabotaging equipment to prevent Lawler from winning.

The Westchester County board of elections initially blamed the fault on “the thickness of the paper ballots” in a statement issued two hours after polls opened. But 20 minutes later, county officials updated the statement, removing the reference to the thickness of the paper and instead blaming a general “issue involving paper ballots.”

In a separate statement published online, Westchester County executive Ken Jenkins said that once the issues with the ballot machines are resolved, he’ll “convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again.” “I want to be absolutely clear,” Jenkins wrote. “This situation is unacceptable.” Later in the day, New York State officials put out an additional statement, saying that the problem was that most machines in the county had outdated programming, which meant they could not recognize and process Election Day ballots.

“The immediate priority is to restore scanning capability to at least one voting machine at every polling location, with additional machines being brought online as the day progresses,” officials said. They added that the programming issue had only caused ballots to be rejected, not tabulated incorrectly, so voters should have full confidence that “every valid vote will be counted.”

In a post on X, the Republican National Committee wrote that, together with Democrats, it is “seeking a joint court order to require central tabulation of ballots at the County Board of Elections.”

Representative Claudia Tenney of New York—who has backed efforts to challenge the results of the 2020 election—also jumped into the fray. “No surprise,” Tenney wrote. “The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat.” Conservative broadcaster Mark Levin shared Tenney’s post to his 5 million followers.

All manner of MAGA-world influencers have also weighed in. “This is how the Left steals elections,” wrote Katie Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller.

“Ban voting machines and prosecute those who’ve used them to cheat,” wrote president Donald Trump’s former spokesperson Liz Harrington.

“Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” wrote MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. Loomer also weighed in on polling location problems elsewhere. “The Democrats are already cheating” she wrote on her Loomer Unleashed account, in response to a post about power outages forcing closure of voting centers in Maricopa County.

The Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington, which tracks online rumors about elections, found that posts on X about the malfunctioning machines—“often with a conspiratorial framing”—were coming about 150 times a minute just after 10 am EST.

While Lawler urged voters to “stay in line” and cast their ballots despite the issues with the scanners, pro-Trump influencer Phillip Buchanan, known as Catturd, shared Lawler’s post, writing: “Every. Single. Election. It's always somthing [sic].” Catturd also boosted conspiracies about “Democrat shenanigans” in Florida’s Broward County, which suffered technical difficulties which were quickly resolved. MJ Ultra, a prominent pro-Trump QAnon account on X, added: “Broward County Florida is corrupted as hell.”

Rogan O’Handley, known online as DC Draino, called what was happening in Westchester the “Maricopa Method of stealing” while also boosting conspiracy theories about Broward County. Meanwhile Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Jamaica, Kari Lake, also shared conspiracy theories about the issues in Westchester and called out so-called liberal “shenanigans” in Maricopa County. Lake has baselessly claimed her 2022 Arizona gubernatorial race and her 2024 Senate race were rigged.

While all of this has been unfolding on X, Trump has been largely preoccupied with other matters. He spent the better part of the morning complaining on Truth Social that people had taken him seriously when he announced—jokingly, he says—on Tuesday his plans to rename the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to “The Trump Reflecting Pool.” He eventually got around to posting about Lawler’s race but didn’t mention the issues with the ballot scanners.

Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist

Wired November 03, 2026

For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.

Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.”

At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.

Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.”

While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.

Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.

If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote

Wired November 03, 2026

As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.

But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.

Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.

Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.

According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that conflated the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.

Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.

Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. Pink slime sites present as mainstream news websites but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.

Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the pink slime sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing pink slime sites in 30 percent of cases.

“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag

Wired November 03, 2026

Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.

Although it hasn't been officially announced, Roli reportedly ousted its CEO and founder, Roland Lamb, earlier this year. Since then, Roli has all but dissolved. (In August, a new company called Instrumental Intelligence was registered with the UK government under Lamb's name, a potential move by the founder to acquire Roli's assets).

On Monday, Roli emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators of Roli on October 20. The company went into administration, the UK process that manages corporate insolvency. This is the second time Roli has gone bankrupt.

That has left a small but bereft community of customers with no word on getting the products they paid for. The Roli community has expressed sadness, anger, or outright confusion. In Facebook groups, the r/Roli subreddit, and other forums, dismayed users have struggled to find recourse for Roli equipment purchases ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars. The Roli subreddit has been awash with posts from customers who say they paid for orders months or years ago and have received no response or refund since then.

Existing owners also worry about the long-term impact. Roli instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps to connect, map sounds, and configure settings. While the hardware still functions, users fear that lack of software support will eventually leave their gear bricked.

Roli’s Lumi keyboard.

Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.

Roli has faced financial struggles before.

The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.

That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.

Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”

Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.

“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”

In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace. One 16-page PDF is titled “Keeping Roland Happy” and includes multiple sections about how to handle interacting with a pathological narcissist. Several former employees independently described what they viewed as Lamb’s narcissistic behavior, describing him as an arrogant visionary.

“Roland is the archetype of a pathological narcissist,” one employee told WIRED. “Unfortunately, that's what he became. Incredibly brittle when challenged, absolutely shameless, quite reckless, incapable of learning or growth, would rather gamble than take any lessons from the previous experience. It was very disheartening to see.”

The Roli Airwave.

“The tragedy here is that it was always fundamentally a great company,” another former employee says. “A lot of what made it great was the sort of all-powerful vision of the founder. But that was so obviously the critical flaw.”

Along with other touch-sensitive devices like the Linnstrument and the Sensel Morph, Roli was a key company in the rise of MIDI polyphonic expression (MPE) devices. MPE technology lets players control a note’s pitch and timbre through touch-based movement. Pressing or sliding fingers over the device’s surface produces varying MIDI notes that capture more expressive playing.

While inventive, Roli’s instruments were altogether very niche—a hard product category to build an Apple-sized audience around. Roli certainly tried, partnering with Apple to sell its Roli Blocks in Apple Stores. Alas, the pandemic caused dire supply chain issues, and the company couldn’t keep up with orders. After the pandemic, bankruptcy, and the rebrand, little remained to push the company forward except the founder's will.

“This was one of the leading lights of music technology in the world,” one former employee said. “It was truly an inventing company—the stuff it made had never been made before. So it's a real shame.”

The response to Roli’s collapse hasn’t been pure dismay. After months of delays and frustration, Reddit users have gathered to mourn the company—and to make sure its devices keep working.

Sam Hocking, a UK audio engineer who runs an audio tools company called Demix. me, also owns multiple Roli Seaboard Blocks. Even before Roli went into administration, Hocking had been building software that could keep the equipment working as a capable MIDI device. He shared his vibe-coded configuration tools in the Roli subreddit and on GitHub, so Roli’s Grand, Rise, Airwave, and Block devices can work without the Roli launcher.

Hocking says his Seaboards are nearly 10 years old and still working. Despite the company’s rocky history and poor communication, he still wants to keep his devices. They’re high quality, cost a good chunk of money, and feel somewhat irreplaceable.

He’s not alone. Other users on the subreddit have joined in, adding their own tweaks and fixes to the software that may keep at least a few of these devices alive.

“They're quite a unique product; there's not another keyboard type out there,” Hocking says. “Nobody likes to spend money and then not be able to use it.”

Review: iPad Mini (2026)

Wired November 03, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

Some thought it might be dead. Some thought it had no place in an iPhone Duo world. But the iPad Mini isn’t being put out to pasture—it’s getting a massive glow-up.

Apple’s smallest tablet has been refreshed—now in its eighth generation—and with it, nearly every aspect of the device has been upgraded. It now has an OLED screen, a faster chip, a thinner chassis, more memory, waterproofing, and much more. That all comes with a higher price, though, and raises the question of just who the iPad Mini is really for among the other choices in the iPad lineup.

I’ll come straight out with it: I love this little tablet. I’ve been using it for about a week, and I happened to take it on a short trip. The perfect time for it to really shine—and shine, it did. It was the perfect companion for long Lyft rides to the airport and wait times at my gate.

Apple iPad Mini (2026)

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The star attraction of the new iPad Mini is its 8.5-inch display. That’s a slightly larger screen than the previous generation, yet the overall dimensions are barely bigger. But the change from IPS to OLED is what matters. It uses an OLED Super Retina XDR display, which is not the tandem OLED seen on the iPad Pro (and OLED MacBook Pro). It doesn’t have the 120-Hz refresh rate, nor is it quite as bright. It can reach 600 nits in SDR and 1,200 nits in HDR, which is 400 nits less than the iPad Pro. It’s more or less similar to the Mini-LED M6 MacBook Pro in terms of brightness, though, which is still impressive for OLED.

The iPad Mini OLED’s brightness is sufficient for most uses, even in bright lighting conditions. But you can take it to the next level by opting for a nano-texture display, which is totally worth the extra $100 it costs. (It’s the model I tested.) It’s not an antireflective coating or a matte layer; it’s actually etched into the glass. The result is a surface that almost entirely diffuses outside light without reducing the screen’s perceived brightness. Reading outside with the iPad Mini is particularly enjoyable, as the nano-texture display not only resists reflections but even gives it a paperlike crispness. This option is also available on the MacBook Pro and iPad Pro, and there’s really nothing else like it.

The iPad Mini one-ups its siblings in sharpness. Its smaller size gives it 19 percent higher pixel density than every other iPad. And yes, it really does look incredibly clear and sharp.

There’s more to it than the display. Part of the magic is how lightweight it is—barely over half a pound, and it doesn’t feel much heavier than my phone in my hand. One-handed use feels completely natural. That’s always been true of the iPad Mini, but this latest version emphasizes that even more.

Lastly, the color options have been pared down from four to just two. The lighter goldish Starlight is still available, but now there’s the introduction of the blackish, navy-blue Midnight. This is a finish carried over from the MacBook Air. The more playful Blue and Purple color options are both gone, as is Space Gray. More options are always better, but for a device that costs $700, I can see why these more professional colors make sense.

Apple has also completely redesigned the iPad Mini’s four-speaker sound system, and a couple of interesting changes are happening. As part of its process of making the device IP67 water-resistant, Apple removed the speaker grille from the sides to create a completely sealed enclosure. Instead, the tweeters sit behind two small slits on the edges of the display glass. And then bass drivers are built directly into the display. Apple calls it an Acoustic Display.

The stereo image sounds fullest when you hold the device in portrait, as long as you keep your fingers away from the display. The vibration caused by the location of the speakers isn’t terribly noticeable unless you have the volume on full blast. Overall, the audio sounds decent for a device this size, but it won’t compare well to larger devices like an iPad Air or MacBook Air. But for watching videos or the occasional movie, it suffices.

Apple iPad Mini (2026)

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The water resistance is a first for any iPad, which is significant. You might still worry about bringing your $700 tablet poolside, but the IP67 rating means it can handle submersion for 30 minutes in about three feet of water. In comparison, iPhones have had an IP68 rating for the past eight years, meaning they can handle twice that depth for 30 minutes.

As always, it has to be said that iPads are not really designed for taking photos. That’s a bit less true with the iPad Mini, if only because it’s so easy to use one-handed. Still, I doubt you’ll use the 12-megapixel rear camera all that much, outside of the occasional document or QR code scan. It’s decent but hasn’t been changed from the previous generation. The front-facing camera, however, got a big upgrade. It’s still a 12-megapixel camera, but it has moved to the side bezel instead of the top. That location makes video calls feel more natural.

One thing the iPad Mini is still missing is Face ID. While it’s a standard iPhone feature, Apple appears to really be reserving it for only the iPad Pro. That’s a shame. This does have Touch ID built into the power button.

A number of other iPad features still apply here, though, that make the iPad Mini feel like something you could work on. It supports extended display mode, letting you connect it to an external monitor without forcing it to mirror the screen. iPadOS also now has windowing and proper cursor support. Without a keyboard, I can’t imagine you’ll use these features as much. On the other hand, the iPad Mini’s size makes it possible to type with your thumbs (like you would on a phone).

Clearly, the 2026 iPad Mini seems to have its sights set on more than just reading books and playing games. As if the OLED display and price tag weren’t already enough to give that away. Most of the demos Apple has been using to show off with the iPad Mini were more creator-focused than I expected. We’re talking running on-device AI models or creative applications.

There are three storage configurations available: 128 GB, 256 GB, and 512 GB. All come with 12 GB of unified memory, four more than the previous iPad Mini and matching the current iPad Air. You’d never know that from Apple’s own spec sheets, though, since it’s never mentioned. Regardless, it’s part of what makes the iPad Mini a more capable little tablet, whether in heavier multitasking or for on-device AI. It’s kind of absurd that this little tablet has 12 GB of memory while the MacBook Neo is stuck at 8.

Apple iPad Mini (2026)

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The iPad Mini’s A20 Pro chip is also more powerful than the MacBook Neo’s. This is the same silicon as in the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone 18 Pro Max—with one caveat. For the first time, the storage options dictate which version of the A20 Pro chip you get. Only the 512-GB model gets the full six-core CPU and dual 16-core Neural Engines. I tested this six-core model, but the other configurations have nerfed performance, with one fewer CPU efficiency core and only a single Neural Engine.

Performance is really solid. The A20 Pro handles games quite well, and I tested several, including Oceanhorn 3, Fortnite, No Man’s Sky, and Assassin’s Creed Mirage. None of these games looked particularly nice here, with textures and effects turned down, but the iPad Mini played them smoothly at 60 frames per second. Visually, the most impressive was No Man’s Sky, which came to iOS and iPadOS just last week. It still feels amazing to play a game this dense on a mere iPad Mini. Of course, the iPad Pro with the M5 will be a substantial upgrade for gaming performance, but if you connect a mobile controller (we like the Backbone One), you’ll have a good time.

I also tried out some local AI in LM Studio. With 12 GB of onboard memory, you’re limited in what models you can use. LM Studio recommended the 4-billion parameter version of Qwen 3.5. This isn’t the kind of model that’s going to blow anyone away, but for simple tasks, it’s nice to run a text model completely locally. This is all GPU-dependent, so performance should be identical without the second Neural Engine that comes exclusively on the 512-GB model. Of course, Siri AI is now a significant part of this platform, and the iPad Mini can run all the advanced features, including the more expressive Siri voices and on-the-fly dictation.

The previous iPad Mini cost $499 when it came out (before the price increases), and that at least felt reasonable. At this new price of $699, it’s a little harder to justify. The iPad Mini has always been a luxe but niche device. It’s sized for reading books, watching movies, and playing games. It doesn’t have the same high-stakes use case as a phone or laptop, which makes that higher premium price harder to swallow.

If you want the most powerful iPad Mini as a professional tool, you’ll probably spend at least $999. Or $1,099 with the nano-texture display. That’s the same price as the MacBook Air! I get it: The iPad Mini is an entirely different device. But I’m wondering whether real professionals would at least prefer a larger display—not only for the extra screen real estate but also for keyboard support.

Apple iPad Mini (2026)

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I will say: The iPad Mini does work remarkably well with the Apple Pencil. If I had to choose an iPad specifically for note-taking, it’d be the iPad Mini. On the other hand, illustrators will likely prefer a larger screen. Like previous versions of the iPad Mini, it’s only compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and USB-C Apple Pencil. Even for those who use tablets in the workplace as a point-of-sale system or for specialized use cases, the higher price seems hard to justify.

Is it all just a plainly disguised way of justifying the higher prices Apple is paying for memory on the backend? The cynic in me says yes. It’s not unlike the direction Apple is heading with its OLED MacBook Pro. But putting the cynicism aside, there’s real quality-of-life value being added here, especially in the form of the OLED screen, waterproofing, and extra memory. For the right person, the iPad Mini will be the perfect product. It’s a dream device for casual use, whether it’s gaming, reading, or browsing. But I’m guessing that demographic has shrunk quite a bit with this increased price.

I’m a little perplexed why Apple isn’t at least offering an 8-GB RAM model that would bring the price down more. I know it goes against the focus on Siri AI, which needs at least 12 GB, but it would at least keep the core audience that would buy an iPad Mini in the first place. It would also help create some more separation between this and the iPad Air. The iPad Mini is $150 cheaper than the iPad Air despite having an OLED screen. The iPad Air, meanwhile, has a larger 11-inch screen and is big enough to use with the Magic Keyboard. You’ll have to weigh a number of trade-offs when choosing between these two.

And with the iPhone Duo’s arrival, the iPad Mini’s size feels even less unique. Sure, the Duo costs $2,000, but it solves the iPad Mini’s main problem: convenience. As your phone, the Duo fits in your pocket, goes with you everywhere, and is far more versatile as a pocket computer. The iPad Mini is less flexible and easier to forget and leave at home. And at $699, you may wonder whether you really need that fancy OLED screen and 12 GB of RAM.

Review: Apple AirPods 5

Wired November 03, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

I’ve owned AirPods since the original pair launched in 2016. Over the years, I’ve tested earbuds from many brands, but I always come back to my trusty AirPods. They’re easy to pair, they integrate well with the Apple ecosystem, and they deliver some of the best-sounding active noise cancellation (ANC) on the market. The latest AirPods 5 continue the trend and deliver more of Apple’s best audio features at a lower price than their predecessor.

The AirPods 5 come in two models: $129 with a standard case and $149 with a wireless charging case that works with Apple Watch chargers, Qi-compatible chargers, and USB-C. Both include ANC, which is a welcome change from the AirPods 4, where you had to pay extra ($179) for the privilege of a feature that’s increasingly standard on most wireless earbuds.

For $149, the AirPods 5 (with a wireless charging case) are an easy recommendation. But after a month of testing, I’d still pay extra to get the AirPods Pro 3. The difference comes down to noise cancellation, fit, and controls.

First and foremost, if you’re buying the AirPods 5, spend the extra $20 on the version with a wireless charging case. You’ll get an extra hour of battery life (up to five hours) on the earbuds and an extra two (up to 22 hours) with the charging case compared to the $129 model. That's the same battery life as the AirPods 4 without ANC, so you’re actually getting more listening time even with noise cancellation.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The inclusion of ANC in both AirPods 5 models is the biggest upgrade here. You no longer have to pay extra just to get noise cancellation, and even the $129 model is a better deal than the standard AirPods 4 were at launch. Both versions also support Conversation Awareness, Live Translation, and Spatial Audio, along with Apple’s Siri features.

And, for semi-open earbuds, the AirPods 5 have exceptional ANC. Apple says the noise cancellation removes up to 50 percent more external noise than the AirPods 4 with ANC, due to a redesigned multi-port acoustic architecture and improved audio processing. I can’t verify that percentage, but the improvement was noticeable during my testing.

I was especially impressed on a domestic flight, where the AirPods 5 did a stellar job at suppressing the sound of the airplane engines. They didn’t make the cabin totally disappear, and the AirPods Pro 3 still deliver stronger isolation, but it was a huge improvement compared to the AirPods 4 with ANC.

Transparency mode sounds even more natural. I found this especially useful with Adaptive Audio, which automatically balances ANC with Transparency mode based on your surroundings. On a run, for example, footsteps approaching from behind prompted the earbuds to lower my music and let more environmental sound through. The transition felt smooth enough that the outside noise almost blended into the song. I could stay aware of my surroundings without getting distracted by every little thing happening around me.

For people who run outdoors or commute, the open-ear design can be more appealing than the tighter seal of the Pros. You sacrifice some isolation, but you get a more natural sense of what’s happening around you.

The notable improvements can't overcome the simple fact that I generally prefer the silicone tips of the AirPods Pro 3 to the semi-open fit of the AirPods 5. The AirPods Pro 3 create a snug seal without making my ears feel clogged, and the interchangeable sizes let me tailor the fit. That seal also makes a noticeable difference when I’m working out. During longer runs, I found the AirPods 5 could start slipping as sweat built up. The Pros stayed put. Their more secure fit also naturally improves noise cancellation.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The AirPods 5 inherit the Pro 3’s volume controls, which let you adjust the volume by swiping up or down on the stem, but I’ve found the feature tricky to use across AirPods models because the stems are so short and slim that I struggle to get the right touch with my long nails. I generally prefer the volume controls on Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, which offer more surface area to work with.

I find the Pro 3’s controls are easier to use than the AirPods 5’s, especially while running. The stem protrudes a little more where it meets the earbud, giving me a more accessible spot to press. With AirPods 5, I’ve had to take an earbud out just to locate the right control spot, which is not ideal mid-run. A few days ago, I nearly sacrificed one to Lake Michigan after fumbling with it. The upgraded IP57 rating means the earbuds can withstand brief immersion in water, but I wouldn’t recommend testing that claim in a lake.

While the AirPods 5 offer a lot for the money, the pinpoint controls and a few missing features make the Pro 3 worth the splurge in my mind. The Pros have integrated heart-rate sensing for workouts, hearing aid features, and longer battery life with ANC enabled.

The $100 price difference between the two is significant, though. For casual listeners, tweens, and teens, the AirPods 5 are great. You still get solid noise cancellation, Apple’s seamless ecosystem integration, and an open-ear design that’s more comfortable for people who don’t like silicone eartips. The smaller charging case is another perk—it slips more naturally into a pocket or the waistband of leggings.

But as an iPhone owner who works out daily and travels frequently, I’d still spend $249 on the AirPods Pro 3. Their secure fit, stronger noise cancellation, and more accessible controls make them the better all-around earbuds for me.

The AirPods 5 are the better value. The AirPods Pro 3 are the better earbuds.

The Endlessly Meme-able Steve Kornacki Is Not a Meme Person

Wired November 03, 2026

Standing in front of a gigantic map isn’t a traditional path to fame. But in 2020, during the presidential face-off between Donald Trump and Joe Biden, Steve Kornacki became America’s sweetheart for his enthusiastic delivery of state-by-state election results. The NBC data analyst gracefully guided teeth-grinding, fist-clenching viewers through Biden’s eventual victory, and the rest is history: That same year, Kornacki was named one of People’s sexiest men alive; the internet became obsessed with his khaki pants; and he earned the nicknames “chartthrob” and “map daddy.”

Kornacki further established himself as the king of election season with the “Kornacki Cam” during 2026 midterm primary election nights, when his nonstop behind-the-scenes livestreams amassed 42 million views. Now that midterm election day is upon us, Kornacki is acutely aware of how many viewers have come to rely on him. “I get very anxious about being prepared for election night,” he says, “and then thinking of all the things that I might not be prepared for, and then just taking the phone out and trying to get prepared.”

For someone who spends a lot of time logged on, Kornacki doesn’t exactly have the habits of someone who is chronically online. He seems to know nothing at all about memes, FaceTime really isn’t his thing, and he isn’t quite sure what a subreddit is. Ask him about who’s most likely to win today’s races, though, and he’ll have no shortage of knowledge to share.

Phone model: iPhone 17 ProBasically, I break one phone per year, so I recently upgraded to it. They always say the camera's better. It never is any different to me, and the battery's always great for 10 days.

Computer model: a DellIt's been in its office probably as long as I've been at NBC. It has a thing on it that says Windows 7 Pro, which I think is old. This thing is on its last leg because I've just been too lazy to replace it. I never really got into Macs. I think I had one once, and I just remember not really liking it. I know it's supposed to be user-friendly, but it actually drove me a little crazy.

Average daily screen time: 3 hours, 35 minutesThat is depressing. That's more than 12.5 percent of my life. And then you take out the eight hours of sleep, it's an even bigger piece of the pie. I thought about taking dramatic steps to change it and, like most of my thoughts about dramatic steps to change my life, I never actually do it.

It’s texting, email, definitely there's social media, which is a lot of just trying to make sure I'm not missing something that's happening in my world. This time of year, with the election, I'll have a panicky thought about a particular state that I'm going to cover on election night and some aspect of it, and then I'll think of some blind spot that I have and I'll try to fix it on the spot.

Music app: SpotifyIt's fun at the end of the year, they give you your top songs. It says my all-time top song is “My Girl” by the Temptations.

Is Spotify the one that did your listening age or something a couple years ago? Mine was 87 or something.

Number of unread emails: 53,828When it was at about 5,000 it overwhelmed me, but now it's just part of the furniture.

Number of unread texts: 75It's amazing what you can get yourself accustomed to, I guess.

I will occasionally—probably once every week or two—sit down with the texts to get it down to zero. That one I can still control, but with email I wouldn't even know where to start. It's almost like a game now to see how high I can get it.

A regular series that quantifies the tech lifestyles of the rich and/or famous.

Last person you FaceTimed: CousinIt’s from over the summer. We were doing a family reunion thing.

But I never really got into that. I like just talking on the phone where you don't have to worry about appearances or anything. You can get up, walk around, whatever. I don't think you need to see each other unless it's some kind of formal meeting. I got so sick of Zoom with Covid, if I can avoid it, I will.

Last thing you Googled: Boothbay Harbor 2024 presidential election resultsFor part of the election prep, looking at Maine, obviously the Senate race. Results come in by town in Maine, which is not the case in a lot of states where it’s by county. Some of them I need to research on my own, and that's one of them.

Last photo you took: Sergeantsville, New JerseyI had about two hours on Saturday of actual free time before getting on a train to DC and drove through there.

Last thing you asked AI: “Can you overlay these numbers onto the attached map of Minnesota counties?”I created benchmarks for the candidates in the Senate race there. This has been new for me this year, and I don't know if I like it. I used to just handwrite them myself on county maps, and now I had AI do it, and I printed the map out, which is much cleaner. It looks much better. Maybe the act of writing them out myself actually maybe helps me internalize it better. I don't know. Maybe this was a bad move.

I have a lot of queasiness and misgivings about AI, but like I said, I have all these files with the maps and these benchmarks on spreadsheets, and I was like, geez, this really would save an hour.

Your top three or most recent most used emojis: N/AThe closest thing I can give you is that I use the thumbs-up thing on text. I really don't use emojis, or, as I mistakenly pronounce them, emoj-eyes. I do think I will use the wink one, because my jokes don't always come through to people.

Favorite social network: X and YouTubeI use Twitter or X or whatever they call it now to keep me aware of things, but I'm not sure it's a healthy thing to use. We've used YouTube for these livestreams that we did in the primary season and built a community on there with the folks who were tuning in and watching these things. It's kind of cool to see that come into being.

Favorite news source: The New York PostBesides my employer, NBC, I really like the old-school print edition New York Post—picking up a tabloid newspaper. I love newspapers, I always will, and you still get that old-school feeling with it. I've thought about subscribing. I probably should just do that, but I also like the act of going to a newsstand.

Favorite subreddit: N/AI don't know, I don't know too much. I don't think so. Is that the dark web?

Favorite tech product: Anker chargerI have this super-fast Anker charger. I was at an event once and somebody showed me and gave me the link to order, and it is transformative. I can put it in for 10 minutes and I'm set for a long time.

Favorite meme: N/AI guess I'm not really a meme person.

Number of burner accounts you have: N/AIf I had burner accounts, I don't think I would tell you.

Technology you’re most nostalgic for: Cable TVI am kind of nostalgic for the cable TV bundle, which seems to be going away. You really feel it this time of year when trying to watch football games. Now you have to have this streaming product and that streaming product. It used to be you could find a cable package that would give you everything, and you could just flip the channel. It's a lot more complicated now.
